stories.title: Witness to the Treaty of Doaksville
stories.hook: His name is on the 1837 treaty, and his trading post fed Choctaw families arriving from Mississippi.
body: On 17 January 1837, "at Doaksville, near Fort Towson, in the Choctaw country," the Choctaw and Chickasaw nations signed the treaty that let the Chickasaws settle inside the Choctaw Nation. The witness list reads: Wm. Armstrong, Henry R. Carter, Josiah S. Doak, Vincent B. Tims, Daniel McCurtain (U.S. Interpreter)… followed by the marks of the three Choctaw district chiefs.

Born in South Carolina (family accounts say Chester County), Vincent was a trader and the partner of Josiah Doak, whose trading post gave Doaksville its name; a missionary later remembered the town's founders as "Josiah Doak and Vinson Brown Tims, an Irishman." Doak & Tims held the government contract to feed Choctaw families arriving on Removal, at 13 cents a ration, and handled the annuity payments that drew crowds to Doaksville. Notices in the Arkansas Intelligencer dissolved the partnership in 1844.

On 29 May 1847 he bought the Dancing Rabbit Creek treaty allotment of Henry Graves, "son of Chief Netachachie," one of the three district chiefs whose marks appear on the 1837 treaty. That December the Washington (Arkansas) Telegraph reported that "Jos. R. Berthelet and Vincent B. Tims of the Choctaw Nation" were invited within the bar at the Red River Raft Convention, which pressed Congress to clear the great logjam that blocked steamboats on the Red River.

He and his full-blood Choctaw wife stayed at Doaksville the rest of their lives. Family accounts say Vincent died at Doaksville in June 1864, while Confederate troops held Fort Towson a mile away, but he was still signing letters as the Confederate postmaster there on 9 September and 1 November 1864 (see "A postmaster's letters, August to November 1864").

The trader's origins, in the one local history that traces him, are modest: 'Born in South Carolina, V.B. Tims is said to be of Irish descent.' He came to the Doaksville area with Josiah Doak in the early 1830s. In March 1843 he ran an office there for letters to the Agent for Claims, and in February 1844 the partnership with Doak was dissolved 'by mutual agreement,' after which he kept the business on his own.

Three of his children are known by name: Vinson W. (born 1838), Edward Ward (born 1842) and a daughter, Phoebe, who died before final enrollment. His grandson Joel said that 'Venson Brown Tims' was the first postmaster at Doaksville and that Edward succeeded him on his death. The postmaster rolls show Edward appointed on 24 October 1887 and a 'V. B. Tims' on 17 May 1871, seven years after the family date of Vincent's death. Local history says that in 1861 he was 'designated' to be Indian Agent for the Choctaws had the Confederacy won, but this rests on one source.

An 1891 sketch of William Gardner, a Choctaw merchant born in 1830, says that "after he had been to work for E. B. Tims, the sutler at Doaksville," he opened his own store at Hamilton, in Blue County (O'Beirne, Leaders and Leading Men of the Indian Territory, p. 124). The book prints the initials "E. B." rather than "V. B.," but the trade and the town point to the Doaksville trader, so this is probably Vincent.

Two more records show him as a man of business. A New Orleans commission house advertising in the Washington (Arkansas) Telegraph of 10 December 1845 named "Doak & Tims, Doaksville, C. Nation" among its references, next to Maj. William Armstrong of the Choctaw Agency. And a list of stockholders in the Cairo & Fulton Railroad Company of Arkansas, to June 1854, includes "V. B. Tims, Choctaw Nation," with 10 shares at $25 each, among other Choctaw Nation stockholders; the road was chartered to link Cairo, on the Mississippi, with Fulton on the Red River.

The signed army contracts behind the thirteen-cents-a-ration figure are printed in House Report No. 271 (1843): contracts nos. 41 and 42 of 1 January 1838 and no. 44 of 1 January 1839, each naming "Doak & Tims." They are told under "Thirteen cents a ration."

In April 1841 a clerk in the Doaksville trading house wrote home that "Mr. Tims one of the men I am living with is now in New York purchasing a stock of goods." The letters, printed in the Chronicles of Oklahoma in 1931, are told under "Mr. Tims one of the men I am living with."

The U.S. Official Register prints the post office he is remembered for. The edition for 30 September 1877 (Post-Office Department, p. 537, the Arkansas list, which also carries the Choctaw Nation offices) reads across: "Doaksville," "Choctaw," "V. B. Tims," "37 77", a year's compensation of $37.77. The 1871 Register's Arkansas list (p. 502) likewise carries a "V. B. Tims" among the postmasters on the page that holds Doaksville. The initials are the trader's. Whether the postmaster of the 1870s was Vincent himself or his son Vinson, who would have used the same initials, the printed register does not say.

The Dawes card of his son Edward names Vincent's wife. On Card 1437 Edward W. Tims's parents are written "Vincent B. Tims," dead, a non-citizen, and "Betsy Tims," dead, of Towson County. Betsy Thompson, born in 1870, was a granddaughter of that Betsy Tims and shared her name.

stories.note: Vincent was white, so the family's Choctaw citizenship came through his wife, whose name has not been found. His date of death is given as 14 June 1864 in a descendants' account and 17 June 1864 in family files, but he signed letters as Doaksville's Confederate postmaster on 9 September and 1 November 1864, so both dates look wrong. The postmaster rolls name a 'V. B. Tims' on 17 May 1871, which may be Vincent himself. The 'first postmaster' detail rests on Joel's memory, and the Confederate office had an earlier postmaster, J. P. Kingsbury, in 1862-63. A card for his son Edward may name Vincent's wife.

stories.title: An indentured boy from London
stories.hook: Bound for seven years' service in Maryland at 15, he ended up a landowner and overseer of a Quaker meeting.
body: Cane Creek's records say Anthony Chamness was the son of John and Ann, born about 1713 in East Smithfield, London. On 9 February 1724/5, giving his age as 15 and his home as Whitechapel, he bound himself to John Cooke, a London victualler, for seven years' service in "Maryland (his Majesty's Plantation in America)."
On 24 November 1735 he married Sarah Cole in St. Paul's Parish, Baltimore County; her own family's story is told under Sarah (Cole) Chamness.

The Chamnesses moved with the Quakers from Gunpowder Meeting in Maryland to Monocacy (1741), Carver's Creek in North Carolina (1749), and Cane Creek, where Anthony received a 490-acre grant in June 1751. When Cane Creek Monthly Meeting was organized that year he was named its overseer. His farm, a mile west of the meetinghouse, had a grist mill. He married three times and died on 20 September 1777.

His son Joseph, born in Baltimore County in 1740, married Margaret Norton at Cane Creek in 1763 and later farmed near Providence in Randolph County. Joseph's daughter Martha married Robert Moffitt at Centre Meeting in 1797.

Anthony married three times: Sarah Cole in 1735; then Rachel Haworth, the widow of Stephanus Haworth, who died on 19 March 1775 and is buried at Deep River; and, on 9 May 1776, Margaret Evans Williams, a widow. He made his will on 24 November 1776 in what was then Chatham County and died the next September.

A Hussey family genealogy written in 1928 by Charles Chaney Baker records a Chamness tradition that differs from the indenture. Baker quotes a letter of 30 April 1917 from Dr. John M. Hussey of Somerville, New Jersey, stating "that Martha Chamness, who married Stephen Hussey, was the daughter of Anthony Chamness and his wife, Sarah Cole; that Anthony Chamness had been kidnapped in England as a child and brought to America where he was 'bound out' till he reached a certain age; that he was the heir of an estate in England, which he had to go to England in order to claim but his wife would not consent to his going." Baker thought the inheritance "somewhat of a myth," since immigrants often told such stories. The kidnapping tale and the indenture of February 1724/5, in which a fifteen-year-old of Whitechapel bound himself to a London victualler for service in Maryland, may be two tellings of one event. The same book dates Martha's marriage to Stephen Hussey to September 1762.
He and his wife Sarah signed as witnesses at their son Joseph's wedding at Cane Creek on 17th of the 3rd month 1763; Hanson's 1922 history prints the certificate and the witness list.

The London parents of Anthony's father John Chamness are not shown by any cited birth record. WikiTree proposes Anthony Chamness and Ann Pitts, who married at St James, Duke's Place, on 23 September 1686, but John's baptism in November 1682 is earlier than that wedding.

Zimri Hanson's 1922 Chamness history describes the home Anthony and Sarah kept near Cane Creek, as remembered by a neighbor about a century earlier: "The farm lay a mile west of Cane Creek Friends church, was a good body of land and lay fine. The dwelling was large, perhaps 20x80 feet, consisted of two main rooms, made of hewn oak logs, with two shed rooms with porch the whole length on the front side." A small creek ran through the farm with a grist mill, and in the barn stood "a stationary thrashing machine propelled by horse power," to which neighbors hauled their wheat. Hanson calls the home "one of hospitality, and a kind of social center," and says Sarah taught her daughters to spin and weave. The family register in his book lists the children's births in Baltimore County, Maryland, then in Frederick County, Maryland (1742 to 1746), then in Orange County, North Carolina (1749 to 1761). Sarah, he writes, was "the mother of thirteen children" and died probably about 1773; he adds a tradition that Anthony was drafted for the army but not forced into it because of his conscience, and judges that tradition "barely credible" given his age.

stories.title: Union soldier, 42nd Indiana
stories.hook: Enlisted in 1861 and marched through a Kentucky winter of mud and measles. How long he served is a family puzzle.
body: Daniel Waters O'Neal was born on 25 October 1838 in Tennessee, the year before his parents settled in Gibson County, Indiana. He married Vashti Pearson on 5 January 1860. On 21 October 1861, at 23, he was mustered in as a private in Company F, 42nd Indiana Infantry, the company raised at Oakland City.

The regiment's first winter was its hardest. At Calhoun, Kentucky, the men camped on ground "fully ankle-deep in mud in its best parts," and within twenty days a third of them were in the hospital, many with measles. At Sacramento, Kentucky, they raided the hen-roosts and were arrested until the chaplain talked them free. When they marched into Nashville on 25 February 1862 they found an unlocked pork-house, and by the time headquarters sent a search party "not an ounce of the meat could be found."

A family biography says Daniel was discharged for disability, blindness, at Nashville on 15 March 1862. The regimental rosters list him with no remark, which usually meant a man served out his three years. Company F went on to Perryville, Stones River, Chickamauga, Missionary Ridge and the Atlanta campaign.

Daniel farmed in Gibson County, and he and Vashti raised ten children, among them Parsis Jane, born in 1868. He is buried in Somerville Cemetery under a family stone, with a side stone reading "DANIEL with Co. F. 42 Reg. Ind. Vol." His father, Archibald O'Neal, died in 1841; his widowed mother, Parses Shaw, later married Hugh Watt.

Daniel's funeral was held by Rev. Wright at the United Presbyterian Church of Somerville. He and Vashti lie in the same plot. A twenty-five-foot limestone monument to Company F was raised in 1893 at Oakland City, and it is said to carry the name 'D. O'Neal'; the stone has not been seen, so the name on it is unconfirmed.

The 1884 History of Gibson County prints the roll of Company F, and beside his name it reads: "O'Neal, Daniel W., vet. mustered out July 21, '65." (page 115). "Vet." marks a man who reenlisted as a veteran when the 42nd did in January 1864, and 21 July 1865 is the day the regiment mustered out. If the roll is right, Daniel stayed in Company F to the end of the war rather than leaving in March 1862, and the regiment's later campaigns at Chickamauga, Atlanta and Bentonville would have included him. His application for an invalid pension in December 1865, five months after the muster-out, fits a man who came home with the regiment.

Gil. R. Stormont's 1913 booklet says the Company F monument at Oakland City, dedicated in September 1893, carries "the names of all the original members of the company and the recruits, 143 in number," and beneath a scroll "Starved to death at Andersonville" the names of eleven company men who died as prisoners after Chickamauga. See the stories on the monument and on Company F's war.

Calhoun left a story that the regiment itself told. In Horrall's telling, Col. James G. Jones kept a canteen of whisky in his quarters against "the bad weather and poisonous miasma" of the Calhoun camp, and one morning found it empty: "That d——d Lieutenant-Colonel Denby has been at my canteen, drank it all." The sentinel before headquarters, "being also a little afraid of malaria," had emptied it himself. The same camp sent a third of the men to the hospital within twenty days, and of the measles cases a few "transferred to Evansville died." The story of Daniel's company and its captain is told under "Company F: the men around Daniel O'Neal" and "Captain Cockrum: Stones River to Libby Prison."

Of his ten children, WikiTree traces seven to adulthood: Mary Elizabeth (1860-1960), William Allen (1863-1933), John Sherman (1866-1940), Parsis Jane (1868-1956), George Johnson (1875-1965), Daniel Clinton (1878-1954) and David Commodore (1881-1955), plus the youngest daughter Charity Louisa (1887-1979). William was born in Tennessee, probably in 1863 while Daniel was in the army, though the 1880 census says Indiana; George, in 1880, says Missouri. Three of the five sons died at Somerville, one at Evansville and one in Pike County, all within about thirty miles of the farm. Mary and Parsis went west. Their stories are told under the O'Neal family entries.

stories.title: A murder trial in early Maryland
stories.hook: Anthony Chamness's wife came from a Baltimore County family whose patriarch was murdered.
body: Anthony Chamness, the London boy indentured to Maryland, married Sarah Cole on 24 November 1735. Her father Joseph Cole had died young: his will, written 22 January 1720/1 in Baltimore County, names his wife Susanna and his little daughter Sarah. Nearly fifty years later her uncle William Cole's 1769 will still called her "dau. and heir of testator's bro. Joseph." The Cane Creek Quaker records in North Carolina name her as "daughter of Joseph and Susanna Cole."

Joseph was the son of John Cole and Johanna (Hannah) Garrett. Johanna's father, Dennis Garrett, was murdered. John Cole testified at the trial of a Captain John Oldton for the killing of his father-in-law.

Dennis's widow Barbara remarried, to John Broad. In August 1712, as Barbara Garrett Broad, she deeded property to "her grandson Dennis Garrett Cole, s. of John and Hannah Cole," a boy named for the grandfather he never knew.

quotes.t: Sarah, dau. and heir of testator's bro. Joseph.
quotes.c: Will of William Cole, 1769

stories.title: Court day at Sulphur Springs
stories.hook: A log courthouse, a whipping post, and a justice system built on keeping your word.
body: Cedar County was created by the Choctaw Nation's Doaksville Constitution of 1860 and lasted until statehood in 1907. Each county elected a judge for a two-year term to oversee county business, a sheriff, who collected taxes and took the census, and a ranger, who sold stray livestock. When an arrest or a sentence had to be carried out, the sheriff called on the district Lighthorsemen.

The Cedar County court met at Sulphur Springs, near present-day Rattan, on the first Monday of each month, in "a large log house, constructed of long, straight logs" that also served as a Choctaw Methodist church. Families camped at the springs on court days. A stump from the tree used as the whipping post is kept by the Pushmataha County Historical Society in Antlers.

Choctaw law punished crimes such as theft with lashes, fifty for a first offense and one hundred for a second. H. B. Cushman, who knew the Nation, described what came after: the whole crowd shook hands with the man who had been whipped, and the matter was never spoken of again.

From 1866 the Nation's death penalty was carried out by rifle. By custom a condemned man went home to plant and harvest his crop and came back on the appointed day, often choosing a friend or relative to fire the shot so no one would seek revenge. Capital cases went to the district court, not the county judge, so when Joel said his father "could have sentenced criminals to be shot," the whippings are the part that fits a county judge.

quotes.t: ...the whole assembly came out and shook hands with the 'Fummah' (whipped), thus reinstating him to his former position in society, and the subject was then and there dropped, never to be mentioned again.
quotes.c: H. B. Cushman, 1899

quotes.t: Never was a full-blood Choctaw known to evade the death penalty ... by flight.
quotes.c: H. B. Cushman, 1899

stories.title: Postmaster and judge of Doaksville
stories.hook: Vinson's brother was a Towson County judge and Doaksville's postmaster, and he was considered for Principal Chief.
body: Doaksville was the capital of the Choctaw Nation from 1858 to 1863. By 1850 it was the largest town in Indian Territory, and in 1860 a convention there adopted the constitution that governed the Choctaw Nation until 1906. At the end of the Civil War there were two surrenders at Doaksville: Principal Chief Peter Pitchlynn surrendered the Choctaw forces on 19 June 1865, and General Stand Watie surrendered his Cherokee, Creek, Seminole and Osage troops on 23 June, the last Confederate general to lay down arms.

Edward Ward Tims, Choctaw by Blood No. 4009, served as District Trustee of Apukshunnubbee District in the early 1880s and for many years as County Judge of Towson County. On 24 October 1887 he was appointed postmaster at Doaksville, succeeding James T. Fleming; the office closed in 1903, when the name changed to Fort Towson.

On 29 April 1888 in Towson County he married Willie Jane Maxwell of Arkansas. After statehood he retired to his allotment southeast of Hugo. He died on 7 February 1923, four months after Willie Jane, and is buried in Springs Chapel Cemetery near Hugo.

His second wife, Willie Jane, was born on 27 July 1870 and died on 8 October 1922, four months before him. Their children were Lucy Ann (1889-1970), Minnie (1891-1930), Edmond (1893-1918), Benjamin (1897-1969), Myrtle (1899-1988), Abel (1901-1966) and Nora (1906-1977). By his first wife Polly, a full-blood Choctaw, he had a son, Columbus, born on Christmas Day 1860, who died on 21 October 1918 and is also buried at Springs Chapel.

In January 1940 the Paris News reported that his old log house, a quarter mile northeast of Fort Towson, had been proposed as a museum, and wrote that Tims was 'once county judge of Towson County' and was 'once considered for the position as principal chief of the Choctaw Nation.' The house was said to have been the setting for talk of the 1860 Council and the 1837 treaty. That detail is local lore, not a record. Joel Thompson remembered him simply as the man 'who was post master and Judge at Doaksville for so many years.'

His own Dawes card is 1437, applied for on 8 May 1899, post office Doaksville. It lists "Tims, Edward W.," age 58, one-half blood, Roll No. 4009, with parents "Vincent B. Tims," dead, a non-citizen, and "Betsy Tims," dead, of Towson County. Edward's son Columbus, born in 1860, is on Card 1238 as "Tims, Columbus," 40, three-quarter blood, Roll No. 3355, with parents "E. W. Tims" and "Polly Tims," the latter dead.

The jacket for Card 1437 has the details of his second marriage. The Commission's decision gives the wedding as 29 April 1888, and a copy of the certificate, signed by R. S. Frazier, reads the same; family summaries that give 19 April are a few days off. Their youngest child on the card, Abel E., was born on 14 December 1901. The card also includes a ward, Adam Nanomantubbe, whom O. W. Seay of Oscar called Edward's orphan grandson in a letter of 1903.

stories.title: The Pisachubbes of Speer and Jeter
stories.hook: A full-blood Choctaw farmer who registered for both world wars and lived with his daughter's family in 1940.
body: Full-blood Choctaw, Dawes Roll No. 4467, enrolled at age 11 on his widowed mother Eunice's card. In 1917 he was 28, married with one child, farming for himself at Speer; the registrar wrote "Indian" for race, black eyes and black hair, medium height, slender. In 1942, at 53, he registered again for the WWII draft of older men, still at Speer, naming his wife Lizzie.
In 1940 he and Lizzie were living with their daughter Frances and son-in-law Simon Thompson at Jeter, with their niece Alice and nephews Eli and Edward: twelve people in the house.

The three young relatives were orphans. Robert's older brother, William Harrison Pisachubbe, had married Lizzie's younger sister Adline Austin, so two Pisachubbe brothers had married two Austin sisters, and their children were double first cousins of Frances. Adline died at Speer in 1929 and William Harrison in 1937.

William Harrison's obituary in the Hugo Daily News (11 May 1937) gave a family history from his relative Judge T. W. Hunter: the Pisachubbes came from Mississippi with the first group of Choctaw exiles in 1832 and settled at Fort Coffee, near present-day Spiro. His funeral was held at the family home near the Long Creek school house, with Choctaw Presbyterian minister Rev. Logan Harlin officiating.
The name Pisachubbe ends the way many Choctaw war-names do; its exact meaning is not recorded.

The county land records bring his land forward. A 1979 decree of heirship for his daughter Frances Pisachubbe Thompson covers Section 29, Township 5 South, Range 17 East, the same section as his allotment. An order in his own estate was entered in 1982.

His 1896 census number was Kiamitia No. 10433, listed right after his mother, and the 1899 card gives his age as 11 and his father as the dead Joseph Pisachubbe. He was approved as Choctaw by Blood No. 4467 on 12 December 1902. His wife Lizzie came from the Austin family of Fowlerville (Card 1363), whose roll numbers ran 3736 to 3740; her brother James, who died in 1899 before enrollment, was struck off by the Department on 16 September 1904.

quotes.t: He was a full blood Choctaw Indian, and was well known among the white people as well as among members of his tribe.
quotes.c: Hugo Daily News, 11 May 1937, on William Harrison Pisachubbe

stories.title: Working at Camp Pike
stories.hook: In 1918, George Hulsey registered for the draft while working at Camp Pike near Little Rock.
body: George Washington Hulsey was forty-two when he registered for the draft on 12 September 1918. He gave his birth date as 24 December 1875 and his permanent address as Story, in Montgomery County, Arkansas. For work he was away at Camp Pike, the Army’s large training camp near Little Rock, employed as a laborer by the Stewart-McGehee Construction Company. His nearest relative was Sarah Rebecca Hulsey at Story. The card describes him as short and slender, with blue eyes and black hair.

He married Sarah Rebecca Graves on 22 December 1901, when she was seventeen. They had ten children, among them Oscar, born in 1910. George died in 1935 and is buried in Breashears Cemetery near Story. Family accounts also place a Benjamin F. Hulsey there, but the shared cemetery does not by itself establish their relationship.

Rebecca and George Washington Hulsey had ten children: William Roy (1904), John Wesley (1906), Noah (1908), Oscar Franklin (1910), Fred (1913), Ruby Ellen (Stipe, 1915), Grady (1918), Louis Daniel (1920), Grace Irene (Dunagan, 1923) and George Paul (1925). Oscar was the fourth. Rebecca was 17 at the wedding and 41 when the last child was born.

Published sources differ on George’s exact death date, including 5 August and 21 August. The year 1935 is more secure. The 22 December date in the earlier tree appears to repeat his wedding anniversary.
At Oscar’s death in 1982, two sisters and four brothers survived him. Of his nine siblings, three had therefore died before him.
When he died in 1935, the oldest child, William Roy, was about 30 and the youngest, George Paul, about 9 or 10; his widow, Sarah Rebecca, was 51. She died at Bandon, Oregon in 1972.

Camp Pike was under heavy strain when he signed. Eleven days after the draft card, on 23 September 1918, the camp base hospital admitted 214 influenza cases in a single day, and by the end of October 12,393 men had reported sick with the disease. See "The camp where George Hulsey was working when the influenza came."

In June 1880, B. F. Hulsey, a thirty-two-year-old Georgia-born miner, lived in Center Township with his wife Sarah G., thirty, and children Margaret M., six, George W., four, and infant Charles F. George’s later December 1875 birth date fits the child’s age. These records point toward this household as his childhood family, although the connection remains probable.

stories.title: Benjamin Hulsey: from Georgia to Arkansas
stories.hook: A Georgia-born Benjamin appears in a blacksmith’s household, an Arkansas cavalry roster and later family accounts; the links between those records remain uncertain.
body: The Hulsey family accounts trace Benjamin Franklin Hulsey to the mountains of Union County, Georgia, and a household headed by the blacksmith Salathiel Hulsey and Elizabeth. The original census of 11 November 1850 lists Benjamin as three, with a six-year-old girl immediately above him. The San Diego society’s published transcription reversed those two ages. Three fits the family birth date of 2 February 1847, but the census supplies no exact birthday and does not establish this child’s identity with the later Arkansas man.

Company D of the 4th Arkansas Cavalry, a Union regiment recruited during the winter of 1863–64, lists a private Benjamin F. Hulsey. A grave account instead attributes Confederate cavalry service to Benjamin. The similar unit names can obscure the distinction between opposing armies; without an identifying service or pension file, his military service remains a lead.

Family accounts name Sylvania Susane Partin as a wife, while a 1977 Hulsey query names Margaret Partain. The 1880 Montgomery County household that probably includes young George Washington Hulsey gives the wife’s name as Sarah G. None of those women has been securely identified with another, and Sylvania has not been established as George’s mother.

In Garland County, a September 1893 marriage bond names Benjamin F. Hulsley and Lucy Morgan. The license is dated 25 September and gives Lucy’s age as fifteen. The printed century on the bond was altered by hand to 1893. The return does not supply a readable completed ceremony date, so the license date should not automatically become their wedding date. This couple’s connection to the 1880 household remains unresolved.

The Hot Springs Sentinel-Record of 13 February 1910 records a $175 land transfer from B. F. Hulsey and wife to C. Floyd Huff: the west half of the northwest quarter of section 10, township 2 south, range 19 west. The notice gives neither his full name nor his home address, leaving it a possible match.

A family account places Benjamin’s death at Story on 16 December 1924 and his burial at Breashears Cemetery; the 1977 query instead gives 1921. These accounts preserve clues worth following, but they do not yet establish one continuous life or prove that he was George Washington Hulsey’s father.

stories.title: A WPA laborer in the Ouachitas
stories.hook: Out of work 48 weeks of 1939, on a government job, with five children in a rented house.
body: Born at Hot Springs, Arkansas, on 27 October 1910. In April 1940 the census taker found Oscar, 29, and Katie, 29, renting a house valued at $2 at South Fork in Montgomery County, Arkansas, with Leon 11, Delis 9, Benney 6, Glen 4 and Mary 2. Oscar was a laborer in "Government work" (the Depression-era WPA), had been unemployed 48 weeks, had worked 16 weeks in 1939 and earned $140. He had five years of schooling.

He had married Katie Stevenson on 27 October 1927, his 17th birthday; she had turned 17 twelve days earlier. He registered for the WWII draft at Mount Ida on 16 October 1940. The family later moved to the lumber towns of McCurtain County, Oklahoma. Oscar died at his home at Holly Creek on 17 June 1982, at 71, and was buried at Wheelock Cemetery near Millerton, the old Choctaw mission ground.

Oscar and Katie had seven children: Franklin Leon (1929-2015), Delphia (1931-2005), Bennie George (1933-1947), Glen (1935-2001), Mary Ellen (1938-2002), Charlie (1940-2010) and Willis Delane (1943-2004). Mary Ellen was born at Broken Bow, Oklahoma, and the family was back in Montgomery County by 1940.

Oscar's obituary in the McCurtain Gazette of 20 June 1982 says he was born at Hot Springs, 'lived in the area for many years,' and died at his home at Holly Creek, between Broken Bow and Wright City in the old sawmill country. His funeral was held at 2 p.m. on Sunday at Wheelock Cemetery, with Rev. Bob Lewis officiating. He was survived by four sons, two daughters, two sisters, four brothers, ten grandchildren and nine great-grandchildren.

Wheelock was the Presbyterian mission to the Choctaws; its church was organized in December 1832 by Rev. Alfred Wright, whose 1853 gravestone in the same graveyard is copied in a 1914 book. Oscar was buried among the missionaries' graves in 1982.

A McCurtain County marriage license lists him by name late in the war years. The Oklahoma State Courts Network index of McCurtain County District Court carries case MLI-2024-00524, a marriage license filed 27 February 1943 in the style "HULSEY, OSCAR F VS. STEVESON, KATIE," with both named as Applicants and the single docket entry "TEXT IMPORTED LICENSE - Document Available at Court Clerk's Office." The spelling Steveson is the clerk's, and Oscar F. with Katie fits the couple (probable; the index gives no ages or residences). The family's own account puts the marriage on 27 October 1927 and their children began in 1929, so the 1943 license may be a later or second legal marriage, or a re-licensing; the index does not say, and the paper license is held by the clerk in Idabel.

Four records bear on the middle of his life. In January 1938 he was arrested after a two-day search and charged with assault with intent to kill in the stabbing of Eddie Stevenson, his brother-in-law (see the story "A family quarrel ends in a stabbing"). He was divorced from Katie in Arkansas on 26 September 1941 and married Hester May Whittington at Mount Ida on 3 November 1941. In 1945 Katie sued for divorce in McCurtain County, and in 1947 he is named as living at Wright City in the obituary of his son Bennie, who was killed on a bicycle near Hugo.

stories.title: The Choctaw removal
stories.hook: Several ancestors were born in the old Choctaw Nation in Mississippi before the Trail of Tears.
body: Our tree lists Pisachubbe "Wilson" (born 1807), Nancy Te-hol-ba-ta-bi (born 1825), Jackson Gardner (born about 1820) and O-we-na as born in the old Choctaw Nation in Mississippi. The Choctaw were the first nation removed under the Indian Removal Act, walking and riding west in 1831–1833.
These families settled in the Kiamitia, Blue and Towson districts of the new Choctaw Nation, where their grandchildren were enrolled by the Dawes Commission seventy years later.

A 1937 newspaper account of the Pisachubbe family says they came from Mississippi with the first group of exiles in 1832 and settled first at Fort Coffee, near present-day Spiro. At Doaksville, the trading firm of Doak & Tims, Vincent Tims's partnership, held the contract to feed arriving families at 13 cents a ration.

Two cautions on the Mississippi-born names. None of them has yet been found on the Armstrong Roll or another removal-era list. The tree's proposed mother-and-son link between Nancy Te-hol-ba-ta-bi and Joseph Pisachubbe is unproved; her age on the Dawes roll alone does not resolve it.

Dawes Card 1278 names a full-blood Nancy Pisachubbi, 69, whose father was Te-hol-ba-ta-bi, dead, and whose mother, Malindy, was dead and listed under Mississippi. She appears to be the tree's Nancy Te-hol-ba-ta-bi, though the card does not say whose mother she was.

The best-documented part of the removal's first winter is the stretch from the Mississippi to the Red River. About 18,880 Choctaws were counted in Major Francis Armstrong's census of 1831; by the first week of November four thousand were on the road, and between 26 November and 8 December about 2,500 were landed at Arkansas Post in a blizzard. A Choctaw letter of February 1833 shows Doaksville already a place where annuities were issued and 'a small town' of white traders stood below the Kiamichi. These are told under 'With the first group of exiles' and 'Doaksville before the store.'
src: Family tree records; Dawes enrollment cards for their descendants; Hugo Daily News, 11 May 1937; Hughes, 'Trader V. B. Tims of Doaksville' (2020); Dawes Card 1278; Thoburn and Wright, Oklahoma: A History of the State and Its People (1929), vol. 1, pp. 165-70; Senate Doc. 512 (1835), vol. 4

stories.title: The Depression, house by house
stories.hook: The 1940 census caught both of Dad's and Mom's families at the bottom of the hard years.
body: In April 1940 the census takers wrote down how many weeks each man had worked the year before. Grady Moffitt in Hugo: 12 weeks, $100, unemployed 50 weeks, eight children at home in a rented house. Oscar Hulsey at South Fork, Arkansas: 16 weeks on a government relief job, $140, unemployed 48 weeks, five children in a house worth $2. Simon Thompson at Jeter: 52 weeks on his own farm, worth $400, feeding twelve people, including his in-laws and their nieces and nephews.
Within a few years John Moffitt was in the Navy, the Hulseys had moved to the Oklahoma lumber towns, and the three families' children would meet and marry in Hugo.
src: 1940 U.S. Census: Hugo and Jeter, Choctaw County, Okla.; South Fork, Montgomery County, Ark.

stories.title: Doaksville: the biggest town in Indian Territory
stories.hook: A trading post by the Kiamichi grew into the busiest town in the Choctaw Nation, then faded within a lifetime.
body: Doaksville took its name from Josiah Stuart Doak, co-owner of a trading post. He and his brother first set up at the mouth of the Kiamichi River, then moved about a mile west after the U.S. Army founded Fort Towson in 1824. Choctaw people relocated from Mississippi settled here, and steamboat access on the Red River made it a principal town of the Nation.

By 1840 it had several stores, a gristmill, a blacksmith and a hotel. In 1842 the Indian agent William Armstrong called it one of the most orderly and quiet towns in the West. A post office opened in 1847, and by 1850 it was the largest town in Indian Territory, with more than thirty buildings and two newspapers, one printed in Choctaw.

The Army left Fort Towson in 1854 and the town's importance began to slip. The Civil War wrecked the plantation economy around it, an 1870 railroad bypassed it, and most businesses moved to Fort Towson. The post office closed in 1903. Only the Fort Towson-Doaksville Cemetery remains; the Oklahoma Historical Society acquired the site in 1960 and it was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on May 29, 1975.
This is the town and neighborhood of the Cedar, Towson and Kiamitia county families, framed here as the place they lived near, not as a record of any one relative.

quotes.t: one of the most orderly and quiet towns that you will find in the west
quotes.c: Agent William Armstrong, 1842, as quoted in Wikipedia, Doaksville, Choctaw Nation

src: Wikipedia, Doaksville, Choctaw Nation; Oklahoma Historical Society, Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture (Fort Towson, Choctaw County)
stories.note: Place history from secondary sources; not tied to a named relative.

stories.title: The 1860 constitution written at Doaksville
stories.hook: A convention at Doaksville set the framework that governed the Choctaw Nation until its government ended in 1906.
body: In 1860 a convention at Doaksville ratified the Doaksville Constitution, which guided the Choctaw Nation until 1906. Doaksville served as the capital in this period; sources differ on the exact dates, and the capital later moved to Chahta Tamaha in 1863.

The constitution created Cedar County and others in the Nation's district system. Each county elected members to the National Council and also a county judge, a sheriff and a ranger to two-year terms. The judge ran county administration, the sheriff collected taxes, watched for intruders and took the census, and the ranger advertised and sold stray livestock.
For families in the Kiamichi country this was everyday government: the people holding these offices were their neighbors.
src: Wikipedia, Doaksville, Choctaw Nation; Wikipedia, Cedar County, Choctaw Nation
stories.note: Capital dates are inconsistent between sources; stated loosely on purpose.

stories.title: The last Confederate general lays down arms near Fort Towson
stories.hook: The Civil War ended in Indian Territory in the Choctaw Nation, a few miles from where these families lived.
body: After the Army abandoned Fort Towson in 1854, the post saw a brief resurgence during the Civil War when Gen. Samuel Bell Maxey chose it as headquarters for Confederate forces in Indian Territory.

On June 23, 1865, Cherokee Brig. Gen. Stand Watie surrendered his First Indian Brigade at Doaksville, near the fort, signing with two Union commissioners. He is generally called the last Confederate general officer to surrender. Some sources place the signing at Fort Towson itself; the date is consistent.

The war had wrecked the plantation economy around Doaksville, and the town never recovered. For Choctaw families of the area the surrender was the end of four years in which their homeland was a Confederate district.
src: Oklahoma Historical Society, Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture, Fort Towson entry; Wikipedia, Doaksville, Choctaw Nation
stories.note: Place and event history; no specific family member is documented here. Whether a relative served is a lead to check in Confederate Choctaw rolls.

stories.title: Fort Towson: the army post built to receive the Choctaw
stories.hook: The Army established Fort Towson in 1824, before the forced removal of the Choctaw from Mississippi.
body: In May 1824 a company of the Seventh Infantry camped on Gates Creek near the Kiamichi and Red rivers. The outpost, Cantonment Towson, was named for Gen. Nathan Towson.

It was abandoned in 1829. After the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek it reopened in 1830 as Camp Phoenix and was soon renamed Fort Towson. The Oklahoma Historical Society says the fort was meant as a buffer for the Choctaw slated for removal to the area, and it later served as a terminal on the Choctaw Trail of Tears.
Troops left for good in 1854. The state acquired the property in 1967 and a visitor center and sutler's store are open to the public.
src: Oklahoma Historical Society, Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture, Fort Towson (FO044)

stories.title: Allotment and the persistence of Choctaw government
stories.hook: The Thompson family’s enrollment and land selections unfolded as Choctaw leaders faced federal pressure to divide the Nation’s land.
body: On 23 April 1897, representatives of the Choctaw and Chickasaw Nations and the Dawes Commission signed the Atoka Agreement. It set terms for dividing tribal lands into individual allotments and reserved coal and asphalt lands. The agreement treated Freedmen and their descendants unequally, assigning them smaller allotments.

The agreement scheduled the end of the tribal governments for March 1906. The Choctaw and Chickasaw governments ratified it in November 1897, but Chickasaw voters rejected it in December, as Chickasaw law required a popular vote. The Curtis Act of 1898 required resubmission, and the agreement passed in a joint election on 24 August 1898.

The Dawes Commission had been established in 1893, before the agreement. Its enrollment process later produced cards naming the Thompson, Tims and Pisachubbe families. Betsy Tims Thompson applied with her family in 1899, and her son Simon’s birth that May required separate affidavits from Betsy and his grandmother Emeline Tims.

In 1902 Choctaw and Chickasaw leaders and the federal government negotiated a supplemental agreement. A Choctaw executive committee circulated information and invited citizens to raise concerns before the vote. That October, Choctaw voters also chose a principal chief in a contested race; Green McCurtain was declared the winner. There is no record here of how any member of the Thompson family voted.

Allotment changed the relationship between families and land. In 1903 Joseph Thompson selected tracts for Betsy and their children, including a homestead for Simon. Tribal land was divided into individual holdings, while federal restrictions governed transactions in many allotments. Choctaw Nation’s historical account describes allotment as a process that made it easier for Choctaw land to pass out of Choctaw hands.

The Nation did not disappear when federal policy reduced the government’s authority. Choctaw community members continued to meet and organize, and an advisory council emerged in the 1930s. In 1971 Harry J. W. Belvin became the first elected principal chief in decades to serve without the required presidential appointment. In 1978 a Choctaw council formed to develop a new constitution and restore representative government. Simon Thompson lived through these changes; the surviving records do not establish his personal political activities.
src: Matthew Rex Cox, 'Atoka Agreement,' Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture, Oklahoma Historical Society, https://www.okhistory.org/publications/enc/entry?entry=AT004; 1902 Supplemental Agreement with the Choctaw and Chickasaw, https://treaties.okstate.edu/treaties/agreement-with-the-choctaw-and-chickasaw-1902-22427; Choctaw Nation Cultural Services, 'A New Chahta Homeland: 1900–1910,' https://www.choctawnation.com/news/iti-fabvssa/a-new-chahta-homeland-a-history-by-the-decade-1900-1910/; Choctaw Nation Cultural Services, 'A New Chahta Homeland: 1930–1940,' https://www.choctawnation.com/news/iti-fabvssa/a-new-chahta-homeland-a-history-by-the-decade-1930-1940/; Choctaw Nation Cultural Services, 'Architectural History of the Choctaw Nation Capitol at Tuskahoma,' https://www.choctawnation.com/news/iti-fabvssa/architectural-history-of-the-choctaw-nation-capitol-at-tuskahoma-1883-present/; Dawes Card 1283 and the Thompson allotment applications.
stories.note: Choctaw Nation history provides context for the Thompson family’s records. No evidence here identifies how a family member voted or whether they participated in the later organizations.

stories.title: A monument for both armies
stories.hook: On the courthouse lawn in Morgantown stands a Civil War monument that honors soldiers from both sides.
body: Butler County, Kentucky, was created by the General Assembly on January 18, 1810, from parts of Logan and Ohio counties, and named for Major General Richard Butler, who died at the Battle of the Wabash in 1791.

Kentucky stayed in the Union but sent men to both armies, and Butler County felt it directly. Fighting broke out near Morgantown on October 29, 1861, and a skirmish followed the next day where Confederate forces were encamped. The war slowed the county's growth.

In 1907 the Confederate-Union Veterans' Monument was dedicated on the courthouse lawn. It is described as one of only two Kentucky Civil War monuments honoring soldiers from both sides, a sign of how neighbors and kin had been divided and then lived side by side.
src: Butler County, Kentucky, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butler_County,_Kentucky)

stories.note: Place story. It describes the county where Smith and Satterfield kin lived. It does not claim a named ancestor served in either army.

stories.title: Allen County and its county seat
stories.hook: Allen County was cut out of Barren and Warren counties in 1815 and named for a colonel killed in the War of 1812.
body: Allen County was established in 1815 from parts of Barren and Warren counties. It honors Colonel John Allen, a state senator and soldier killed at the Battle of Frenchtown in Michigan during the War of 1812.

The county seat began as a settlement on Bays Fork in 1797 that grew into a stagecoach station. The town was laid off in 1816, established in 1817 and named for Charles Scott, Kentucky's fourth governor. Early on it was also called Allen Court House and Scottville. It was incorporated in 1860.
A fire at the courthouse in 1902 destroyed some county records, which is why some Allen County families are hard to trace in local papers.
src: Allen County and Scottsville, Kentucky, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allen_County,_Kentucky; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottsville,_Kentucky)

stories.title: A crossing on the Sulphur River
stories.hook: Hagansport began as a river crossing, and its post office came and went over 70 years.
body: Hagansport grew up at a Sulphur River crossing called Hagan's Port, named for an early settler. The spelling Hagansport was in use by 1857, when F. M. Sims was postmaster. The post office closed in 1866, reopened in 1876, and closed for good in 1929.
By 1884 the community had about 150 people, four churches, a school, a mill and a cotton gin. In 1896 its one-room school had 69 pupils.
By the 1930s the center had moved south to Farm Road 71 and later shifted again to its present spot. About 40 people lived there in 1985, and about 40 still in 2000.
src: Handbook of Texas, Hagansport (https://www.tshaonline.org/handbook/entries/hagansport-tx)

stories.title: Cotton, rails and tenant farms in Franklin County
stories.hook: Between 1879 and 1929 the county's cotton acreage grew more than fourfold while yields fell by more than half.
body: Franklin County was created in March 1875 and named for Benjamin C. Franklin. White settlers had come from the late 1830s, mostly from Tennessee and the upper South. The St. Louis, Arkansas and Texas Railway crossed the county in 1887 and became the main route to market.
In 1879, 706 farms planted 8,660 acres of cotton. By 1929, 1,678 farms planted 37,969 acres. Yields fell from about half a bale per acre to about one-fifth.

Tenants were 34 percent of farmers in 1880 and 62 percent in 1930. The county's population peaked at 9,331 in 1910, then declined as the Depression and the shift to livestock took hold. Cotton fell to 16,582 acres by 1940.
src: Handbook of Texas, Franklin County (https://www.tshaonline.org/handbook/entries/franklin-county)

stories.title: Grant began as a railroad stop in the Choctaw Nation
stories.hook: Grant was born in 1887 as a station on the Frisco line, when the land was still part of the Choctaw Nation.
body: Grant was founded as a station stop on the St. Louis and San Francisco Railroad, which opened through Indian Territory in June 1887. It was named for President Ulysses S. Grant.
A post office opened at Grant, Indian Territory, on January 31, 1889. At its founding the town lay in Kiamitia County, part of the Apukshunnubbee District of the Choctaw Nation.
The town counted 289 people in 2010 and 190 in 2020.

Charles Oscar and Artie Smith are buried at Grant Cemetery. Grant began about 1885 with Basil Gooding's store. A Red River ferry six miles south connected residents with Texas markets, and when the Arkansas & Choctaw laid its track five miles north, business drifted to Hugo. Grant had 416 people in 1910 and 296 in 1930, with a cotton gin, bank, hotel and a newspaper, the Grant Graphic. By 1930, 73 percent of Choctaw County's farmers were tenants.
src: Grant, Oklahoma, Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grant,_Oklahoma)
stories.note: Place story. It does not claim a Choctaw citizenship record for a named ancestor.
stories.place: Grant, Choctaw County, OK

stories.title: From Evansville to Perryville and Stones River
stories.hook: Raised in October 1861 from six southwestern Indiana counties, the 42nd was in the field at Perryville within a year and at Stones River by New Year's.
body: The 42nd Indiana Infantry was organized at Evansville and mustered in for three years on October 9, 1861, under Colonel James Garrard Jones. Its men came from six counties of southwestern Indiana.

In the autumn of 1862 the regiment moved into Kentucky, pursued Bragg's army from October 1 to 15, and fought at the Battle of Perryville on October 8. One of its lieutenant colonels, Charles Harvey Denby, left after Perryville to command the 80th Indiana.

The regiment then returned to Nashville and advanced on Murfreesboro on December 30, 1862. At Stones River (December 30, 1862 to January 3, 1863) Lieutenant Colonel James M. Shanklin commanded and was surrounded and captured on 3 January 1863.
From January 1863 the regiment belonged to the XIV Corps, Army of the Cumberland.

Horrall gives the Perryville losses plainly. On the morning of 8 October 1862 the regiment "numbered less than five hundred effective men. The entire loss, officers and men, killed, wounded and missing, was 166, or fully one-third of the entire command." Company G, one of the largest, had 52 rank and file in the fight and lost 22 killed and wounded. The regiment's actual fighting, the book says, "was not to exceed two hours." Horrall writes that this was "the first general engagement the regiment was in, and its loss was by far the greatest of any of the succeeding ones."

At Stones River, on the morning of 31 December 1862, the regiment fought in the cedar woods beside the 15th Kentucky, whose colonel was killed. Company F's captain, William M. Cockrum, was wounded in the right shoulder, and his company's part in the day is told under "Captain Cockrum: Stones River to Libby Prison."
src: Wikipedia, 42nd Indiana Infantry Regiment (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/42nd_Indiana_Infantry_Regiment); NPS Stones River people page (https://www.nps.gov/people/guest-joseph.htm); Horrall, History of the Forty-second Indiana (1892), pp. 153–154 (Perryville), 167–168 and 178–179 (Stones River)

stories.note: Regimental facts are documented. The connection to this family rests on Daniel O'Neal's service in the 42nd, covered in his own story.

stories.title: Chickamauga, reenlistment, and the road through Atlanta
stories.hook: After Chickamauga and Missionary Ridge the regiment reenlisted and fought on to Atlanta, Savannah and Bentonville, losing 310 men in all.
body: At Chickamauga (September 19-21, 1863) the regiment was commanded by Lieutenant Colonel William T. B. McIntire. In November 1863 it fought at Lookout Mountain and Missionary Ridge.

The 42nd reenlisted on January 1, 1864, and served in the Atlanta Campaign from May 1 to September 8, 1864: Resaca (May 14-15), Kennesaw Mountain, Peachtree Creek (July 19-20), the Siege of Atlanta (July 22 to August 25) and Jonesboro (August 31 to September 1).

It went on to the March to the Sea, the siege of Savannah and the Carolinas, fighting at Bentonville March 19-21, 1865, and marched in the Grand Review at Washington on May 24, 1865. It mustered out at Louisville on July 21, 1865.
Total losses were 310: 113 killed or mortally wounded, and 197 dead of disease.

At Chickamauga the regiment lost "eight killed, fifty-three wounded, and thirty-two missing, making a total of ninety-three," nearly all the missing taken prisoner; Company F's captain was among them. Horrall describes the reenlistment that followed: the government "offered inducements to the men to re-enlist, or veteranize, on the first day of January, 1864," and "there were but few in the 42d Indiana who did not re-enlist." The regiment reached Indianapolis on 28 January 1864, where Governor Morton and others addressed a public reception, and the soldiers "became recruiting officers" to fill the ranks.

Company F paid for the Atlanta campaign in names: David W. Johnson (killed 14 August 1864), John Warick (7 August 1864) and David W. Wallam (31 May 1864, at Altoona or Allatoona). Horrall adds that he could not give the regiment's losses by name for the campaign, because "the day's and month's losses were reported in the aggregate, and not in detail." The last of Company F's dead, Lt. John Q. A. Steele, fell at Bentonville on 19 March 1865. See "Company F: the men around Daniel O'Neal."
src: Wikipedia, 42nd Indiana Infantry Regiment (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/42nd_Indiana_Infantry_Regiment). Fuller sources: Horrall, History of the Forty-second Indiana Volunteer Infantry (1892); Horrall, History of the Forty-second Indiana (1892), Chickamauga pp. 189–193; reenlistment pp. 206–207; Atlanta campaign p. 258
stories.note: Regimental history is documented. Daniel O'Neal's own dates of service should be checked against it.

stories.title: A company town built around a sawmill
stories.hook: Wright City began about 1909 as a Dierks lumber company town, with the mill, houses, stores, bank and hotel all owned by the company.
body: The Choctaw Lumber Company, a subsidiary of Dierks Lumber and Coal, founded the town about 1909 beside a large timber-processing plant. Its first log was cut July 13, 1910, and a post office was chartered March 24, 1910. Renamed Wright City on May 18, 1920, it honors William Wiley Wright, the county's first war casualty.

The company supplied a sawmill, planer, railroad shops, housing, stores, a bank, a hotel, an ice factory and fire and police protection, and donated land for a school and churches. A company railroad ran from Valliant to De Queen, Arkansas.
Together the Wright City and Broken Bow mills could cut nearly 250,000 board feet of pine and 60,000 of hardwood a day. Workers struck for two months in 1947 and won an eight-cent hourly raise.
Weyerhaeuser bought the Dierks holdings in 1969, and the town incorporated in 1966. Its Little Cheyenne Rodeo dates to 1933.
src: Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture, Wright City (https://www.okhistory.org/publications/enc/entry?entry=WR002) and Forest Culture (https://www.okhistory.org/publications/enc/entry?entry=FO024)

stories.title: The Oath, the Burned Fields, and the Road West
stories.hook: For the families who stood at Alamance, the battle lasted an afternoon. What came after lasted years.
body: Governor William Tryon's militia of about 1,000 won the field on May 16, 1771. Casualty figures are disputed: 9 to 27 government dead, and perhaps 100 or more Regulators.

James Few was executed at the camp the next day. Twelve more prisoners were tried and sentenced to hang; six were pardoned at the last minute, and six were hanged at Hillsborough on June 19, 1771, among them Benjamin Merrill, Robert Matear, James Pugh and Captain Robert Messer.
Tryon then marched across Regulator country, burning homes and destroying crops. Residents were made to sign oaths of allegiance and surrender their firearms.

Many Regulators and their families moved west. Some went to Tennessee, where the Watauga Association formed in 1772 and the State of Franklin in 1784. Later study found that of 883 known Regulators only 34 became Loyalists, while 289 were Whigs.

quotes.t: Many Regulators and their families migrated westward, beyond North Carolina.
quotes.c: Summary of the aftermath of Alamance

stories.title: A Town Born at a Railroad Crossing
stories.hook: Hugo did not grow from a farm or a fort. It sprang up where two railroad lines crossed in the Choctaw Nation.
body: The Frisco built a north-south line through the area in 1887. In 1902 the St. Louis, San Francisco and New Orleans Railroad built a line from Hope, Arkansas, to Ardmore. The territorial town that sprang up at the crossing became Hugo.

It was founded in 1901 in Kiamitia County, part of the Pushmataha District of the Choctaw Nation, and named for the French novelist Victor Hugo. The name was suggested by the wife of surveyor W. H. Darrough, a fan of his books.
Agriculture, timber and ranching have been mainstays of the local economy since the start, which fits the family's timber work in Choctaw County.
In 1941 the Al G. Kelly and Miller Brothers Circus relocated to Hugo from Kansas, and for decades about twenty circuses at times wintered there.

stories.title: The County That Had Two Names
stories.hook: Etowah County was created under one name and renamed two years later, so records from the late 1860s can sit under either.
body: Before 1866 the area was split mainly between DeKalb and Cherokee counties.
On December 7, 1866, the first postwar legislature created Baine County, named for David W. Baine, a politician and Confederate officer who died in battle in 1862. Gadsden was made the county seat.
On December 1, 1868, after the 1868 constitutional convention abolished Baine County, the same boundaries became Etowah County, from a Cherokee-language word.
Anyone searching for family records of the period should look under DeKalb or Cherokee before 1866, Baine from 1866 to 1868, and Etowah afterward.
src: Wikipedia, Etowah County, Alabama (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etowah_County,_Alabama)
stories.note: Place story with a practical research tip for the family; no named ancestor is tied to it here.

stories.title: Four documents, one name: William Moffitt in 1768
stories.hook: In a single spring and autumn, William Moffitt's name went onto a petition, a committee list and the Governor's list of men too dangerous to pardon.
body: The Regulators kept their papers, and so did the royal government. William's year can be followed in print. On 30 April 1768 the Regulators issued their eighth Advertisement, and "William Maffet" is among the signers, alongside nearly the whole leadership. The meeting agreed to "send 12 men that we have chosen to meet on the said 11th day of May at Thomas Lindley's," the mill on Cane Creek.

The ninth Advertisement, the petition on public fees, carries roughly 450 names. "Wm Moffit" signs on page 734; a "James Moffitt" signs on page 737, probably a relative. Then on 21 May 1768, at George Sally's house, the Regulators chose a committee to collect their grievances and carry them to the Governor. The list begins "Wm Maffit." His name is first.

The Governor's answer came on 3 October 1768 at Hillsborough. His proclamation pardoned the insurgents except thirteen men, and "William Moffitt" is on the Council's list between Malachi Fyke and Christopher Nation. A general pardon of 9 September 1769 covered "all persons concerned in the said late Insurrection" and listed no exceptions; the pardon text does not say outright that it reached the thirteen.

His name does not appear in 1771. The reward proclamation outlawed only four men, and the sixteen men excepted from the June 1771 pardon include no Moffitt. Whether he stood on the field at Alamance on 16 May 1771 is not recorded.
In 1901 the boys' novel The Boy Spies with the Regulators printed Tryon's list, with "William Moffat" on it, as the names of "the patriots of upper Carolina in the opinion of William Tryon."

stories.title: What William did after Alamance
stories.hook: The records leave William out of the 1771 outlaw lists, and family accounts say he fed the Patriots rather than fought in the Revolution.
body: After the Regulators were beaten at Alamance in May 1771, the Governor outlawed four leaders and named sixteen more for exception from pardon. William is on neither list. He went home to the farm on Richland Creek.

A family history says he took the oath that followed Alamance, never to bear arms against the King, and stayed neutral in the Revolution because of it. No militia service record for him has been found. Instead, the family account and the Alamance Battleground Book of Remembrance both say he supplied provisions to the Patriots, and one compiled record cites a North Carolina pay voucher (no. 156) for provisions furnished.

The mill is where the sources disagree. The community of Moffitt, North Carolina, takes its name from the mill on Richland Creek, and a post office called Moffitt's Mills ran from 1823 to 1935. The state gazetteer credits Hugh Moffitt, William's probable brother, with the first mill. Family histories say William and Hugh built it together, and a Patriot record credits a James Moffitt of Brush Creek with "supplied sundries to the militia; ran Moffitt's Mill." That is likely another brother, and the vouchers have not been checked for the payee's name.
Be careful with the Roberts. A Patriot named Robert Moffitt, born 1762 of Brush Creek, is a different man, and his service should not be credited to William's son Robert.

A county history of Randolph County, 1779–1979, records the militia's first court meeting on 16 September 1801. Governor Caswell commissioned John Collier, Richard Owen and Joseph Shepherd as the regiment's officers, and the nine company captains were Shubal York, Joseph Smith, Dobson Burrow, Robert Redding, Samuel Moffitt, Colon Steed, John Brown, Charles Duncan and John Craven. A Samuel Moffitt among them is a lead only: no record seen ties him to William and Mary's household or to Hugh Moffitt's.

stories.title: A wagon, a still and 250 acres: two Moffitt wills
stories.hook: William's will of 1796 and Mary's of 1820 show a working farm: a wagon, a still, a new field on the river, and eight grown or growing children.
body: William's will begins "I William Moffitt of Randolph County in the province of North Carolina, being weak in body." He gave his sons Robert, William and David land, and his daughters Naomi (Neomi Macky), Catharine Cox, Hannah Cox, Mary Wilkinson and Margaret £3 each, with Margaret also getting cows, sheep and a bed.

Robert received the 250 acres William had bought of William Cox, except "the new field that is cleared upon the River," which his mother kept for life. William got the 225-acre plantation where his father lived, with a share reserved for Mary while she was a widow. David, who was clearly under age, got land on Tibs Run, wagon iron "brought from Pig River," and a quarter of a lot in Campbelltown in Cumberland County. If David died young, his brothers inherited and each sister would get £15.

"My Loveing Wife Mary Moffitt" received the wagon, the still, the plantation tools and the stock, and was named executrix with "my son Robart Moffitt" as executor. The witnesses were Hugh Moffitt and Charles Moffitt.

Mary outlived him by more than twenty years. She dated her own will "the 23rd day of the 9th month, 1820," in the Quaker style, naming the same five daughters and "my three sons," Robert, William and David. Her daughter Margaret was executrix and David executor, and William Cox and Stephen Cox witnessed. It was filed in 1822. Robert, her son and our ancestor, was alive in 1820.

quotes.t: my Loveing Wife Mary Moffitt Executrix & my son Robart Moffitt Executor
quotes.c: Will of William Moffitt, Randolph Co., N.C.

src: Will of William Moffitt (1796), Randolph Co. Will Book 2, pp. 30-31 (FamilySearch film 007640058); will of Mary Moffitt (1820, filed 1822)
stories.note: The last digit of William's will date is faint: one reading gives 1790, but the 1796 reading fits Robert as executor. Online trees give his death as 10 August 1797 or 1799; no record settles it. Mary's death is given as February 1822.

stories.title: Two weddings at Cane Creek, sixteen days apart
stories.hook: In the spring of 1763 the Cane Creek meetinghouse saw Joseph Chamness marry Margaret Norton and William Moffitt marry Mary Davies. Their children would marry each other in 1797.
body: Cane Creek Monthly Meeting was organized in 1751, with Anthony Chamness named its overseer. By 1763 the Chamnesses had been in North Carolina for fourteen years, since a transfer from Monocacy in Maryland to Carver's Creek Meeting in 1749, followed by a 490-acre grant on Cane Creek dated 24 June 1751.

On 17 March 1763 Anthony's son Joseph, born in Baltimore County, Maryland, married Margaret Norton, daughter of Edward and Elizabeth Norton, who had arrived from Virginia in 1762. Joseph became the meeting's recorder of marriage certificates. Margaret bore eleven children and died in 1784.

Sixteen days later, on 2 April 1763, William Moffitt, 23, married Mary Davies, 22, at the same meeting. Her father Charles Davies had crossed the Atlantic as a bound youth, married Hannah Matson of Merion in Pennsylvania in 1732 or 1733, and followed the Quaker migration south. He was recorded as a minister at Cane Creek in 1761 and was disowned by the meeting five years later, after complaining that the women's minutes were "mixed with an untruth." He bought 187 acres in Orange County on 2 August 1758 and died on 13 May 1801; Hannah died on 25 October 1812.

Margaret's daughter Martha was born in 1778. On 20 September 1797 she married Mary's son Robert at Centre Meeting, and the Chamness and Moffitt lines joined. Their son Nathan carried the Moffitt name to Arkansas.

The Chamness-Norton certificate itself is printed in Zimri Hanson's History and Genealogy of the American Descendants of John and Ann Chamness (1922, pp. 17-18). It reads: "Whereas, Joseph Chamness, son of Anthony Chamness and Sarah, his wife, of Orange County, in the Province of North Carolina, and Margaret Norton, daughter of Edward Norton and Elizabeth, his wife, of Rowan County; and Province aforesaid; having declared their intentions of Marriage with each other before several Monthly Meetings of the people called Quakers, held at Cane Creek, in Orange County, and Province aforesaid, according to the good order used amongst them, and having consent of parents, or parties concerned, their said proposals of marriage were allowed by said meeting." The day was "the Seventeenth day of the Third Month in the Year of Our Lord One Thousand Seven Hundred and Sixty-three," when the two stood up "in a public meeting of the said people, held at their meeting house at Cane Creek" and each promised "with Divine Assistance" to be a faithful and loving spouse until death.

Beneath the signatures of "Joseph Chamness" and "Margaret Chamness," twelve witnesses signed: "John Marshall, Joseph Pike, William Piggott, John Stout, John Davis, William Marshall," and, in the second column, "Thomas Branson, Anthony Chamness, Edward Norton, Sarah Chamness, Elizabeth Norton, Elizabeth Chamness." Hanson comments: "We note, also, the parents of Joseph and Margaret and his oldest sister all signed the certificate." So the page carries the names of all four grandparents of Martha Chamness, who would marry Robert Moffitt in 1797: Anthony and Sarah Chamness, and Edward and Elizabeth Norton. Hanson adds that Joseph was made recorder of marriage certificates in 1764 and that the meeting's records from then until 1769, when he moved into Providence Meeting in Randolph County, "must be" in his writing.

stories.title: Robert Moffitt's year: a father's will in 1796 and a Chamness wedding in 1797
stories.hook: Robert Moffitt was named executor of his father's will in 1796 and married Joseph Chamness's daughter Martha at Providence meeting on 20 September 1797.
body: On 20 September 1797, Robert Moffitt and Martha Chamness married at a public Quaker meeting at Providence. The Centre Monthly Meeting certificate names Robert as the son of William Moffitt, deceased, and Mary, of Randolph County; Martha was the daughter of Joseph Chamness and Margaret Norton. The witnesses include William Moffitt, Joseph Chamness, Hannah Chamness and Mary Moffitt: the groom's mother Mary, a William Moffitt who was probably his brother, the bride's father, and Hannah, who was Joseph's second wife and Martha's stepmother. Margaret had been dead since 1784, when Martha was five.

Robert had come to the altar with an estate. His father William's will of 1796 named "my son Robart Moffitt" executor and left him 250 acres bought of William Cox, except "the new field that is cleared upon the River," which Mary kept for life. His brother William got the 225-acre plantation, and the youngest, David, land on Tibs Run, wagon iron brought from Pig River and a quarter of a lot in Campbelltown. Mary got the wagon, the still and the stock. Martha, born 6 October 1778, was eighteen when she married him. Her father had served the meeting as its recorder of marriage certificates, and she was a granddaughter of Anthony Chamness.

They raised nine children in Randolph County. Randolph had been cut from Guilford in 1779, and Asheboro, its seat, was incorporated in 1796, the year William Moffitt wrote his will. The children were Naomi (1800), Sarah (1801), David (1802), William C. (1803), Aaron (1805), Hannah, Lydia (1811), Nathan (1814) and Robert (1815). Robert was alive in 1820 when his mother dated her will "the 23rd day of the 9th month, 1820," naming "my three sons," and he is in the Randolph County census of 1830 and 1840. Martha lived until 1865.

The family that Robert and Martha founded scattered with the century. Sarah and Naomi went to Iowa with their Barker husbands; Sarah died at Lorimor in 1860; Hannah and Lydia stayed in Randolph County; Nathan went to Arkansas in the early 1840s, and the youngest Robert died at Hutton Valley, Howell County, Missouri, in 1872. Their grandson Veno died in 1864 as a Confederate prisoner at Elmira. Both of the families behind that wedding, Moffitt and Chamness, signed the same certificate in 1797.

As executor in 1796, Robert was probably born by about 1775. Martha’s death is given as 11 October or 11 November 1865. Her parents and the children’s list come from compiled Quaker abstracts. The records do not establish that Robert was the Patriot Robert Moffitt of Brush Creek or Robert son of Hugh; neither married Martha.

Martha, born 6 October 1778, a daughter of Joseph Chamness, lived until 1865. Their children included Mary, Nathan, David, Naomi, William, Hannah, Lydia and Aaron.

stories.title: Nathan the wheelwright, and a son in blue
stories.hook: Nathan’s census trail runs from North Carolina through Arkansas to Missouri; a Union cavalryman of the same name may have been his son.
body: Nathan married Rebecca Williams on 13 October 1835 in Randolph County, North Carolina, and he is in the 1840 census of the county's South Division. A son, Calvin, was born there on 4 December 1841. By 1850 the family was farming in Strawberry Township, Lawrence County, Arkansas.

Lawrence County in the 1850s was a mix of small farms, a county seat at Smithville, and 494 enslaved people among 8,875 white residents in 1860. By then Nathan was a wheelwright with $1,200 in land. Patrick was born in May 1853 and Henry in 1855. The war brought jayhawkers and bushwhackers to the county, though no major battle. A National Park Service index lists a Calvin V. Moffitt as a private in Company L, 4th Arkansas Cavalry (Union), but whether that soldier was Nathan's son remains unconfirmed. Family profiles place Nathan's son later at Duncan, Oklahoma, where he died on 13 February 1913.

By 1870 Nathan and Rebecca were in Dent County, Missouri, farming with no land of their own. Oregon County, where they next lived, was largely pro-Southern and suffered raids; its Alton courthouse burned in October 1863, and the historical marker adds that Lee's surrender "did not end the Civil War in Oregon County." Rebecca died there in 1871. That year Nathan married a widow, Nancy (Rowe) Cole.
Nathan died on 23 December 1873 in Oregon County. That August his son Patrick had married Alice Ann Cole there. A photograph labeled "Nathan Moffitt," shown with children, is kept in the family tree.

Nathan's brothers and sisters spread widely: Sarah and Naomi to Iowa, Robert to Strawberry Township and then Howell County, Missouri, and Hannah, Lydia, Aaron and William C. stayed in Randolph County. Aaron's son Veno Moffitt died in 1864 as a Confederate prisoner at Elmira.

The 4th Arkansas Cavalry (Union) was organized at Little Rock in December 1863, and Company L, where the NPS database lists a Calvin V. Moffitt, was made up in Montgomery County, far from Lawrence County. Whether the National Park Service entry belongs to this Calvin remains a lead. Company L's petition of March 1864 and the regiment's scouts are told under "The 4th Arkansas Cavalry: Union men from the Ouachita hills."
src: 1840 U.S. Census, Randolph Co., N.C.; 1850 and 1860 Censuses, Lawrence Co., Ark.; 1870 Census, Dent Co., Mo.; NC Marriages, Randolph Co. (1835); Missouri Marriages (1871); NPS Civil War Soldiers database; Encyclopedia of Arkansas, 'Lawrence County'; Alton marker (HMDB 179894); WikiTree Moffitt-107, Moffitt-400
stories.note: The NPS record documents a soldier named Calvin V. Moffitt; identifying that soldier with Nathan's son remains a lead. Patrick is given as born 11 May 1853 at Sylamore and as dying on 20 December 1905 at Mountain View in one source, and as dying in November 1904 and buried at Sallisaw in another. Who burned the Alton courthouse is disputed: the marker says Union troops, a 2024 survey says Southern partisans.

stories.title: 1901: a death in Mountain View and 22 years of widowhood
stories.hook: Henry died at 46 in the Stone County hills. Hannah, who could not read or write, kept the family together for another two decades.
body: Stone County was only 28 years old when Henry died. It was created in 1873, and Mountain View, its seat, had 99 residents in 1880, was incorporated on 14 August 1890, and got its first wooden courthouse in 1888. Henry, a farmer who owned his land free and clear in the 1900 census, died there in 1901 at 46. Family records give the date as 9 September. No grave has been found and he has no memorial anywhere; Arkansas did not register deaths in Stone County until 1914.
The same spring, on 26 May 1901, Henry's brother Patrick lost his wife, Alice Ann (Cole) Moffitt, who is buried at Levisy Flat Cemetery in Stone County.

Hannah stayed. In 1910 she was renting a house in Franklin Township with Tom, who worked as a railroad section hand, and Grady, who made barrel staves. She had borne seven children and six were living: among them Josephine, Jesse, Gimsa, Bertha, Tom and Grady. Jesse Gee Moffitt went to Texas and died in Amarillo in 1957; Tom died in Paris, Texas, in 1953.

She spent her last years at Herpel, a Rocky Bayou community six miles east of Mountain View with a grist mill, cotton gin, stave mill and sawmill by the early 1900s. Its post office opened in 1907, and the Herpel Missionary Baptist Church laid its cornerstone on 5 March 1923. Hannah died there on 4 April 1923, about a month later, and is buried in Herpel Cemetery, where her stone reads "Wife of Henry H Moffitt."
src: 1900 and 1910 U.S. Censuses, Franklin Twp., Stone Co., Ark.; Find a Grave (Hannah Moffitt, Herpel Cemetery; Alice Ann Moffitt, Levisy Flat; Jesse Gee and Thomas Berry Moffitt); Encyclopedia of Arkansas, 'Stone County' and 'Herpel'

stories.title: A timber camp and a rented house in Hugo
stories.hook: Grady and Mary raised their family in Oklahoma and Texas and buried three of their children.
body: Grady and Mary married about 1914. Their first son, Alvin, was born in September 1915. In 1917 Grady's draft card puts him at Ervin, Oklahoma, a place that existed only from 1904 to 1922, as a timberman for C. D. Neese. Which sawmill that was is not recorded. The county's biggest one was the Pine Belt Lumber Company at Fort Towson, begun in 1902.

Hugo was a young town. It was founded in 1901 where the Frisco's north-south line crossed the Arkansas & Choctaw, and the Frisco depot went up in 1914. Grady's family rented there at 411 North H Street by 1940.

Family trees name the following children, with these dates: Alvin B. (1915-1994, U.S. Army Air Corps in World War II), Odas Eugene (1918-1995; "Odis" in the census, and "Ottis" in 1920), Dois L. (1921-1947), Jimmie Gaynell (1923-1926), John Winfred (1925-1990), the twins Alton V. (1928-1975) and Eldon Herman (1928-2014), Donald K. (1931-2014) and Henry Wayne (1934-1937). The two toddlers who died were three years old.

In 1930, with six boys, they were living with Mary's parents, John Morgan and Lizzie Shackleford, in Martin County, Texas. That is the county where Mary's father is buried. In 1940 Grady, 48, had been out of work for 50 weeks and earned $100.

Grady's brother Tom farmed beside him in 1920 and later lived in Paris, Texas, where he died in 1953, with a stone marked WW I and WW II. Their brother Jesse is buried at Tahoka, Texas. Grady and Mary lie at Shoat Springs Cemetery near Hugo.
The Shoat Springs transcription confirms the full dates for the two children who died young: Jimmie Gaynell, 17 January 1923 to 26 October 1926, and Henry Wayne, 13 January 1934 to 12 May 1937.

stories.title: Mary's people: from Etowah County to Texas and Oklahoma
stories.hook: An Alabama marriage in 1889, a Texas household in 1930, and Lizzie’s later home near her children at Apache.
body: John Morgan Shackleford was born on 30 September 1862 in Alabama and married Catherine Elizabeth "Lizzie" Newton on 1 December 1889 in Etowah County. Etowah County had been created only 21 years before, and for two of those years, 1866 to 1868, it was called Baine County. In the 1900 census at Gilbert, John was 37 and Elizabeth 28, with five living children. Mary, born 4 June 1895, was the "May, 5."

Her siblings were Balis Anthony (1892-1982, who died in Los Angeles County), Robert Yates (1897-1961), John Newton (1906-2002), Hazel Marzee King (1908-1980), Edward Richard (1910-1988) and Helen Elizabeth Josey (1915-1997).

By 1930 John Morgan was in Martin County, Texas, with his wife and children; Grady and Mary and their six boys were living with them. John died on 22 May 1930 and is buried at Evergreen Cemetery in Stanton. Lizzie died on 8 November 1951 and is buried at Fairview Cemetery, Apache, Caddo County, Oklahoma. In 1933 Lizzie moved from Dawson County, Texas, to Apache. She spent her final years near several of her grown children, and died at son Ed’s home southwest of town.

The Shackelfords of Virginia trace to an immigrant, Roger, who received a grant in Gloucester County in 1658. A Shackleford family history of 1940 says the family had no coat of arms, and Mary's descent from Roger is not proved.

The 1900 census household at Gilbert lists John, 37, Elizabeth, 28, and five children: "Balous" 8, Myrtle 6, May 5, Robert 3 and Eddie 8 months. Two later obituaries (Chico Enterprise-Record, 23 June 1961; Lamar County Echo, 1 January 1981) name sisters Josephine Haskell, Eulah Tillman and Beulah Hutchins who do not fit that list. Hazel was born at Rattan in Delta County, Texas, so the family was in northeast Texas about 1908 before reaching Martin County.

Lizzie’s marriage papers preserve a family moment just before the wedding. On 28 November 1889, her father, Balas Newton, gave permission for her to marry John. John carried that consent into the probate office and, two days later, certified that he had written and signed it at her father’s direction. A separate affidavit names her as Lizzie Newton.
