stories.title: One man, two names: William Harrison Pisachubbe enrolled twice
stories.hook: A boys' school list in 1899 put "Harrison Pisachubbe" on the Choctaw rolls, and he was already there as William H. In 1911 the Interior Department sorted it out.
body: On Dawes Card 1580, filled out on 10 May 1899 for Kiamitia County with the post office Goodland, line 2 is "William H.," son of the widow Eunice Pisachubbe, 16 years old and full-blood, Roll No. 4466. A note on the card says he had been on the 1896 roll as "William Harrison." His father, Joseph Pisachubbe, is written as dead.

Three months later, on 22 August 1899, a list of students at Armstrong Academy, a Choctaw school, was sent to the Commission, and it included "Harrison Pisachubbe." That name was also put on the final roll as No. 10559, approved on 4 February 1903. In the meantime William H. had received a complete allotment under his first number, and in 1905 the Commission, not knowing about the doubling, made a second, arbitrary allotment in the name of Harrison. The certificates were mailed to Academy, Oklahoma, and came back marked "unclaimed."

On 2 August 1909 William H. testified at Hugo that he had told the postmaster to send the certificates back, as he already had his allotment as William H. Pisachubbe. Eunice, Harrison Nohio and Thomas Hunter also gave testimony. On 1 August 1911 the Commissioner at Muskogee wrote to the Secretary of the Interior that it showed "that Harrison Pisachubbe, Choctaw by Blood Roll No. 10559, is a duplicate enrollment of William H. Pisachubbe, No. 4466 on the same roll." The Secretary's office approved a notation on the roll on 16 August 1911: "Duplicate enrollment of No. 4466; not entitled to land or money under this number."

William H. had a son, Colbert, born on 26 June 1906 at Hugo, whose mother Mamie signed her application with a mark and whose birth was attended by a midwife, Cassie Davis. His enrollment was refused: the Commissioner decided on 27 November 1906 that, because Colbert "was not living March 4, 1906," the cutoff in the Act of 26 April 1906, he had no authority to consider it, and the Secretary affirmed on 26 February 1907. Mamie is called a non-citizen in the decision.
William Harrison Pisachubbe died in May 1937; his obituary in the Hugo Daily News is the source of the family's account of the removal from Mississippi in 1832.

stories.title: Edward Pisachubbi's land letter, 1903
stories.hook: Edward, listed as Eunice's ward on Card 1580, wrote to the Commission in January 1903 about land he had picked for himself and his wife Frances.
body: Line 4 of Eunice Pisachubbe's card is not one of her sons. "Edward," 17, full-blood, Roll No. 4468, is written as her ward, and the card gives his dead parents as "Simpson Pisachubbe" and "Sallie Pisachubbe," of Jackson County. A note says he was the husband of Frances Byington, whose own card is No. 956.

On 31 January 1903 the Commission wrote to him at Hugo, answering his letter of 16 January, "in which you state that you have selected certain lands for the allotments of yourself and your wife, Frances Pisachubbi." He had added that part of the land he described was claimed by another citizen. The Commission told him it had "no means of recording the selections of citizens" and could not settle disputes about possession; the matter would be heard when land offices opened in the Nation, which it expected between the first of March and the first of April. A follow-up letter said admission to the land office would be by tickets handed out on or after 16 April 1903.
His letters show how the land was chosen in the Choctaw Nation in 1903: families walked the ground first and wrote to the Commission, and then had to apply in person at the land office.

quotes.t: in which you state that you have selected certain lands for the allotments of yourself and your wife, Frances Pisachubbi.
quotes.c: Commission to the Five Civilized Tribes to Edward Pisachubbi, Hugo, 31 January 1903 (Choctaw 7-956, 7-1580)

stories.title: Doak & Tims in the Texas Supreme Court, 1849
stories.hook: A Doaksville store's unpaid account from 1840 to 1844 ended up before the Supreme Court of Texas, in a case titled Love v. Doak & Tims.
body: Doak & Tims, the Doaksville trading firm of Josiah L. Doak and Vincent B. Tims, appears in the law reports of Texas. The case, Love v. Doak & Tims, was decided at the December 1849 term and printed in volume 5 of the Texas Reports, at page 343.

The court summarized the suit this way: it "was brought in the names of the appellees as copartners, trading as merchants, for the use and benefit of Josiah L. Doak, one of the said copartners." It was an action on a store account against a man named Love who lived across the Red River in the Choctaw Nation. The first item in the account was dated 1840 and the last 30 July 1844; the suit was begun in Grayson County, Texas, on 24 January 1848. A witness testified that he had sold Love goods up to 28 August 1840, "that at the time said account was made the defendant was a resident of Mississippi," and that Love "did remove in 1841" to the Choctaw Nation. A second witness said that in 1844 he had presented the account for payment and asked Love for an order on a Colonel Upshaw, or his note, and Love said he would settle it himself.

The trial jury found for Doak & Tims. On appeal, Chief Justice Hemphill reversed and dismissed the case on the law of limitations: the debt was more than two years old, and nothing in writing acknowledged it. The partnership is the one the family's Doaksville records describe, from the army ration contracts of 1838 and 1839 through the store letters of 1841; the suit of 1848 came four years after the partners dissolved their business by mutual agreement in 1844, and it is brought for the use and benefit of Doak alone.
The account shows the store selling goods on credit over four years, with the bill pursued years later in a Texas court.

quotes.t: brought in the names of the appellees as copartners, trading as merchants, for the use and benefit of Josiah L. Doak, one of the said copartners.

stories.title: Edward Tims on the ballot for Principal Chief, August 1886
stories.hook: A New York Times wire from Little Rock on 5 August 1886 names Edward Tims among four candidates for Principal Chief of the Choctaw Nation.
body: The Paris (Texas) News said in 1940 that Judge Tims was "once considered for the position as principal chief of the Choctaw Nation." A newspaper from the time shows how far it went. On 6 August 1886 the New York Times printed a short dispatch headed "Choctaws Hold an Election," dated Little Rock, Ark., 5 August: "The election for principal chief of the Choctaw Nation was held yesterday." It names four men: Ben Smallwood, Thompson McKinney, J. P. Folsom (printed Fulsom) and Edward Tims. It adds that a large vote was cast and that unofficial returns pointed to the election of McKinney.

Edward Tims was then in his mid-forties, a county judge of Towson County and, since the early 1880s, a trustee of Apukshunnubbee District. The Doaksville post office came to him the next year. The dispatch gives no vote totals; Thompson McKinney went on to serve as Principal Chief, so Edward Tims was a losing candidate in a four-man race for the highest office in the Nation.
He is the same Edward Tims whose 1888 marriage near Doaksville is on the Dawes jacket, and whose enrollment card names his father as Vincent B. Tims.

quotes.t: The election for principal chief of the Choctaw Nation was held yesterday.
quotes.c: "Choctaws Hold an Election," The New York Times, 6 August 1886, dispatch from Little Rock, Ark., 5 August

quotes.c: The Paris (Texas) News, January 1940

stories.title: Nancy Pisachubbi: a card that names her father, Te-hol-ba-ta-bi
stories.hook: Dawes Card 1278 names Nancy Pisachubbi’s parents, but no examined record connects her to Joseph Pisachubbe.
body: Dawes Card 1278 was made out in May 1899 for "Pisachubbi, Nancy," age 69, a full-blood woman of Eagle County, post office Luk-fa-tah, Indian Territory, Roll No. 3474. She is alone on the card, and her enrollment was approved on 12 December 1902.

The columns for her parents give two names: her father was "Te-hol-ba-ta-bi," dead, of Eagle County, and her mother was "Malindy," dead, with Mississippi written as her county. Her stated age suggests a birth around 1830, but the card does not identify her birthplace.

One family tree gives Joseph a mother named Nancy Te-hol-ba-ta-bi, born about 1825 in Mississippi. Card 1278 lists a Nancy Pisachubbi whose father was Te-hol-ba-ta-bi, but it does not list a husband or children, and no examined record establishes that she was Joseph’s mother or that the two Nancy entries represent the same person (lead only). A Case Pisachubbi on neighboring Card 1277 has a father called Pisachubbi and a mother called Noise; their relationship to Nancy is not established.

stories.title: "Rosey Ann Tims": a notary's letter and a grandmother who delivered the babies
stories.hook: Betsy's sister Rosie married James Wilson. In October 1900 a Doaksville notary wrote to the Dawes Commission to say who she was, and her mother Emeline attended her children's births.
body: Rosie does not appear under the Tims name on the roll. She was enrolled on 24 April 1899 on her mother's Card 778 as "Rosanna Tims," and when she married James Wilson she was moved to his card. Dawes Card 1281, filled out on 1 May 1899 at Doaksville (the same day as Henry W. Thompson's Card 1282 and Joseph P. Thompson's Card 1283), lists "Wilson, James," age 24, full-blood, of Cedar County, with parents "Simon Wilson" and "Melissie Wilson," both dead; his wife "Rosanna," 18, three-quarter blood, with her parents written "Benson Tims," dead, and "Emiline Tims," of Towson County; and a baby son. A note on the card says Rosanna was "transferred to this card with her husband, Oct. 26, 1900."

How she was found is in the jacket. In September 1900 the notary R. L. Carter of Doaksville sent in an application for the baby, Islam Wilson, born on 10 August 1900. The Commission sent it back because it could not identify the mother, who gave her age as eighteen and had clearly been married since she was listed. On 19 October 1900 Carter replied: "Rosey Wilson the wife of James Wilson was registered as Rosey Ann Tims and has been married since she was registered. Her mother name is Emaline Times her father died before he was registered." The Commission wrote back on 27 October that it had identified her as "Rosanna Tims the daughter of Emiline Tims, who was listed for enrollment April 24th, 1899." It still wanted the marriage certificate, and on 19 August 1902 acknowledged one between "James Wilson and Rosa Tims."

Two more children are on the jacket. A son was born on 23 March 1903, and Rosanna swore the birth affidavit on 25 March 1905 with her mark, her husband James Wilson and John Aaron as witnesses. The midwife's affidavit, sworn on 19 April 1905, is signed "Emeline Tims," Rosanna's mother, who swore the same kind of affidavit for her grandson Joseph W. Thompson ten days later. A daughter, Candace, was born on 16 June 1905; in May 1906 the Commission acknowledged "the affidavits of Rosanna Wilson and Emeline Tims to the birth of Candace Wilson."
Rosie's husband is probably the James Wilson who swore with her brother Mitchell Tims in 1902 to the death of Mitchell's baby daughter.

stories.title: The boy who died before the roll was taken
stories.hook: Born 15 November 1898, dead by April 1899, and still on a federal roll until 1904 when the Department struck him off.
body: James Austin was the second child on his parents' card. His father Legion swore at Fowlerville in early May 1899 that the boy was born on 15 November 1898 and was "now living." The card gave his age as 1 and entered him as No. 3739, with a note: "No. 4 died April 1899."

The boy's birth proof is as plain as such papers get. The form's printed "Affidavit of Mother" is crossed out and "Father" written over it, and Legion signed by mark as a 33-year-old citizen by blood. The second affidavit, normally for a doctor or nurse, was sworn by a neighbor, Leonidas Willis, who "knew" of the birth and also made his mark.

Proof of the death reached the Commission on 2 December 1902. The Secretary of the Interior approved the other four on 12 December 1902; the card stamps James "Died prior to September 25, 1902" and runs a red rule through his line. The Department did not cancel his enrollment until 16 September 1904.

quotes.t: No. 4 died April 1899: Enrollment cancelled by Department Sept. 16, 1904

stories.title: A baby on a card that was nearly closed
stories.hook: Born 5 August 1900, a year after her family applied, and added by a letter and an affidavit signed with two marks.
body: Adline was born on 5 August 1900, a year after her parents' application and two years before the roll was approved. Her father wrote to the Commission from Garvin that October; on 9 October the Commission replied with a blank infant application and the instruction that if the mother or the midwife could not write, two disinterested witnesses must attest each mark.

Her mother, "Mulcy Austin," swore on 19 April 1901 that she was 25, a citizen by blood and "the lawful wife of Leageon Austin," and that a girl was born 5 August 1900 and named Adline Austin. The midwife, Sinie Hall, swore the same. Both signed with a mark before the notary William Swink at Fowlerville, with two witnesses, one of them Sallie Johnson.

The Commission acknowledged it on 5 June 1901, "the same being in proper form," and listed the child as Choctaw by Blood No. 3740. The roll was approved on 12 December 1902. Adline later married William Harrison Pisachubbe, whose younger brother Robert had married her sister Lizzie, and died at Speer in 1929.

stories.title: Four counties on three cards
stories.hook: The grandparents' counties were Choctaw counties, not Oklahoma ones, and the 1896 census numbers show which was which.

subject.name: Towson, Red River, Blue and Kiamitia

body: The Dawes clerks recorded where each person was counted in 1896, and where their dead parents had lived. On the three cards for this line the answers are four Choctaw Nation counties: Towson for Legion and Molsey Austin and for Emeline Tims; Kiamitia for Eunice Pisachubbe, her sons and the ward Edward; Blue for her parents Jackson and Viney Gardner; and Red River for Molsey's parents Brazil and Siney.

Under the Choctaw constitution and its acts, as printed in 1894, Towson belonged to the Apukshunnubbee District, while Blue and Kiamichi were counties of the Pushmataha District, each sending one senator. In 1886 the Council cut Jackson County out of Kiamitia, Blue and Atoka, which is why Edward Pisachubbe's dead parents, Simpson and Sallie, are written as of Jackson County in 1899 while he was counted in Kiamitia.

The cards give both a county and a post office. The Austins were Towson County people with a Fowlerville post office, renamed Valliant in 1902, and Eunice was a Kiamitia County woman at Goodland. The old counties vanished at statehood in 1907, and the families that had been counted in four of them came together in Choctaw County, Oklahoma, where Simon and Frances settled at Jeter.

stories.title: Calvin Moffitt, from North Carolina to Oklahoma
stories.hook: Nathan and Rebecca’s son moved through Arkansas to Oklahoma; a Union soldier of the same name may have been him.
body: Calvin was the oldest of Nathan and Rebecca Moffitt's sons known by name, born 4 December 1841 in Randolph County, North Carolina, and eight years old when the family was counted at Strawberry Township, Lawrence County, Arkansas, in 1850. He was still in the same township in 1860, a year after his parents' twin daughters were born, and when Henry was a child of four.

A soldier index lists "Calvin V. Moffitt" (also written Moffett) as a private in Company L of the 4th Arkansas Cavalry, a Union regiment, and a Federal service record from 1864 gives his age as 22. The soldier’s identification as Nathan and Rebecca’s son remains a lead. The 1870 census has him married and living at Lebanon Township, Sharp County, Arkansas. His wife was Matilda Dailey (born 23 January 1849 in Polk County, Missouri).

The family tree names six children. Andrew Webster was born in Sharp County on 17 January 1869 and died 24 December 1899. Sarah A. (born 1874 in Missouri) died 11 September 1883, and John W. (born 1877 in Missouri) died 7 February 1885, both as children. Milburn Green (1880-1956) lived and died in Arkansas. Wilson Cornelius, born at Golden City, Missouri, on 14 January 1889, farmed in Stephens County, Oklahoma, later lived in Johnson County, Arkansas, and died at Norco, California, in 1971.

The last child, Girdy Emalah, is shown as born and dying on 19 July 1891. Matilda died the next day, 20 July 1891, at New Pocahontas, Arkansas. In 1900 Calvin, a widower, was head of a household at Reyno, Randolph County. By 1910 he was at King Township, Stephens County, Oklahoma, near his son Wilson, and he died in nearby Duncan on 13 February 1913. A Civil War pension index entry was filed from Oklahoma.

kv: Widowed head of household, Reyno, Randolph Co., Ark.
stories.note: The NPS soldier record names a Calvin V. Moffitt; whether that soldier was Nathan's son is unconfirmed. The family-tree profiles and the Strawberry Township household establish a separate family lead. The dates of Matilda's and the infant's deaths come from a tree import and no certificate has been seen. An 1880 census entry at Janes Creek, Randolph County, attached to him in that profile does not fit his children being born in Missouri through 1889, so it is not used here.
stories.place: Born in Randolph County, N.C.; raised in Lawrence County, Ark.; died at Duncan, Stephens County, Okla.

stories.title: Patrick: the brother who stayed in Stone County
stories.hook: Patrick married in Missouri the year his father died, then lived on in Mountain View, where Henry settled, and buried his wife four months before Henry died.
body: Patrick Green Moffitt was born on 11 May 1853 at Sylamore, in the Ozark hills along the White River. He was two years older than Henry. After the family went north into Dent and Oregon counties, Missouri, he married Alice Ann Cole there in August 1873, four months before Nathan's death on 23 December.

Alice Ann was born on 18 December 1857 in Missouri. Nathan's second wife was a widow, Nancy (Rowe) Cole, whom he married in 1871. It is likely, though unproved, that Alice was a Cole child of that household, which would make Patrick's bride his stepsister.

The couple returned to Arkansas and settled at Mountain View, where Henry's family was by 1889. Their daughter Lillian was born in 1894 and died in 1988. Alice Ann died on 26 May 1901 and is buried at Levisy Flat Cemetery; Henry died that September.

Patrick's own death is recorded two ways: WikiTree has 20 December 1905 at Mountain View, and another tree has November 1904 with burial at Sallisaw, Oklahoma. The 1905 date is the more widely repeated.
src: WikiTree profiles (api.wikitree.com, 2026): Moffitt-106 (Patrick Green Moffitt), Cole-3005 (Alice Cole), Moffitt-105 (Lillian); Missouri marriages 1750-1920 index entry for Nathan Mofit, 1871; Find a Grave (Levisy Flat Cemetery)
kv: Aug 1873, Oregon Co., Mo., to Alice Ann Cole (1857-1901)
20 Dec 1905, Mountain View (one source: Nov 1904, buried Sallisaw)
stories.note: Alice as Nancy Cole's daughter is a guess from the surname; no record names her parents.
stories.place: Born at Sylamore, Ark.; married in Oregon County, Mo.; lived and died at Mountain View, Stone County, Ark.

stories.title: Uncle Robert, one house over in Strawberry Township
stories.hook: Nathan's youngest brother followed him to Strawberry Township, Arkansas, by 1860, buried most of his early children, and ended up in the Missouri Ozarks.
body: Robert was the youngest of Robert and Martha (Chamness) Moffitt's nine children, born 19 June 1815, a year after Nathan. He married Cynthia Gardner, born in North Carolina on 29 April 1815, and in the 1850 census they were in District 17 of Henderson County, Tennessee, with seven children: John 17, Mary Ann 12, Malcy 10, Alzia 8, Henry P. 6, James H. 3 and Martha E., a baby.

By the 1860 census Robert, 45, and Cynthia, 45, were in Strawberry Township, Lawrence County, Arkansas (page 224), where his brother Nathan was a wheelwright. The household had shrunk to Alzira 18, Parker 15, James 13, Martha 10, Jane 8 and Franklin 5. John, Mary Ann and Malcy do not appear again in any record found, and Parker is last seen in 1860.

The family moved on into Missouri. Robert died on 9 November 1872 at Hutton Valley, Howell County, and was buried in what is now called Moffitt Cemetery near Willow Springs. Cynthia lived until 9 October 1895.

Three of the children have traceable lives. Alzira Adelaide (1842-1923) married James Thomas Loving in 1867, bore seven children and is buried at Willow Springs. James Henderson Moffitt (1848-1916) became a physician at Redford, Reynolds County; the Ellington Press of 20 January 1916 reported, "We were greatly pained to hear of the death of Dr. Moffitt which occurred at Redford the evening of the 7th." Martha Elizabeth (1850-1931) died at Springfield and Margaret Jane (1852-1923) at Montier, Missouri.

quotes.c: The Ellington Press, Ellington, Mo., 20 Jan 1916, p. 4 (as transcribed on WikiTree)

H. Moffitt, 1916

stories.note: The census citations are given in the WikiTree profile; the census pages themselves were not viewed. Cynthia Gardner is from North Carolina and no link to the Choctaw Gardner family on the maternal side has been found.
stories.place: Born in Randolph County, N.C.; farmed in Henderson County, Tenn., and Strawberry Township, Lawrence County, Ark.; died at Hutton Valley, Howell County, Mo.

stories.title: Nathan's nephew, who died in the Elmira prison camp
stories.hook: From Randolph County, North Carolina, Veno was captured in Virginia and died at Elmira; a soldier with his cousin Calvin’s name served the Union in Arkansas.
body: Nathan's older brother Aaron C. Moffitt (6 December 1805 to 20 June 1877) stayed in Randolph County, North Carolina. He married Mary "Polly" Brady on 7 August 1827 and is in the 1850 and 1870 censuses with her. Their son Veno, called Zeno in the 1860 census, was born about 1828.

Veno married Charlotte L. "Lottie" Gardner (1824-1904), and they had Mary Jane (1860-1920) and the Rev. James Alfred Moffitt (1864-1926). At 34 he enlisted in the Confederate army on 8 April 1863 and joined Company F, 24th North Carolina Infantry.

The roll of honor card says that he was captured near Drewry's Bluff, Virginia, on 16 May 1864. He was sent to the prison camp at Elmira, New York, where he died of chronic diarrhea on 11 October 1864. He is buried in Woodlawn National Cemetery at Elmira.

The war touched Moffitt families in several places. A Union cavalryman in Arkansas shared the name of Veno's cousin Calvin, though the identification remains unconfirmed. Lydia Moffitt Rains lost two sons in the war in North Carolina.

stories.place: Randolph County, N.C.; died as a Confederate prisoner at Elmira, N.Y.

stories.title: William C. and his three Randolph County wives
stories.hook: Nathan's brother stayed in North Carolina, married three times, and lost two sons by 1873; his first wife was a Williams, like Nathan's.
body: William Cornelius Moffitt, born about 1802, married Thalitha (Aletha) Williams on 7 August 1827, the same day Aaron, his brother, married Polly Brady. Thalitha was born 16 September 1804 at Deep River, Randolph County, and died before 1866. The 1850 and 1860 censuses show them with children.

Their children were Milo (1828-1881, died in Chatham County), Dennis (1830-1886), Reuben Elwood (1833-1915), Mahala Adeline (1835-1903), Marshall (1839-1863), Mary Delphina (1842-1898, died at Decatur, Indiana) and John Tyler (1843-1873). Marshall died in 1863, which fits the Civil War, but no record of his service has been seen.

William married Elizabeth Fesmire on 2 September 1866; she appears in the 1870 census and died about 1873. On 7 October 1873 he married Araminta Hicks (1844-1932), and the 1880 census shows them with two young children, Hannah V. (born 1875) and William Dufoe (born 1876). He died in 1884 aged about 82; the birth date on his Find a Grave memorial is regarded as doubtful.

Nathan's wife was Rebecca Williams, also from Randolph County. Whether Rebecca and Thalitha were sisters is not shown by any record; it is a lead worth checking in the Randolph County Williams families.

stories.title: Two sisters who went to Iowa with their Barker husbands
stories.hook: Nathan went west to Arkansas; his sisters Sarah and Naomi married two Barkers and settled in Iowa, where Sarah died on a sled being hauled home.
body: Sarah and Naomi were the oldest of Robert and Martha Moffitt's children. Naomi married Robert Barker on 5 March 1822, and Sarah married the Rev. Beeson Barker in 1821. Both families left Randolph County for Union County, Iowa.

Sarah's WikiTree profile preserves a family memory of her death: "Mrs. Beeson Barker was born in 1800 and died in 1860 in the early winter. She took sick at the home of her son, Jerry, in Winterset. She wanted to come home so Marion Carey took a yoke of oxen hitched to a pin sled with a wagon box on it and putting a feather bed in it, brought her home. She lived only a few days. This broke up the active home of Rev. Barker." She is buried at Groesbeck Cemetery, Lorimor.

Sarah and Beeson had eight children: Aaron Dennis (1824-1881), Jeremiah Harmon (1826-1885), Robert Moffitt (1830-1834), Martha Jane (1831-1838), David Pearce (1834-1918), Mary Rahab (1838-1891), Sarah Ann (1841-1850) and William Beeson (1842-1926).

Naomi and Robert Barker's daughters Mary D. (1823-1899) and Deborah L. (1824-1907) both married their Moffitt cousins, Solomon C. and Stancil, sons of Charles Moffitt and Mary Beeson, and both died in Union County, Iowa.

quotes.c: Family account quoted on WikiTree, Moffitt-1914

stories.title: The sisters who never left: Hannah and Lydia
stories.hook: Nathan's sisters Hannah and Lydia stayed in Randolph County, and Lydia lost two sons in the Civil War.
body: Hannah Moffitt, born 11 December 1806, married Isaiah Craven and in 1850 lived in his household in Randolph County. They had at least Hiram Peter (1835-1900), Peter W. (1837-1861), Molcy, and Lewis Pickett (1846-1924). Hannah died on 24 January 1888 and is buried at Concord Cemetery, Coleridge.

Lydia, born 18 June 1811, married Alford Rains on 29 June 1833 and appears in the censuses of 1850 through 1880. Her seven children were Nathan (born 1834), Mary (1836), Susannah (1838, died young), William Anderson (1841), Alfred Evans (1844), Daniel (1845) and Robert Monroe (1853). WikiTree records that Nathan and William Anderson "died in the Civil War."
Lydia died on 2 March 1885 and is buried in the Rains-Caveness family cemetery at Ramseur. Her brother Nathan, far away in Missouri, had died twelve years earlier.

stories.title: Tom, the brother next door
stories.hook: Tom was born at the old Buck Horn settlement, worked the railroad, and followed his brother Grady to Choctaw County.
body: Thomas Berry Moffitt was born on 17 February 1889 at St. James in Stone County, Arkansas, the first of Henry and Hannah's children known to be born in Stone County. In the 1910 census he was living with his widowed mother in Franklin Township and working as a railroad section hand.

By 1920 he was farming next door to Grady in Wilson Township, Choctaw County, Oklahoma. His wife, Vesta, was born in Arkansas on 2 March 1892 and died at Holdenville, Hughes County, Oklahoma, on 15 October 1930.

Tom later lived at Paris, Texas, where he died on 21 March 1953. His grave marker is carved with World War I and World War II service, and WikiTree gives him as the son of Henry H. Moffitt and Hannah Grimes and the brother of Grady.

stories.title: Grady's older brothers and sisters
stories.hook: Four of Henry and Hannah's seven children are known only by a census line or a gravestone, and one of them went to the Texas plains.

subject.name: Josephine, Jesse Gee, Gimsa and Bertha Moffitt

body: The 1880 census at Janes Creek Township, Randolph County, lists Henry and Hannah with Josephine, 3, and Jesse, 1. Hannah told the 1910 census taker that she had borne seven children and six were still living, so one died young and has left no record.

Jesse Gee Moffitt (1879-1957) went to the Texas plains; he is buried at Tahoka in Lynn County, and family notes place his death at Amarillo. Josephine, Gimsa and Bertha are with their parents in the 1900 census at Franklin Township, Stone County, along with Tom and Woodford (Grady).
A Bertha May Moffitt Barham (1888-1930) is buried at Herpel Cemetery, near her mother, and may be the Bertha of the census. That is not proved.

stories.title: Grady and Mary's sons
stories.hook: Grady and Mary raised five more sons to adulthood beside John and Dois, and lost two toddlers and Dois himself.

subject.name: Alvin, Odas, Alton, Eldon and Donald Moffitt

body: Alvin B., born in September 1915, was the first of Grady and Mary's children. He served in the U.S. Army Air Corps in World War II and died in 1994.
Odas Eugene (1918-1995) was "Odis, 21" in the 1940 census and "Ottis" in 1920. The twins Alton V. and Eldon Herman were born in 1928 and were 11 in 1940; Donald K., born in 1931, was 8.

Two children died at three years old: Jimmie Gaynell in 1926 and Henry Wayne in 1937. They and Dois, who died after breaking his neck in the Red River in 1947, were three of the children who died before their parents.

stories.title: The Grimes farm on Hardin Creek
stories.hook: A Blackshear daughter from Jones County, North Carolina, married a South Carolina Grimes and raised a family at the Haggard farm near Waynesboro, where David H. Grimes was born.
body: John Grimes was born in South Carolina about 1775. Penelope, called Penny, was the daughter of Jesse and Hannah (Huggins) Blackshear of Jones County, North Carolina, and she was born there on 6 June 1789. Jesse took his family to Williamson County, Tennessee, between 1800 and 1810. John and Penelope's first known child, James B., was born in Williamson County about 1807.

In October 1814 the Williamson County court settled the estate of Jesse Blackshare, deceased: his widow had remarried as Hannah Mairs, and the balance was due to "Penny Blackshare and James Blackshare" and the other heirs. The Grimes site dates Penelope's first child to about 1807, so she was already married by then; the court may simply have used her maiden name for the share due to her.

The Grimes family later moved to Wayne County. John died there on 14 June 1844 and was buried on the Haggard farm. The Grimes family website lists their children as James B. (about 1807), a daughter (1810-1815), Elisha S. (about 1817), a daughter (1820-1825), John Anderson (born October 1823), an unnamed son (1825-1829) and William Jasper (born 1826). David H. Grimes, born in 1829 in Wayne County, fits the unnamed son, and a family tree names a John Grimes as his father.
A 1954 Blackshear genealogy lists "A dau., m. Grimes" as the first child of Jesse Blackshear of Jones County and Williamson County. Penelope is shown still living after 1850.
src: Grimes Family Genealogy, "Our Grimes Line" (descendants of John Grimes and Penelope Blackshear); Genealogy.com Grimes forum, Pamela Bryant, 17 July 2003; Williamson Co., Tenn., Probate Court Wills vol. 2, p. 109 (Oct. 1814), as cited on WikiTree Blackshear-160; P. L. Blackshear, Blacksheariana (1954); Ancestry family tree for David H. Grimes
kv: Born c.1775 in South Carolina; died 14 Jun 1844, Wayne Co., Tenn.; buried Haggard Farm
Born 6 Jun 1789, Jones Co., N.C.; living after 1850 (one list: after 1864)
James B., Elisha S., John Anderson, William Jasper, and probably David H.
stories.note: David H. Grimes is not named in the Grimes family website; he fits the unnamed son of 1825-1829. The tree that names John Grimes as his father calls him "John Jasper" born 1784, which does not match the site's John, born about 1775. WikiTree gives Penelope an 1814 death date that cannot be right if she was living in 1850 or 1864.
stories.place: Williamson County, then Wayne County, Tenn. (Hardin Creek, near Waynesboro)

stories.title: "John A. Grimes, my brother, as executor"
stories.hook: In 1872 William Jasper Grimes made a will leaving his land to his second family and his first wife's children, and named his brother John executor.

subject.name: William Jasper, John Anderson and the other Grimes brothers

body: John Anderson Grimes, born in October 1823 in Wayne County, married Mary C. Arnett about 1852. In the 1860 census he was a farmer, 37, with $4,000 in land and $3,500 in personal property, with Mary, 27, and children Nancy E., 7, George (Kearney), 5, Sarah F., 3, and John, 1. They are still on the family farm in the 1900 census, run by their son George.

William Jasper Grimes was born in 1826. He married first Malaha Keaton and had twelve children between 1844 and 1868, among them Sarah J., Margaret G., John Q. A., Lucinda, Mary P., William Jasper K., Sevilla, Nancy C., Jasper Wayne, Benjamin Stout (a Blackshear name), Fannie and Mahulda Vista. His second wife was Tennessee Ann McClanahan.

His will was probated on 1 July 1872. It leaves his wife Tennessee Ann the home farm for her life and the land bought from John H. Cole, requires that "each of our children at the age of 21 years or at marriage" receive "one good horse, Bridle and Saddle, one cow and calf, one bed, bedstead and furniture," gives his two sons John A. and W. J. Grimes the tract bought from John B. Rutledge, and ends: "I nominate and appoint John A. Grimes, my brother, as executor to this my will."
James B. (born about 1807) and Elisha S. (born about 1817) both lived in Wayne County, Elisha on the Haggard farm.

quotes.t: I nominate and appoint John A. Grimes, my brother, as executor to this my will.
quotes.c: Will of W. J. Grimes, Wayne Co., Tenn., probated 1 July 1872 (transcription by Pamela Bryant)

stories.title: A Williamson County estate and a daughter named Penny
stories.hook: The 1814 court order dividing Jesse Blackshear's estate is the paper that names Penny Blackshear, who married John Grimes.
body: Jesse Blackshear was born about 1767 in Jones County, North Carolina, son of Susannah and Elisha Stout Blackshear. He moved to Williamson County, Tennessee, between 1800 and 1810; two of his sons remained in North Carolina until after 1810.

In October 1814 the Williamson County court heard the settlement of "Jesse Blackshare, Dec'd." Hannah, his widow and administrator, was by then "Hannah Mairs, wife of Isaac Mairs," and the "balance of $227.30" was divided between "Penny Blackshare and James Blackshare and the above named Legatees," Ezekiel, Elisha, Luke, David, Elijah, Jacob and Jesse. Hannah died on 4 June 1829 and is buried in Brown Cemetery, Wayne County.

The 1954 Blacksheariana traces the sons. Ezekiel (born 13 July 1792) lived in Williamson County in 1820, in Haywood County in 1830, and died at Brownsville on 23 April 1837; his widow, Isabella Dobson, was "bur. in the Ozarks" in 1882. Elisha (about 1794) farmed in Marshall County in 1840. Jacob (born 26 January 1802) moved to McNairy and Obion counties. The first child in the book is "A dau., m. Grimes."
src: Tennessee Probate Court Books, Williamson Co., Wills 1812-1819, vol. 2, p. 109 (Oct. 1814), as cited on WikiTree Blackshear-160 and Blackshear-2; P. L. Blackshear, Blacksheariana (1954), entries for Jesse, Ezekiel, Elisha, Jacob; WikiTree Huggins-10

Williamson Co., Tenn.; WikiTree gives 26 Jul 1803
Ezekiel, Elisha, Luke, David, Elijah, Jacob, Jesse, Penny and James
stories.note: WikiTree gives Jesse's death as 1803, which does not fit an estate settled in 1814 with a guardian; the settlement could follow years after his death. Penelope's place as the "dau., m. Grimes" rests on the name Penny and the Grimes family site.

stories.title: A militia oath before a Grimes justice of the peace
stories.hook: Penelope's brother Elijah swore never to fight a duel, in front of a Wayne County Grimes.
body: Elijah Blackshear was born on 9 June 1800, the son of Jesse Blackshear. He lived in Waynesboro, Tennessee, and married Dicena McMahon about 1820. Their children were Lucinda (1823), the twins Jesse Marion and James Newton (1826), and Hannah Permelia. James Newton married a Grimes, Elizabeth Anne, daughter of Isaac G. Grimes, on 11 April 1847.

The Blacksheariana prints two oaths Elijah signed on 29 March 1830: "I do solemnly swear that I will support the Constitution of the U. S., and the State of Tenn.," and "I, Elijah Blackshear do solemnly swear that I will not give or accept a challenge either written or verbal to fight a duel, nor will I be the bearer of a challenge for such purpose." Both were sworn before Isaac G. Grimes, J.P., the same man who is the father of his son's later wife.
Isaac G. Grimes's relationship to John Grimes has not been traced.

quotes.t: I do solemnly swear that I will not give or accept a challenge either written or verbal to fight a duel.
quotes.c: Oath of Elijah Blackshear, 29 March 1830, Wayne Co., Tenn., as printed in Blacksheariana

stories.title: A Lincoln husband, a Sheffield-side bride and one surviving son
stories.hook: A couple married at Rotherham in 1609 and had a son Peter who may have been the later Sandwich settler.
body: Thomas Gaunt was baptized at Silkstone in the West Riding on 22 July 1571, though the register does not name his parents. On 28 August 1609 he married Susan Bate at Rotherham, about thirteen miles from Silkstone and ten from her home parish of Norton, south of Sheffield. Susan had been baptized at St James, Norton, on 23 September 1571, the daughter of James Bate.

Thomas was almost certainly marrying for the second time. His will of 1621 names children George, James, Anne and 'Dynes' as well as Peter, and Susan's own will says Peter was her only son. A Peter Gaunt was baptized at Lincoln on 29 June 1610, the year after the wedding; identifying him with the couple’s son and the later Sandwich settler requires further evidence. The family lived in Lincoln, where Thomas was buried on 14 April 1621; Susan was buried there in February 1626, leaving a will that also names her brothers and sister, Thomas, Adam and Alice Bate.

WikiTree separates this Thomas Gaunt from a Thomas Gaunt of Pinchbeck, Lincolnshire, who married Isabel Wheelwright in 1602, and it removes an older, unsourced pair of parents (Thomas Gaunt and Elizabeth Wheelwright) that online trees had given him. His own parents are not known.
src: FamilySearch Yorkshire Bishop's Transcripts 1547-1957 (marriage of Thomas Gaunt and Susan Bat[e], Rotherham, 1609; Blagg, Yorkshire Marriage Registers, West Riding, vol. 1, p. 50); Simpson, Parish Registers of S. James' Church, Norton, vol. 1 (1908), p. 8; wills of Thomas Gaunt (1621) and Susan Gaunt, Lincoln, as cited on WikiTree Gaunt-202 (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Gaunt-202) and WikiTree Bate-1462 (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Bate-1462)

Baptized 23 Sep 1571, St James, Norton, daughter of James Bate; buried Feb 1626 Lincoln

stories.note: The marriage, Susan's baptism and both wills are record-based. The link from Peter Gaunt of Sandwich to this Lincoln couple rests on the wills naming Peter, as summarized on WikiTree; Thomas's parents are not known.
stories.place: Rotherham, Norton and Lincoln, England. Peter Gaunt, who crossed to Sandwich in Plymouth Colony, was the only son of their 1609 marriage.

stories.title: The Bates of Jordanthorpe
stories.hook: Susan Bate's father James is known only from the Norton baptisms of his children; where he came from is not recorded.
body: James Bate and Dorothy Harrison married in 1569, and their children were baptized at St James, Norton, a mile north of the hamlet of Jordanthorpe: William in 1570, Susan in September 1571, Jane in 1576. James is called 'of Jordanthorpe' at the marriage of his daughter Elizabeth and at his own death in March 1608. Dorothy outlived him by four years.

WikiTree says plainly that James Bate's origins are not known. A baptism for a James 'Batty', son of Robert, at Kirkburton about twenty-five miles away in January 1547/8 fits his estimated birth year, but the name is too common to claim him.
Susan carried the Bate name to Lincoln when she married Thomas Gaunt in 1609, and she remembered her brothers Thomas and Adam and her sister Alice in her will.
src: Simpson, Parish Registers of S. James' Church, Norton, vol. 1 (1908); FamilySearch England, Yorkshire Parish Registers 1538-2016; as cited on WikiTree Bate-357 (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Bate-357) and WikiTree Bate-1462 (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Bate-1462)
stories.note: Parish registers name James as father of Susan; his own parents are unknown. Dorothy's parents are not given.
stories.place: Jordanthorpe, in the parish of Norton just south of Sheffield, on the Yorkshire and Derbyshire border.

stories.title: Friends of Newhey, and the son who crossed the Atlantic
stories.hook: William and Elizabeth Croasdale were buried side by side at Settle Meeting; a family history calls it 'highly probable' that they were the emigrant Thomas's parents.
body: William Croasdale of Newhey in the Forest of Bowland died on the 29th day of the 11th month 1666 and was buried on the 31st at the Friends' burial ground at Settle Meeting, Newton. His wife Elizabeth died in the 4th month of 1672 and was buried next to him.

The Welcome Society's reference work and Patterson's list of Quaker emigrants both place a Thomas, son of William and Elizabeth, at Settle. Cleaver, the family genealogist cited on WikiTree, calls it 'highly probable' that William and Elizabeth were the parents of the Thomas who emigrated to Pennsylvania in 1682, while noting that other parentage has been suggested. Henry Croasdale of Newhey is another proposed earlier ancestor, but the generations connecting him to the emigrant need original records.
Elizabeth's surname Hayhurst is taken from the same compiled sources; her WikiTree profile cites no original record.
src: McCracken, Welcome Claimants Proved, Disproved and Doubtful, vol. 2; Patterson, Quaker Emigrants to America (Swarthmore); Cleaver, Ancestry of Allenn Grinnell Cleaver and Martha Irene Jessup, 1989, pp. 328-9; as cited on WikiTree Croasdale-17 (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Croasdale-17)
kv: Died 29th of 11th month 1666; buried 31st, Settle Meeting, Newton
Died 18th of 4th month 1672; buried 20th beside him
The emigrant Thomas Croasdale; parentage and reported birth date need confirmation
stories.note: Burial dates come from the Settle Meeting register as abstracted by the cited authors; the parent link to Thomas is secondary-source probable, and Elizabeth's surname is unconfirmed.
stories.place: Newhey (Newah) in the Forest of Bowland, Yorkshire. Quakers of Settle Monthly Meeting; buried at Settle Meeting, Newton.

stories.title: Henry Croasdale of Newhey, yeoman
stories.hook: A Bowland yeoman named his son William as administrator in his September 1652 will and was buried at Waddington three weeks later.
body: Henry Croasdale lived at Newhey in the Forest of Bowland, within the parish of Waddington. The register records three of his children between 1616 and 1621: Elizabeth, buried 1 June 1616; Edward, baptized 13 January 1617/8; and William, baptized 24 October 1621.

His burial reads 'Henry Croasdell buried Oct: 10' (1652). He had made his will the month before, on 21 September 1652, as 'Henrie Croasdale, yeoman; Newhay within Bolannd', with his son William as administrator; it was registered in 1654. The printed will index identifies the surviving register as Alchin, folio 337, under 1654. That reference points to the original probate record; the index itself supplies no wife’s name.

WikiTree makes this Henry the grandfather of the Thomas Croasdale who emigrated in 1682. That step is a family-history inference: the William baptized in 1621 would have been about 23 if Thomas was born in 1644, and some published lines give a different Henry (died 1595).

No evidence in the reviewed index names Janet Harrison as his wife, and no such relationship is established here.

stories.title: A father who died the year his daughter was born
stories.hook: Agnes Hawthornthwaite was baptized in 1633, the year her father William died at 26.
body: WikiTree gives Agnes Hawthornthwaite, later wife of Thomas Croasdale, a birth on 13 July 1633 in Tatham parish. Her father William Hawthornthwaite, born in 1607, is said to have married Elizabeth in Lancashire in 1631 and to have died in 1633, aged 26.

The profile's sources are database indexes of Lancashire parish registers and burials, not images of the register entries, and it does not say how Agnes is tied to William beyond the dates. The link stays a lead until the Tatham register is read.
Agnes came to Pennsylvania with the Settle Friends in 1682 and died at Neshaminy in 1686.

stories.place: Tatham (Tethem) parish, on the Yorkshire and Lancashire border. His daughter Agnes married Thomas Croasdale and sailed to Pennsylvania in 1682.

stories.title: A 1686 marriage in Duke's Place
stories.hook: A London record shows an Anthony Champneys marrying Anne Pitts in 1686, but their son John was baptized four years earlier.
body: WikiTree makes John Chamness, who married Ann Wearey at St John's, Wapping, in 1704, the son of Anthony Chamness and Ann Pitts. The only document cited for the parents is the marriage of Anthony 'Champneys' and Anne Pitts at St James, Duke's Place, on 23 September 1686.

That date is four years after John's baptism, which WikiTree places in November 1682 at St Saviour's in Southwark. The profile says there is 'no geographical or chronological reason to dispute' the link; the order of dates is a reason to be careful. John could have been baptized before his parents formally married, or the baptism belongs to another family.
WikiTree also says Anthony 'appears to be' the son of a John Chamness of Stansted Mountfitchet, Essex, and his wife Mary Reffell. Those Essex generations are not added here.

stories.title: A Quaker family on the Kent
stories.hook: A Chesterfield Meeting birth record gives a John Rogers born in 1687 to John and Mary; whether he is the John Rogers whose son Thomas married Ann Staples is not settled.

subject.name: John Rogers & Mary (Groom) Rogers of Burlington

body: The Burlington County Quaker John Rogers, born about 1656 at Rotherham, is said to have crossed with Friends on the Kent, which loaded at London in March 1677 and landed at the Delaware in 1678. He married Mary Groom, who died on 13 February 1693, and the couple had at least five children.

WikiTree attaches this family to the John Rogers born 'the 5th day of the 1st month 1687' at Nottingham, Burlington County, on the strength of the Chesterfield Monthly Meeting birth record, and gives that John a wife Martha Middleton, whose mother's 1712 will names a 'son-in-law John Rogers'.

The will calendars distinguish two estates that have been attached to John Rogers in online genealogies. John Rodgers of Burlington made his will on 23 January 1764; it was proved on 26 March 1767 and gave his son Thomas one-third of the residue. John Rogers of Windsor made a different will on 6 January 1769, proved on 10 April 1776, naming seven sons and two daughters but no Thomas in the published abstract. Neither calendar entry supplies the testator’s parents. The identity of the John born in 1687, and his connection to our Thomas Rogers, therefore remain unresolved.

Van Doren Honeyman, Calendar of New Jersey Wills, vol. IV, 1761–1770 (1928), pp. 360–361, John Rodgers of Burlington, will dated 23 Jan 1764, proved 26 Mar 1767; citing Lib. 13, p. 57. Independently examined printed abstract: https://archive.org/details/calendarofnewjer04newj/page/360/mode/2up . Calendar of New Jersey Wills, vol. V, 1771–1780, p. 431, John Rogers of Windsor, will dated 6 Jan 1769, proved 10 Apr 1776; citing Lib. 17, p. 354. Independently examined printed abstract: https://archive.org/details/calendarofnewjer05newj/page/431/mode/1up .

Born c.1665 Byberry, Pa.; d. 13 Feb 1693, Burlington Co.
stories.note: The Chesterfield birth record is cited through online genealogy, not independently examined here. The two published probate abstracts establish distinct estates; neither proves the parentage of our Thomas Rogers’s father.
stories.place: Quakers of Nottingham township, Burlington County, New Jersey. John is said to have come from Rotherham, Yorkshire, on the ship Kent in 1677.

stories.title: From the Isle of Man to Belfast to Iredell
stories.hook: A 1720 marriage record at Downpatrick is the only solid piece in the chain behind James Stevenson of Iredell County.
body: WikiTree records Henry Stevenson's marriage to Ann Curlett on 2 June 1720 at Saul parish, Downpatrick, in two Irish marriage indexes. Ann had been baptized on 27 May 1698 at Braddan on the Isle of Man, a daughter of William Curlett. The couple's children, listed from family trees, include a James born about March 1721 at Belfast.

That James is the James Stevenson who died on 5 March 1820 in Iredell County, North Carolina, and whose obituary in the Raleigh Star calls him a native of Ireland, nearly 90 years old, married 65 years, with 208 descendants. His estate was probated in Iredell in 1820.

Henry's own birthplace and his parents (given as William Stevenson and Katherine Alison) have no cited source. Whether this James is the father of the James Stevenson (1746-1828) in the Stevenson line here is itself only a lead.

stories.place: Downpatrick and Belfast, County Antrim, Ireland. If the line is right, they are the parents of the Scots-Irish James Stevenson who died in Iredell County, North Carolina, in 1820.

stories.title: Cedar Creek Friends move south
stories.hook: Robert Johnson and Virginia Elmore were received by certificate from Cedar Creek Meeting in 1766; both ended in the Springfield Meeting graveyard.
body: The 1988 Johnson genealogy abstracts the Cedar Creek Meeting minutes: 'Robert Johnson married Virginia C. Elmore of Louisa Co. 11-19-1759' and 'Robert and Virginia Johnson rec. on cert. from Cedar Creek M.M., Va., dated 1766-3-29'. Both were buried at Springfield Meeting in North Carolina. Robert's estate file was opened in Stokes County in 1808.
Robert was born 8 February 1738 in New Kent County, a son of Ashley Johnson and Martha Woody. Virginia, born at Black Creek in 1737, was a daughter of Thomas Elmore and Cecilia Ellyson.

A GEDCOM import on WikiTree, with no sources, lists Martha Johnson, born 28 August 1766 at Deep River, who married Aden Nordyke in 1787, among their children. The Quaker minutes support the couple but do not themselves name Martha.

stories.title: A gift of everything for 'love and affection'
stories.hook: In 1794 Ashley Johnson deeded his whole estate to his son Elijah in return for keeping him and Martha for the rest of their lives.
body: Ashley Johnson was born about 1710 in St Peter's Parish, New Kent County, and married Martha Woody in Henrico or New Kent County; the sources give 12 December 1734 and 10 or 12 October 1735. They raised at least eight sons and five daughters, including Robert, born February 1738.

Two Louisa County deeds fill in the later years. On 9 November 1778 Ashley gave his son Elijah 241 acres on Chamberlain's Creek. On 3 February 1794 he gave Elijah all his estate, real and personal, 'for love and affection and maintenance of the said Ashley Johnson and Martha his wife during their natural lives', except 210 acres jointly to David and James, with a feather bed and furniture each for Martha, Elizabeth and David.
Martha died on 6 September 1802 and Ashley about 1803, aged about 93; both are buried at Roundabout Castle Cemetery in Louisa County.

stories.title: John Johnson’s land on Black Creek
stories.hook: A 1705 patent traces 252 acres beside Black Creek and credits John Johnson with the importation of five named people.

subject.name: John Johnson of St Peter's Parish

body: John Johnson first appears in the family’s St Peter’s Parish record references on 22 November 1702, when a son John was baptized. An original Virginia patent dated 2 November 1705 grants John Johnson 252 acres in St Peter’s Parish, New Kent County, on the north side of Black Creek. It credits him with the importation of five people into the colony; it does not identify them as relatives or state their terms of service.

The five names written beside the grant appear to read Wm Davies, Saml Mitchel, Joan Hillard, Dan Gibbs and George Abraham. Their spellings are tentative readings of the handwriting. The boundary runs between marked trees and along the creek: a pine, a white oak, a maple at a small branch and Thomas Snead’s line. The tract had first been granted to Thomas Reynolds on 25 October 1695, then deserted and granted again to Johnson under a General Court order of 17 October 1705.

A separate original patent, dated 9 February 1727/8, names John Johnson of Hanover County and grants him 200 acres in Henrico County on the south side of Chickahominy Swamp. This time the instrument records a payment of twenty shillings. Later deed references say John and his wife Elizabeth sold that land on 1 November 1736. Those deed and death details still require independent original review; the reported death date is 5 September 1737.

Hinshaw's Quaker abstract names Ashley Johnson's mother as Lucretia Massie, but WikiTree notes that Friends' records call John's wife Elizabeth and treats Lucretia as 'purported' and unsourced; her claimed Massie parentage rests on uncited published histories. John's own parents are also marked disputed.
src: Virginia Land Office Patents and Grants 1697-1706, pp. 703-704, and 1725-1730 (Library of Virginia); Henrico County deed of 1 Nov 1736; Hinshaw, Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy vol. 6; WikiTree Johnson-2045 (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Johnson-2045) and WikiTree Massie-73 (https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Massie-73); Library of Virginia, Virginia Land Office Patents, Patent Book 9 (1697–1706), pp. 703–704, John Johnson, 252 acres, New Kent County, 2 November 1705; original manuscript images independently examined: https://image.lva.virginia.gov/LONN/LO-1/009/009_0725.tif and https://image.lva.virginia.gov/LONN/LO-1/009/009_0726.tif; Patent Book 12 (1725–1730), p. 201, John Johnson of Hanover County, 200 acres in Henrico County, 9 February 1727/8; original manuscript image independently examined: https://image.lva.virginia.gov/LONN/LO-1/012/012_0217.tif.

stories.note: The 1705 and 1727/8 patent manuscripts have been independently examined. The five people’s names are tentative readings; the patent says persons, not servants, and gives no ship, arrival dates, kinship or service terms. These patents document land grants and do not establish Ashley Johnson’s parentage, the identity of John’s first wife, or his earlier ancestry. The 1736 sale and reported 1737 death remain based on the separately cited references. This proposed ancestral connection remains probable.

stories.title: A Spotsylvania will with six sons
stories.hook: John Paine's will names six sons, one of them a William, and the line to the Stevenson wife Lydia Payne runs through that name.
body: John Paine was born in Drysdale Parish, King and Queen County, in 1705, a son of Barnett Paine. He witnessed a Spotsylvania County deed in 1740 and died there between the date of his will, 25 July 1764, and the executors' bond of 20 September 1770. The will names his wife Frances and sons John (eldest), Thomas, Barnett, William, Robert and George.

Frances is thought to be a daughter of Robert and Mary (Clayton) Coleman, but WikiTree says the choice among Coleman families is the subject of 'considerable disagreement'. A 1750 will reportedly calls her 'Francis Pain'.

The link to the Stevensons is by way of Rev. Elam Stevenson's wife Lydia Payne, whose father William Paine (1754-1807, Burke County, N.C.) WikiTree lists as one of John's sons. That William is attached to Lydia only through a Find a Grave memorial, and two men named William Paine have been merged on Catherine Arnold's profile, so the whole link is a lead.

Payne, The Big Payne Book, 2007)

stories.title: The stone house on Sugaw Creek
stories.hook: Esther (Alexander) Garrison is listed among the eleven children of Hezekiah and Mary Alexander of Mecklenburg County.
body: Hezekiah Alexander was born on 13 January 1728 at New Munster in Cecil County, Maryland, and settled in the Sugaw Creek congregation in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina. He married Mary Sample, a daughter of William Sample Sr. and Esther Garrison, and they raised eleven children. He is a DAR-recognized patriot ancestor, and his homesite in Charlotte is kept as a museum.

Their daughter Esther, born 28 September 1762, appears in the lists of his children on WikiTree. She is the wife of Samuel Garrison, whose son John Milton Garrison lived in Allen County, Kentucky, but her own profile cites no record, so the tie from Hezekiah to our Garrison family is a lead.

stories.title: Two wills on one day
stories.hook: William and Esther Sample each signed a will on 26 January 1769, and he was dead that month.
body: William Sample Sr. was born about 1690, in either Northern Ireland or Scotland, and lived in Cecil County, Maryland, before the family moved to Mecklenburg County. He signed a will on 26 January 1769 and died that same month; his wife Esther Garrison signed her own will the same day. The loose estate papers name five children: William, John, Joseph, Mary and Agnes.
Their daughter Mary, born 31 January 1734, married Hezekiah Alexander in 1752. Esther's parentage is not carried further here.

stories.title: Twelve children from one Bible list
stories.hook: James Alexander of Cecil County married two McKnitt sisters in turn and fathered seventeen children, among them Hezekiah.
body: James Alexander was born between 1690 and 1695 at Manokin in Somerset County, Maryland, and married Margaret McKnitt (1693-1736). A family list gives twelve children by her, including Hezekiah in 1722. After her death he married her sister Abigail and had five more.

Three separate marriage-record compilations give his birth as 1690, and DAR recognizes him as a patriot ancestor. He died in Cecil County on 31 May 1779 and was buried at the Head of Christiana Church cemetery near Newark, Delaware.
This is as far as the Alexander line goes in print: WikiTree itself warns that its sketches of the 'Seven Brothers' Alexanders from Donegal are 'speculative' and not primary sources.

stories.title: A Continental private and the road to Kentucky
stories.hook: Samuel Garrison's name rests on a DAR number and an unsourced profile, so he is entered as a lead.
body: WikiTree gives Samuel Garrison a birth on 24 August 1762 in Halifax County, North Carolina, a Revolutionary service as a private in the Continental Line, and a burial in Old Scottsville Cemetery in Kentucky. His wife Esther Alexander was born in Mecklenburg County in 1762, but her place of death is given as Coles County, Illinois, which does not fit a husband buried in Kentucky.

John Milton Garrison's WikiTree profile says he came from Mecklenburg County to Warren, later Allen, County, Kentucky, with his parents before 1809, which matches Samuel's move. No cited record names John Milton as Samuel's son. Samuel's father, John Garrison of Salem, New Jersey, has no source at all on WikiTree.

stories.title: The oldest of the ten Hulsey children
stories.hook: Eldest of ten, he was about six at the 1910 census and about thirty when his father died.
body: William Roy was the eldest of the ten children, born in 1904, three years after his parents married on 22 December 1901. By the April 1910 census he was about five or six and the family was in Mountain Township, Garland County, Arkansas, listed with his parents and two younger brothers, John W. and Noah, before Oscar was born in October of that year at Hot Springs.

He was the child who saw the whole move. His father was a laborer on the Camp Pike construction job near Little Rock in September 1918 and living at Story in Montgomery County; by the 1920 census the household was in Sulphur Township, McCurtain County, Oklahoma, farming as tenants, and in 1930 it was near Wright City. When his father died on 5 August 1935 William Roy was about 30 or 31, the oldest of the nine surviving children (the youngest, George Paul, was 9 or 10).

Four of Oscar's brothers survived him in 1982, so at least two of his eight siblings had died by then. Whether William Roy was one of them, whom he married and where he lived as an adult are still open (lead). A Roy Hulsey, 34, married Bonnie Meredith, 15, in Montgomery County, Arkansas on 22 Jan 1938 (marriage index, Montgomery Co., book J, p. 635); that age fits William Roy (b. 1904) but is only a lead until checked against a record that names his parents.

stories.title: John Wesley, the second son
stories.hook: The second son, three years old at the 1910 census in Garland County.
body: John Wesley, called John W. on the 1910 census, was born in 1906 and was the second son. In April 1910 he was three or four years old in the Mountain Township, Garland County household with his father George, mother Rebecca and brothers William R. and Noah. His father, then farming in Garland County, was also a preacher.

He was twelve when his father registered for the draft at Story in September 1918, and about fourteen when the family moved west over the line to McCurtain County, Oklahoma, a county then filling with sawmill and railroad work. His brother Oscar later worked government relief jobs and lumber towns in the same corner of the state.
His marriage, children, death and burial are not yet traced (lead). Four of Oscar's brothers were still living when Oscar died in 1982; whether he was one of them is unknown.

stories.title: Noah, the brother between Wesley and Oscar
stories.hook: Third of ten, born 1908, the baby of the 1910 census household.
body: Noah was born in 1908, two years before Oscar and the third of the ten. He is the youngest child named in the April 1910 census household in Mountain Township, Garland County, where he would have been one or two years old beside William R. and John W.
He grew up as the family moved from Garland to Montgomery County, Arkansas (where his father was working on Camp Pike in 1918) and on to McCurtain County, Oklahoma.
Noah's adult life, spouse and death are not yet found in any record seen (lead).

stories.title: Fred, the brother born in 1913
stories.hook: Born in 1913, he was seven when the family counted six children at home in Oklahoma.
body: Fred was born in 1913, three years after Oscar, and was five years old when his father registered for the draft at Story in September 1918.

He was about seven at the 1920 census, the year the household was recorded as tenant farmers in Sulphur Township, McCurtain County, Oklahoma with six children at home. By the 1930 census, when the household of ten was renting a farm near Wright City, he was about sixteen or seventeen.
Fred's marriage, military record and death are not yet found (lead). A WWII draft registration would be expected, since he was 27 at the first call-up in October 1940, but no card has been matched.

stories.title: Ruby Ellen, who became a Stipe
stories.hook: The first Hulsey daughter, born 1915 and married to a Stipe.
body: Ruby Ellen was the first daughter after five sons, born in 1915 when her mother Rebecca was about thirty. She married a Stipe, and that is how she is recorded in the family list. Two sisters survived Oscar in 1982; Ruby was either one of them or had died before him.
She was a girl of five at the 1920 census in McCurtain County, Oklahoma, and fourteen or fifteen in 1930 near Wright City. She was about twenty when her father died in August 1935.
Her husband's first name, the date and place of the marriage and her death are not yet found (lead).

stories.title: Grady, born the year of the draft card
stories.hook: Born in 1918, the year his father was building Camp Pike.
body: Grady was born in 1918, the year his father registered for the draft at Story, Montgomery County, while working for Stewart-McGehee on Camp Pike. He was the seventh child and probably the last born in Arkansas (lead).

He was about two at the 1920 census in Sulphur Township, McCurtain County, and about twelve in 1930. He was about seventeen when his father died in 1935, and in 1940, at 21 or 22, he was old enough for the first peacetime draft registration of 16 October 1940.
His registration card, marriage and death are not yet found (lead).

stories.title: A gunshot near his mother's farm, January 1948
stories.hook: Louis Daniel Hulsey, 27, a World War II veteran and timber worker, was found dead near Mena, Arkansas, on 13 January 1948; the certificate gives suicide.
body: Louis Daniel Hulsey was born at Bethel, Oklahoma, on 11 May 1920, a son of George Hulsey and Rebecca Graves. He was a World War II veteran, single, a timber worker, and had lived 13 months in the Acorn community by Mena, Polk County, Arkansas, on his mother's farm (Mena Route 3).

His Arkansas death certificate says he died on 13 January 1948. The cause of death is written "Gun shot wound. Self inflicted bullet entered right temple going thru front part of head. Was found dead about 1/4 mile from his mother's farm house in the Acorn community at 6:30 AM Jan-13-1948." Item 22 reads "Suicide," and the coroner O. R. Wood of Mena signed on the same day. His mother Rebecca Hulsey signed as informant. He was buried on 15 January 1948 at Storey, Arkansas.
The McCurtain Gazette of Idabel, 14 January 1948, carried the headline "Gunshot Wound Is Fatal for Former Wright City Man" over an article naming him.

stories.title: Grace Irene, who became a Dunagan
stories.hook: Born 1923 and married a Dunagan; one of the two sisters in her brother's 1982 obituary, unless she had died.
body: Grace Irene was born in 1923, the ninth child and second daughter, when her mother was about 39. She married a Dunagan, and the family list records her under that name.

She was about seven in 1930 in the renting household of ten near Wright City, and about twelve when her father died in August 1935. Her mother, Sarah Rebecca, later left Oklahoma and died at Bandon, Coos County, Oregon on 23 December 1972; whether Grace lived near her in Oregon is not known (lead).
Her husband's first name, her marriage and her death are not yet found (lead). She and Ruby Stipe appear to be the two sisters who survived Oscar in 1982.

stories.title: George Paul, the last child
stories.hook: The youngest of the ten, nine or ten when his father died.
body: George Paul was the youngest, born in 1925 when his father was 48 or 49 and his mother Rebecca 41. He shared his first name with his father, George Washington Hulsey.

He was four or five at the 1930 census near Wright City and nine or ten when his father died on 5 August 1935 and was buried at Breashears Cemetery near Story. At seventeen, in 1942, he would have been of age for the draft within the following year, in the middle of the Second World War.
No record of his adult life has been matched (lead).

stories.title: Margaret Crumpton and the Graves family
stories.hook: An 1884 Garland County marriage register names Margaret Crumpton and Jesse Graves. How she connects to Sarah Rebecca is still being researched.
body: In 1880, the census of Mountain Township, Garland County, listed a widowed Margarett J. Crumpton, age 25, in a household with Rebecca Cornett, age 69, and John W. and William H. Crumpton, ages four and two. The matching name, age and county make this a possible match for the 1884 bride, not a proven identification. A later Graves family genealogy identifies Rebecca as Margaret's mother and the boys as Margaret's sons; the FamilySearch census index does not state those relationships.

A Margaret Cornett, age six, appeared in the 1860 census of Searcy County with Edward and Rebecca Cornett. That is a promising lead, but linking her to the woman in the 1880 household requires more evidence. Rebecca's reported ages differ substantially between the two records, and the 1860 census did not state relationships.

On 31 January 1884, a Jesse Graves married Margaret Crumpton in Garland County. The register records Margaret as 28 and Jesse as 38. A family query published in 1977 names Margaret as a wife of Jesse Graves and Sarah Rebecca as his daughter, but does not say which wife bore Sarah. The age on the 1884 register conflicts with an age attributed to Jesse in an 1871 marriage record, so whether both records concern the same man is unresolved.

The Graves Family Association identifies Margaret as Sarah Rebecca's mother and reports that Margaret died on 5 May 1884, the day Sarah was born. A record directly confirming the parentage and the death account has not yet been found. The genealogy gives two possible maiden names, Speer and Cornett, without resolving the conflict.

stories.title: Married at fifteen in a neighbor's house
stories.hook: Jesse Graves's first wife was 15 when they married at Jack Phillips's house in 1871.
body: The Graves family genealogy identifies Emma as a daughter of Nicholas Fisher and names Sarah L. Garrett as her probable mother. It describes Sarah's marriages to William Gray, a man named Kirkland, Nicholas Fisher and Jack Phillips, whose home in Mountain Township was the location given for Emma's marriage.
The marriage record, Book A, page 278, is quoted in the Graves genealogy: Jesse was "18 years old and Emma was 15." They married on 2 April 1871 at the residence of Jack Phillips.

They lived in Garland County, and the family was recorded there on the census of 11 June 1880. The family genealogy lists Abraham Nicholas, Catherine Eunice and Greenbury H. as the children born by then, and a son Vestal born in 1881. Emma is not recorded after that census. A 1977 family query identifies Margaret Crumpton as another wife of Jesse, although the identity of the Jesse in the 1884 marriage record still needs verification.

stories.title: Nancy Cutter and the Graves household
stories.hook: An 1889 Garland County marriage record names Jesse Graves and Nancy Cutter. Family accounts offer different surnames for Nancy.
body: A Garland County marriage register records a Jesse Graves marrying Nancy Cutter on 19 September 1889. The register lists the groom as 38. A 1977 Hulsey family query names Nancy Wilborn Sutton as a wife of Jesse Graves, while the Graves Family Association calls her Nancy Wilborn Kyle Cuttler. The different names need further research before the records can be tied together with confidence.

The Graves family genealogy says Nancy had earlier married John B. Kyle and Samuel B. Cuttler, and names children Isaac and Prince. It also lists Lucinda, William Vestal, Pearl Mae and Cora Ellen as children of Nancy and Jesse. Those relationships are reported by the genealogy and need independent confirmation.

The same genealogy places Nancy in Garland County in the 1920 and 1930 censuses, reports that Jesse died in 1910 and says Nancy died on 20 November 1932. The 1977 query names Sarah Rebecca as Jesse's daughter, but does not identify which wife was her mother; the relationship between Sarah and Nancy remains to be established.

stories.title: A possible route from Georgia to Arkansas
stories.hook: Robert in Salathiel’s Georgia household may be the Robert Hulsey recorded in Arkansas in 1860; the connection remains open.
body: The original 1850 Union County, Georgia census lists Robert, 17, in the household of Salathiel, 43, and Elizabeth, 35. The other young Hulseys include Maryan, 19; Elizabeth, 12; Jesse, 10; Jennings, 8; a girl transcribed Lillean, 6; Benjamin, 3; and Nancy, 1. The published San Diego extract gives Robert a middle initial R. and reverses the ages of Benjamin and the girl above him.

The original 1860 census of Carouse Township, Hempstead County, Arkansas, records Robert Hulsey, 27, born Georgia, a farmer with $240 in real estate and $80 in personal estate. Sarah A., 20, born Mississippi, and a one-year-old male born Arkansas occupy the same dwelling, numbered 961. Robert has no middle initial on this page. The infant’s name is indexed as Selatha G.; its handwritten spelling is uncertain, and the published extract’s reading Salathel G. should not be treated as a secure match to Salathiel. The census records no relationships, and Benjamin is not listed in this household.

If this is the same Robert, he was in Arkansas by 1860. The shared 1850 household suggests that he and Benjamin may have been brothers, but it does not state their relationship. The identity of the Benjamin F. Hulsey on the 1864 Union roster also remains unconfirmed.

stories.title: Gilliam Graves and the orphans of Samuel and Sarah
stories.hook: In 1854 Gilliam Graves was named guardian of the children of Samuel and Sarah Graves; one of them, William Riley, died without a will in 1861.
body: In January 1854 Gilliam Graves was appointed guardian for the children of Samuel and Sarah Graves of Montgomery County, Arkansas. The Graves genealogy suggests the parents are Samuel Graves and Sarah Cole, who were married on 30 March 1837 in Randolph County, North Carolina, by Moore Graves.

Gillum and Moor Graves are both on the 1840 census of Cherokee County, Georgia, and "it is believed that Moore Graves died in the 1840s." The widow Sarah appears on the Montgomery County tax lists from 1851 and bought a 40-acre tract, the NW SE of section 11.

The 1860 census lists the children as a household of their own: William (Riley), 22, farmer, and Alley, 17, Ursa, 15, Alison, 14 and Madison, 11, all born North Carolina. In April 1861 Gilliam is again named guardian for the minor heirs Alley, Ultha, Alison and Madison. William Riley died intestate on 1 November 1861.
How these children were related to Gilliam, whether nephews and nieces or otherwise, is not established (lead).

quotes.t: It is believed that Moore Graves died in the 1840s.
quotes.c: Graves Family Association, Gen. 242

stories.title: Married at nineteen, then to a man twice her age
stories.hook: Polly Gray was 19 when she married Franklin Washburn in 1859; by 1864 she had a daughter by Gilliam Graves.
body: Polly Gray was the daughter of William Andrew Gray and Sarah L. Garrett, a woman who married four times (Gray, Kirkland, Fisher and Phillips). She was born about 1840 in Hot Spring County and, on 1 February 1859, married Franklin W. Washburn: the record lists him as 21 and her as 19.

By 1864 she was Gilliam Graves's wife, and their daughter Mary Elizabeth was born on 13 August 1864, two months before Gilliam deserted from the Union army (12 October 1864) and returned on Christmas Day. The 1880 census shows the Graves children by Polly living with Andrew Washburn, her son by Franklin, and his wife Amanda.
Polly died about 1879 at Cedar Glades. Gilliam, who is supposed to have been killed by robbers in January 1876, is buried next to Polly in Mountain Valley Cemetery, once called Mt. Pleasant Cemetery.

stories.title: The women named in the Hulsey records
stories.hook: A census, a marriage bond and a family query preserve different names; each belongs to its own record until the connections can be established.

subject.name: Sarah G., Margaret Partain, Sylvania Partin and Lucy Morgan

body: In June 1880, B. F. Hulsey’s wife was recorded as Sarah G., thirty, born in Arkansas. Three children—Margaret M., George W. and Charles F.—were in the household. The census identifies her as the wife of their father, but it does not explicitly identify her as their biological mother.

A family query printed in 1977 calls Benjamin’s wife Margaret Partain. Other family accounts use Sylvania Susane Partin. Neither name has been linked securely to Sarah G. Similar surnames and a recurring Benjamin are clues, but they do not establish a mother for George Washington.

The September 1893 Garland County bond and license name Benjamin F. Hulsley and Lucy Morgan. The license, issued on 25 September, calls Lucy fifteen. The bond’s printed century was corrected to 1893 in handwriting; the ceremony return is blank or unreadable. The documents establish this couple’s application for marriage, while their relationship to the 1880 family remains open.
