stories.title: "Dr. Brown, of Cedar Glades, was shot down": a Union petition, March 1864
stories.hook: Weeks after Gilliam Graves joined the Union cavalry at Cedar Glades, Union men from the same county begged the army for help against murder and plunder.
body: Gilliam Graves, 45, volunteered for the Union 4th Arkansas Cavalry at Cedar Glades on 14 January 1864. Less than two months later, on 10 March 1864, a letter went from Little Rock to Col. C. C. Andrews, who commanded the post. It was signed by Oliver Adair "and others" who called themselves "citizens of Montgomery County, Ark., and members of Company L, Fourth Arkansas Cavalry." The printed letter reads Company L, which may be a misprint for D, the company raised at Cedar Glades; the family's own man is on the roster of Company D.

The men wrote that "Deeds of cruelty and barbarity that would shame Indians are of daily occurrence." They gave three cases from a single day: "On the 1st instant the wife of Mr. James Dosier was shot through the shoulders, and her child (one year old) shot through the arms. On the same day Dr. Brown, of Cedar Glades, was shot down, mortally wounded, and his brains then blown out. William Gray (citizen) was shot in a brutal and cowardly manner on same day."

They added that "the plundering of houses, breaking and burning of cotton cards, wheels, &c., belonging to Union citizens is of common occurrence," and asked that about 100 cavalry be sent into the county, where forage and mills were plentiful. Because "our company is not armed," they suggested that guides be taken from among themselves. The army's own list of operations for March 1864 has a "Skirmish at Cedar Glade, Ark." on 1 March, the same day as the shootings, with the note that no circumstantial reports are on file.

The letter does not name Gilliam Graves, and nothing seen says he or any Hulsey signed it. What it shows is the neighborhood he enlisted from: Union families in the Ouachita hills in the winter of 1864, with their cavalry company still unarmed while their neighbors were being shot at home. Gilliam's later death, "supposedly killed by robbers" in Garland County in 1876, came in the same kind of country.

quotes.t: Deeds of cruelty and barbarity that would shame Indians are of daily occurrence.
quotes.c: Oliver Adair and others, Montgomery County, 10 March 1864

quotes.t: On the same day Dr. Brown, of Cedar Glades, was shot down, mortally wounded, and his brains then blown out.
quotes.c: Official Records, vol. 34, pt. 2, p. 631

src: The War of the Rebellion: Official Records, Series I, vol. 34, part 2 (1891), p. 631, Oliver Adair and others to Col. C. C. Andrews, Little Rock, 10 March 1864; vol. 34, part 1, p. 3 and Index (Skirmish at Cedar Glade, Ark., 1 March 1864). archive.org full text of vol. 34.
stories.note: The event and the petition are proven by the printed Official Records. That Gilliam Graves or B. F. Hulsey took part in it is not shown; the OCR text reads "Company L".
stories.place: Cedar Glades, Montgomery County, Arkansas

stories.title: Scouts "to secure all guerrillas and bushwhackers," 1864
stories.hook: The orders and reports that sent the 4th Arkansas Cavalry back through Montgomery County in 1864, with the wounded and missing it cost.

subject.name: The 4th Arkansas Cavalry in Montgomery and Hot Springs counties

body: A Union company recruited at Cedar Glades had to be used somewhere, and the army's papers show where. On 11 April 1864 Col. A. H. Ryan, commanding the 4th Arkansas Cavalry at Lewisburg, was ordered to send 2nd Lt. John N. Jones with 75 men to Hot Springs County. The general "wishes the detail to start at the earliest practicable moment. He orders that no houses be burnt by them and no property destroyed, but he wishes them to secure all guerrillas and bushwhackers who may fall in their way."

On 11 June 1864 an expedition was organized "to make a scout in Saline, Hot Springs, Montgomery, and Perry Counties," with 100 men of the 4th Arkansas Cavalry, four companies of the 3rd U.S. Cavalry and part of Merrill's Horse, under Maj. G. Harker, "to be gone six or eight days." Fifteen days later, on 26 June, Capt. Joel Brown of Company A wrote General Steele about the loyal families crowded into Dardanelle: "mostly soldiers' families," "without medical aid, and not enough of men in town to bury the dead."

The army's monthly summary for August 1864 records the result: "14th, a battalion of the Fourth Arkansas Cavalry returned from scout through Saline, Hot Springs, and Montgomery Counties. Fought with small bands of the enemy daily until arriving at Farr's Mill. Captain Green, with twenty-five men of this battalion, engaged Cook's and Crawford's companies, numbering about 100 men, drove them and killed 4 and wounded 6 of the enemy." The battalion itself lost "1 private killed, Captain Quin and Lieutenant Spiva and 6 privates wounded, and 3 men missing."

None of these papers names Gilliam Graves or Benjamin Hulsey. They show the war they were in: a cavalry that was short of arms and horses, scouting the hills it came from, with soldiers' wives sheltered in river towns and bushwhackers threatening to burn out Union households. Deserters were a constant trouble for the regiment; in the fall a scout at Helena arrested one Company I man at his home. Gilliam's own absence from 12 October to 25 December 1864 fits that same autumn, but the reason for it is not recorded.

quotes.t: to secure all guerrillas and bushwhackers who may fall in their way
quotes.c: Order for a scout to Hot Springs County, 11 April 1864

src: Official Records, Series I, vol. 34, pt. 3 (Hdqrs. Detachment Seventh Army Corps, 11 April 1864); vol. 34, pt. 4, pp. 322-323 and 561 (11-12 June, 26 June 1864); vol. 41, pt. 1, Chap. LIII, Itinerary of the Seventh Army Corps, August 1864 (archive.org full text).
stories.note: Page numbers are from the OCR text of the volumes and should be checked against page images. No document seen names Gilliam Graves or Benjamin Hulsey.
stories.place: Montgomery County, Arkansas

stories.title: "Starved to death at Andersonville": the Company F monument, 1893
stories.hook: Daniel O'Neal's company raised its own limestone shaft at Oakland City and carved on it the names of eleven men who died as prisoners.

subject.name: Company F, 42nd Indiana: the eleven who starved at Andersonville

body: The monument stands on a small triangle of ground beside the railroad in Oakland City. Gil. R. Stormont's 1913 booklet says it was put up by the surviving members of Company F, 42nd Indiana, "as a loving tribute to the memory of their comrades who gave up their lives in defense of the flag." It was built in the summer of 1893 and dedicated that September, with an address by Capt. A. J. McCutchan of Company A.

A committee of Col. W. M. Cockrum, John W. Corder, James T. Bell, John P. Simpson and Washington Strickland raised the money, and Cockrum deeded the lot to the county. The contract went to William Kelley of Oakland City for nearly $1,000. The shaft is of oolitic limestone, twenty-eight feet tall, with a carved soldier on top. "On the several sides of the dies are the names of all the original members of the company and the recruits, 143 in number." That should include Daniel W. O'Neal, who is on the company roll, but the stone has not been read for his name.

On one side is a scroll reading "Starved to death at Andersonville," and beneath it eleven names: Chesterfield P. Dill, Alford Farmer, J. M. Hunter, H. H. Hunter, John H. Martin, Adam Canon, Wm. A. Reavis, W. W. Oliver, A. H. Mariner, Jacob Strickland and A. C. Coleman. Stormont adds: "These all were taken prisoners at the battle of Chickamauga and died at Andersonville." Most can be matched on Horrall's roll of Company F, though spelled a little differently: Christfield P. Dill, Alfred Farmer, Henry H. Hunter, Adam Cannon, William A. Revis, William W. Oliver, Adolphus H. Marriner and Andrew C. Coleman.

The shaft also lists the company's battles: Perryville, Stone's River, Stevenson, Flint River, Chickamauga, Lookout Mountain, Mission Ridge, Ringgold, Buzzard Roost, Big Shanty, Snake Creek Gap, Chattahoochee River and Bentonville. Whether Daniel was present for all of them or left in March 1862 is the open question about his service; the men who built this stone, his neighbors from the same few townships, would have known.

quotes.t: Starved to death at Andersonville.
quotes.c: Inscription on the Company F monument, Oakland City, 1893

src: Gil. R. Stormont, Gibson County in the Civil War (Princeton, 1913), "Co. F, 42nd Indiana Monument" (archive.org, gibsoncountyinci00stor); S. F. Horrall, History of the Forty-second Indiana (1892), roll of Company F, pp. 64-67.
stories.note: That Daniel W. O'Neal is among the 143 names has not been confirmed by a reading of the stone.
stories.place: Oakland City, Gibson County, Indiana

stories.title: William Thomas Camp, hanged at Princeton, 22 November 1872
stories.hook: A murder over a $75 note ended with Gibson County's first execution, while Daniel and Vashti O'Neal were raising their young family in the county.

subject.name: The first legal hanging in Gibson County

body: The 1884 History of Gibson County calls it "the first legal execution in this county." William Thomas Camp and J. R. Bilderback, both of Pike County, walked and rode to Haubstadt on 31 July 1871 and, finding no lodging, lay down to sleep in a piece of woods near the village. Camp had picked up a hickory club to use as a cane. As Bilderback slept "with his head on the roots of a tree," Camp "struck him on the head several times and killed him."

"There had been no grudge or quarrel between them, but the motive for the crime was shown by the larceny of a note for seventy-five dollars which Bilderback held on Camp." Camp threw the body into a fallen treetop, took some of the dead man's clothes and rode his horse to New Harmony, where the dead man's brother William had him arrested. Back at Haubstadt he showed where the body lay; a coroner's jury found it "horribly mangled by hogs," and Camp confessed under oath.

Jailed at Princeton, he escaped before trial and hid near his mother's home, was later picked up in Kentucky for horse-stealing and jailed at Owensboro, and was brought back. He was convicted of first-degree murder in July 1872 and sentenced to hang on 4 October. Gov. Baker gave him a respite until Friday, 22 November 1872, "when, at 2 o'clock p.m. of that day, he was executed by Sheriff F. W. Hauss." His lawyers were Col. Charles Denby, who had left the 42nd Indiana to become colonel of another regiment, and C. A. Buskirk.

Daniel O'Neal's household was then on its farm in Columbia Township, with Parsis (born 1868) a small child; the case was the talk of the county but is a place story, not a family one. No O'Neal is named in the account.

quotes.t: There had been no grudge or quarrel between them, but the motive for the crime was shown by the larceny of a note for seventy-five dollars.
quotes.c: History of Gibson County, 1884

src: History of Gibson County, Indiana (Chicago, 1884), "First Legal Hanging," in the chapter on the county courts (archive.org, historyofgibsonc0000jast).
stories.note: Page number not recorded from the OCR text. Stormont's booklet says Denby was transferred from the 42nd Indiana and commissioned colonel of another Gibson County regiment after Perryville.
stories.place: Princeton and Haubstadt, Gibson County, Indiana

stories.title: A Sunday-evening cyclone, 27 February 1876
stories.hook: The worst storm in Gibson County history took the roof off a church at "church time" and carried a house thirteen feet.
body: The county history of 1884 says that "on Sunday evening, Feb. 27, 1876, the most severe cyclone which ever passed over Gibson County struck Princeton." It came from the southwest and "destroyed almost the entire southern part of Princeton, doing damage to the extent of over fifty thousand dollars." It "happened about church time and few of the people were at their homes." The roof and steeple of the C. P. Church were taken off.

The Sutton family's two-story frame house was "large," "comparatively new." "The wind lifted the house and it came down over the fence, distant thirteen feet from the foundation," breaking it "into three parts, one part going north, another east and another west." Ten persons were inside, "Mrs. Sutton and seven children, a son-in-law and his children." A two-year-old was found "hanging by its hands to a rafter on top of the fallen house"; a nine-year-old blown out of an upstairs window walked about four hundred feet to a neighbor's door and knocked, "remarking 'his house was blowed.'" Eight of the family were found huddled in a space about ten feet square, saved by a bureau, and "crawled out" through a hole sixteen inches across.

Parsis O'Neal, Katie Stevenson's mother, had been born at Princeton in 1868, and the family's farm was in Columbia Township a few miles south. The history does not mention any O'Neal in connection with the storm; it is told here as the county's worst disaster of the years they lived there.

quotes.t: It happened about church time and few of the people were at their homes.
quotes.c: History of Gibson County, 1884

src: History of Gibson County, Indiana (Chicago, 1884), chapter on climate and natural events ("Cyclones") (archive.org, historyofgibsonc0000jast).
stories.note: The O'Neal link to this storm is by place only. The text says the storm "passed out northeast of Oakland" in the OCR, which may be misread.
stories.place: Princeton, Gibson County, Indiana

stories.title: A Stevenson cousin in the 32nd Tennessee, 1862-1865
stories.hook: While Daniel O'Neal wore Union blue in Indiana, a first cousin of his future son-in-law wore Confederate gray from Giles County.
body: Goodspeed's 1886 History of Tennessee prints the sketch of Coleman L. Stevenson, "a first-class farmer and stock-raiser" of the Ninth Civil District of Giles County, born 26 December 1832. He was the eldest son of William P. Stevenson, a brother of Rev. Abner A. Stevenson, and so a first cousin of Frank Stevenson.

Goodspeed says: "In 1862 Mr. Stevenson enlisted in the Thirty-second Tennessee Regiment of Volunteers, and served until the close of the war. He participated in most of the principal battles, and was a brave and gallant soldier." The 32nd was a Confederate regiment. His family was large: two wives, who were sisters (Louisa and Dorcas Jackson), his own children, and "three orphan children to raise," Martha V., Nancy M. and Mary J. Jackson, daughters of his wife's dead brother and sister-in-law.

The same sketch is where the family's own roll of Rev. Elam Stevenson's children is printed, and it records that William P. "has four brothers who are ministers of the gospel." Coleman held 265 acres at home and 400 more elsewhere in Giles County in 1886, was a Democrat, and belonged, like his uncles, to the Methodist Episcopal Church South.
The Stevensons were Giles County people, and Frank's O'Neal in-laws were Indiana Unionists, so the two sides of the family met only after the war, in Frank's marriage to Parsis O'Neal.

quotes.t: In 1862 Mr. Stevenson enlisted in the Thirty-second Tennessee Regiment of Volunteers, and served until the close of the war.
quotes.c: Goodspeed, History of Tennessee, 1886

src: Goodspeed Publishing Co., History of Tennessee (1886), Giles County Biographical Appendix, sketch of Coleman L. Stevenson, p. 871-872 (archive.org, historyoftenness00good).
stories.note: Goodspeed does not say the 32nd was Confederate; that is from the regiment itself. Whether Abner or his own sons served is not known.
stories.place: Ninth District, Giles County, Tennessee

stories.title: "I saw him die, and closed his eyes": Elam Stevenson and Philip Bruce
stories.hook: The old itinerant whose books Elam hauled in his wagon died among the Stevensons' neighbors, and Elam shaved and shrouded him.
body: In 1869 Elam Stevenson, then 81 and housebound, dictated to the Methodist historian John B. McFerrin his memories of the preacher Philip Bruce, who came to Giles County in 1813 and "made our neighborhood his home." Bruce, in Elam's telling, was a Virginia Conference man who never married, who had once been offered a rich young Charleston woman's plantation and declined it ("he thought she had about money enough to send him to ruin"), and who after his health failed lived with his brother Joel and taught a day school for the neighborhood's children, giving to the poor every dollar the Conference sent him.

Elam was at the deathbed. "I saw him die, and closed his eyes, shaved him, and assisted in shrouding him. His death was calm and peaceful; there was not a struggle nor a groan. He did not move a muscle, only a slight quiver of the upper lip when the last breath left the body." A few days earlier the circuit preacher had preached to him: "It was a high day with him. He was very happy, and spoke in raptures of heaven." Bruce died in May 1825.

He was buried in the country graveyard "about two miles distant from our church (Bee Spring), by the side of his sainted mother and two of his brothers." His stone, Elam says, was put up by the Virginia Conference and reads: "To the memory of the Rev. Philip Bruce, an itinerant Methodist preacher nearly fifty years. He was born December 25, 1765, and died May, 1825. He loved God and the souls of mankind, many of whom became seals to his ministry."

The same letter records the cost of the Civil War to Elam's church. The first Methodist church in Giles County, Rehoboth, was replaced "by a large frame-church, which was destroyed by the Federal soldiers during the late war." It also tells of Meshach Boyce's son William, who "went to Arkansas at an early day as a missionary, and was drowned in a small stream, the second year of his labors."

quotes.t: I saw him die, and closed his eyes, shaved him, and assisted in shrouding him.
quotes.c: Rev. Elam Stevenson, 1869

quotes.t: a large frame-church, which was destroyed by the Federal soldiers during the late war
quotes.c: Rev. Elam Stevenson on Rehoboth church, 1869

src: John B. McFerrin, History of Methodism in Tennessee, vol. 2 (Nashville, 1871), pp. 180-190, letter of Rev. Elam Stephenson, Elkton, 28 July 1869 (archive.org, historymethodis00mcfegoog).
stories.note: McFerrin prints the name as Stephenson. Page numbers are approximate from the OCR text (182-183 for the Bruce passage).
stories.place: Bee Spring, Giles County, Tennessee

stories.title: Ten Hulseys in one house: Union County, Georgia, 1850
stories.hook: The original census puts Benjamin at three, with a six-year-old girl above him; a published extract had reversed their ages.
body: On 11 November 1850 the census taker recorded the household of a Georgia-born blacksmith, Salathiel Hulsey (indexed as Salathel Halsey), 43, in District 85, Union County, Georgia. The household included Elizabeth, 35; Maryan, 19; Robert, 17; Elizabeth, 12; Jesse, 10; Jennings, 8; a girl transcribed Lillean, 6; Benjamin, 3; and Nancy, 1. Arminda Burnett and J. C. Bell were also listed in dwelling and family 998.

The original resolves an age discrepancy in the published San Diego Genealogical Society extract: Benjamin is three on line 34, and the girl immediately above him is six on line 33. Those ages had been reversed in the extract. Three is consistent with the family’s 1847 birth year for Benjamin, although the census does not give his exact birthday. It also contains no relationship column, so it cannot establish that Elizabeth was each child’s biological mother or prove this child became the later Arkansas Benjamin.

The compiler of the San Diego extract suggested that Robert in this household was a man recorded in Hempstead County, Arkansas, in 1860. The Arkansas original does show a Georgia-born Robert Hulsey, 27, but no middle initial. It lists Sarah A., 20, and an infant male whose name is indexed as Selatha G.; the handwriting is uncertain. The extract’s Salathel G. therefore cannot be used as a secure naming link to Salathiel. The identification of the two Roberts, like Benjamin’s connection to Arkansas, remains open.
In 1840 Salathiel was counted in Hall County, and in the 1830 Hall County Hulsey list he is one of seventeen men named Hulsey, living among the Hulseys of Charles and Adler.
src: San Diego Genealogical Society, Hulsey Families (2000), "1850 Union Co., GA" and "1860 Hempstead Co., AR" census extracts (archive.org, sdgsfamilies64); 1850 U.S. Census, Union Co., Ga. Original 1850 U.S. census, District 85, Union County, Georgia, 11 Nov 1850, p. 273B (handwritten p. 145), dwelling/family 998, lines 26–37, NARA M432 roll 84, RG 29; indexed as Salathel Halsey: https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/8054/records/18983349 ; image 148 of 170, https://www.ancestry.com/imageviewer/collections/8054/images/4191561_00433?pId=18983349 . Original downloaded and independently read; Benjamin is 3 on line 34, girl immediately above him is 6 on line 33. Original 1860 U.S. census, Carouse Township, Hempstead County, Arkansas, Albany post office, dwelling/family 961, lines 18–20, NARA M653 roll 42, RG 29, indexed p. 830; enumeration date fields blank. Independently read and downloaded image 12 of 30: https://www.ancestry.com/imageviewer/collections/7667/images/4211301_00318?pId=13097887 ; index and citation https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/7667/records/13097887 . Original names Robert without a middle initial; infant indexed as Selatha G., handwriting uncertain.

stories.title: Seventeen Hulsey households in Hall County, 1830
stories.hook: The 1830 Hall County census names seventeen Hulsey households; Salathiel’s relationship to the others remains unknown.

subject.name: The Hulsey cluster of Hall County, Georgia

body: The 1830 census of Hall County, Georgia, a county formed in 1818 from the Cherokee cession, lists seventeen heads of household named Hulsey, among them Charles, Adler Jr., Joel, Elija, Demsey, William, Sarah, Pleasant, James, Adler Sr., Armistead, Hiram, Micajah, Jesse, Salathiel, Charles F. and Vincent. Printed lists of the 1832 Cherokee land lottery also carry Hall County names such as Pleasant T. Hulsey, James Halsey and Alder Halsey Jr., all in Hall County districts.

A 1997 newsletter article, drawing on The Hulsey Book by Lou Pero, traces the senior line: Charles Hulsey and his wife Hannah, married about 1752, lived in Pittsylvania County, Virginia, in the 1770s, near the North Carolina line, then in Greenville County, South Carolina. A Greenville deed of 1792 names their sons "James, Charles, Jesse, Adonijah and Adler." The article says the family name was spelled "interchangeably Huddlesy, Hulsey, Huldsey."

Where Salathiel fits is unknown. Online trees give him a father Jesse Hamilton Hulsey and a mother Mary Tharp, but no record has been found; the Hall County Jesse of 1830, and the Jesse among Charles's sons, are both possible fathers by name alone. Salathiel was born about 1807 in Georgia, which puts a South Carolina-born parent in Hall County at the right time.

The 1850 Hall County census, which the compiler calls "a very hard to read film," still shows a Charles Hulsey, 55, farmer, real estate $2,000, born in South Carolina, with Hannah, 52, also born in South Carolina, and a widow, Sally Hulsey, 33, with children. None of this ties to Salathiel, but it is the neighborhood he came from.
src: San Diego Genealogical Society, Hulsey Families (2000), 1830 and 1850 Hall Co., Ga. extracts and "Extended Branches" Nos. 12-13 (1997), quoting Lou Pero, The Hulsey Book; J. T. Smith, Cherokee Land Lottery (1838), lists for Hall County (archive.org).
stories.note: A lead only. Salathiel's parentage is not established.
stories.place: Hall County, Georgia

stories.title: The 4th Arkansas Cavalry: Union men from the Ouachita hills
stories.hook: A Union regiment raised in Arkansas included Gilliam Graves and soldiers named Benjamin F. Hulsey and Calvin V. Moffitt.
body: The 4th Regiment Arkansas Volunteer Cavalry (Union) was organized at Little Rock in December 1863 and, by Dyer's Compendium, mustered out on 30 June 1865. Its companies were raised among Arkansas Unionists. Company D was recruited in Montgomery County in the winter of 1863–64, and on 14 January 1864 Gilliam Graves volunteered at Cedar Glades, at 45, a farmer, five feet ten inches tall with black eyes. The roster of the same company has a private "Hulsey, Benjamin F." The National Park Service database also lists a Calvin V. Moffitt in Company L, but his identification as the son of Nathan Moffitt remains a lead.

Dyer's list of the regiment's actions reads like a calendar of small, hard marches. A skirmish on the Saline River on 15 February 1864. A move to Cedar Glade on 1 March, which the Official Records index also lists as a skirmish that day (no report was filed). A scout from Little Rock to Benton on 27–31 March, led by Capt. E. H. Vance, who arrested three women hauling cotton for guerrillas and wrote that "the bushwhackers made a desperate rally to get the captured wagon and their fair friends, but they failed to get either." Mount Elba on 30 March. Then the Camden expedition of April 1864, in which Dyer lists Jenkins' Ferry. In mid-May the regiment was at Dardanelle, and from 25 September to 13 October it took part in an expedition from Little Rock to Fort Smith.

The regiment's own story had darker edges. Union men in Montgomery County were hunted by neighbors, and the March 1864 petition from Company L, told under "Union families of Montgomery County ask for cavalry," names a wife and child shot and a doctor killed at Cedar Glades. In September 1864 a detachment out of Helena went looking for "deserters from the Fourth Arkansas Cavalry" and took one, Benjamin Davis of Company I. Gilliam Graves's own roll entry reads that he "deserted on 12 October 1864 and returned on 25 December 1864." The roll gives no reason, and no record seen places Company D on any particular march that month.

In November 1864, Maj. Harris S. Greeno led 130 men of the regiment out of Devall's Bluff, where the regiment had its cavalry depot, toward Batesville and Searcy and reported that Price's army had been "badly whipped at every point." The regiment finished the war at Little Rock, scouting to the Saline River and Bayou Metoe in April and May 1865, and was mustered out on 30 June.

quotes.t: the bushwhackers made a desperate rally to get the captured wagon and their fair friends, but they failed to get either
quotes.c: Capt. E. H. Vance, Fourth Arkansas Cavalry, scout from Little Rock to Benton, 31 March 1864, Official Records, Series I, vol. 34, part 1, p. 859

src: Dyer, Compendium of the War of the Rebellion (1908), vol. 3, p. 999, as summarized in the regiment's Wikipedia article; Official Records, Series I, vol. 34, part 1 (Capt. Vance, 31 Mar 1864) and part 4; vol. 41, part 1 (Maj. Greeno, 15 Nov 1864; Helena scout, Sept 1864) (https://archive.org/details/warofrebellion013401rootrich, https://archive.org/details/warofrebellion014101rootrich); Index to Compiled Service Records of Union Soldiers from Arkansas (NARA M383); NPS Soldiers and Sailors database; Graves Family Association, Gilliam Graves
kv: Co. D, volunteered 14 Jan 1864 at Cedar Glades, age 45; deserted 12 Oct 1864, returned 25 Dec 1864
Private, Co. L (NPS Soldiers and Sailors)
stories.note: A soldier named Calvin V. Moffitt is listed in Company L, whose members in March 1864 were men from Montgomery County; how he came to be in that company is not shown, so the identification stays a lead.
stories.place: Montgomery County and Little Rock, Arkansas

stories.title: Buck Horn in the Official Records, March 1864
stories.hook: Two Union reports name Buck Horn: one orders cavalry to "kill, capture, and destroy" a camp there, the other says the farmers wanted "peace on any terms."
body: Buck Horn, in what is now Stone County, Arkansas, is the old settlement near St. James where Henry and Hannah Moffitt's son Tom was born in 1889. Twenty-five years earlier it appears twice in the Union record of the war. On 14 March 1864 the district headquarters at Batesville wrote to Lt. Col. William Baumer, First Nebraska Cavalry, to take men across White River at Ramsay's Ferry and go to Round Bottom, near Sylamore, for forage, protecting the steam transport Miller. The order goes on: "You will endeavor to hunt up the enemy reported to be in camp at McDermott's, near Buck Horn, and kill, capture, and destroy them."

The order shows the care its writer thought necessary. Baumer was to recapture any mules taken from the Union train that he found with local people, "leaving the women and children of the family undisturbed and in possession of their household goods and such work-cattle as they need to cultivate their farms." He was told to be "kind and courteous in your dealings with the defenseless citizens," to give receipts for everything he took, and to "prevent your men from entering houses, pillaging, or burning any houses or fence rails." "Incendiarism or unnecessary severity," the order says, "you are strictly charged to prevent."

A week later Maj. Lewis C. Pace of the Eleventh Missouri Cavalry reported from Batesville on a seven-day scout of 206 miles (15–21 March 1864) after a Confederate force under Rutherford. On the last day he marched "down the river through Buck Horn. Here I could gain no information of Rutherford." His men were out of rations and many horses barefooted. He added a note on the country that fits the hills the Moffitts later farmed: "a rough, rocky, and mountainous country, destitute of forage excepting in the valleys and coves of the mountains," where "the farmers generally are busily engaged preparing their ground for planting, and express a great desire for peace on any terms."

These are two glimpses, not the story of a battle. The county's bloodiest fight of the war came at Buck Horn in May 1864, when Jo Shelby's Confederates attacked a band of bushwhackers; that is told under Henry and Hannah in the Ozarks.

stories.title: The runner's morning: Company D at St. Etienne
stories.hook: Edmond Tims's company got lost in the French sector that day, but his battalion lost its commander and half its runners to a single shell.
body: The 36th Division's book of 1920, Story of the 36th, describes the morning of 8 October 1918 from the front. The 142d Infantry was ordered forward at 5:15 a.m. to take the village of St. Etienne-a-Arnes, in Champagne, after the Marines in the 2d Division had taken the ridge. The Second Battalion jumped off from Hill 140 and went through machine-gun fire. The First Battalion, Companies A through D, followed in support. Companies A and B were in the first wave and C and D in the second.

To reach the jumping-off place, Chastaine writes, the men of the First Battalion had to pass "in squad columns, or single file, through the trees down the northern slope of Blanc Mont and through the barrage placed by the enemy's batteries to cut off the supporting troops from the fight." They suffered heavy casualties from shell fire and lost their commanding officer, Capt. Charles Kuhlman: "The burst of a shell wounded half of the battalion headquarters group, including several runners." Edmond Tims was a company runner, and a company runner's job was to carry messages between the company and the battalion.

Company D's morning went wrong in a different way. "In this advance the men of Company D failed to follow the wake of Company B and wandered into the French sector to the left, where they remained through the balance of the day." Captain Kuhlman was so badly hurt that his loss "did not become known to his company commanders until the middle of the afternoon." The high-explosive shells were mixed with gas, and many gas casualties followed later in the day. Company B, whose wake Company D had been told to follow, lost its first lieutenant, Arthur J. Matheny, "killed instantly just after he had crossed the last belt of wire," and the second lieutenant, Thomas F. Collins; "more than thirty men in Company B had been killed and more than fifty wounded."

The Honor Roll printed at the back of the book lists "TIMS, EDMOND, Private, Co. D," with the date 8 October 1918. The regiment's own report, written in January 1919 and quoted in Edmond's own story, says a fellow runner spoke to him at 8 a.m. on the 9th and found him killed an hour later. The two dates are a day apart and both fall inside the 142d's fighting at St. Etienne. Before the war he had served in Company L of the First Oklahoma Infantry, the National Guard regiment that Chastaine says was assembled at Fort Sill in the spring of 1917, after months of border duty the year before.

quotes.t: The burst of a shell wounded half of the battalion headquarters group, including several runners.
quotes.c: Ben H. Chastaine, Story of the 36th (Oklahoma City, 1920), p. 117

stories.title: The camp where George Hulsey was working when the influenza came
stories.hook: George W. Hulsey signed his draft card on 12 September 1918 as a laborer at Camp Pike, and eleven days later the camp's base hospital admitted 214 influenza cases in a day.
body: On 12 September 1918 George Washington Hulsey, 42, filled out his draft card at Story in Montgomery County. It gave his employer as the Stewart-McGehee Construction Company at Camp Pike, the Army training camp near Little Rock. The camp had been established on 18 July 1917 and was the mobilization point for the 87th Division.

The Army's medical commission that studied pneumonia and influenza in the camps reached Camp Pike on 5 September 1918. Its report says the camp's death rate from lobar pneumonia, over its whole history, was third among the 32 camps in the country, and from bronchopneumonia fourth. The report adds that "beginning September 1 there had been a gradual increase of the number of patients admitted with the diagnosis of acute bronchitis." On 23 September, 214 cases of influenza were admitted to the base hospital in a single day, and that is the day the commission dates the epidemic.

"The epidemic was at its height from September 27 to October 3, during which period there were in the neighborhood of 1,000 new cases daily." By 31 October it was over, and a second, milder wave came at the end of November. Counting from 1 September to 31 October, the commission recorded 12,393 men reporting sick with influenza and 1,499 cases of pneumonia, with 466 deaths. These are figures for soldiers; the report says nothing about the civilian construction crews working on the camp.

Nothing seen says whether George Hulsey was working at Camp Pike during those weeks, or whether he was ill. His draft card is the only record that puts him there. By the 1920 census he was a tenant farmer in Sulphur Township, McCurtain County, Oklahoma.

stories.title: Four registration days and the men who signed
stories.hook: On 5 June 1917, 12 September 1918, 16 October 1940 and 27 April 1942, the family's men lined up to give a clerk their name, age and employer.
body: The first World War registration was on 5 June 1917 for men aged 21 to 30. Grady Moffitt was 25, a timberman at Ervin, Oklahoma, married and supporting his wife, his mother and a child; the card describes him as tall and stout, with gray eyes and dark hair. Robert Pisachubbe, 28, farmed for himself at Speer, black eyes, black hair, medium height, slender. By age Joel Thompson (b. 29 January 1892), Peter P. Thompson (b. about 1896), Wavey Lincoln Satterfield (b. 28 December 1895, at Morgantown, Kentucky) and Edmond Tims (b. about 1893) all fell into the same registration. No card has been seen for Joel or Peter, and nothing seen shows that either was inducted. Wavey served as a private in the Army, and Edmond served first in Company L, First Oklahoma Infantry.

The third and widest registration, on 12 September 1918, took in men aged 18 through 45. Simon Thompson, 19, signed as a farmer working for his father at Corinne. George Washington Hulsey, 42, signed at Story, Arkansas, as a laborer at Camp Pike. Edmond Tims died on the fields of St. Etienne less than a month later.

The World War II draft began on 16 October 1940 with men aged 21 to 35. Oscar Franklin Hulsey, 30, registered that day at Mount Ida, Montgomery County. When the war began, Congress required all men aged 18 through 64 to register. The fourth registration, on 27 April 1942, was for men 45 to 64, and was nicknamed "The Old Man's Draft." Its purpose was an inventory of skills and available labor; those men were not liable for service. Charles Oscar Smith, 52, signed as "Charlie Oscar Smith" of Forney, Choctaw County, working on a farm, with mail at Hugo Route 1, naming "Mrs. Pearl Smith" as the person who would always know his address. Robert Pisachubbe, 53, signed at Speer, naming his wife Lizzie.

Their sons went in different ways. Dois Moffitt enlisted in the U.S. Navy on 3 September 1942, aged 21, and served as a ship's cook until 27 January 1946. John Winfred Moffitt enlisted on 17 December 1943, at 18, and served as a corpsman. No record seen gives service dates for their older brothers Alvin and Odis, or for the Hulsey brothers of Oscar's generation.

stories.title: Three months in the 9th Kentucky
stories.hook: James Satterfield joined the Union army in 1861 and left after three months; the regiment he joined lost 357 men, 250 of them to disease.

subject.name: James H. Satterfield and the 9th Kentucky

body: James H. Satterfield told the authors of Kentucky: A History of the State in 1885 that "in 1861 he enlisted in the Ninth Kentucky (Federal) Infantry, remaining in the field but three months, after which he was engaged in the recruiting service." He was 23, a young farmer in Allen County, and his father, Henry, died that same year.

The 9th Kentucky Infantry was organized at Camp Boyle, Adair County, and mustered in for three years on 20 November 1861. Its first winter was spent in camp at Columbia, Kentucky, until February 1862. If James joined in the autumn of 1861, the three months he describes would have ended about the time the regiment marched to Bowling Green and then Nashville, leaving camp on 15 February. His own account does not say whether he was discharged, detailed or transferred, and the roll that would show it has not been seen.

The regiment was in the rest of the war. Dyer lists it at Shiloh on 7 April 1862, the siege of Corinth, Perryville (in reserve), Stones River, Chickamauga, Missionary Ridge, the Atlanta campaign and Jonesboro. It mustered out on 15 December 1864. Its dead number 357: 8 officers and 96 enlisted men killed or mortally wounded, and 3 officers and 250 enlisted men dead of disease. In the 9th Kentucky, disease killed more than twice as many men as the enemy.
Butler County, where James settled in 1876, put up a veterans' monument in 1907 on the courthouse lawn to the soldiers of both armies. It is described as one of two such Kentucky monuments.

quotes.t: In 1861 he enlisted in the Ninth Kentucky (Federal) Infantry, remaining in the field but three months, after which he was engaged in the recruiting service.

stories.title: Two brothers' wives from one Clark family
stories.hook: John C. Satterfield's brother Sidney married a Johnson girl whose mother was a sister of Samantha Johnson's mother.
body: Sidney Rufus Satterfield was born on 2 September 1865 in Kentucky, the second son named in his father's 1885 biography ("Henry W., John C., Sidney R., James D., Martha A. and Mary C."). Find a Grave gives his parents as James Henry Satterfield and Malissa A. Gibson, so he was John C. Satterfield's full brother. He died on 19 November 1949 at Richardsville, Warren County, and was buried at Satterfield Cemetery, near Jetson in Butler County.

His wife was Eliza "Ancie" Johnson, born 19 July 1871, died 27 December 1951. Her parents were James P. Johnson (1840-1884) and Martha J. Clark (1839-1923), and Martha J. was an older sister of Melvina (Clark) Johnson, the mother of Samantha "Mantha" Johnson. That makes Ancie a first cousin of the woman who married Sidney's brother John C. in 1892. Two Satterfield brothers married into the same Clark-Johnson family.

Sidney and Ancie had at least three children: Walter, born and died in 1890; Mary Cecil (Woosley), 1891-1989; and Lillie (Embry), 1893-1946. All of them are shown on Find a Grave with the Satterfield Cemetery burials.

stories.title: The brother who went to Arkansas
stories.hook: James D. Satterfield, born in Allen County just before the family left for Minnesota, ended up in Clay County, Arkansas.
body: James Doiser Satterfield was born in February 1867 in Allen County, Kentucky, a son of James Henry Satterfield and Malissa Gibson. The 1885 county history lists him as "James D." among the six children of the first marriage. He was born the year his father says the family "removed to Dakota County, Minn."

On Find a Grave he is shown as married in 1889 to a wife recorded as Iverson Embry Satterfield (1871-1926), with five children: Laura Myrtle Hooper (1890-1951), Juvanda McKinney (1892-1922), Claud Edward (1899-1963), Fannie Esther Dobbins Tisdal (1902-1977) and James Ralph (1909-1983).

He died on 10 July 1929 at Hickoria, Clay County, Arkansas, and is buried at Redenbo Cemetery in that county. That is a different part of the Mid-South from his half-brothers at Texarkana, and from John C., who went to Franklin County, Texas.

stories.place: Born in Allen County, Kentucky; died at Hickoria, Clay County, Arkansas

stories.title: A daughter born in Minnesota, dead at twenty-one
stories.hook: One Satterfield child was born during the eight years the family spent in Dakota County, Minnesota, and came home to Kentucky to die a year after her wedding.
body: James H. Satterfield's 1885 biography says that "in 1867 he removed to Dakota County, Minn., and in 1875 he returned to Kentucky." A Find a Grave memorial supplies the only child known to have been born there. A. M. Satterfield was born on 23 July 1870 in Minnesota, a daughter of James Henry Satterfield and Malissa Gibson and a full sister of John C. Satterfield.

She married Calvin H. Coots (1869-1932) in 1891 and died on 25 May 1892, aged 21. She is buried at Butler Phelps Cemetery in Butler County. Her mother had died in 1877, soon after the move back, and her father had remarried in 1878 to Lucinda Belle Phelps, a Butler County woman.
Her Minnesota birth is a small piece of independent support for the Minnesota years in the 1885 sketch, which no other record seen so far confirms.

stories.title: James Satterfield's second family
stories.hook: After Melissa died in 1877 James H. Satterfield married a 21-year-old neighbor and had nine more children, most of whom ended up around Texarkana.

subject.name: Lucinda Belle (Phelps) Satterfield and her nine children

body: Lucinda Belle Phelps was born on 30 May 1857 in Butler County, a daughter of Solomon Phelps and Sarah J. (Deweese). She married James H. Satterfield on 2 June 1878, a year after Melissa Gibson's death. A Bowie County family group sheet, which says the compiler holds a copy of the marriage bond, lists nine children: Martha Belle (born Nov 1879), Alonzo Thomas (1882), Minnie E. (1884), Joe Griffin (1886), Laura E. (1887), Charles J. (1890), George Franklin (1892), Grover C. (1894) and Effie J. (1899). Find a Grave gives Lucinda's death as 5 June 1917.

By 1909 the grown children were marrying in Bowie County, Texas, or across the Arkansas line: Charles J. to Alma Morgan on 5 December 1909; Alonzo to Zoda Mae Slader Reed in September 1914; Grover to Norah Walker on 28 May 1917 at Maud; Joe Griffin to Lennia Champion on 11 November 1917; George to Eula Viola Martin on 2 September 1917 at Hatfield, Polk County, Arkansas. Laura married a Douglas Henry and died in October 1975.
The sheet shows Minnie E. married to a "(?) Smith." That could be a coincidence of a common name, and nothing links her husband to Charles Oscar Smith's family.

James himself died in Bowie County on 28 November 1922 (Find a Grave; the group sheet says 24 November 1922 or 1924) and is buried at Reed Cemetery. His 1885 biography already credits him with 1,340 acres in Butler County and another 425 acres in Tennessee.

stories.title: A corporal in the Arkansas training regiment
stories.hook: John C.'s half-brother George, born at Brooklyn, Kentucky, served as a corporal in 1917-18 and married in Polk County, Arkansas, five months after the United States entered the war.
body: George Franklin Satterfield was born on 10 May 1892 at Brooklyn in Butler County, a son of James H. Satterfield and Lucinda Belle Phelps. His father died in Bowie County, Texas, in 1922.

On 2 September 1917, according to the Bowie County family sheet, he married Eula Viola Martin at Hatfield, Polk County, Arkansas. His headstone is marked "ARKANSAS CPL CO E 3 TRAINING REGT WORLD WAR I."
He died on 4 January 1958 at Texarkana and was buried at Odd Fellows Cemetery, Lockesburg, Sevier County, Arkansas.

subject.name: Alonzo Thomas and Grover Cleveland Satterfield

body: Alonzo Thomas Satterfield was born on 6 June 1882 in Butler County, one of the three children named in his father's 1885 biography. In September 1914 he married Zoda Mae Slader Reed in Bowie County, Texas. He died there on 18 December 1950.
Grover Cleveland Satterfield was born on 5 April 1894 in Butler County. He married Norah Walker at Maud, Bowie County, on 28 May 1917, and died at Maud on 13 December 1966.
Both brothers appear as children on the Find a Grave memorial of their half-brother Sidney Rufus Satterfield, and in the Bowie County family sheet.

stories.title: A headstone that gets the birthday wrong
stories.hook: Artie Pearl's older brother was a private in the Army in the First World War; his Oklahoma stone and his draft cards disagree about his birth date.
body: Wavey Lincoln Satterfield was the oldest surviving child of John C. and Samantha Satterfield. His stone at Soper Cemetery gives his birth as 9 January 1896, but the Find a Grave memorial says his World War I and World War II draft registrations both give 28 December 1895 at Morgan Town, Butler County, Kentucky. The memorial treats the stone as the error.

The stone is marked "TEXAS PVT. U.S. ARMY World War I." That fits the family's move to Franklin County, Texas, about 1907. In 1925 he married Jewel Dale Weems (1908-1984), and they later lived in Choctaw County, Oklahoma, where Samantha and her second husband had settled.
He died at Soper on 24 March 1952, aged 56, and is buried there in plot E4, the same plot as his mother Samantha.

stories.title: The brother who married a Riddle
stories.hook: James Bethel Satterfield and his sister Stella both married into the Riddle family.
body: James Bethel Satterfield was born on 12 May 1901 in Butler County, Kentucky, and was about six when the family moved to Franklin County, Texas. He married Alice Elizabeth Riddle (1900-1976), and Find a Grave shows seven children born between 1922 and 1940, one of whom, Charlie, died in 1940 at about ten.
His sister Stella had married Clifford Calvin Riddle (1898-1975). Whether Alice and Clifford were brother and sister is not shown in the records seen, so the two marriages are a lead only.
James died on 7 December 1964 at Paris, Texas, and is buried at Soper Cemetery in Choctaw County, Oklahoma, near his mother.

stories.title: Stella, dead at seventeen
stories.hook: Artie Pearl's youngest sister married a Riddle and died at 17.
body: Stella B. Satterfield was born on 6 October 1907 and was one of the two children John C. and Samantha had after the move to Texas (the 1910 census shows her at about two). Her mother married again in 1917 and moved with Stephens to Oklahoma.

She married Clifford Calvin Riddle (1898-1975). She died on 25 January 1925, aged 17, and is buried at Chillicothe Cemetery, Hardeman County, Texas, far from Soper and Hugo where her mother and sister lie. No cause of death is given.
The Hagansport household of April 1910 lists her as "little Stella."

stories.hook: Ira served in the Army in the Second World War; Jewel was born at Talco, Texas, five years before his mother remarried.

subject.name: Ira L. and Jewel Thompson Satterfield

body: Ira L. Satterfield was born in 1905 in Kentucky and was five in the April 1910 census at Hagansport. He is buried at Grant Cemetery, the same cemetery as his sister Artie Pearl and Charles Oscar Smith, in plot B2, with a stone marked "AMRY WWII." He died in 1977.

Jewel Thompson Satterfield, the last child, was born on 3 May 1912 at Talco in Titus County, Texas. He married Marie Nabors in 1929, when he was 17, and had five children. He died at Hugo on 13 January 1995 and is buried at Mount Olivet Cemetery there.

stories.title: The widower Samantha married in 1917
stories.hook: Samantha Satterfield's second husband was a 59-year-old widower whose first wife was part Choctaw and who went back to Texas after Samantha died.
body: Billy Alexander "Bird" Stephens was born on 16 February 1858 in Tennessee, a son of Calaway "Cal" Stephens (1824-1863) and Sarah Ann Little (1822-1913). He appears in Find a Grave as the youngest of six children.

The biography on Samantha's memorial says he married Martha Adeline Liles in Newton County, Arkansas, on 28 March 1878, and that she was one-quarter Choctaw. She died in 1916 and is buried at Old Saltillo Cemetery in Hopkins County, Texas. The memorial gives them eight children, of whom seven are linked: John Harvey, Nancy Ann (Brown), Mary Adeline (Simmons), Joseph Carroll, Wiley Alexander, Francis Henry and Tomie Delmane, who died at 10 in 1907.

On 28 July 1917 at Mount Vernon, Franklin County, the 59-year-old widower married 44-year-old Mrs. M. D. Satterfield. They moved to Oaks Township, Choctaw County, and were there in the 1920 census. After Samantha died in October 1928 he went back to Titus County, Texas, and died at Mount Pleasant on 23 January 1944. He is buried at Bridges Chapel Cemetery.

stories.title: The Clarks of Brooklyn, Kentucky
stories.hook: Newton’s 1850 household includes Polly; Melvina’s later death certificate names her parents as Newton Clark and Mary Dunn.

subject.name: Newton Jasper Clark & Polly Clark (maiden name unresolved)

body: Newton Jasper Clark was born on 6 August 1817 and died on 3 April 1878 in Butler County. Compiled profiles identify his parents as William Clark (1785-1856), born in Granville County, North Carolina, and Levina Willis (1785-1877). WikiTree credits William with service in the War of 1812; that is not checked.

WikiTree reports a marriage to Polly Elms on 20 January 1839 in Butler County and cites the county marriage register on FHL film 928,314; that original marriage entry has not been examined here. Her compiled dates are 1818–1888. The original 1850 census lists Newton and Polly Clark, both 32, in Butler County, household 629. It gives no maiden name and no relationships.

Melvina’s 1929 death certificate names Newton Clark and Mary Dunn as her parents. Dunn and Elms are not established alternative names for the same woman. Identifying Mary Dunn with Newton’s census companion Polly remains probable; the marriage original and further records are needed to resolve the mother’s identity. The existing maternal tree link is retained with that qualification.

Family memorials place Newton’s burial at Newton Clark Cemetery, Brooklyn, and give Polly’s death as 16 February 1888 and burial at Clark Cemetery, Morgantown. They link Martha J., Stanford C., Beverly L. "Belva" and Melvina as children. These compiled links are not independently proved by the relationship-free 1850 schedule; Stanford’s census age of 8 also conflicts with the later 1844 birth date attributed to him.

stories.title: A Union cavalry private
stories.hook: Samantha Johnson's uncle Stanford Clark rode with the 12th Kentucky Cavalry.
body: Stanford C. Clark was born on 6 June 1844 in Kentucky, identified in compiled family profiles as a son of Newton Jasper Clark and Polly Elms. His headstone at Belmont General Baptist Church Cemetery, Morgantown, is marked "PVT TRP A 12 REGT KY CAV CIVIL WAR." The 12th Kentucky Cavalry was a Union regiment.

On 9 February 1867 he married Serenia Hunt (1851-1918) in Butler County. He died on 12 June 1913 at age 69. By then his niece Samantha and her husband John C. Satterfield had left Butler County for Texas.

stories.title: The Clark brother who went to Oklahoma
stories.hook: Melvina’s reported brother Belva Clark died at Cushing, Oklahoma, at 88, with eight children behind him.
body: Beverly L. "Belva" Clark was born on 2 October 1850 in Butler County, Kentucky, identified in compiled family profiles as a son of Newton Jasper Clark and Polly Elms. In 1877 he married Margaret Ann Coots (1861-1944).

Find a Grave lists eight children: Palvena (Smith), Sardena (Flener), William Pearl, Fannie Ellen (Coots), Purnie Dee (Noteware), Carrie (born and died in 1891), Martha D. (Fulkerson) and David Carl. Most were born in Kentucky; the Clark family was in Oklahoma by the time he died.
He died on 18 February 1939 at Cushing in Payne County, Oklahoma, and is buried at Fairlawn Cemetery there.

stories.title: Melvina's older sister
stories.hook: Martha Clark married James P. Johnson; their daughter Ancie married a Satterfield and is buried at the cemetery that carries the Satterfield name.

subject.name: Martha J. (Clark) Johnson & James P. Johnson

body: Martha J. Clark was born on 1 February 1839 in Butler County, identified in compiled family profiles as the eldest child of Newton Jasper Clark and Polly Elms. She married James P. Johnson (7 January 1840 - 30 June 1884). Find a Grave names three of their children: Mary Isabella "Isey" (Phelps), 1868-1936; Eliza "Ancie" (Satterfield), 1871-1951; and William Miligan Johnson, 1875-1950. The memorial notes two more, Oliver P. and Drucilla.
James died in 1884 and Martha lived on as a widow for 39 years. She died on 13 February 1923 in Butler County. Both are buried at Satterfield Cemetery near Jetson.
James P. and Melvina's husband, who is not named in the records seen, shared the surname Johnson. Whether the two husbands were brothers or cousins is unchecked.

stories.title: Samantha's brother who stayed
stories.hook: Samantha went to Texas and Oklahoma; her brother Charlie lived and died within a few miles of where they were born.
body: Charlie Johnson was born on 27 April 1885 at Brooklyn in Butler County, a son of Melvina Clark Johnson, 13 years after his sister Samantha. He died on 14 February 1959 at Welchs Creek, Butler County, and is buried at Clark Cemetery, Morgantown, with his mother's Clark family.

He had two wives. The first was Martha Alice Satterfield (27 August 1886 - 22 July 1918), buried at Clark Cemetery; she died at Riverside, Warren County, aged 31. The second was Pernie Brooks (1905-1944). Find a Grave lists eight children, among them Carlie, Cooper F., James Wallace, Artie Mae Roberts, Cevil, Golda Marie Hunt, Chester and Cova Myrl Felty.
Martha Alice's parents are not named, so whether she belonged to the same Satterfield family as her husband's brother-in-law John C. is unknown.

stories.title: Hazel Shackleford King and her brothers and sisters
stories.hook: Hazel's family stretched from Texas to Oklahoma and California, and three Moffitts carried her casket.
body: Hazel Marzee Shackleford was born in 1908 at Rattan in Delta County, Texas, and died on 22 December 1980 at Paris, Lamar County. The Lamar County Echo of 1 January 1981 printed: "Mrs. King was born in the Rattan community of Delta County, a daughter of John Morgan Shackleford and Kathryn Elizabeth Newton. She attended schools in Delta County and married John Wesley King who preceded her in death in 1968."

The paper named her brothers and sisters: "four sisters, Mrs. Joe Haskell, Mrs. Beula [sic] Hutchings and Mrs. Helen Josey, all of Apache, OK, and Mrs. Eular Tillman of Lawton, OK; three brothers, Balis Shackleford of CA, John S. Shackleford and Edward Shackleford, both of Apache, OK." Mary Moffitt had died in 1962, and Robert Yates in 1961.

The pallbearers were "Loyd Mathews, Roy Chadwick, Bill Halliday Sr., Donald Moffitt, Odis Moffitt and Tommy Moffitt." The three Moffitts are very likely sons of Grady and Mary, which would make them Hazel's nephews, but the paper does not say so. She is buried at Meadowbrook Memorial Park, Paris.

quotes.t: Mrs. King was born in the Rattan community of Delta County, a daughter of John Morgan Shackleford and Kathryn Elizabeth Newton.
quotes.c: The Lamar County Echo, 1 January 1981 (transcribed on Find a Grave memorial 200655081)

stories.title: Mary's oldest brother, who went to California
stories.hook: The 1900 census lists the Shackleford children at Gilbert, Alabama; Balis, the oldest, spent his last decades in Los Angeles County.
body: Balis Anthony Shackleford was born on 5 February 1892 in Alabama. The 1900 census at Gilbert, Etowah County, as transcribed on his Find a Grave page, lists "John Shackleford 37, Sep 1862, married 10 yrs, b. AL, parent GA" and wife Elizabeth, 28, "5 children born, 5 living," with "Balous" 8; Myrtle, 6 (Aug 1893); May, 5 (Jun 1894); Robert, 3 (Oct 1896); and Eddie, 8 months (Sep 1899).

That list holds two children not in the later obituaries. Myrtle (born Aug 1893) and Eddie (born Sep 1899) do not appear among the survivors named in 1961 and 1981. They may have died young or may be known by other names; unchecked. The Edward Richard Shackelford who lived to 1988 was born in 1910, a different child.

Balis married Bertha Mae Fox (1895-1970); a daughter, Jewell Irene Denman, lived 1914-1978. He died on 9 January 1982 in Los Angeles County and was buried on 2 February at Green Hills Memorial Park, Rancho Palos Verdes. The California death record gives his name as Balis Anthony Shackelford.

stories.title: An obituary from a California paper
stories.hook: The Chico Enterprise-Record named all his brothers and sisters, including 'Mamie Moffett' of Oklahoma.
body: Robert Yates Shackleford was born on 25 October 1897 at Gadsden, Etowah County. The Chico Enterprise-Record of 23 June 1961, page 3, said: "Robert Y. Shackleford died early this morning in an Oroville Hospital. He was 63. Born in Alabama, he was a resided of Gridley for 10 years... He was a veteran of World War I."

The survivors section reads: "three brothers. Bayles of Los Angeles and Ed and John of Oklahoma; six sisters, Mrs. Josephine Haskell, Mrs. Helen Josey, Eulah Tillman and Mamie Moffett, all of Oklahoma; Beulah Hutchins and Mrs. Hazel King, both of Texas, and 16 grandchildren." Mamie Moffett is Mary Tinsley Shackleford Moffitt, who died the next year. His widow was Mae and he had eight children.
He is buried at Gridley-Biggs Cemetery in Butte County, California; the stone carries a World War II marker, while the paper says World War I.

stories.title: Three sisters known only by married names
stories.hook: Two obituaries from 1961 and 1981 list sisters of Mary Moffitt who do not appear in the 1900 census household.

subject.name: Josephine Haskell, Eulah Tillman and Beulah Hutchins

body: The Chico paper of 1961 and the Paris, Texas, paper of 1981 together name three sisters of Mary Shackleford Moffitt who are not in the earlier list of siblings: Mrs. Josephine (Mrs. Joe) Haskell, Eulah (Eular) Tillman of Lawton, Oklahoma, and Beulah (Beula) Hutchins (Hutchings). Both papers also name Helen Josey and Hazel King, whose Find a Grave pages are linked as John Morgan Shackleford's children.

The 1900 census lists John and Elizabeth with five children, the youngest born in 1899. Josephine, Eulah and Beulah were therefore born after 1900, between about 1901 and 1915, or Myrtle (born 1893) may be one of them under another name. Without a birth record this cannot be settled.
The family lived in Delta County, Texas, around 1908, in Martin County, Texas, by 1930, and later in Caddo County, Oklahoma, where Lizzie is buried at Fairview Cemetery, Apache.

stories.title: Where Hagansport buried its dead
stories.hook: The cemetery where John B. Smith and Emma Langley lie holds about 250 graves, begun in the 1880s.
body: Historical Records of Franklin County, Texas, compiled by B. F. Hicks and Doris Meek between 1967 and 1972 and reproduced by the county's TXGenWeb page, describes the cemetery: "Hagansport Cemetery is in the Hagansport Community and has around 250 graves. Burials probably started in the 1880's. The people of the community had probably used the Pierces Chapel Cemetery previous to the start of Hagansport Cemetery."

The earliest marked grave is Laura Terry's, born 13 June 1870 and died 13 October 1876. Smaller family burying places nearby, now lost, include the Cannon cemetery two miles south of Hagansport and the Singleton cemetery two miles northeast, where "there were once about ten wooden stakes marking gravesites."

Emma Langley Smith, who died on 15 March 1905, and John B. Smith, who died in 1918 and whose grave was marked with a wooden stob, were buried here. Some of John B. and Emma's children also grew up here: Charles Oscar Smith and his sisters Vera, Luina, Lona and Allie and brother Jimmie are the children recorded in 1900.
src: Historical Records of Franklin County, Texas (B. F. Hicks and Doris Meek, 1967-72), cemetery descriptions at https://www.txgenwebcounties.net/franklin/cemetery.htm; 1900 U.S. Census, Franklin Co., Tex.
stories.place: Hagansport, Franklin County, Texas

stories.title: A Butler County burying ground with the family's name
stories.hook: At least five of the Satterfield and Johnson kin are buried at Satterfield Cemetery near Jetson, Kentucky.
body: Find a Grave places Satterfield Cemetery at Jetson, Butler County, at 37.2579 N, 86.5703 W. Among those memorialized there are Sidney Rufus Satterfield (1865-1949), his wife Eliza "Ancie" Johnson (1871-1951), their infant Walter (1890), Ancie's father James P. Johnson (1840-1884) and her mother Martha J. Clark Johnson (1839-1923).

The cemetery is the burial place of those who stayed. John C. and Samantha moved to Texas about 1907; Sidney and Ancie stayed on the farm country of Butler and Warren counties, and Sidney died at Richardsville, Warren County, in 1949.
The Satterfields buried here are the sons and daughters of James H. Satterfield, who farmed in Butler County from 1876 and, by his own 1885 account, owned 1,340 acres there.

stories.title: Buried among the missionaries at Wheelock
stories.hook: Oscar Hulsey's funeral in 1982 was held at a mission graveyard where stones from the 1850s still stand.
body: Wheelock was a Presbyterian mission to the Choctaws. Its church was organized in December 1832 by Rev. Alfred Wright, who removed to the Choctaws' new land in October 1832, and the buildings stood about two miles northeast of the later town of Millerton. A 1914 book on the neighborhood says what remained: 'the two mission school buildings, a strongly built stone church 30 by 50 feet, a two story parsonage and cemetery.'

The same book copies one stone from the graveyard: 'Sacred to the memory of the Rev. Alfred Wright who entered into his heavenly rest March 31, 1853, age 65 years. Born in Columbia, Connecticut, March 1, 1788. Appointed Missionary to the Choctaws 1820. Removed to this land October, 1832. Organized Wheelock Church December, 1832. Received to its fellowship 570 members.' In 1947 the Oklahoma Historical Society's journal listed Wheelock among the state's 'historic old cemeteries ... that offer much fine material.'

Oscar Franklin Hulsey died at his home at Holly Creek on 17 June 1982, at 71. His funeral, according to the McCurtain Gazette of 20 June, was held at 2 p.m. at Wheelock Cemetery with Rev. Bob Lewis officiating. He was laid there in a graveyard where, a teacher at the mission school wrote of a three-year-old's burial there in the 1890s, the child was placed 'beside missionaries who had passed away half a century before.'

No transcription of Wheelock is posted among the McCurtain County cemetery files, so the family's information for Oscar rests on the newspaper notice and on the memorial listing already cited in his entry, not on a published list of stones. His wife Katie is buried at Mount Olivet in Hugo.
src: R. E. Flickinger, The Choctaw Freedmen and the Story of Oak Hill Industrial Academy (1914), p. 22 (archive.org/details/choctawfreed00flick); Chronicles of Oklahoma 25:3 (Autumn 1947) and 26:3 (Autumn 1948); McCurtain Gazette, 20 June 1982 (obituary of Oscar Hulsey, quoted in his entry); McCurtain County cemetery files, USGenWeb Archives (files.usgwarchives.net/ok/mccurtain/cemeteries/, no Wheelock file)

stories.title: Two Stevenson stones in Block 2
stories.hook: A year-2000 canvass of Hugo's Mount Olivet lists Frank and Parsis Stevenson side by side, with one birth year that cannot be right.
body: Mount Olivet is Hugo's old municipal cemetery. The county list calls it 'Originally called Burgoyne Cemetery,' and a gravestone-studies newsletter dates it to 1907, 'very nearly to the town's beginning.' It is better known as the home of Showmen's Rest, the circus performers' section dedicated in 1961, with its granite dancing elephant at the entrance.

In 2000 Ron Henson canvassed Block 2 and posted 652 names. Two lines read: 'Stevenson  Frank N.  1860  1950' and 'Stevenson  Parsis Jane  1887  1956.' This is the only transcription found that confirms a stone for Gilbert Franklin 'Frank' Stevenson, who died at Hugo on 9 May 1950, and for his wife Parsis Jane.

Two points need care. Frank's stone gives birth as 1860 while his family record has 17 November 1861; the 1870 and 1880 censuses fit either year, and the middle initial N is not in his known name. Parsis Jane's death year, 1956, matches the family record, but a birth in 1887 is impossible for the mother of children born from 1884; her birth was 1868, so the listed 1887 is a misreading or a carving error. The transcription gives no inscriptions beyond names and years.
Their daughter Katie Cornelia Hulsey died on 30 January 2009, with burial at Mount Olivet. That is nine years after the canvass, so her stone is not in this listing.

stories.title: Five Moffitt stones at Shoat Springs
stories.hook: The cemetery list confirms the dates of Grady, Mary and three of the boys they buried.

subject.name: Shoat Springs Cemetery: the Moffitt graves

body: The Shoat Springs transcription lists five Moffitt entries in a row: 'Moffitt, Dois L. -- Feb 16, 1921 - Aug 25, 1947; OK SC1C USNR WWII', 'Moffitt, Jimmie Gaynell -- Jan 17, 1923 - Oct 26, 1926', 'Moffitt, Henry Wayne -- Jan 13, 1934 - May 12, 1937', and 'Moffitt, Woodford Grady -- Nov 6, 1891 - Jun 21, 1972; Mary Tinsley -- Jun 4, 1895 - Aug 26, 1962.'

These match the dates already in the family record. Dois's date of 25 August 1947 is the date on his Texas death certificate, four days after the Red River accident of 21 August. The rating on his stone, SC1C, is Ship's Cook First Class in the U.S. Naval Reserve, the job he held through the war.
Jimmie Gaynell and Henry Wayne were each three; their parents joined them in 1962 and 1972. The county list places the cemetery in the community of Hugo, in section 4, T7S R18E.
The transcription gives names and dates only, with no epitaphs, so the wording on the stones is not recorded.

stories.title: The meeting ground where the Chamness stone stands
stories.hook: Anthony Chamness has a 1975 memorial in the Cane Creek cemetery, placed by descendants, not a stone of his own day.
body: The Cane Creek Meeting history records that on 14 February 1764 William Marshall transferred 26 acres on Cane Creek, next to Simon Dixon's mill dam, to the trustees Peter Stout, Jeremiah Piggott, Benjamin Piggott and David Vestal 'for the use and benefit of Cane Creek Meeting.' It adds: 'This is the property where the Meeting House and burial grounds are presently located.' A separate Marshall account says William and Rebecca Marshall gave the 26 acres and the house on it.

Of Anthony Chamness the book says: 'In 1975 friends and family erected a large stone in the Cane Creek Meeting's cemetery to commemorate these early pioneers and their devoted service to the Cane Creek congregation.' It dates him 'circa 1713-1777,' says he and Sarah Cole 'were among the first overseers of the Cane Creek Meeting,' and notes that his will was made on 24 November 1776. 'Chamness descendants still come yearly to stroll between the quiet graves.'
The same book says British troops took over the meeting-house during the Revolution and 'some English soldiers are buried in the cemetery.'

The memorial stone is a modern commemoration. This source does not say where Anthony, Sarah, William Moffitt or Mary Davies lie, and Quaker burials of that time were commonly unmarked, so those graves remain unlocated.
src: From Whence We Came: Cane Creek Meeting Sesquibicentennial Reunion (Snow Camp, N.C., c. 2000), archive.org/details/fromwhencewecame00cane
kv: 26 acres and a house, 14 Feb 1764, 'for the use and benefit of Cane Creek Meeting' (trustees Peter Stout, Jeremiah and Benjamin Piggott, David Vestal)
Large stone placed 1975 for Anthony and Sarah Chamness
Not individually confirmed: early Friends graves were unmarked and no grave list for William Moffitt, Mary Davies or Sarah Cole appears in this source
stories.place: Cane Creek Meeting, Snow Camp, Alamance County, North Carolina.

stories.title: A small graveyard with four Hulsey stones
stories.hook: Both Benjamin and George Washington Hulsey are said to rest at Breashears, but the public list names only the surname count.
body: Breashears Cemetery lies east of the Montgomery County town of Story, in a field off a gravel road, 'fenced, with a bench under the shade of an old tree.' The ARGenWeb page says it has been transcribed at least three times: online in 2008 with 139 names, and in the county's published cemetery books of 1986 and 1998, which recorded 117 names and 106 unmarked graves.

The surname count in that page is 'Breashears (15), ... Holmes (7), Hulsey (4), ... Kilby (10), Lamb (12), Lenderman (9) ...,' with the majority of the stones belonging to eight families. The Hulsey stones are not itemized: the page is a photo study of selected stones, not a transcription.

Rev. George Washington Hulsey (d. 5 August 1935, age 58) and his father Benjamin Franklin Hulsey (d. 16 December 1924) are the two Hulseys the family has placed here. The four-stone count is consistent with that, but the page does not confirm either name. Other burials listed there show the kind of neighbors who surround them: Rev. H. H. Holmes (July 2, 1863 - May 15, 1935, 'The Lord is my shepherd'), M. R. Lenderman (1858-1935) and Gertrude A. Breashears (1881-1952, 'Mother is Resting').
Nothing posted names a church for the cemetery, which has no stated affiliation.

stories.title: What is left of Bee Spring is the graveyard
stories.hook: The church where Elam Stevenson preached for decades was blown down in 1909; by 1956 only the cemetery survived, neglected.
body: The Methodist history of middle Tennessee says the original Bee Spring church 'was organized in 1815 by Rev. Elam Stevenson,' son of a Revolutionary captain, who 'professed religion in 1804,' united with the church in 1806, was licensed to preach in 1813 and 'the same year moved to Tennessee.' The first house was logs; a larger log church followed in 1822 or 1823, and a frame church in 1855 whose building committee included J. G. Stevenson. Its members were 'largely the families of the McClaurines, Loyds, McGuires, Sherrills, Moseleys, Bruces, Rowes, and Stevensons.'

Elam's own 1869 account mentions the church-yard: Rev. Meshach Boyce, who helped build the first house, 'died in the faith, and his dust now sleeps in our church-yard at Bee Spring.' A visitor in 1878 wrote that 'here repose the sacred dust of old Father Stevenson and his beloved consort,' which is the newspaper item already cited for Elam and Lydia.

'On the night of April 29, 1909, the Bee Springs Memorial Methodist Church was totally destroyed by the memorable and terrible tornado which passed through this section of Giles and Lincoln Counties.' The congregation rebuilt at Bryson, three miles away. Of the old site the 1956 history says: 'All that remains of this today is the cemetery, sadly neglected.'

No transcription of the Bee Spring graves appears in the Giles County cemetery archives, so the stones of Elam, Rev. Abner A. Stevenson (d. 1896) and Martha Still Watson (d. 12 July 1887) are known only from the family's memorial listing and the 1878 newspaper.

stories.title: Hugh Moffitt plans a move west
stories.hook: In 1799 Hugh prepared to leave North Carolina with his family; a later family account says he died near Chillicothe, Ohio.
body: The Bible Record of Abijah Moffitt says "William and Hugh married Davis daughters of North Carolina," and the 1928 Moffitt Genealogy names the wives as Mary and Hannah. In an 1853 letter, Joseph Moffitt named his father Hugh, mother Hannah Davis, and Hugh's brother William. Joseph also said Hannah's sister Mary married a Moffitt; identifying that man as the William in our Randolph County line remains an inference.

A transcribed will dated 1 October 1799 identifies Hugh Moffit of Chatham County, names his wife Hannah and son Joseph, and says he had disposed of his affairs in order to move with his family to the Northwest Territory. It also names six of the brothers Joseph later listed in his letter. These overlapping details strongly support identifying the will and letter with the same Hugh, although the original will and the original letter have not been examined.

The later Bible record says Hugh went to Ohio in 1798 or 1799 and died near Chillicothe about 1800. The 1799 will supports an intended move and is consistent with a departure later that year, but makes a definite 1798 departure doubtful. Neither the will nor Joseph's letter establishes that Hugh completed the journey or died in Ohio; those details remain a family lead.

Weeks's 1896 study of Southern Quakers reports that in 1798 Westfield Monthly Meeting in Guilford County sought advice on members moving to the Scioto River. He also says Cane Creek certificates to Ohio began in 1804. These records provide context for movement west, but do not name Hugh or establish his route.
src: Hugh Moffit will, 1 October 1799, Chatham County Will Book A, p. 189b, transcription: https://www.ncgenweb.us/chatham/court/wills_lmn.html; Joseph Moffitt letter, 4 August 1853, printed in The Nebraska and Midwest Genealogical Record, July 1924, p. 130: https://negenweb.net/NEHolt/The_Nebraska_and_Midwest_Genealogical_Re.pdf#page=139; Bible Record of Abijah Moffitt (WikiTree Moffitt-65); Moffitt Genealogy (1928), p. 3; S. B. Weeks, Southern Quakers and Slavery (1896), pp. 256 and 265, archive.org/details/southernquakerss00week
stories.note: The 1799 will records a planned move, not a completed journey. The 1853 letter and the will identify the same immediate family, but the original documents and an Ohio death or burial record have not been seen. The connection to William Moffitt and Mary Davies is supported by family testimony and later genealogy, but remains a lead.
stories.place: Chatham County, North Carolina; possible move to Ohio

stories.title: Silas Moffitt's wagon: Randolph County to Hamilton County, October 1823
stories.hook: A first cousin of our Robert Moffitt rode ahead to Indiana in 1822, built a cabin, and brought his wife and two children north in a single wagon in the fall of 1823.
body: Silas Moffitt (1794-1873) was the son of Charles Moffitt, one of William Moffitt's brothers, and Mary Cox; our Robert Moffitt was William's son, so the two were first cousins. Silas married Hannah Wilkinson (1799-1886) in Randolph County, North Carolina, on 4 May 1820. Hannah was the daughter of William Wilkinson, an Englishman, and Mary Moffitt, William Moffitt's daughter, who married on the 26th day of the 3rd month, 1795 by the family's papers. That makes Hannah Robert's niece, and Silas her first cousin once removed.

The 1928 genealogy says the son-in-law and father-in-law "both seemed to think the Northwest Territory offered them better opportunities, so two years after the wedding they started for Indiana on horseback in quest of their future homes." The land "was bought direct from the government, and so far as is known, most of it was bought in Wilkinson's name." They built "rude cabins" and went back for the families. Wilkinson, "unable to return the following year," died in Carolina before he could make the trip, and his family left soon after.

Silas and Hannah, "with their two children Mary and Charles, along with another family whose names have been lost, made the trip in the early fall and reached the site of their future home on the 8th day of the golden month of October, 1823." The book quotes Haines's history of Hamilton County: "The family made the trip from North Carolina with a four-horse team and all their possessions in one wagon." Their eldest son Charles W. was born in North Carolina only weeks before they started.

They lived in the log cabin for three years. Then Silas built a brick house out of brick he made himself, the second brick house in the township. When he died on 28 August 1873, nearly 79 and a few weeks short of fifty years on the place, he owned several hundred acres and had served as county commissioner and for two terms as treasurer of the township trustees. The book says he "lived and labored for half a century on the old Moffitt homestead." He and Hannah are buried in Carmel Cemetery. The Wilkinsons owned land, slaves and a tan yard, and the family left a slaveholding county for a free state, the same road Weeks documents for hundreds of Carolina Quaker families.

quotes.t: The family made the trip from North Carolina with a four-horse team and all their possessions in one wagon.
quotes.c: Haines, Hamilton County history, quoted in the Moffitt Genealogy (1928)

src: Moffitt Genealogy: Silas Moffitt and Hannah Wilkinson Moffitt (1928), pp. 3-5, quoting Haines, History of Hamilton County, Indiana, archive.org/details/moffittgenealogy00moff; S. B. Weeks, Southern Quakers and Slavery (1896)
