stories.place: Randolph County, North Carolina to Hamilton County, Indiana

stories.title: Two Quaker families, one road: Davies and Norton to Cane Creek
stories.hook: A Welsh-named indentured servant and an Irish Quaker's son took the same Pennsylvania-Virginia-Carolina road, twelve years apart.

subject.name: Charles and Hannah (Matson) Davies; Edward and Elizabeth (Brown) Norton

body: Charles Davies and Hannah Matson were married at Radnor Meeting, Pennsylvania, in the twelfth month (February) of 1732/3. The Davis family book of 1985, whose title names "Charles Davies, the immigrant to Pennsylvania about 1725, from there to North Carolina," gives the marriage. Hannah was "daughter of John Matson of Merion"; the family's own note in the back of the Cane Creek minute book says Charles "was brought over the ocean and sold to pay his passage." The Davies surname, with its alternate spelling Davis, is Welsh, and Radnor and Merion were Welsh townships in the Quaker settlement west of Philadelphia.

From Pennsylvania the couple went to Virginia. The same family book quotes a minute that a certificate "having been made for Charles Davis and Hannah, his wife to Hopewell Monthly Meeting, therefore this meeting [appoints]," and says the early Hopewell minutes were burned, so the exact year of the move is lost. It says Charles and Hannah were charter members of Cane Creek Monthly Meeting and moved "in or before 1750." Cane Creek was set up in the tenth month of 1751; Orange County, in which the land fell, was cut from Johnston, Bladen and Granville in 1752. Charles bought 187 acres from Henry McCullogh on 2 August 1758 and died in 1801.

Edward Norton's son, also Edward, was the other traveler. His 1739 marriage record at West Nottingham Meeting calls his father "Edward Norton, dec., of the County & Parish of Armagh, in the Kingdome of Ireland." The Nortons are said to have moved to Hopewell in Virginia, then to Fairfax, and reached Cane Creek in 1762, the year before their daughter Margaret married Joseph Chamness. Weeks's survey of the Southern meetings describes exactly this stream: in 1754, the first year of New Garden Monthly Meeting, "we have settlers coming in from Pennsylvania, from Hopewell and Fairfax meetings, Virginia," and he concludes that "the large settlement of Friends in Alamance, Chatham, Guilford, Randolph and Surry counties was formed by Quaker immigrants, not by the expansion of the native element."

Those two sentences are the family's story in small. The Davieses reached Cane Creek about 1750, the Chamnesses in 1749-51, and the Nortons in 1762. By 1763 the three families met at the meetinghouse for two weddings, sixteen days apart: Joseph Chamness and Margaret Norton on 17 March, William Moffitt and Mary Davies on 2 April.

quotes.t: we have settlers coming in from Pennsylvania, from Hopewell and Fairfax meetings, Virginia.
quotes.c: Weeks, Southern Quakers and Slavery, on New Garden Monthly Meeting, 1754

quotes.t: Charles was brought over the ocean and sold to pay his passage.
quotes.c: Family note in the Cane Creek minute book, as quoted in the tree entry for Mary (Davies) Moffitt

Weeks, Southern Quakers and Slavery (1896), pp. 101-103, archive.org/details/southernquakerss00week; Corbitt, Formation of the North Carolina Counties; Cane Creek and West Nottingham Quaker records as quoted in the tree entries for Charles Davies and Edward Norton

stories.place: Radnor and Goshen, Pennsylvania; Hopewell and Fairfax, Virginia; Cane Creek, North Carolina

stories.title: From Whitechapel to Cane Creek in four moves
stories.hook: A fifteen-year-old London apprentice bound for Maryland in 1725 left a line that stayed in Randolph County for a hundred and forty years.
body: Anthony Chamness was baptized at St John's, Wapping, in February 1713, the son of John Chamness and Ann Weary, who had married there on 4 January 1704. The parish clerk wrote the name "Chamniss." Cane Creek Meeting later wrote him down as "Anthony Chamness, s. John & Ann, b. about 2 mo. 1713, Est. Smithfield, London." On 9 February 1724/5, giving his age as 15 and his home as Whitechapel, he bound himself for seven years to John Cooke, a London victualler, for service in "Maryland (his Majesty's Plantation in America)."

He was out of his time by 1732. On 24 November 1735 he married Sarah Cole at St. Paul's Parish, Baltimore County, in the family of the Coles who had been in the county since the 1690s. They were Friends of Gunpowder Meeting. About 1741 they moved to Monocacy, then, in 1749, to Carver's Creek Meeting in North Carolina, and in June 1751 he took up 490 acres at Cane Creek. When Cane Creek Monthly Meeting was organized that autumn, Anthony was its overseer. Weeks writes that "the large settlement of Friends in Alamance, Chatham, Guilford, Randolph and Surry counties was formed by Quaker immigrants," and Anthony is one of them: an English servant boy who became a landowner and the officer of a meeting.

His son Joseph, born in Baltimore County in 1740, married Margaret Norton at Cane Creek on 17 March 1763 and became the meeting's recorder of marriage certificates. Their daughter Martha was born on 6 October 1778 at Centre, then in Guilford County; Randolph County was not cut from Guilford until 1779. She married Robert Moffitt there in 1797 and lived until 1865. Martha's son Nathan Moffitt, born in 1814, left Randolph County for Arkansas in the early 1840s rather than for Indiana.

The Chamness name did also leave by the Quaker road. In Weeks's appendix of removals, Dover Monthly Meeting's list of Friends who took certificates to Indiana between 1830 and 1860 includes "Camness," one more spelling of a name the Wapping clerk had written "Chamniss" a century earlier. The match is by surname only.
src: Cane Creek Meeting records and the London indenture, as quoted in the tree entry for Anthony Chamness; St John of Wapping registers (1704, 1713); S. B. Weeks, Southern Quakers and Slavery (1896), pp. 101 and 278; Corbitt, Formation of the North Carolina Counties (Randolph, 1779)
stories.note: Martha's birthplace is given as Center, Guilford, in the tree; if Centre Meeting's neighborhood fell in Randolph County in 1778 the county named at birth would differ. The Dover 'Camness' is a surname match only.
stories.place: Whitechapel, London; Baltimore County, Maryland; Monocacy; Carver's Creek and Cane Creek, North Carolina

stories.title: Six homes in forty-four years: the Nordykes, 1761 to 1805
stories.hook: From a New Jersey meeting to an Ohio farm by way of Virginia, Georgia, North Carolina and Tennessee, in time for a wolf-haunted winter in a one-sided shelter.
body: A Nordyke family history, the Terrell-Nordyke Genealogy of 1960, gives the stations of Abraham and Mary Nordyke in order. They married in 1761 and were Quakers "members of Chesterfield Monthly Meeting" in New Jersey. "In 1771, they moved to Virginia where they became members of Hopewell Monthly Meeting, which was located near Winchester. They then lived for eight years in Georgia. In 1788, we find them having transferred their membership to Deep River, Westfield Monthly Meeting in North Carolina. Then, in 1798, they moved again, this time to Lost Creek Monthly Meeting located near New Market, a few miles north of Knoxville, Tennessee. From there, in 1805, the family moved to Ohio."

Their son Micajah, the line the book follows, "was born in 1771 in Stafford County, Virginia. At the age of four, he, with the family, moved to Georgia where, because of imminent danger of an Indian invasion, he lay, secreted in a dense woods, through a whole night." Another son, our Aden, was shot in the arm in Georgia in an Indian attack, according to an Ohio county history. The book copies out the Quaker habit of recording the hour of birth: "Aden was born at 7:00 P.M.; Israel at 3:00 P.M.; Benajah at 9:00 P.M."

Lost Creek in 1798 was already a settlement with a history of trouble. Weeks reports that in 1787 Friends at Lost Creek, near the Holston River, asked New Garden Monthly Meeting for the right to hold meetings and were refused, because they had "settled on lands the title to which was still in dispute with the Indians," and were told to move off. The Western Quarterly Meeting added in 1792 that no Friend should "remove and settle out of the limits of a Monthly Meeting without first applying to and having consent." A meetinghouse went up at Lost Creek in 1796. The Nordykes reached it two years later, and it was from there that Weeks says many Tennessee Friends "drifted on, like Charles Osborn and William Williams, to the Northwest."

The last move, in 1805, put Micajah, then 34, his wife Charity, 26, with an infant in her arms and children of three, five and seven, and the "aging grandparents" on the road north. They bought land near what became New Vienna, Clinton County, Ohio, and "helped start a Friends Meeting which was called East Fork," on a lot that was part of the Nordyke farm. "Micajah had to go to Chillicothe, forty miles distant, to get flour and sugar," and Charity kept wolves off with brimstone on the fire. Mary died in 1814. Abraham's burial at East Fork was recorded in 1825, at 89; the tree gives 1822, so the death year is unsettled.

quotes.t: In 1771, they moved to Virginia where they became members of Hopewell Monthly Meeting, which was located near Winchester. They then lived for eight years in Georgia.
quotes.c: Terrell-Nordyke Genealogy (1960), p. 13

src: C. Clayton Terrell, Terrell-Nordyke Genealogy (1960), pp. 13-15, archive.org/details/terrellnordykege00terr; S. B. Weeks, Southern Quakers and Slavery (1896), pp. 251-54, archive.org/details/southernquakerss00week
stories.note: Terrell dates the Ohio move to 1805 and Weeks's context supports Tennessee in 1798; the tree entry for Abraham gives Clinton County in 1806. The Georgia meeting is not named. A diary of the road from Tennessee to Ohio is quoted in the same book but is not attributed to the Nordykes.
stories.place: Burlington County, New Jersey; Virginia; Georgia; Deep River, North Carolina; Lost Creek, Tennessee; East Fork, Ohio

stories.title: Those who left and those who stayed: Aden Nordyke, Sicily Shaw and Parses
stories.hook: Aden Nordyke died in Indiana in 1842, while his daughter Sicily and her husband Noble Shaw stayed in Guilford County; Parses Shaw turns up in Gibson County in 1839.

subject.name: Aden Nordyke, Sicily (Nordyke) Shaw and Parses (Shaw) O'Neal

body: Aden Nordyke was born in Burlington County, New Jersey, in 1762, and came south with his parents. In the twelfth month of 1787 Deep River Monthly Meeting recorded the marriage intention of Adin Nordyke and Martha, and Hinshaw's index lists their daughter "Sicily b. 8-2-1790" first among their children. Aden's brother Micajah went to Ohio in 1805; Aden went on to Indiana, where trees give his death as 9 May 1842.

Sicily stayed. She married Noble Shaw, a member of Dover Monthly Meeting in Guilford County, whose register records him as born 22 April 1787 with children Aaron (16 December 1809), Parris (7 July 1817, died 30 May 1818) and Mary (17 November 1820). Noble died on 25 December 1855 and Sicily on 16 May 1861; in the spring of 1857 she and J. H. Leak advertised his 268-acre farm at Oak Ridge. Weeks's count for Dover Monthly Meeting is seventy-one certificates between 1816 and 1860, "nearly all" of them to Indiana; the Shaws were among the Friends who watched neighbors go and stayed behind.

Parses is the loose end. The 1884 History of Gibson County calls Mrs. Parsis Watt "a native of Lawrenceburg, Ohio," who "came to this county in 1839." Lawrenceburg, on the Ohio River near the mouth of the Great Miami, is in Dearborn County, Indiana, in the heart of the White Water country where Weeks says the Carolina Quakers headed. Parses was about 28 when she and Archibald O'Neal, a Tennessean, came to Gibson County; their son Daniel had been born in Tennessee in October 1838. Archibald died there on 25 April 1841 and she married the County Down Irishman Hugh Watt.

Whether Parses was a child of Noble and Sicily Shaw is not proven. The Dover register has a Parris who lived a year in 1817-18, and Parses, born about 1811, would have to be an earlier child missing from the page. The simplest reading is that her people belonged to the Shaw families who moved from North Carolina to the Ohio-Indiana line; no record has been seen naming her parents.
src: C. Clayton Terrell, Terrell-Nordyke Genealogy (1960); Hinshaw, Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy, vol. 1 (Nordyke and Shaw entries); Dover Monthly Meeting register; History of Gibson County, Indiana (1884), Columbia Township and directory, pp. 212 and 239; S. B. Weeks, Southern Quakers and Slavery (1896), pp. 264-65; The Times, Greensboro, 26 March 1857
stories.note: Parses Shaw's parentage and the 'Ohio' of her birthplace (the town of that name is in Indiana) are unresolved. Aden Nordyke's Indiana death place comes from the tree and has not been checked against a record.
stories.place: Deep River and Dover Meetings, Guilford County, North Carolina; Indiana; Gibson County, Indiana

stories.title: Where the Hulseys came from, and how they got to Arkansas
stories.hook: A Georgia memoir says the pioneer Hulsey came from England and a Virginia-born son went to South Carolina as a child; a Union County blacksmith's sons turn up in Arkansas by 1860.

subject.name: Salathiel Hulsey's household and the Hulseys of Hall County

body: The 1850 census for Union County in the north Georgia mountains, as transcribed in the San Diego Genealogical Society's Hulsey compilation, shows Salathiel Hulsey, 43, born in Georgia, with Elizabeth, 35, and children Mary Ann, Robert R., Elizabeth, Jesse, Jennings, Benjamin, Lillian and Nancy, with an Arminda Burnet, 20, in the house. An earlier reading of the same household gives Benjamin as 3; the transcription prints 6. This is the Salathiel the tree places as Benjamin Franklin Hulsey's father, a link not yet proved. He was in Hall County in 1840.

Hall County had Hulseys earlier. The Georgia land lottery of 1832, which gave away Cherokee land, lists "Charles Hulsy" of Hamilton's District, "Pleasant T. Hulsey" and "James Halsey," a soldier, of Dobbs's District, and "Alder Halsey, Jr.," of Hamilton's, all in Hall. Tax lists for Franklin County, Georgia, on 31 October 1820 name James Hulsey Sr., Joel Hulsey and Pleasant Hulsey. None of these has been tied to Salathiel.

The family's origin shows in a Georgia memoir quoted in the same compilation. The sketch of Col. William Hulsey, born in DeKalb County on 1 October 1839, says: "JENNINGS HULSEY, native of Virginia, immigrated to South Carolina with his parents while he was a child. Came to Georgia, married REBECCA PATE" and died in DeKalb County, and adds: "The pioneer Hulsey from England." So the best account of the surname is Virginia, then the South Carolina upcountry, then north Georgia, a path that matches the Hulseys of Franklin and Hall counties. Salathiel named a son Jennings, which may be a clue to a connection and is no more than that.

Arkansas came next. The compiler notes a Robert R. Hulsey, 27, in Hempstead County, Arkansas, in 1860, and a child named Salathel G. born in Arkansas, which may be Salathiel's son Robert and a grandson named for him. Benjamin F. Hulsey, then 16 or 17, is on the roster of Company D, 4th Arkansas Cavalry, a Union regiment raised in Montgomery County in the winter of 1863-64; so was Gilliam Graves, the grandfather of the woman Benjamin's son George Washington Hulsey would marry in 1901. Montgomery County had been organized on 9 December 1842, and the Ozark region history of 1894 says its settlers "came into the valleys of Montgomery in the thirties."

quotes.t: JENNINGS HULSEY, native of Virginia, immigrated to South Carolina with his parents while he was a child. ... The pioneer Hulsey from England.
quotes.c: Memoirs of Georgia, as quoted in the SDGS Hulsey compilation

src: San Diego Genealogical Society, Families: Hulsey (2000), compiled census abstracts and Memoirs of Georgia (Southern Historical Association) extracts, archive.org/details/sdgsfamilies64; James F. Smith, The Cherokee Land Lottery (1838), archive.org/details/cherokeelandlott00smit; A Reminiscent History of the Ozark Region (1894), Montgomery County sketch, archive.org/details/reminiscenthisto00unse
stories.note: Salathiel's place in the line depends on Benjamin being G. W. Hulsey's father, and the Hall County Hulseys are not tied to Salathiel. The Memoirs' Jennings is the grandfather of a DeKalb County man, not a proven ancestor.
stories.place: Virginia; South Carolina; Hall and Union counties, Georgia; Hempstead and Montgomery counties, Arkansas

stories.title: Toms Creek to Cedar Glades: Gilliam Graves's three states
stories.hook: He married in Randolph County in 1832, sat on Georgia juries in 1835 and 1838, and was farming in the Arkansas Ouachitas by 1853.
body: Gilliam Graves was born about 1813 on Toms Creek in Randolph County, North Carolina. He married Mary Tyler there on 18 August 1832. The county had been cut from Guilford in 1779, and his neighbors on the Deep River side included Friends whose meetings Weeks shows draining toward Indiana. Gilliam went south instead. By 1835 he was in Cherokee County, Georgia, where he served on county juries in December 1835 and again on 5 November 1838, and he is in Cherokee County in 1840.

By 1853 he was on the tax lists of Montgomery County, Arkansas, at Cedar Glades, and on 18 August 1845 he had married Delila Hawthorne there, so the move may be earlier than the tax list. The 1894 history of the Ozark region describes the county he came to: it "was organized December 9, 1842," its settlers "came into the valleys of Montgomery in the thirties," "in 1845 there were twenty-one slave-owners," and "the spinning-wheel and loom have not yet disappeared." Its seat is Mount Ida.

The Civil War put him in blue. On 14 January 1864, at 45, he volunteered at Cedar Glades for Company D, 4th Arkansas Cavalry, the same company that carried Benjamin F. Hulsey. He deserted on 12 October 1864 and came back on 25 December. His son Jesse is said to have been born about 1855 in Blount County, Alabama, which does not square with an Arkansas tax roll in 1853 and is unresolved.

Gilliam died in January 1876, supposedly killed by robbers, in Garland County, and is buried beside his third wife Polly in Mountain Valley Cemetery. Garland County was not yet three years old: the 1894 history says it "was established April 5, 1873," with Hot Springs the seat, and that "the greater part is mountainous, leaving only a small area worthy of the labor of the husbandman." Hot Springs is where G. W. Hulsey was born on 24 December 1876, and where Oscar Hulsey was born in 1910.
src: Tree entries for Gilliam and Jesse King Graves (Randolph Co., N.C., marriage 1832; Cherokee Co., Ga., jury lists 1835 and 1838; Montgomery Co., Ark., tax lists 1853; Union Army enlistment papers, 4th Arkansas Cavalry); A Reminiscent History of the Ozark Region (1894), Garland and Montgomery county sketches, archive.org/details/reminiscenthisto00unse; Corbitt, Formation of the North Carolina Counties (Randolph)
stories.note: Jesse King Graves's Alabama birth conflicts with Gilliam's Arkansas tax record in 1853; the tree also gives different details for Gilliam's death.
stories.place: Toms Creek, Randolph County, North Carolina; Cherokee County, Georgia; Cedar Glades, Montgomery County, Arkansas; Garland County, Arkansas

stories.title: Four families, two states and one county line: the Satterfield road
stories.hook: From a Carolina Piedmont county to Warren County, Kentucky, with a detour through Tennessee and a widow of 77 who moved to Missouri.

subject.name: The Satterfields and Garrisons: North Carolina to Kentucky to Texas

body: John Satterfield was born about 1766 in Orange County, North Carolina, a county that had been formed in 1752 and has since been divided until the part he came from is Person County. He lived in South Carolina and settled in Warren County, Kentucky, where his will was proved on 10 November 1847 and names thirteen children, among them Ephraim. His son Ephraim, whom his grandson's 1885 sketch calls "a native of Virginia," married Ruth Knowles in Warren County on 12 November 1809. Ruth was born in Virginia about 1783; her father Joshua Knowles, born about 1747, was in Warren County in 1830, and his will of 11 November 1824 names a son John "of Franklin County, Virginia," and a daughter "Ruth Saterfield."

The second generation shows a Tennessee stop. The Butler County sketch of 1885 says Ephraim's son Henry Satterfield was "a native of Maury County, Tenn.; died in 1861, at the age of fifty years," so, if Henry is Ephraim and Ruth's son, as WikiTree has it, they were in Maury County about 1811, two years after their marriage. At the same moment another future ancestor was passing the same way: J. M. Garrison married Patsey Cannon, born in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, at Wilson County, Tennessee, on 6 December 1809, and the couple settled in Warren County, Kentucky. In 1815 Allen County was cut from Warren and Barren, and the Garrisons found themselves in a new county. Their daughter Mary, born 17 October 1811, married Henry Satterfield. The Kentucky General Assembly dissolved the Garrisons' marriage by an act of its December 1847 session.

Ephraim died about 1850. His widow Ruth is in Allen County in 1850 with her daughter Elizabeth and in 1860, at about 77, in Gasconade County, Missouri, with Elizabeth and her husband Jesse Agee. She died there in 1864, a long way from Warren County.

Henry and Mary's son James H. Satterfield was born in Allen County on 14 April 1838 and married Melissa Gibson there on 17 September 1859. In 1867 he moved to Dakota County, Minnesota; in 1875 he returned to Kentucky and settled in Warren County, and in 1876 in Butler County, a county created on 18 January 1810 from Logan and Ohio. By 1885 he held 1,340 acres there and 425 acres in Tennessee. Melissa died in 1877, and in 1878 he married Lucinda Belle Phelps in Butler County. He died in Bowie County, Texas, on 24 November 1922. His son John C., born in 1864, farmed at Horse Mill in Butler County in 1900. About 1907 the family left for Franklin County, Texas; John died there between 1912 and 1916, and in 1917 his widow Samantha crossed the Red River into Choctaw County, Oklahoma. Their daughter Artie Pearl, born at Morgantown in Butler County on 13 August 1898, married Charles Oscar Smith in 1914.
src: Kentucky: A History of the State (1885), Butler County sketch of James H. Satterfield, p. 676; Warren County, Kentucky, Will Book D, p. 262 (John Satterfield, proved 10 Nov 1847); Joshua Knowles will, written 11 Nov 1824, proved Oct 1832; Wilson County, Tennessee, marriage 6 Dec 1809 (Garrison-Cannon); Acts of Kentucky General Assembly, Dec 1847; 1850 and 1860 censuses, Allen Co., Ky., and Gasconade Co., Mo.; Corbitt, Formation of the North Carolina Counties (Orange, 1752)
stories.note: WikiTree gives Ephraim's birth as South Carolina in 1787, while the 1885 sketch says Virginia; the Maury County birthplace for Henry rests on the same sketch.
stories.place: Orange County, North Carolina; South Carolina; Warren and Allen counties, Kentucky; Maury and Wilson counties, Tennessee; Butler County, Kentucky; Franklin County, Texas

stories.title: Three Arkansas counties and a Red River crossing: the Moffitt road west
stories.hook: The Moffitts did not come to Arkansas by way of Alabama; they came straight from the North Carolina Quaker country, and left it by the timber trade.
body: The family's Alabama link is a marriage, not a route. Nathan H. Moffitt, born in 1814 in Randolph County, North Carolina, a son of Robert Moffitt and Martha Chamness, grew up in the Centre meeting community; the North Carolina Manumission Society counted sixty-five members in its Centre branch in April 1819, and a New Garden member quoted by Weeks recalled that the little anti-slavery band there "continued to meet at New Garden until the majority of the members emigrated to the west, preferring to live in a free state." Nathan's own children's birthplaces tell the route: North Carolina up to about 1842, Arkansas from about 1843. In 1850 he was farming in Strawberry Township, Lawrence County. The mother county of northeast Arkansas, Lawrence was created in 1815, according to the county's own history.

His son Henry, born there in August 1855, was farming in Janes Creek Township, Randolph County, in June 1880, with his wife Hannah and two small children. By 1889 the family was in Stone County, where Tom was born at St. James. Stone County was brand new: the 1894 history says it "is one of the new divisions" organized "April 21, 1873," with Mountain View the county seat, and it counted 5,089 inhabitants in 1880 and 7,043 in 1890. Henry's youngest son Grady was born there on 6 November 1891, and Henry died at Mountain View in 1901 at 46.

Grady left the Ozarks in the timber trade. In June 1917 he was a timberman for C. D. Neese at Ervin, Oklahoma, a sawmill town that existed from 1904 to 1922; in 1920 he was a tenant farmer in Wilson Township, Choctaw County. He had married Mary Tinsley Shackleford about 1914, and her people had themselves moved west, from Gilbert in Etowah County, Alabama, in 1900, to Martin County, Texas, by 1930. So Alabama enters the Moffitt line through Mary, whose parents are on the 1900 census at Gilbert and the 1930 census at Stanton, Texas. In 1930 Grady, Mary and their six sons were living with her parents. By 1940 they rented a house at 411 North H Street in Hugo, in the Choctaw Nation, where Grady had been out of work for 50 weeks.

So a family that left Randolph County, North Carolina, for Arkansas in the early 1840s, and Arkansas for Oklahoma in the 1910s, finished its western moves a few miles from the Red River and the old Doaksville road, a few miles from where the Tims family had traded at Doaksville since the 1830s.

stories.title: Frank Stevenson's road: Pulaski to Indiana to Danville to Valliant
stories.hook: His grandfather came to Giles County by pack horse in 1813; Frank spent seventy years going back west in short hops.
body: Giles County, Tennessee, where Frank was born on 17 November 1861 at Pulaski, was itself new when his grandfather Elam Stevenson came: it was formed in 1809 from Maury County, and Elam, licensed to preach in 1813, brought his wife Lydia Payne from Burke County, North Carolina, the same year. Elam's own letter of 1869 says Philip Bruce asked him to carry some of his books "in my wagon," which sits oddly with the family story that the move was made by pack horse. A neighbor remembered the family settling near Bee Spring church "in 1815 or 1816."

Frank is in his father Abner's household at Pulaski in 1870 and 1880. In January 1881 the Pulaski Citizen said his father had "abandoned the idea of going to Texas," and in May that his brother "Judge Geo. Stevenson" had "returned from Texas last week." Frank himself went north to Gibson County, Indiana, where his wife Parsis Jane O'Neal's family lived; her grandparents Archibald and Parses O'Neal had come to the county from Tennessee in 1839. Their first three children, Iva Myrtle (1884), Adison Galiton (1886) and Nellie Vashti (1889), were probably born there.

The 1910 census gives the rest of the order. Frank, 51, a clergyman, was renting at Danville in Yell County, Arkansas, married 25 years, with seven children "born in Indiana, Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas." Yell County had been organized on 5 December 1840, and the 1894 Ozark history notes it had two county seats, Danville and Dardanelle. Katie Cornelia was born at Danville on 15 October 1910.

By January 1919 his mother-in-law Vashti's obituary placed her daughter at "Valiant, Oklahoma." In 1920 Frank farmed a rented place on South Millerton Road in McCurtain County; he died at Hugo on 9 May 1950 and is buried at Mount Olivet. Katie married Oscar Hulsey, born at Hot Springs, in 1927, and their daughter Mary Ellen (1938-2002) is buried at Hugo beside William Thompson Jr.
src: Pulaski Citizen, 27 Jan and 5 May 1881; McFerrin, History of Methodism in Tennessee (1871), vol. 2, pp. 178-90; Goodspeed, History of Tennessee (1886); 1870-1920 censuses; Obituary of Vashti O'Neal, Jan 1919; The Tennessee Handbook (2002) (Giles County formed 1809 from Maury); A Reminiscent History of the Ozark Region (1894), Yell County sketch
stories.note: The order of the Texas and Oklahoma births between 1889 and 1902 is not established from the sources seen.
stories.place: Pulaski, Tennessee; Gibson County, Indiana; Texas; Oklahoma; Danville, Yell County, Arkansas; Valliant and Hugo, Oklahoma

stories.title: With 'the first group of exiles': what the winter of 1831-32 was like
stories.hook: The Pisachubbes told their newspaper that they came west with the first group of exiles in 1832 and settled at Fort Coffee. The official record of that first winter, and of Fort Coffee, sets the story's dates.

subject.name: Joseph Pisachubbe's family and the first Choctaw exiles

body: When William Harrison Pisachubbe died in May 1937, the Hugo Daily News printed a family history from his relative Judge T. W. Hunter: the Pisachubbes "came from Mississippi with the first group of Choctaw exiles in 1832 and settled at Fort Coffee," near present-day Spiro. William Harrison and Robert were the sons of Joseph Pisachubbe, who is on Dawes Card 1580 only as a dead father. No roll of the removal has yet been seen that names him.

The record of the first removal fills in what that sentence meant. Major Francis W. Armstrong took the Choctaw census in the summer of 1831 and counted about 18,880 Choctaws. By the first week of November, Thoburn's history of Oklahoma says, "four thousand Choctaws, some in wagons, some on horseback, some on foot, were on their way to the Mississippi River": five hundred went north to Memphis and took steamboats for Arkansas Post, the rest to Vicksburg. A "fierce winter storm" followed. Between 26 November and 8 December about 2,500 were landed at Arkansas Post. "Few blankets and moccasins or shoes were seen among them; the women generally were barefoot and the young children naked, especially those from the extreme southern part of the nation in Mississippi." There were only forty government wagons for the 350 miles to the Kiamichi country, and the roads were frozen. More than a thousand others went by the Red and Ouachita rivers to Ecore de Fabre. The last parties of 1831 reached the Red River region "during the first week in March, 1832"; on 30 April 1832 Lieutenant Stephenson recorded 3,749 rations being issued at four stations on the Red River, and 536 near the Choctaw Agency by Fort Smith.

The ration was the one Doak & Tims would later be paid for. Thoburn's note gives it as "one and a half pounds of beef or pork, one pint of corn, or an equivalent of corn-meal or flour, with two quarts of salt to the hundred rations," with the corn raised to a quart a day in the fall of 1831.

A family that came "in 1832" is therefore either from the last of the 1831 parties, the winter exiles, or from the 1832-33 removals that the War Department reorganized in May 1832. Fort Coffee, however, was not there to settle at. The garrison at Fort Smith was moved twelve miles up the Arkansas to a new post called Fort Coffee only in June 1834, and the post was abandoned on 27 July 1838. The family's 1937 words most likely name the neighborhood where they put down roots by the agency and the later fort and Skullyville, not a place that existed in 1832. By 1899 the sons were in Kiamitia County, well over a hundred miles south, where Eunice Gardner Pisachubbe and her boys were enrolled at Goodland.

quotes.t: By the first week in November, four thousand Choctaws — some in wagons, some on horseback, some on foot — were on their way to the Mississippi River.
quotes.c: Thoburn and Wright, Oklahoma: A History of the State and Its People (1929), vol. 1, p. 168

src: Hugo Daily News, 11 May 1937 (obituary of William Harrison Pisachubbe); Dawes Card 1580; Joseph B. Thoburn and Muriel H. Wright, Oklahoma: A History of the State and Its People (1929), vol. 1, pp. 165-70 and note 17, archive.org/details/oklahomahistoryo01thob; Fort Coffee entry in the same volume's chapter on military posts
stories.note: No removal roll naming Joseph Pisachubbe has been seen. Fort Coffee was established in June 1834, so a settlement there in 1832 cannot be literal.
stories.place: Mississippi; Arkansas Post and Little Rock; the Arkansas River near Fort Smith and Fort Coffee

stories.title: Doaksville before the store: 1833 in the removal papers
stories.hook: A Choctaw district's letter of February 1833 complains of white traders in 'a small town below Kiametia' and names Doaksville as the place where annuities were received.
body: Doak & Tims is usually dated by its contracts of 1838-39. The removal correspondence puts Doaksville on the map five years earlier. In Senate Document 512, the printed correspondence on the emigration of the Indians, a letter dated at Horn Prairie on Red River on 6 February 1833 is signed by the treaty captains of Nittuckachee's district. They write that their people "are entirely satisfied with our new country" and ask that their annuity be delivered at Horn Prairie, because "at Doaksville, where we have generally received our arms and articles mentioned in the treaty, our horses have suffered much, as there is no winter range." There was a complaint too: "We have to inform you that we have too many white traders in our country, we wish you to have them removed. ... They have built a small town below Kiametia, consisting of white traders, with the exception of two." They would not object to "a few traders ... but we do not wish to be crowded."

The same volumes carry a smaller clue to the man the town was named for. In the account of Lieutenant J. R. Stephenson, the officer in charge of the subsistence depot at Fort Towson, a line lists Josiah S. Doak with "28 lbs. bacon and 4 lbs. sugar," for the first and third quarters of 1833. The printed columns are garbled in the scan, so what Doak was paid for is unclear, but it shows a Josiah S. Doak dealing with the removal's quartermasters on the Red River in the year of the letter.

Vincent B. Tims was a witness, with Doak, to the Treaty of Doaksville on 17 January 1837 and was feeding Chickasaw emigrants under contract by 1 January 1838, at thirteen cents a ration. His partnership with Doak was dissolved in 1844. A New Orleans advertisement in the Washington (Arkansas) Telegraph of 12 October 1845 lists references that begin with "Maj. Wm. Armstrong, Choctaw A[gency]" and include "Doak & Tims, Doaksville, C. Nation." Armstrong was the Choctaw agent, and his brother Francis had taken the 1831 census and run the removal; by 1845 the agent himself stood as a reference for the firm. The Oklahoma history of 1954 lists the Doak & Tims Mercantile Company among the stores of Doaksville, with a blacksmith shop and a hotel.

No document seen puts Tims himself at Doaksville in 1833. Family accounts say he was born in South Carolina in 1803 and had a Choctaw wife; his earliest record at Doaksville that has been seen is the January 1837 treaty. The 1833 letter shows what he walked into: a Red River town already built by white traders, already resented by the Choctaw districts around it, and already the place the government's goods and annuities were handed out.

quotes.t: At Doaksville, where we have generally received our arms and articles mentioned in the treaty, our horses have suffered much, as there is no winter range.
quotes.c: Treaty captains of Nittuckachee's district, Horn Prairie, 6 February 1833, in Senate Doc. 512

stories.title: Peter Gaunt, who knew no visible worship in the world
stories.hook: Called before the Plymouth court in 1655 for staying away from church, Peter Gaunt of Sandwich said he knew no public visible worship in the world, and was fined in cattle for the Quaker meetings that followed.
body: Peter Gaunt settled at Sandwich on Cape Cod, in Plymouth Colony, with his wife Lydia, whose surname is unknown. One proposed identification links him to a Peter baptized at St Peter at Gowts, Lincoln, on 29 June 1610, son of Thomas Gaunt and Susan Bate. That identification remains unproved. Thomas and Susan married at Rotherham on 28 August 1609, and Susan's will calls Peter her only son.

The colony’s court books follow Peter Gaunt for six years. At the court of 6 March 1654/5 he was called in "to answare for neglecting to frequent the publick worship of God." Asked to speak to the charge, the record says, "Peter Gaunt affirmed hee knew noc publicke vizable worship now in the world, whereunto the said Ralph Allen assented, but Gorg Allen dissented; the case was left to further consideration." Within three years the same court was fining him for Quaker meetings.

On 2 March 1657/8 Gaunt, Daniel Wing, Ralph Allen Jr. and William Allin were summoned "for a tumultuose carriage att a meeting of the Quakers att Sandwich." The court cleared them of that charge, "notwithstanding, for theire vnreuerent carrying themselues before the Court, coming in before them with theire hatts on," it fined each of them twenty shillings. Thomas Butler, whose daughter Dorothy would marry Peter's son Hananiah in 1678, was summoned for the same disturbance and was "admonished and cleared."

The fines were collected in cattle. In June 1660 a note was entered in the court's record that Marshal George Barlow "tooke from Goodman Gaunt, for his fine of 24li, these particulares: seauen cowes & heifers, two steers, seauen bushells and an halfe of pease; and after, when one of the cowes died, hee tooke another liue one in stead therof, because Barlow had not the hide of the dead cow deliuered to him." Thomas Burgis Jr. owned in open court that he had made the report, and was himself fined thirty shillings for refusing to help the marshal. Joseph Besse's Sufferings of the People Called Quakers, in a list of goods taken from Plymouth Colony Friends about 1658, prints "Peter Gaunt 43 l. 14 s. 6 d."

The summonses kept coming. In October 1660 a long list of people "fined for being att Quakers meetings," ten shillings each, includes "Peter Gaunt, Dorithy Butler, Obadiah Butler." In February 1660/1 the Sandwich constable was ordered to bring Gaunt and nine others to Plymouth "to answare for theire tumultuouse carriages against the marshall and cunstable of Sandwich in the execution of theire offices in the cecuring of two Strang Quakers." A ten-shilling fine on Gaunt "was leuied vpon a mistake" and was given back. In 1661 a list given into the court of those who had sheltered visiting Friends reads: "Wiliam Allin entertained Christopher Holder. Wiliam Newland entertained one forraigne Quaker. Peter Gaunt entertained two forraigne Quakers."

Family trees date Peter’s death at Sandwich to 10 May 1678, the day of his son Hananiah’s marriage to Dorothy Butler, but the date needs independent confirmation. Lydia died in April 1692. Their sons included Israel and Hananiah, who went to New Jersey. A 1661 court case involving Thomas Burgis Jr. names a Lydia Gaunt; the record does not identify her as Peter’s wife, so it does not establish an event in this family. (Lead)

stories.title: The Butlers of Sandwich and the marshal
stories.hook: Thomas and Dorothy Butler were fined in cattle and money for Quaker meetings; their son Daniel was publicly whipped in June 1660.
body: Thomas Butler was at Sandwich, Plymouth Colony, soon after the town was founded in 1637. In March 1657/8 he was summoned with Peter Gaunt and others over a Quaker meeting and "admonished and cleared." In 1658-9 he was fined ten shillings "for refusing to assist the marshall, Barlow, in the execution of his office," and the court assigned another fine, fifty shillings for refusing to serve as constable, to Barlow himself.

In June 1660 the court passed two sentences on the family: "Daniell Butler, for rescuing a Strang Quaker, when apprehended by the marshall, Barlow, and for his breakeing away when taken p'soner, is sentanced to bee publickly whipt, which accordingly was pformed." The next reads: "Thomas Butler, and Dorithy, his wife, for turbulent cariages the same night that theire son Daniell was serched for att theire house, fined forty shillings." In October 1660 Dorothy Butler, almost certainly the mother, was fined ten shillings for being at Quaker meetings.
The court later returned twenty shillings taken from Thomas for his wife and son attending a Quaker meeting. Its October list also names Obadiah Butler among those fined.

Thomas was also a land-hunter. In 1665 the court sent Richard Bourne and William Bassett "to view and purchase some lands desired by Edmond Freeman and Thomas Butler lying towards Saconeesett," and when the Indians would not part with that parcel it gave them leave to buy other land for him. In 1667 the court granted Butler "a necke of land called Tassacausett, lying neare to Edmond Freemans land," which he had "bought ... of an Indian called Charles, alias Pampmumitt, for a yoake of oxen," provided the Indian returned three pounds to Butler.

Dorothy died on 9 August 1675 and was buried the next day. Thomas died on 12 March 1690. Their daughter Dorothy, born 23 January 1649/50, married Hananiah Gaunt at the Quaker meeting at Sandwich in 1678, and they carried the Quaker family to New Jersey. Thomas's origin and Dorothy's maiden name are not known.

stories.title: Thirty-five head of cattle: Sandwich in December 1658
stories.hook: A magistrate's letter to a friend in London, printed by Joseph Besse, describes the town where the Gaunts and Butlers lived as nearly all Quaker and being stripped of its cows.
body: In December 1658 J. Cudworth (James Cudworth of Scituate), a Plymouth Colony magistrate who had lost his seat on the bench and his militia captaincy for "entertaining some of the Quakers at my House," wrote to a friend in London. Joseph Besse printed the letter in his Sufferings of the People Called Quakers. Of Sandwich, Cudworth said: "almost the whole Town of Sandwich is adhering towards them: And give me leave a little to acquaint you with their Sufferings, which is grievous unto, and saddens the Hearts of most of the precious Saints of God."

He described the method. The Quakers would not swear, so the old law that every man take the oath of fidelity was revived: refuse it and pay five pounds or leave the colony. "When the Time is come, they are the same as they were; then goes out the Marshal, and fetches their Cows and other Cattle ... On this Account thirty five Head of Cattle, as I have been credibly informed, have been, by the Authority of our Court, taken from them the latter Part of this Summer." Some families had one cow, some two, "and many small Children in their Families, to whom, in Summer-time, a Cow or two was the greatest outward Comfort they had for their Subsistence."

A poor weaver with seven or eight small children, lame himself, had two cows, and both were taken. "The Marshal asked him, What he would do, he must have his Cows? The Man said, That God that gave him them, he doubted not, but would still provide for him." The court then fixed fines for the meetings themselves, ten shillings a meeting, which Cudworth reckoned at one hundred and fifty pounds for Sandwich men, "Newland ... for himself and his Wife" being twenty-four of it and the weaver twenty.

The town was watched. "Sandwich Men may not go to the Bay, lest they be taken up for Quakers," Cudworth wrote, and a man who went on business was put in prison for twenty-four hours while witnesses were sent for. By the colony's newest law, anyone who entertained a Quaker "if but a Quarter of an Hour" forfeited five pounds. Besse follows the letter with a list of other people whose goods were taken at about the same time, for refusing to swear or for absence from public worship. It includes "Peter Gaunt 43 l. 14 s. 6 d.," and the whole list amounts, Besse says, to about six hundred and sixty pounds.

Peter Gaunt's goods and the Butler family's fines are in the colony's own court books, told under "No publicke vizable worship now in the world" and "Daniel Butler's whipping, June 1660." Twenty years later Peter's son Hananiah and Thomas Butler's daughter Dorothy were married at the Sandwich Friends meeting, and within a few years they left for New Jersey.

stories.title: Hananiah Gaunt's deeds: 500 acres, a hundred sold, and a share of West Jersey
stories.hook: The East and West Jersey records show Hananiah Gaunt, "of Rhode Island, yeoman," buying 500 acres in May 1685, selling a hundred of them in 1687, and buying into a West Jersey proprietary share in 1690.
body: The New Jersey Secretary of State's calendar of records has three deeds for Hananiah Gaunt. On 11 May 1685 George Hutcheson of Burlington conveyed "to Hananiah Gaunt of Rhode Island, yeoman, for 500 acres in the First Tenth." The Proprietors' survey returns for July 1685 enter "500 a. near Honeonickon, adjoining George Hutcheson," the Indian place-name that became Oneanickon and then Springfield Township. The deed calls him of Rhode Island. An alphabetical list of Dartmouth land owners for 1684-1694 in Lands of Old Dartmouth carries his name; a Ricketson family history notes undivided Dartmouth land deeded by him to William Ricketson on 13 January 1684.

He added to the farm. A later survey is entered for him, "of 220 a. adjoining Samuel Houghton and Tho. Clark; incl. 9 a. of meadow on a brook near Mount Pisgah; 20 a. of the whole being an allowance for highways for other land." A neighbor's survey for Daniel Leeds of 188 acres at Oneanickon is described as lying beside "said Gaunts 9 a. lot," the meadow ground on the brook.

On 18 May 1687 "Hananiah Gaunt of near Oneanickon, yeoman," sold "to William Bustill of Shrewsbury, East Jersey, carpenter, for 100 acres, N. grantor, E. Ralph Trenoweth, part of 500 a., bought of George Hutchinson May 11, 1685." The deed puts Ralph Trenoweth on the east side of the hundred acres and Hananiah's own land on the north.

On 3 November 1690 George Hutcheson, now called a distiller, deeded Hananiah, then "of Burlington Co., yeoman," one twenty-fourth of a share of West Jersey that Hutcheson had bought of Godfrey Newbold of Handsworth, Yorkshire, on 22 August 1684, "excepting 200 acres." A West Jersey share was a proprietary right to a portion of the province's unsurveyed land, and such rights were bought and sold in England and Burlington before the land was laid out.

Hananiah and his brother Israel had exchanged their Sandwich land for New Jersey land on 4 May 1678, the week before his marriage to Dorothy Butler, according to the Sandwich Friends records cited by WikiTree. By 1686 and 1689 the Biddle surveys at Springfield describe other men's land as adjoining his.

stories.title: A "madman" at the table: William Dewsbury and Richard Browne
stories.hook: The Nottingham Friends' family memorandum says our Browne ancestor became a Quaker when William Dewsbury shared his table, and that his landlord then made him pay his rent twice.
body: In 1786 East Nottingham Monthly Meeting entered into its book of births and burials an account of the English father of William Brown the emigrant, written down from the stories of a great-nephew of William's in his eightieth year. It places the father in "Puddington" near Wellingborough, today's Podington, and says he had been "some time in communion with the Baptists, afterwards joining with the sect called Puritans, and is said to have been a teacher among both, and a seeking, religious man." The memorandum calls him William, but the Wellingborough Quaker registers give the father's name as Richard.

The story is that William Dewsbury, "about the first going forth" of that minister, came to the town, and the man noticed "the solidity of his countenance" and asked him in to "break bread." When they sat down the host said grace. Dewsbury sat in a grave manner and answered, "if thou wilt first partake with me I shall be free to partake with thee." After a short silence he was moved to speak, "beginning with these words, 'O Earth! Earth! hear the word of the Lord,'" and the host was convinced. When he came home with Dewsbury his wife asked why he had brought "that madman" to their house. "Why woman," he answered, "he hath brought the Eternal Truth of God to us." She thought it over and was convinced too.

The cost came quickly. The landlord, "a wild airy man and given to sporting," sent his tenant two young hounds to feed and raise. The tenant would not, and the landlord waited. Rent had been paid every half year to a steward without a receipt, so the landlord demanded it again, and said, "except you will take your oath that it is paid, you shall pay it to me." Browne held that Christ had forbidden swearing, so "this Friend had to pay his rent over again," and was then turned off the farm. It took him a considerable time to find another, where he did well. Dewsbury came back, the memorandum adds, and Browne got him leave to speak in the parish church, where "many people were convinced."

Richard died about 1664 by the memorandum's reckoning (a Quaker burial record in the registers gives 1662), and on his deathbed told his wife, "thou shalt live to bring up all our children, and they shall be blessed and be all favoured to keep their habitations in the Truth." The memorandum makes William, born about 1656 in its reckoning, the youngest of nine, six other sons and two daughters. The original Wellingborough register instead gives his birth as the twenty-ninth day of the first month 1658 and names his father Richard; it does not name his mother. The same pages say that when Penn's province was proposed, some Friends doubted whether to go, and Dewsbury, preaching among the Brownes in Northamptonshire, told them: "The Lord is about to plant the wilderness of America with a choice vine or noble seed which shall grow and flourish."

Besse's Sufferings of the People Called Quakers records, in its Northamptonshire section, a meeting at Findon where Daniel Brown and Joane Brown, both "of Puddington in Bedfordshire," were taken with some forty other Friends, held overnight in an alehouse, fined forty shillings each, and sent with the rest to the county gaol for six weeks. Nothing in either source ties them to Richard, and the match rests only on the village name, so it remains a lead.

stories.title: "He is in a wrong spirit": William Brown, his brother James and George Keith
stories.hook: Before the Nottingham Lots, William and James Brown lived at Marcus Hook, where George Keith tried to win James to the separatists and William talked him out of it.
body: William Brown came over about 1682 or 1683 with a first wife, Dorothy, who "could not give up to it cheerfully." The Nottingham memorandum says he felt a clear sense of duty and that "the Lord wonderfully made way for and assisted him," and adds that on the voyage his wife died at sea. Their son Joseph had been born in England on 12 June 1682. William went first to his older brother James, a weaver, who was already at Marcus Hook on the Delaware.

James had been in Pennsylvania before Penn's grant, by Gilbert Cope's reckoning. He married Honour Clayton, whose father William Clayton came in 1677, and on the 20th of the 12th month 1683 (February 1683/4 in modern reckoning) he took a patent for 115 acres on Chichester Creek, which he named "Podington" after the home village. He conveyed it to his son William in 1706.

About 1692 George Keith, once a leader among Friends, split the Quakers of the Delaware. At Chichester meeting Keith "spake or preached largely, using some arrogant and lofty expressions, beyond the simplicity of the gospel." James Brown, "having at first a favourable opinion of Keith," asked his brother afterwards, "what he thought of George Keith now; was not he satisfied?" William, "a deep feeling man," answered, "I am satisfied, but it is in this, that he is in a wrong spirit."

James took it badly and started to leave. William stepped after him and asked whether he remembered "how they used to feel at their meetings when in England, though they were but as lads," the love and melting seasons "under the powerful operation of the pure principle of Love and Light." He went on: "In this country we have come under a different dispensation ... We have been looking out and allowed to provide towards an outward inheritance, and settlements for ourselves and families, free from disturbance or persecution; but let us remember that the truth is still as precious as ever."

The next day Keith held a meeting at the house of Henry Reynolds and called at James's door on the way, asking if he was coming. James hesitated; Keith got down from his horse and went in, saying that if James was growing dissatisfied he would satisfy him, "though he used many words, all did not avail, for James went not to meeting." James later settled in the same neighborhood at Nottingham and died about 1715, "a religious man and of a good character, but not favoured with a capacity or talent equal to his brother William." William's son Richard married Hannah Reynolds of Chichester in 1717; the host of Keith's second meeting was a Henry Reynolds "who lived near."

quotes.t: I am satisfied, but it is in this, that he is in a wrong spirit.
quotes.c: William Brown to his brother James about George Keith, in the East Nottingham memorandum of 1786 (Cope, The Browns of Nottingham)

stories.title: Lots 23 and 33: William Brown on the Nottingham Lots
stories.hook: William Brown is said to have cut the first tree on the Nottingham Lots in 1701; the plat gives him Lots 23 and 33 and his sons the lots beside them, and the first meeting was held in his house.
body: The Nottingham Lots were thirty-seven rectangular lots of Penn's land laid out in 1701-02 on the border with Maryland. A 1902 bicentennial history of the Brick Meeting House at Calvert, Maryland, says "all agree that William Brown was the first Friend to settle on the Nottingham lots." The family memorandum says he moved his family there in 1702, "accounted far back in the wilderness." The bicentennial history adds a tradition that Penn himself rode out in the early spring of 1701 with a party that included William Brown, James Brown, John Churchman, Edward Beeson and Henry Reynolds, and that in the fall the two Brown brothers went to the site on pack horses from New Castle to clear ground for corn.

The plat as the history gives it assigns "No. 23 to William Brown" and "No. 33 to William Brown," with "No. 14 to James Brown" and Nos. 26 and 27 to James, and "No. 28 to Messer Brown." Messer is William's son Mercer, born in February 1685/6, whose first name was his mother Ann Mercer's maiden name; the history prints it as Messer, as it was commonly written. William's lot was beside a spring about a mile east of the present Rising Sun, near the road to the Brick Meeting House.

Tradition, "which is now upon record," says William "was the first to take his axe in hand and strike it into a tree, one of the monarchs of the forest," and said, "In humble trust we commence our labor." The spring is said to have been an Indian camping ground on the trail from Pennington to the mouth of the Susquehanna, which an old resident, Jesse Pugh, remembered tracing as a boy.

The records are firmer about the meeting. At Concord Monthly Meeting in the 2nd month of 1705, "two Friends of Nottingham desires on behalf of the rest a First Day meeting at the house of William Brown, and a Fourth Day meeting once a month," and Concord Quarterly Meeting on 9 April 1705 "approves of until further order." The first brick meetinghouse followed in 1724. Penn's spoken gift of forty acres for a meetinghouse, burial ground and school in 1701 was the only title Friends had until 1765, when his sons Thomas and Richard Penn issued a patent to William Brown, Timothy Kirk, William Churchman and Benjamin Chandlee in trust.

William Brown the emigrant died, by the family memorandum, on the 23rd of the 6th month 1746 (23 August), "in the 91st year of his age," having lived at Nottingham about 44 years "in good repute for his integrity; being an elder in the Church, and a substantial Friend." Ninety-one would put his birth near 1655; the Wellingborough register gives 1658. His great-nephew and namesake William Brown, a minister, traveled in Europe with John Churchman from 1750 to 1754 and was the man in whose eightieth year the memorandum was written down.

quotes.t: In humble trust we commence our labor.
quotes.c: Words attributed by tradition to William Brown as he struck the first tree, in Bi-centennial of Brick Meeting-House (1902)

stories.place: Nottingham Lots, Chester County, Pennsylvania (now Cecil County line)

stories.title: Three cows, two mares and 500 acres: Thomas and Agnes Croasdale on the Neshaminy
stories.hook: Two inventories preserve a family’s Pennsylvania household: livestock, bedding, tools and a 500-acre holding on Neshaminy Creek.
body: Thomas Croasdale of New Hay, Yorkshire, married Agnes Hawthornthwaite of Wyresdale on 1 May 1664. The marriage was recorded by Lancaster Monthly Meeting. Eighteen years later, the couple prepared to leave England with six children. The certificate issued at Settle on 7 June 1682 names the whole household, placing their move within a group of Quaker families rather than an isolated voyage.

Before leaving, Thomas arranged to buy land in Pennsylvania by deeds dated 21 and 22 April 1682. The family history describes a purchase of a thousand acres, but the estate papers later describe a 500-acre holding. The records concern different stages of acquiring and settling land; they should not be treated as two measurements of an unchanged farm.

One of those documents survives. The Friends Historical Library at Swarthmore College catalogs the 21 April 1682 indenture from William Penn to Thomas Croasdale as a vellum document with a red seal, signed by both men. The catalog describes a yearly rent of one peppercorn. The document was made before the family crossed the Atlantic; its catalog does not itself describe their voyage.

Thomas died on 2 November 1684, about two years after the move. Agnes became administrator of his estate. On 8 December, James Dillworth and Thomas Constable valued his belongings: clothing, bedding, pewter and brass, cushions, wooden vessels, chests, linen, ironware and hogs. Two mares were worth £8 10s; three cows, a calf and a yearling were valued at £12. The goods totaled £47 9s. The 500 acres were listed but left unvalued.

Agnes’s inventory gives the household another outline: brass and pewter, pots, a bed and bedding, a chest, a saddle, hogs, three cows, two bullocks, a heifer, two mares and a colt. This time the land was valued at £50, nearly half the £106 5s total. Small things also survived into the account—a blanket, nails and the tools used around the house and farm.

Agnes died on 20 October 1686, according to the family account, and sons William and John received administration on 1 November. The inventory’s printed date is in 1685, creating a conflict that the transcript does not resolve. The children’s list names William, John, Elizabeth, Mary, Bridget and Alice. Bridget’s marriage to John Cowgill carries this branch into the Brown, Norton, Chamness and Moffitt families.

The same archive preserves a later trace of the family’s land. In 1728 John Wildman and his wife Mara, the widow of Thomas and Agnes’s son John Croasdale, transferred land in Middletown to a Thomas Croasdale identified in the catalog as John’s son. He was Bridget’s nephew. Other documents in the collection describe a debt involving a Thomas Croasdale and a sheriff’s sale in 1733; whether this was the same nephew requires further research.

stories.note: Thomas Maxwell Potts’s 1895 book reproduces the inventories and meeting entries; these are printed transcriptions, not images of the original manuscripts. Thomas’s inventory supports his death in 1684 rather than 1682. Agnes’s printed inventory year conflicts with the reported 1686 death and administration. Their own birth dates and parents remain unverified. The ship name is disputed in later accounts. The Swarthmore finding aid describes the 1682 and 1728 documents; their original text has not been independently examined. The 1733 debtor’s identity is not established.
stories.place: From New Hay, Yorkshire, to Neshaminy Creek, Bucks County, Pennsylvania. The Settle certificate of 1682 names Thomas, Agnes and six children.

stories.title: Ellen Cowgill, widow of Giggleswick, and the sons who came as servants
stories.hook: The 1682 Settle certificate calls her "Ellen Cowgill widow & her children"; two of her sons landed in Pennsylvania in service.
body: On 7 June 1682 Settle Monthly Meeting, in the Yorkshire dales, issued a certificate for a party of Friends bound for Pennsylvania. It lists Cuthbert Hayhurst "his wife & family," Thomas Wrigglesworth and Alice, Thomas Walmsley and Elizabeth, Thomas Croasdale "Agness his wife & six children," Thomas Stackhouse and his wife, Nicholas Waln "his wife & three children," William Hayhurst, and "Ellen Cowgill widow & her children." No child is named. Ellen was born near Giggleswick about 1639, so she was about forty-three. Later genealogical research identifies her children as Edmund, Jennet, John, Jane and probably Ralph; the certificate does not name them.

Her husband's name is not documented. Many trees name Ralph Cowgill, said to have been hanged in 1682 as a Quaker, but that has no documentation, and the Cowgill family association thinks Edmund Cowgill, baptized in 1634 at Thornton in Craven, more likely. Her maiden name is also disputed: some books give Stackhurst, and several Stackhouse histories say she was not a Stackhouse, so a Thomas Stackhouse of Giggleswick and Anna Evans are not added as her parents.

John, probably about seventeen, came as a servant to Cuthbert Hayhurst. Hayhurst, born at Easington in Yorkshire about 1633, had been among the Friends imprisoned in the West Riding in the 11th month of 1660 for refusing the oath of allegiance. In 1668 he held a meeting at the house of Richard Betteris in Oxford and was arrested while speaking and held for a month by the vice-chancellor. His neighbor Nicholas Waln wrote that "he went through many great exercises and imprisonments." He died in the first month of 1683, only months after landing in Bucks County.

Ralph Cowgill came by a different ship, landing about 28 September 1682. Under Randolph Blackshaw of Hallingee, Cheshire, a list of Bucks County residents prints: "These servants below came in the ship the 'Friend's Adventure.' The Mr., Thomas Wall. Arrived in this river the 28th 7th M., 1682. Servants to Randulph Blackshaw, William Beasy, Ralph Nuttall, and Ralph Cowgill, each to serve 4 years, and to have 50 acres of land apiece." Passengers and Ships Prior to 1684 (1970) lists both John and Ralph as apparently Ellen's children: John, "servant to Cuthbert Hayhurst" and a probable passenger on the Lamb of Liverpool, and Ralph, who came on the Friend's Adventure.

Which ship carried the Settle families has been told two ways. Potts's Our Family Ancestors (1895) and the 1915 Stout family history say they sailed in Penn's own Welcome, and Potts adds that smallpox killed thirty on that ship. The later study says at least four of the seven Settle families sailed on the Lamb of Liverpool, and a Watson family history lists the Lamb, "John Tench, master, from Liverpool," as arriving on 22 October 1682. The party's own certificate does not name a ship.

Ellen settled at Middletown, Bucks County, and is buried in the Middletown Friends cemetery; she died in 1705. John served his time, married Bridget Croasdale at Neshaminy in 1693, and had four children by her before her death in 1701, among them Elizabeth, born in 1694, who married William Brown Jr. John married Rachel Bunting in 1703/4. Jennet married Bernard Lane at Burlington on 2 February 1688. Elizabeth's daughter Elizabeth Brown married Edward Norton, and the line came down through the Nortons and Chamnesses to the Moffitts.

stories.title: A tan-yard on Black Bird's Creek, and two Cowgill sisters who married two Brown brothers
stories.hook: John Cowgill left Bucks County about 1713, set up a tan-yard on Black Bird's Creek, and his daughters Elizabeth and Ellin married William Brown Jr. and Thomas Brown of Nottingham.
body: John Cowgill, the servant boy of 1682, married Bridget Croasdale at Neshaminy on the 19th of the 8th month 1693 (19 October). Their children were Elizabeth (born the 24th of the 6th month, 1694), Thomas (21st of the 4th month, 1696), John (8th of the 5th month, 1698) and Ellin (14th of the 10th month, 1700). Bridget died on the 26th of the 2nd month, 1701. In 1703/4 he married Rachel Baker, the widow of Job Bunting of Darby, and had four more children: Rachel, Mary, Ebenezer and Eleazer. Quaker months started in March, so the 6th month is August; some family trees convert the first birth to June.

About 1713 or 1714 he moved to the lower part of New Castle County, Delaware. The land records the Stout family history quotes say that on the 26th of the 3rd month 1715 (26 May) a warrant was signed to John Cowgill "for the resurvey of a tract of land in a fork of Appoquinimink Creek," and on the 1st of the 5th month 1715/6 he "desired the grant of about 100 acres of vacant land, near his other tract in New Castle county, where he had planted a tan-yard." On the 10th of the 3rd month 1718 (10 May), "having erected a tan-yard on a branch of 'Black Bird's Creek,'" he asked for another hundred acres on rent.

His sons Thomas and John followed him, and married sisters, daughters of Joshua Clayton of Little Creek Hundred. Thomas had Thomas, Ezekiel and Jane. John married Lydia Clayton in 1720 "of Kent county." The daughters were already settled among the Nottingham Quakers. The Duck Creek Monthly Meeting records the marriage of "Elizabeth Cowgill, daughter of John Cowgill, of Duck Creek in New Castle, and William Brown, son of William Brown, of Nottingham," on 1 December 1715 by the Quaker count (the Nottingham registers say 1715). Her sister Ellin married Thomas Brown, William Jr.'s brother, in 1718/9.

Elizabeth died before 1721 and left a daughter, also Elizabeth, who in 1739 married Edward Norton. William Jr. married Margaret Davis in March 1721/2, died about 1727, and Margaret then married William Kirk. Ellin's husband Thomas Brown died on the 19th of the 12th month 1746/7 (19 February). She married again on the 13th of the 11th month 1768 (13 November 1768) Lewis Clothier of Kent County, Maryland, and died on the 5th of the 1st month 1772 (5 January), aged 71. John Cowgill himself died on 2 July 1731. His grandson John Cowgill of Little Creek was hauled through Dover in a cart in the Revolution for refusing Continental money; that is told in "Carted through Dover."

Cope's Browns of Nottingham lists the four marriages of William Brown the emigrant and the children of each, and the Maryland Quaker Records for Nottingham Monthly Meeting repeat the Cowgill marriages from the meeting's own books.

stories.title: Carted through Dover: John Cowgill of Little Creek, 1776
stories.hook: Elizabeth Cowgill's nephew refused Continental paper money on conscience, was declared an enemy to his country by the Kent County Committee in January 1776, and was driven to Dover in a cart with a paper pinned to his back.
body: John Cowgill of Little Creek Hundred was the son of John Cowgill and Lydia Clayton, and the grandson of the tanner John Cowgill of Black Bird's Creek, which makes him a nephew of Elizabeth (Cowgill) Brown, our ancestor. On 4 January 1776 the Committee of Inspection and Observation for Kent County, Caesar Rodney and Thomas Rodney among its members, resolved "that it appears to this Committee, by the confession of John Cowgill, a residenter of Little Creek Hundred, in this County, that he has refused, and, from conscience, shall refuse, to take said Continental money in discharge of debts, or for other purposes, when tendered to him." The committee decided he was "an enemy to his country, and ought to be treated as such by every friend of American liberty; and that they ought to have no further dealings with him."

His daughter Mary Corbit described the arrest in a letter of 1824 to her brother John, who passed it on to Samuel R. Fisher. It began when he asked a tenant to pay rent in specie. He was taken before the Assembly at Dover and threatened with "a heavy fine," and, when he declined to take any part in encouraging war, was let go. Later "going to Meeting on a fifth day, mother and I being in the chaise, and my father on horseback with one of my little brothers behind him," a man in regimentals rode with him half a mile where armed men were waiting. "The child was taken from behind him, and he was ordered to dismount and get into a cart." Friends coming to meeting followed as far as the meetinghouse, where "my father called out and bid us farewell." "A paper was pinned to his back."

Before they entered the town the officer stopped the cart, and, taking his calm for ignorance, said, "Mr. Cowgill you are not aware of the danger you are in!" He answered: "I fear not them that can kill the body, and after that have no more power that they can do; but I fear Him who after he hath killed the body, hath all power." At the liberty pole in Dover it was proclaimed that he had no protection and that anyone dealing with him did so at their peril; "the miller was threatened with the destruction of his mill if he ground for his family, and the school-master forbid receiving his children at school."

The man was let go, and many Friends rode home with him. His daughter wrote, "When we went to bed at night we did not know what would be the issue before morning, and in this way we lived for several years." She told of one of the party who took him that day. The roads were wet and muddy, and Cowgill, seeing the man walking beside the cart, said, "Thee had better get up and sit with me, as the walking is wet and I am fearful thee will take cold." The man said long afterward that he never regretted any act of his life more than being concerned in the affair against "one of the best of men."

Duck Creek Monthly Meeting, on 27 June 1778, received "an account of the sufferings of John Cowgill for refusing Continental Currency" and sent it to the Quarterly Meeting committee. John married Mary Worrell and had a large family; his daughter Mary married William Corbit of Odessa, Delaware.

stories.title: Two Nortons from Armagh and two Browns at Nottingham
stories.hook: Edward Norton's son and daughter, Irish Quakers from Armagh, married a Brown nephew and uncle at West Nottingham in 1739 and 1733, and Mary Norton's widow's settlement was inspected by a Virginia meeting.

subject.name: Edward Norton of Armagh and his children

body: The Irish Quakers' certificate list for Nottingham Monthly Meeting records two Norton marriages. "Mary Norton, daughter of Edward Norton, 'of ye County of Armagh,' Ireland, was married 9 Mo. 24, 1733, under auspices of Nottingham Mo. Mtg., to Richard Brown, son of William Brown, of West Nottingham." And: "Edward Norton, of West Nottingham, Chester County, son of Edward Norton of 'ye City and Parish of Armagh,' Ireland, deceased, was married 8 Mo. 16, 1739, at Nottingham Mo. Mtg., to Elizabeth Brown, daughter of William Brown."

Richard was the son of William Brown the emigrant and his second wife Ann Mercer, born in 1693; he had married Hannah Reynolds in 1717 and Rachel Beeson in 1730/1 before Mary Norton, who was his third wife by the Nottingham count (Cope lists the same three marriages but gives the third as the 24th of the 5th month). Elizabeth was the daughter of William Brown Jr. and Elizabeth Cowgill, so the bridegroom Edward Norton married his sister Mary's husband's niece. Elizabeth's mother had died before 1721 and her father about 1727, and she married at West Nottingham as an orphan. The meeting's book calls her "dt William & Elizabeth (Cowgill), both dec."

Both couples went to Virginia. Edward and Elizabeth Norton took a certificate to Hopewell Monthly Meeting on 19 January 1739/40, and Richard and Mary Brown with their family took one to Hopewell too. Mary and Richard's three children were Richard (born 18 September 1734, died 4 September 1738), Joseph (1 April 1736, died 19 May 1751) and Mercer (7 May 1740). Richard died before 1747, leaving a will; his widow's second marriage was to Elizabeth's step-family, as below.

The editors' abstract of the Nottingham minutes says that Fairfax Monthly Meeting appointed a committee on the 28th of the 12th month 1746/7 (28 February) to inquire into the settlement of Richard Brown's last will and testament, to protect the children, and that it was found satisfactorily settled. On the 21st of the 1st month 1746/7 (21 March) Nottingham gave William Kirk, the widower of Margaret Davis, a certificate to Fairfax, clear to marry Mary Brown, and in April 1747 he married Mary (Norton) Brown, widow of Richard Brown and daughter of Edward Norton "of Co. Armagh, Ireland, dec." Margaret Davis, who had died in February 1744/5, had been the second wife of Elizabeth's father, so Mary Norton's new husband was Elizabeth's stepmother's widower.

Edward and Elizabeth Norton later lived at Rowan County, North Carolina, according to their daughter Margaret's marriage certificate of 1763, when Margaret Norton married Joseph Chamness at Cane Creek. If the Edward and Elizabeth Norton of that certificate are the couple of 1739, as the names and the Hopewell and Fairfax trail suggest, then Margaret's grandmother was Elizabeth Cowgill of Neshaminy, and the line from the Settle certificate of 1682 runs through Brown and Norton to the Chamness wedding that put the family into Robert Moffitt's household.

quotes.t: Edward Norton, of West Nottingham, Chester County, son of Edward Norton of 'ye City and Parish of Armagh,' Ireland, deceased, was married 8 Mo. 16, 1739, at Nottingham Mo. Mtg., to Elizabeth Brown, daughter of William Brown.
quotes.c: Albert Cook Myers, Immigration of the Irish Quakers into Pennsylvania, 1682-1750 (1902), p. 376

src: Albert Cook Myers, Immigration of the Irish Quakers into Pennsylvania, 1682-1750 (Swarthmore, 1902), Nottingham Monthly Meeting, https://archive.org/details/immigrationofiri00myer_0; Maryland Quaker Records: Nottingham Monthly Meeting (Brown entries for William Jr., Richard and Margaret Davis); Cope, The Browns of Nottingham (1864).
stories.note: The marriages and the Brown relationships are proven by meeting records; that the Rowan County Nortons of 1763 are this couple is probable, not proven.
stories.place: West Nottingham, Chester County, Pennsylvania; later Hopewell and Fairfax, Virginia

stories.title: A cane and a sword
stories.hook: Wills and inventories from 1731–32 trace three generations of a Perkins family and their connection to the Nordykes.
body: In May 1731 administration of the estate of Jacob Perkins of "Wellenborrow," Burlington County, who died without a will, went to his son Jacob Perkins, yeoman. The inventory, made on 20 May by Robert Lucas and Joseph Fenimore, comes to 91 pounds 18 shillings 5 pence and "includes cane and sword, £1.10; debt of 14 shillings from Benja. Perkins; 8 years rent due from Benja. Perkins and Wm. Makintass, £1."

The son, Jacob Perkins Jr., made his own will on 26 October 1731. He left his wife Sarah and his children "Abraham, Rebeckah, David, Mary, Ann, Susannah, Hannah, Sarah, Bethseda and Martha." He disposed of "land in Chester, which I bought of John Ward March 15, 1728," and listed bonds due him "from James Smith, Esq., John Shinn and Henry Nordike." He also left ten pounds to St. Mary's Church, Burlington, the Church of England parish, which points to Church of England ties. His son David was executor and the witnesses were Joseph Fenimore, Eliza Fenimore and Sam. Scattergood. The will was proved on 7 December 1731, and the inventory of 6 December, by Fenimore and Scattergood, was 205 pounds 14 shillings 6 pence.

Henry Nordyke had married Rebecca Perkins at Willingboro on 6 January 1731, the same year. He appears in her father's will as a man who owed him money. Then David died too. His will, made in January 1731/2 "of Wellingborrow, yeoman," leaves his brother Abraham "plantation in Wellingburrow, which came to me by will of my father, Jacob Perkins, dated Oct. 26, 1731," and names his "Sister, Rebecca, wife of Henry Nordike" and "Mother, Sarah Perkins." It was witnessed by Joseph Fenimore, Sam'l Scattergood and Henry Nordike, and was proved on 4 March 1731/2.

So within about a year the Perkins household of Willingboro lost a grandfather, a father and a son, and the new son-in-law Henry Nordyke witnessed the last of the wills. Henry and Rebecca's descendants are the Nordykes of the family tree. Abraham, to whom David left the plantation, was also his executor.

quotes.t: Sister, Rebecca, wife of Henry Nordike. Mother, Sarah Perkins.
quotes.c: Will of David Perkins of Wellingborrow, 1731/2, Calendar of New Jersey Wills, Lib. 8, p. 184

quotes.t: Includes cane and sword, £1.10.
quotes.c: Inventory of Jacob Perkins Sr., 20 May 1731, Calendar of New Jersey Wills, Lib. 3, p. 102

src: Calendar of New Jersey Wills, Administrations, etc. (New Jersey Archives, 1st series), Perkins estates, 1731–32, Lib. 3 pp. 102 and 169 and Lib. 8 p. 184: https://archive.org/details/calendarofnewjer01newj
kv: David Perkins, 1731/2: "Sister, Rebecca, wife of Henry Nordike. Mother, Sarah Perkins."
