stories.note: The calendar abstracts the wills; the originals have not been read. That Henry and Rebecca's son Abraham is the Abraham Nordyke who married Mary Rogers in 1761 comes from the family tree, not from these abstracts. Some trees identify Jacob Sr. with a man from Hampton, New Hampshire, who married Mary Philbrick, but no record has established that this man moved to New Jersey.
stories.place: Wellingborough (Willingboro), Burlington County, New Jersey. Parents of Rebecca, who married Henry Nordyke in 1731.

stories.title: Soldiers on the road to Huntsville: Giles County, 1862-1863
stories.hook: Abner Stevenson's son Gilbert was five months old when the first Federal troops marched into Pulaski.

subject.name: Giles County in the Civil War

body: Gilbert Franklin Stevenson was born near Pulaski on 17 November 1861, to Rev. Abner Stevenson and Martha. Goodspeed's county history says what the next four years were like around the family farm. "The county was continually overrun with both Federal and Confederate soldiers throughout the war, being on the line of march from Nashville to Huntsville, Ala. Pulaski, Lynnville, Elkton and Prospect were each visited by Federal troops in large numbers, and Pulaski and Lynnville were fortified." On Fort Hill above Pulaski "a formidable fort or earth-work was erected."

The first Federals to come in any number arrived in April 1862, when Col. Mark Monday brought a detachment of Gen. Negley's brigade from Columbia to drive off John Morgan's cavalry, who were plundering the Federal wagon trains. Gilbert was then about five months old. Monday camped at Pulaski until September 1862. In August 1863 Col. Hayes raided the county with a regiment of cavalry and camped a day and a night in Pulaski. In the same year, in Goodspeed's words, "Lynnville and Elkton were both raided by the Federals, the whole county, in fact, being relieved of horses, cattle and grain."

That October Gen. Wheeler retreated south through the county with Gen. Wilder after him, and in November "Gen. W. T. Sherman and his entire army passed through Giles County, en route to Chattanooga, making a short stop at Elkton." Bee Spring, the Methodist church Elam Stevenson helped found, stood in the Twentieth Civil District with Mount Pisgah and Mount Zion.

The book does not name Abner's household. What it gives is the setting: a Methodist preacher with a farm, a wife, and a new baby on a road that three armies used. Abner's nephews Coleman and Wilbur Stevenson served the other side from their own farms nearby, in the 32nd Tennessee.

quotes.t: The county was continually overrun with both Federal and Confederate soldiers throughout the war, being on the line of march from Nashville to Huntsville, Ala.
quotes.c: Goodspeed, History of Tennessee (1886), Giles County chapter, p. 759

quotes.t: the whole county, in fact, being relieved of horses, cattle and grain.
quotes.c: Goodspeed, History of Tennessee (1886), Giles County chapter, p. 759

src: Goodspeed, History of Tennessee (1886), Giles County chapter, pp. 758-760 and church list in the district descriptions, p. 766 (archive.org: historyoftenness00good).

stories.title: John Milton Garrison, a Mecklenburg boy who ended up in the legislature's Acts
stories.hook: Born at Cowans Ford in 1788, married in Wilson County at twenty-one, and divorced by the Kentucky General Assembly at fifty-nine.
body: John Milton Garrison was born on 4 October 1788 at Cowans Ford in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, and came as a boy with his parents to Warren County, Kentucky. On 6 December 1809 he married Martha "Patsey" Cannon in Wilson County, Tennessee. Patsey is said to have been born about 1788 in Mecklenburg County. John’s daughter Mary, born 17 October 1811, married Henry Satterfield; whether Patsey was her mother remains a lead because the records examined do not name Mary’s mother. In 1815 Allen County was formed from Warren and Barren counties, placing the family in a newly named county.

WikiTree transcribes the census index entry for "John M Garreson" in Warren County in 1810, and the transcription gives "Numbers of Slaves 1" in a household of five. That is one enslaved person in the household of a man of about 21. The transcribed returns for Allen County in 1820, 1830 and 1840 show no slaves: in each the total of all persons equals the total of free white persons (7, 11 and 7). The 1850 census shows him at 62, a farmer, with real estate valued at $2,250. No 1850 or 1860 slave schedule has been checked, so it is not known whether he held anyone after 1810. The 1810 count rests on a WikiTree transcription of an index, not on the schedule page itself.

The marriage ended in the legislature, by statute. The printed Acts of the 1847-48 session, section 6 on page 410, read: "That the marriage contract now existing between John M. Garrison, and his wife, Patsey Garrison, be and the same is hereby dissolved, and they are hereby restored to all the rights and privileges of unmarried persons." The section gives no reason. The volume's index lists it twice, once under "Garrison, Patsey, an act to divorce" and once, apparently by a slip, under "Harrison, John M."

WikiTree gives a reason from other records, but names no source for it. Its biography says that during the marriage he "fathered children by Sarah Stamps who lived nearby," that he "had the KY legislature declare those children legitimate," and that after the divorce he married Sarah. The 1850 census, as WikiTree transcribes it, lists J. M. Garrison, 62, with an "S" aged 57 and three younger Garrisons aged 21, 19 and 6. The legitimation act has not been located in the volumes searched, so that part is a lead. He died in Allen County on 18 September 1860. WikiTree gives Patsey’s death as about 1850 in Allen County; the estimate has not been independently verified.

Mary Garrison married Henry Satterfield and bore twelve children. The 1885 sketch of her son James calls her father "John M. Garrison, of Allen County, Ky." and adds "(now living at the age of seventy-five years)"; because John died in 1860, the parenthesis most likely describes Mary, who would have been 73 or 74 in 1885. John's parents may be Samuel and Esther (Alexander) Garrison, who came to Warren County from Mecklenburg, though no cited record names John Milton as their son (lead).

quotes.t: That the marriage contract now existing between John M. Garrison, and his wife, Patsey Garrison, be and the same is hereby dissolved, and they are hereby restored to all the rights and privileges of unmarried persons.
quotes.c: Acts of the General Assembly of Kentucky, session of 1847-48, p. 410, sec. 6

src: Kentucky: A History of the State (1885), Butler County, p. 676; Find a Grave; Acts passed at the session of the General Assembly for the Commonwealth of Kentucky (1847–48), ch. 600, sec. 6, p. 410 and index: https://archive.org/details/actspassedatses72kentgoog; WikiTree Garrison-4365, Garrison-3085 and Cannon-4655 (biography and census transcriptions); Tennessee State Marriages 1780–2002, Garrison–Cannon, Wilson County, 1809.

The Sarah Stamps children and their legitimation are a lead: WikiTree states them without a source and the act was not found. No record examined directly names Mary’s mother. Her attribution to Patsey rests on Mary’s birth during the marriage and the Cannon middle name already in the family tree.

stories.title: What a rented farm at Hagansport meant in 1910
stories.hook: The government's 1908 soil survey says what tenants paid, what the land near Hagansport grew, and why the north end of the county was held back.
body: In April 1910 John C. Satterfield, 46, was renting a farm at Hagansport, and John B. Smith and Emma Liza Langley Smith had farmed there in 1900. The U.S. Bureau of Soils surveyed Franklin County in 1908 and wrote about farming in just that corner, without naming any family.

On renting, the survey says that "the rental paid is on the usual share plan, by which the tenant furnishes everything but the land and buildings and receives one-half the crops. When the tenant furnishes only the labor he is given one-third of the corn and one-fourth of the cotton." In 1900 only 44.1 percent of the county's farms were run by their owners, and the average farm was 77.9 acres. Most land could be bought for $5 to $10 an acre, more in the Sulphur River bottoms. The authors add that "since that date many of the tenants have acquired title."

On Hagansport itself: the town sits on a divide between the Sulphur River and White Oak Creek, with bodies of Wilson clay loam "in the vicinity of Hagansport and Lavada." The survey calls that soil "somewhat better adapted to cotton than to corn," says it was nearly all in cultivation, and gives the cotton yield as "from one-third to three-fourths bale per acre." The bottoms along the river were "more or less subject to overflow." Of the north end of the county, the survey says: "Other small centers in the northern part of the county are Daphne, Lavada, and Hagansport. In this part of the county development is seriously hindered by the absence of adequate shipping facilities."
This is a general portrait. It does not say whether the Smiths owned or rented, or whether the Satterfields farmed on halves or thirds, but it describes the terms on which families like them worked.

quotes.t: The rental paid is on the usual share plan, by which the tenant furnishes everything but the land and buildings and receives one-half the crops.
quotes.c: Soil Survey of Franklin County, Texas (1908), p. 931

src: A. E. Kocher and W. S. Lyman, Soil Survey of Franklin County, Texas, in Field Operations of the Bureau of Soils, 1908 (USDA, 1909), pp. 931-947; archive.org: usda-soil-survey-of-franklin-county-texas-1908.

stories.note: The soil survey describes the area, not an individual ancestor; the family details come from census records.

stories.title: Fifteen children at Bee Spring
stories.hook: Frank Stevenson was one of fifteen children of a farming preacher, and a twin; the 1870 census lists eleven of them under one roof.

subject.name: The fifteen children of Abner and Martha Stevenson

body: Rev. Abner A. Stevenson and Martha S. Watson were married on 8 December 1838. A family history compiled from the Stevenson family sketches of the 1950s lists their fifteen children, all born in Giles County: Lucinda C. (3 May 1840), William Elam Fletcher (9 April 1842), Lydia Mary Eliza (20 December 1843), Catherine M. Frances (10 January 1846), Augustus Summerfield (30 October 1847), Ellen Tillman and James Willis (twins, 30 January 1850), Larkin Henry (12 October 1852), Amanda Elizabeth (21 October 1854), Julia Ann Desdemona (July 1857), John Edward Thomas (16 September 1859), the twins Gilbert Franklin and George Washington (both 17 November 1861), Wilson McAlister (15 August 1864) and Manerva Jane (22 July 1866).

The 1870 census, as printed on the WikiTree page for Frank, finds the household in District 10 with A. A. Stevenson, 54, Martha, 47, and eleven children: Lucinda 28, James 20, Ellen 20, Larkin 18, Amanda 16, Julia A. 14, John E. 12, George W. 8, Gilbert 8, Mack 5 and Manerva J. 3. The two eight-year-olds are the twins. By 1880 the house was nearly empty: Abner, 63, "Farming Preacher," Martha, 56, Gilbert F., 18, Wilson M., 16 and Jane M., 12, with three hired or fostered Whittaker children and a one-year-old grandchild named Berry Andrew, born in Alabama. The Andrew grandchild was probably the youngest son of Abner's daughter Eliza, who had died in November 1878 (lead).

Several of the dates check against the Bee Spring graveyard. W. Mack Stevenson is on the cemetery list as born 15 August 1864 and dead 30 June 1940, which matches Wilson McAlister. Nathan A. Stevenson, 12 November 1870 to 21 July 1936, is Abner's grandson Nathaniel, William's son. Werner W. Stevenson, 4 March 1880 to 23 June 1974, is James Willis's son. Abner himself lies there, as does Martha S., 19 February 1823 to 12 July 1887.

The children scattered. Lucinda married Perry Pittman Williams and died in 1920; Eliza Mary married John Newton Andrew on 20 December 1870 and died in 1878; Frances married J. M. Whitaker and died on 18 April 1889; Summerfield went to Arkansas and was buried near Crowley's Ridge; Ellen married James Marion Britton; Julia went to Texas as John Newton Andrew's third Stevenson wife; Edward died in El Paso; George became a judge at Lubbock; James Willis became a Methodist minister; Manerva married Andrew R. Merrill and moved to Ardmore, Tennessee. Frank went to Indiana.

quotes.t: Farming Preacher
quotes.c: Abner A. Stevenson's occupation, 1880 U.S. census, 10th District, Giles County, Tennessee

src: Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm); WikiTree profiles (api.wikitree.com) for Gilbert Franklin Stevenson (Stevenson-12558), Parsis Jane O'Neal (O'Neal-3514) and Daniel Waters O'Neal (O'Neal-2667), with the 1870, 1880 and 1910 census transcriptions printed there; Bee Spring Cemetery listing, Giles County, Tennessee (Giles Co. TNGenWeb cemetery page); Goodspeed list of Elam Stevenson's children, p. 872.
stories.note: The Casey family history names the fifteen children and their births; the 1870 and 1880 census households and the cemetery dates fit it, but the family history has no sources for the exact days.
stories.place: Giles County, Tennessee, with branches in Alabama, Arkansas and Texas

stories.title: Two Stevenson brothers go to Texas
stories.hook: One brother became a judge at Lubbock and the father of thirteen; another died of smallpox at El Paso in June 1886, working for the railway.
body: Frank Stevenson had a twin. George Washington Stevenson was born on the same day, 17 November 1861, and the 1870 census lists both as 8 years old in the same Giles County household. In May 1881 the Pulaski Citizen noted that "Judge Geo. Stevenson, son of Rev. A. Stevenson, returned from Texas last week." The family history says that George later lived at Lubbock, Texas, where he was a judge, and that he was the father of thirteen children. It names none of them.

John Edward Thomas Stevenson, born on 16 September 1859, appears in the 1870 census as "John E," 12. The family history says Edward "moved to Texas where he worked for the Texas and Pacific Railway" and "died of smallpox in El Paso, Texas on June 26, 1886." He would have been 26. The Texas and Pacific reached El Paso in 1881, so the job fits the date.

The pull of Texas runs through this family. In January 1881 their father "abandoned the idea of going to Texas." Their sister Julia Ann followed her husband John Newton Andrew there, and by the 1870s their sister Ellen Britton's growing family was moving between Giles County and Texas. When Frank and Parsis lived there in the 1890s and 1900s, three of their children were born in Texas.

quotes.t: Edward Stevenson moved to Texas where he worked for the Texas and Pacific Railway. Edward Stevenson died of smallpox in El Paso, Texas on June 26, 1886.
quotes.c: Casey family history, Master Publication 3-109

quotes.t: Judge Geo. Stevenson, son of Rev. A. Stevenson, returned from Texas last week.
quotes.c: The Pulaski Citizen, 5 May 1881, p. 2

src: The Pulaski Citizen, 5 May 1881, p. 2 (Library of Congress); Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm); 1870 U.S. census, District 10, Giles County, as transcribed on the Frank Stevenson WikiTree page.
stories.note: The El Paso death and the Lubbock judgeship come from the family history alone, which has no source for them. A Texas death record or a Lubbock County court record would settle both.
stories.place: Giles County, Tennessee; Texas

stories.title: One widower, three Stevenson wives
stories.hook: John Newton Andrew of Giles County married a Stevenson cousin, then a Stevenson sister, then Frank's other sister; the last wife took him to Texas.
body: John Newton Andrew was born in Giles County on 20 February 1841. His first wife was Mary Hamilton, a granddaughter of Rev. Elam Stevenson through Elam's daughter Catherine. His second, on 20 December 1870, was Eliza Mary Stevenson, Frank's sister, who bore him four sons (Baxter, Abner, Truman and Perry) and died on 16 November 1878. His third was Eliza's younger sister Julia Ann Desdemona Stevenson, born in July 1856 or 1857. The family history notes that Julia was thus "John's third marriage to a Stevenson woman."

Julia and John had four children, Ray, George, Tina Tisha and Alice. WikiTree places a son, Roy Jackson Andrew, at Rockwall, Texas, on 30 July 1893 and at his death at Wilbarger County, Texas, in 1964. John died on 28 March 1909 and Julia on 3 July 1928 at Vernon, Wilbarger County, according to WikiTree; its biography page gives 1925 as her death year, so the date is not settled.

Rockwall comes up again in this family. A WikiTree profile for the first husband of Parsis O'Neal, Frank's wife, puts his death in Rockwall County in 1901. If Frank and Parsis were among the Giles County Stevensons around Rockwall in the 1890s, the Texas births of their children Willie, Frank and Elisha would be explained (lead; see the Louderback story).
src: Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm); WikiTree profiles Stevenson-5863 (Julia Ann Desdemona), Andrew-1921 (John Newton Andrew) and Andrew-1917 (Roy Jackson Andrew).
stories.note: Julia's death year is given as 1925 and 1928 in different WikiTree fields, and her birth as 1856 and 1857. A Texas death certificate or Vernon cemetery record would settle it.
stories.place: Giles County, Tennessee; Rockwall and Wilbarger Counties, Texas

stories.title: Ellen Stevenson and the Brittons
stories.hook: A twin born in 1850 who married a Giles County farmer, went to Texas and back, and raised seven children.
body: Ellen Tillman Stevenson was born on 30 January 1850, the twin of James Willis. On 24 December 1871 she married James Marion Britton, born on 3 March 1840 in Giles County, the son of Wilson Britton and Elizabeth Ragains. His brother John Frank Britton died in Collin County, Texas, in 1890.

The family history names seven children: Logan Harwell, Sarah Beulah, Amanda Elizabeth, an infant daughter, Wilson Arrington, James Wilson Lafayette "Fate," and Carlos Erskine. In the 1880 census of Friendship, Crockett County, James and Ellen's household included son L. H., age seven, and daughters B. V., age five, and M. E., age three. The family history gives Logan's birth as 17 September 1872 and Sarah Beulah's as 24 January 1873; these dates are only four months apart and cannot both be accepted without further evidence. By 1900 Ellen and James were back in Giles County.

James died on 18 September 1913 in Giles County and Ellen on 4 March 1927 (Find a Grave gives 4 February); both lie at Mount Zion (New Zion) Cemetery near Pulaski. Their daughter Amanda married Eli Bascom Pitts on 2 March 1892 and had eleven children. Sarah Beulah married Samuel McNeese and had eight, including twins who died the day they were born, 10 June 1902.
src: Robert Casey, Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families, pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (https://www.rcasey.net/acrobat/ste0301b.pdf); 1880 U.S. census, Friendship, Crockett County, Tennessee (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:MDQY-F5F); 1900 U.S. census, Logan Britton (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:MSCB-B5Z); Sarah Bulah McNeece, Tennessee death record, 1957 (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QKM9-KRS9); Find a Grave memorial 88644767; WikiTree profiles Stevenson-3637, Britton-1643 and Britton-2364.
stories.note: Birthplaces and the month of Ellen's death differ between the sources. The family history's 17 September 1872 birth date for Logan and 24 January 1873 date for Sarah Beulah are only four months apart. The 1880 census records a son L. H., age seven, and daughter B. V., age five; Logan's 1900 census gives September 1872. Sarah Beulah's 1957 death record names her parents James Britton and Ellen Stevenson but estimates her birth year as 1873; her grave memorial gives 24 January 1872. The exact dates and the identification of B. V. with Beulah remain unresolved.
stories.place: Giles and Crockett Counties, Tennessee; Texas

stories.title: A third-generation preacher with three wives
stories.hook: Frank's brother James Willis, a twin of Ellen, became a Methodist minister, married three times, and lived until 1943.
body: James Willis Stevenson, born on 30 January 1850, was the twin of Ellen. The family history calls him a Methodist minister. His first wife was a cousin, Nancy J. Stevenson, and their only son was Werner Wesley, born on 4 March 1880. After Nancy died he married Elizabeth A., and then Beatrice, born in October 1870 in Alabama. The 1900 census finds James and Beatrice in Giles County, and he later lived at Ardmore, Tennessee.

His second and third marriages gave him another ten children: Bessie (1885), Bertha (1887), Coleman (1893), Cletis Z. (1897), Lydia M. (1898), and Nore, Clower, Elizabeth, Charlie and Talmadge Dewitt. He died on 9 November 1943 and was buried at Bee Spring, the church his grandfather founded.

Werner Wesley (1880-1974) stayed in Giles County and married Lila Mitchell. Their daughter Nannie married Robert Hulsey, born in January 1904; a family letter of 1997 from "Nannie (Stevenson) Hulsey" is one of the sources for the family history. No connection between this Giles County Hulsey and Katie Stevenson's husband Oscar Hulsey has been shown (lead).
src: Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm) (James Willis Stevenson, Werner Wesley Stevenson); Bee Spring Cemetery listing, Giles County, Tennessee (Giles Co. TNGenWeb cemetery page); 1900 and 1920 censuses, Giles County, as cited in the family history.
stories.note: The 1943 death date comes from the family history; the cemetery list used here has no matching entry for him.
stories.place: Giles County, Tennessee

stories.title: A preacher with soldier sons and a short-lived brood
stories.hook: Elam's oldest surviving son raised eight children on a Giles County farm, buried four before 1857, and sent two sons into the Confederate 32nd Tennessee.

subject.name: Rev. William Payne Stevenson and Malinda (Rowe)

body: William Payne Stevenson was born on 27 September 1810 in North Carolina, the oldest son of Rev. Elam Stevenson. On 14 October 1830 he married Malinda Rowe in Giles County. Goodspeed (1886) says he "has four brothers who are ministers of the gospel," and that he settled on his farm in 1838. He lived to 14 January 1892; Malinda died on 21 January 1888. He is buried at Bee Spring.

The family history lists nine children: an infant son who lived and died in 1831; Coleman Lafayette (26 December 1832); Elam R. (1835); Joseph J. (1837); Sarah Ann P. (10 March 1840); Wilbur Marion (20 January 1841); Presley W. (8 September 1847); William F. (19 January 1853); and John Henry (1856). Six of the nine did not reach adulthood. The family history gives Presley W.'s death as 30 June 1849 (the cemetery list reads 30 July), Elam R. on 2 August 1854, William B. F. on 19 August 1854 and Joseph J. on 15 February 1856. Sarah died on 10 February 1846.

The two grown sons went to war. Goodspeed says Coleman "enlisted in the Thirty-second Tennessee Regiment of Volunteers" in 1862 and "served until the close of the war," taking part "in most of the principal battles." The same book says the 32nd was organized at Camp Trousdale in the summer of 1861, with four Giles County companies, and went first to East Tennessee and Kentucky. Goodspeed's orders of battle for the Army of Tennessee place the 32nd in Brown's Brigade of the division of Gen. C. L. Stevenson (no kin), and the county chapter says it was reorganized at Jackson, Mississippi. Wilbur Marion served in the same regiment until the fall of 1864, "when left the service due to ill health."

Coleman raised not only his own sons but three orphaned Jackson nieces of his wife (Martha V., Nancy M. and Mary J.). He died on 24 October 1908. Wilbur married Martha Jane Hampton on 9 November 1865. She died on 28 December 1918 and he died the next day, 29 December 1918, in Giles County. The sources do not give a cause, but their dates fall in the winter of the great influenza epidemic (lead).

quotes.t: He has four brothers who are ministers of the gospel, and his father was also a very prominent Methodist Episcopal minister.
quotes.c: Goodspeed, History of Tennessee (1886), Giles Co., sketch of Coleman L. Stevenson, p. 872

quotes.t: In 1862 Mr. Stevenson enlisted in the Thirty-second Tennessee Regiment of Volunteers, and served until the close of the war.
quotes.c: Goodspeed, p. 872

TNGenWeb cemetery page).
stories.note: The influenza suggestion is only a guess from the dates. Neither source states a cause for the 1918 deaths.
stories.place: Giles County, Tennessee

stories.title: The Stevenson row at Bee Spring
stories.hook: Four Stevenson burials between 1 February and 3 March 1856, two more in August 1854: the graveyard Elam founded shows how hard those years were.

subject.name: Bee Spring Cemetery, the Stevenson burials

body: Elam Stevenson bought fifteen acres for $20 in 1815 to found Bee Spring church. The cemetery behind it lists about seventy-five Stevenson entries. The tall stone over Elam and Lydia reads, on Elam's side, "Erected to the memory of Reverend Elam Stevenson, born September 24, 1787, died March 13, 1875. Nearly 62 years a minister of the gospel. He was pure in heart and life." On the back: "Erected to the memory of Lydia Stevenson, born August 16, 1787, died March 6, 1872. Nearly 70 years a Methodist. She consecrated her household to God and the church."

The listing shows how the family's children died. In the summer of 1854: Citty on 20 June, Elam R. on 2 August and William B. F. on 19 August. In the winter of 1856: Louisa (Coleman's young wife) on 1 February, Joseph J. on 15 February, Ann Eliza on 2 March and James Elisha on 3 March. An "infant" is dated 6 October 1831 (the first child of William and Malinda). Several more are listed only as "child" or "infant." The list does not record causes.

The family also kept its dead close. Rev. Abner A. is listed there with his wife Martha S. (1823-1887); his brother Rev. James C. (23 June 1813 to 23 February 1899) lies beside Margaret Caroline (8 December 1816 to 11 February 1886); Willis McKendree is there (18 January 1818 to 6 February 1900), as are Coleman L. (1832-1908), with Dorcas (1832-1892), and Thomas C. (1825-1906). The congregation also buried a Stevenson as late as 1994. The Pulaski Citizen noted in 1878 that "Here repose the sacred dust of old Father Stevenson and his beloved consort."

quotes.t: Nearly 62 years a minister of the gospel. He was pure in heart and life.
quotes.c: Elam Stevenson's gravestone, Bee Spring Cemetery, as quoted in the Casey family history, p. 3-98

quotes.t: Nearly 70 years a Methodist. She consecrated her household to God and the church.
quotes.c: Lydia Stevenson's gravestone, same stone, reverse side

src: Bee Spring Cemetery listing, Giles County, Tennessee (Giles Co. TNGenWeb cemetery page) (burial dates for Stevenson entries); Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm) (gravestone inscriptions, p. 3-98); The Pulaski Citizen, 30 May 1878, p. 1.
stories.note: The cemetery list gives no cause of death and does not say which Stevenson household each child belonged to; only the names matched in the family history are placed.
stories.place: Bee Spring Methodist Church, near Bunker Hill and Bryson, Giles County, Tennessee

stories.title: "They who bear the cross shall bear the crown"
stories.hook: Elam's eldest child moved to Alabama with her husband, raised nine children, and is quoted on her gravestone; her sons went on to Texas and Arkansas.
body: Catherine A. Stevenson was born on 2 October 1808 in North Carolina, the oldest of Elam and Lydia's eleven children. She married William B. Hamilton, born in 1808 or 1809 in South Carolina. Their nine children were Lydia J. (1832), Mary A. (1834), James (1839), Elam Carr (1 February 1842), Clatinda I. (20 January 1844), George Worth (1846), Thomas C. (1848), Gilbert William (1850, in Alabama) and John Baxter (30 April 1853, in Limestone County, Alabama). The family was in Limestone County in 1860, 1870 and 1880.

William died on 8 September 1872 and was buried in the Wallace Cemetery in Limestone County. Catherine died on 2 December 1888, and the same cemetery has her stone: "Mrs. C.A. Hamilton born October 2, 1808 died in great peace December 2, 1888. They who bear the cross shall bear the crown." A grandson, Robert J. Hamilton of Ripley, Alabama, described her as "a short, chubby, and very cheerful little lady."

Her children moved west. Her son George became a Methodist minister. Clatinda never married and died on 4 March 1892. Gilbert William married Martha J. Thorpe and lived in Greene County, Arkansas, where their daughter Bessie was born on 31 March 1880; Martha died on 19 May 1881, Gilbert on 6 June 1896, and both were buried at Pruetts Chapel. John Baxter married Mary Arantha Lynch in Kaufman County, Texas, on 31 January 1884 and had nine children there. Her daughter Mary A. became the first wife of John Newton Andrew, who later married two of Frank's sisters.

quotes.t: Mrs. C.A. Hamilton born October 2, 1808 died in great peace December 2, 1888. They who bear the cross shall bear the crown.
quotes.c: Gravestone, Wallace Cemetery, Limestone County, Alabama, as quoted in the Casey family history, p. 3-99

src: Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm) (Catherine A. Stevenson, pp. 3-99 to 3-103); WikiTree Stevenson-8354 (Catherine A. Stevenson) and Hamilton-23815.
stories.note: A 1950 Skinner family genealogy on archive.org (ancestryofcaroly00skin) prints a chart of Elam Stevenson (1787-1875) and what appears to be the opening of his will in Giles County Court, 1875, via the Hamilton line; the book is not available in full text and was seen only in search snippets.
stories.place: Giles County, Tennessee; Limestone County, Alabama

stories.title: A doctor and preacher who moved to Arkansas in 1858
stories.hook: Abner's younger brother carried the family trade to Arkansas, taught his sons the pulpit, and is buried at Booneville, not far from Danville where Frank later lived.
body: Elam Augustus Stevenson was born on 3 February 1829 in Giles County, the son of Rev. Elam and Lydia. He joined the Tennessee Conference of the Methodist Episcopal Church, South. The Minutes of the 1858 Conference record "Elam A. Stevenson, transferred to Wachita Conference" (Ouachita, in Arkansas). A 1930 Arkansas biography of his son says he "came to Arkansas and became pastor at El Dorado and Princeton" in 1858. His son James Baxter was born at Richmond, Arkansas, on 24 October 1860, and WikiTree puts Thomas Elam's birth at Booneville in April 1857, a year before the Minutes record the transfer, so he was in Arkansas earlier than 1858 (lead).

Ten years later he was back in Tennessee, where the 1870 census shows "E A Stephenson," 40, with Alabama-born wife H. S., 27, and sons Thomas, James and John. In 1875 the Minutes list him as "readmitted" and then "transferred to White River Conference," and appoint "Wittsburg, E. A. Stevenson," in the White River Conference of northeast Arkansas. The 1880 census finds him at Addison, Winston County, Alabama, aged 51 and married to Hannah, listed as a "Doctor & Preacher" with seven children at home. Hannah Celia Carolan, born in 1844 at Somerville, Alabama, died on 26 October 1884 at Carolan, Logan County, Arkansas. Elam A. died on 17 April 1886 and is buried at Oak Hill Memorial Cemetery, Booneville.

The 1930 biography says he "was a graduate of the Vanderbilt University" at Nashville. Vanderbilt did not open until 1875, when he was already 46, so the claim must be a family exaggeration. It also names his wife as "Earl (Cook)," which none of the census records supports, so the sons by his first marriage and by Hannah are not yet separated (lead).

quotes.t: Elam A. Stevenson, transferred to Wachita Conference.
quotes.c: Minutes of the Annual Conferences of the Methodist Episcopal Church, South, 1858 (archive.org item 27838123.1858.emory.edu)

quotes.t: Wittsburg, E. A. Stevenson.
quotes.c: Minutes of the Annual Conferences, MECS, 1875, appointments (archive.org item 27838123.1875.emory.edu)

src: Minutes of the Annual Conferences of the Methodist Episcopal Church, South, 1858 and 1875 (Emory/Internet Archive 27838123.1858 and .1875); Arkansas and Its People (1930), vol. 4, sketch of James Baxter Stevenson (archive.org arkansasitspeopl0004vari); WikiTree Stevenson-15611 and Stevenson-15610 with the 1870 and 1880 census transcriptions; Goodspeed list of Elam's children, p. 872.
stories.note: This Elam A. Stevenson is called "Elam A., Jr." in the Casey family history, which gives his wife as Mrs. Hannah Celia Wright.
stories.place: Giles County, Tennessee; Arkansas; Winston County, Alabama

stories.title: Frank's cousin the Arkansas Methodist
stories.hook: A cousin of the Hulsey ancestor Frank preached in Yell County in 1883, was the first pastor of Oklahoma City's Methodist church, and is the Rev. J. B. Stevenson whose 1932 letter is quoted for the family's years of preaching.
body: James Baxter Stevenson was born on 24 October 1860 at Richmond, Arkansas, the son of Rev. Elam A. Stevenson. His 1930 biography says he "grew up in Tennessee, to which State his father had returned when he was six," and that at nineteen he "returned to Arkansas and settled in Booneville, Logan County" (the 1930 text is hyphenated across a line). He was licensed to preach on 21 September 1881. In 1883 "the Arkansas Conference sent him to Yell County, where he remained for two years" and then to the Mulberry Circuit and to Paris, Logan County.

He became "the first pastor of the Methodist church in Oklahoma City" and later served at Guthrie, Fort Smith, Conway, Batesville, Morrillton, Dardanelle, Fayetteville, Paragould, Russellville and Ozark. The Conference Minutes confirm some of this: "Conway Station, J. B. Stevenson" in 1892, "Van Buren Station, J. B. Stevenson" in 1896, "Morrillton Station, J. B. Stevenson" in 1900. From 1927 he was pastor at Atkins. He married Lulu Briggs on 14 May 1885. They had four children, among them Eugene Hendrix, a Rhodes Scholar who studied at Oxford and took a doctorate at the University of Pennsylvania.

This is the J. B. Stevenson who wrote in 1932 that "Uncle Jimmie preached 63 years, Uncle Abner 54 years, Uncle John 48 years, my father E. A. Stevenson 38 years, Uncle Gilbert 25 years." The Giles County site that printed the letter calls it a letter to "Eugene Hendricks Stevenson," which fits his son Eugene Hendrix (lead). His Yell County parish of 1883-85 is the county where Frank Stevenson was living at Danville in 1910, and his father's burial place at Booneville is in the next county.

quotes.t: Uncle Jimmie preached 63 years, Uncle Abner 54 years, Uncle John 48 years, my father E. A. Stevenson 38 years, Uncle Gilbert 25 years.
quotes.c: Rev. J. B. Stevenson, 1932 family letter, Giles County TNGenWeb

quotes.t: In 1883 the Arkansas Conference sent him to Yell County, where he remained for two years.
quotes.c: Arkansas and Its People (1930), vol. 4

src: Arkansas and Its People: A History 1541-1930, vol. 4, sketch of James Baxter Stevenson (archive.org arkansasitspeopl0004vari); Minutes of the Annual Conferences, MECS, 1892, 1896 and 1900 (archive.org 27838123.1892, .1896, .1900 emory); letter of 1932 listed in the Giles County TNGenWeb Stories index.
stories.note: The 1932 letter is attributed on the Giles County site to "Rev. J. B. Stevenson, Elam's grandson"; James Baxter, then 72, is the grandson of that name found in the Minutes and the Arkansas biography.
stories.place: Richmond, Booneville and Atkins, Arkansas; Oklahoma City

stories.title: Golden-wedding preacher, and a general in the family
stories.hook: A Tennessee preacher’s family connects the Stevenson line to an Army Air Forces commander.

subject.name: Rev. James Calvin Stevenson and Margaret Caroline (Brown)

body: James Calvin Stevenson was born on 23 June 1813 in North Carolina and brought to Giles County as a babe. On 19 November 1835 he married Margaret Caroline Brown, born on 8 December 1816. County marriage returns of the 1850s and 1860s name "James C. Stevenson" as the officiating minister at several weddings, among them Swinney-Dyer on 19 January 1852, Young-Huff on 3 November 1852, Stovall-Stephenson on 3 September 1860 and Woodard-Barnfield on 25 August 1862.

On 20 August 1885 the Pulaski Citizen's county correspondent visited "our old friends, Rev. and Mrs. Jas. C. Stevenson of near Bryson," who "speak of celebrating their golden wedding in October." Margaret died on 11 February 1886. James lived until 23 February 1899 and is buried beside her at Bee Spring. His ten children included Catherine Eliza (1838) and another daughter, Sarah, who married James Hollon.

Eliza Catherine Stevenson married the Rev. William Thomas Andrews in 1856. In his 1912 autobiography he named her as the daughter of James C. and Margaret C. Stevenson and listed their son James David Andrews. James David’s 1937 memorial names his son Major General Frank M. Andrews; the Nashville Public Library’s family papers identify him as Frank Maxwell Andrews. He became a lieutenant general and the namesake of Andrews Field, now Joint Base Andrews.

quotes.t: speak of celebrating their golden wedding in October
quotes.c: The Pulaski Citizen, 20 Aug 1885, p. 3

quotes.t: Frank Andrews was a general and died off the coast of Iceland.
quotes.c: Casey family history, p. 3-107

src: Robert Casey, Interactive Family Histories, "Stevenson, Arrington and Tucker Families," Master Publication pp. 3-98 to 3-120 (http://www.rcasey.net/master/steelam.htm and steabner.htm) (James Calvin Stevenson, Catherine Eliza Stevenson); The Pulaski Citizen, 20 Aug 1885, p. 3; Bee Spring Cemetery listing, Giles County, Tennessee (Giles Co. TNGenWeb cemetery page); Giles County marriage returns (Giles Co. TNGenWeb marriage index, grooms S-Y); Wikipedia, "Frank Maxwell Andrews," early life.; W. T. Andrews, Memorial Sketches (1912), pp. 340–341, https://archive.org/details/memorialsketches00andr/page/340/mode/1up; The Pulaski Citizen, 10 Mar 1937, https://tngenweb.org/gilestn/obituaries/GC1930-1939_Obits.html; Nashville Public Library, James D. Andrews Papers, https://assets.library.nashville.gov/documents/finding-aids/Special_Collections_Division_Finding_Aid_AndrewsSeries2.pdf; Goodspeed (1886), https://www.tngenweb.org/goodspeed/giles/bios.html; Elam Stevenson will, https://ahgp.org/tn/giles/wills/stev.htm.
stories.note: The 1912 autobiography, 1937 newspaper account and Nashville Public Library papers identify the generations from James Calvin Stevenson to Frank Maxwell Andrews. Elam Stevenson’s will and the 1886 Goodspeed sketch support the connection between James Calvin and his brother Abner, the direct ancestor.
stories.place: Near Bryson, Giles County, Tennessee

stories.title: Parsis's brothers stayed home
stories.hook: Five of Daniel and Vashti O'Neal's sons and their youngest daughter lived out their lives in or near Gibson County, Indiana, while Parsis and Mary went west.

subject.name: The O'Neal brothers of Gibson County

body: Daniel Waters O'Neal and Vashti Pearson had ten children, and six of them are traced to adulthood on WikiTree. William Allen was born on 15 April 1863 in Tennessee (WikiTree; the 1880 census says Indiana), and died on 11 September 1933 in Pike County, Indiana, with burial at Blackfoot Cemetery. His wife was Nancy Jane Mason, born in 1865 at Oakland City, who died there on 20 June 1923.

John Sherman was born on 15 January 1866, a few months after the regiment mustered out, and died at Somerville on 19 July 1940. He married Jane Minerva Mitchell. George Johnson was born on 16 August 1875; the 1880 census says in Missouri, so the family spent some time there in the 1870s (WikiTree says Tennessee). He lost his first wife, Adella Douglas (born 1875), on 27 February 1906, married Sarah Eleen Reed, and died at Somerville on 12 June 1965 at 89. Daniel Clinton, born 9 June 1878, married Flora Nellie McGregor and died on 3 March 1954. David Commodore, born at Somerville on 22 March 1881, married Birdie Viola Rembe and died at Evansville on 7 May 1955.

The youngest, Charity Louisa, born on 19 December 1887, was the only daughter besides Parsis and Mary to live to adulthood. She married Fred Skomp, born on 7 May 1884 in Greene County, Indiana. He died at Hobart, Indiana, on 5 August 1949, and she died at Valparaiso on 15 November 1979. Vashti's 1919 obituary named her five living sons as William, John, George, Clinton and Commodore, and the daughters as Mrs. Frank Stevenson of Valiant, Oklahoma, and Mrs. Fred Skomp of Somerville.
src: Obituary of Vashti O'Neal, Jan 1919 (Find a Grave 24711779); WikiTree profiles O'Neal-3565, 3566, 3567, 3568, 3569, 3570 and spouse pages; 1880 U.S. census, Columbia Twp, Gibson Co., Indiana, as printed on the Parsis O'Neal WikiTree page.
stories.note: Death dates after 1900 are taken from WikiTree and are not checked against Indiana death certificates.
stories.place: Gibson and Pike Counties, Indiana; Missouri

stories.title: A hundred years from Indiana to Oklahoma
stories.hook: Parsis's oldest sister married three times, raised her children in Arkansas, and was feted at 100 by the Tuttle Times.
body: Mary Elizabeth O'Neal was born on 16 November 1860 in Gibson County, Indiana, the first child of Daniel and Vashti, ten months after their marriage. By 1878 she had married David Raliegh Farris, born in 1856 in Indiana. Their son Elmer Cooper Farris was born on 25 September 1878 at Princeton and died in Sequoyah County, Oklahoma, in 1948. A second son, Daniel Riley, born in Arkansas on 23 March 1881 and recorded as Fairce, died at Mead, Oklahoma, in 1968.

On 10 February 1884, in Arkansas, Mary married Joseph McConnell Rinker, 29, born in Iowa. WikiTree lists their children: Lydia Bell (1885, Sunset, Arkansas), Armenda Mae (1888), Cynthia Jane (1890), Joseph Jonathan (1892, Fayetteville), Vasha (1895, died 1897), Oscar Ashel (1897), Letha Agnes (1900) and Alta (1902, died 1906). Joseph was in Roger Mills County, Oklahoma, in 1910 and died on 27 May 1919 at Wapanucka.

Her obituary in the Tuttle Times of 22 December 1960 says Mrs. Mary Elizabeth Wilson, 100, "was born in Gibson County, Indiana, near Evansville, and spent most of her early life in Missouri, and raised her children in Arkansas. She first came to Oklahoma in 1907 and moved to Tuttle, from Faxton, in 1926." She "celebrated her 100th birthday in Nov 16, 1960, and passed away at her home on Wednesday, Dec 14, 1960." Survivors included "3 sons, 3 daughters, 51 grandchildren, 150 great-grandchildren, & 73 great great grandchildren." She was buried in Fairlawn Cemetery. Her third husband, James Calvin Wilson, born in 1867 at Princeton, Indiana, is listed with her on WikiTree.
Katie's brother Eddie was born in McCurtain County, Oklahoma, in July 1907, the same year Mary first came to Oklahoma.

quotes.t: She first came to Oklahoma in 1907 and moved to Tuttle, from Faxton, in 1926.
quotes.c: Tuttle Times, 22 Dec 1960, obituary of Mrs. Mary Elizabeth Wilson, as transcribed on WikiTree O'Neal-2666

src: Tuttle Times, 22 Dec 1960 (transcribed in Find a Grave 41943603 and WikiTree O'Neal-2666); WikiTree Rinker-451, Farris-3080, Wilson-112326 and the children's profiles.
stories.note: Names and dates for her children and husbands are from WikiTree; the Rinker and Wilson marriages are not checked against a county marriage register.
stories.place: Gibson County, Indiana; Missouri; Arkansas; Tuttle, Oklahoma

stories.title: Seven children in the 1910 census
stories.hook: The 1910 census at Danville, Arkansas, lists Katie, the baby, with six older brothers and sisters born in Indiana, Texas and Oklahoma.
body: The 1910 census, enumerated at Danville, Yell County, on 18 April, lists Frank Stevenson, 51, "Clergyman," his wife Jane, 41, and these children: Delphia, 18, born in Indiana; Willie, 16, Texas; George, 12, Indiana; Frank, 8, Texas; Elisha, 6, Texas; Eddie, 2, Oklahoma; and Katie, under one year, Arkansas. Frank and Jane told the enumerator they had been married 25 years and that seven children had been born. These are the seven.

Delphia was the oldest daughter. In her own obituary in 2009 Katie was said to have been preceded in death by "daughters Delphia and Mary," so she named a daughter for her sister. Willie was born in Texas about 1894. George Sherman Stevenson died on 3 June 1978 at Kilgore, Gregg County, Texas, and his mother Parsis Jane (O'Neal) Stevenson is named on the Texas death certificate cited in WikiTree. Frank, born about 1902 in Texas, is "Frank Lester" in other trees. WikiTree's list of the children calls the sixth one "Allen" where the census has Elisha.

The youngest brother, Horace Edward "Eddie," was born on 13 July 1907 in Garvin, McCurtain County, Oklahoma. He married Edith Marie Shunkey (born 29 July 1911 at Muskogee, died 2 April 2003 at King City, Oregon), and he died on 1 February 1998 at Portland, Oregon.

Other trees give a different list for the same parents: Iva Myrtle (1884), Adison Galiton (1886), Nellie Vashti (1889), Frank Lester (1902), Horace Edward (1907) and Katie. Iva Myrtle, Adison and Nellie would have been 26, 24 and 21 in 1910, so they could have been grown and away; WikiTree's list does not include them, and their link to this family is not documented (lead).
src: 1910 U.S. census, Danville, Yell Co., Arkansas, as transcribed on the WikiTree pages for Parsis Jane O'Neal (O'Neal-3514) and Gilbert Franklin Stevenson (Stevenson-12558); WikiTree Stevenson-5100 (Horace Edward Stevenson); Texas death certificate 1978, George Sherman Stevenson, cited on WikiTree O'Neal-3514.
stories.note: Delphia, Willie, George, Frank, Elisha and Eddie are the names on the 1910 census page; the later given names in other trees are not proven. The census is also the only record yet seen for Willie and Delphia.
stories.place: Indiana, Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas

stories.title: A sixteen-year-old bride in Pulaski County
stories.hook: An Arkansas marriage index records Parsis J. O'Neal, 16, marrying a 40-year-old Otho Louderbank on Christmas Day 1884, and her grave memorial still carries the Louderback name.
body: The WikiTree page for Parsis Jane O'Neal quotes a FamilySearch index of "Arkansas Marriages, 1837-1944": "Parsis J O Neal and Otho Louderback were married 25 December 1884 in Pulaski County, Arkansas. Otho was 40, Parsis, 16 years old." The index spells the groom "Louderbank." Pulaski County is Little Rock. In Gibson County, Indiana, at the 1880 census, Parsis, 11, had been in her father's household. Parsis's sister Mary was also in Arkansas by February 1884.

William Ortho Louderback was born about 1836 to 1844 at Princeton, Gibson County, the same county as the O'Neals. WikiTree gives his death in 1901 in Rockwall County, Texas, and lists a daughter, Henrietta Louderback, born in Illinois and dead in Texas in 1955, as a child of Parsis and him.

The Find a Grave memorial that WikiTree cites for her grave at Hugo is titled "Parsis Jane O'Neal Louderback (26 Mar 1868-26 Jan 1956)," so she was remembered under the Louderback name to the end, while the same WikiTree page lists the Stevenson children after the note "Marriage to Stevenson ..... Citation Needed." The 1910 census says Frank and Jane had been married 25 years, which would put that wedding in 1885, months after the Louderback record. Either the 1910 answer is loose, or the Stevenson household began without a recorded marriage, or the Louderback marriage ended early. No record seen settles it. Willie, Frank and Elisha Stevenson were born in Texas after 1894, where Otho Louderback died in 1901 (lead).
src: WikiTree O'Neal-3514 (Parsis Jane O'Neal), Louderback-86 (William Ortho Louderback) and Louderback-85 (Henrietta Louderback), quoting "Arkansas Marriages, 1837-1944," FamilySearch F73Z-LQF; 1910 census, Danville, Yell Co., Ark.
stories.note: The marriage record itself has not been seen. Both the Louderback surname index and the bride's age should be checked against the Pulaski County, Arkansas, marriage register for 25 December 1884.
stories.place: Pulaski County, Arkansas; Illinois; Rockwall County, Texas

stories.title: A juror in Cherokee County, the year of the roundup
stories.hook: In November 1838 Gilliam Graves sat on a county jury a few months after soldiers emptied the Cherokee farms of his county into a stockade.

subject.name: Gilliam Graves in Cherokee County, Georgia

body: Gilliam Graves is on the Cherokee County, Georgia, jury lists twice, in December 1835 and on 5 November 1838. The county had been carved out of the Cherokee Nation's Georgia land, and the state gave that land to white men by lottery in 1832. Its seat, first called Etowah, is Canton today.

In May 1838 the rest of the story arrived. Gen. Winfield Scott set up at the Cherokee capital, New Echota, and on 10 May told the Cherokee that "before another moon had passed every Cherokee man, woman, and child must be in motion" for the West. About 7,000 regulars, militia and volunteers were used. Stockade forts were built to hold the people until they could be moved, and Mooney lists five in Georgia: Fort Scudder in Lumpkin County, Fort Gilmer in Gilmer County, Fort Coosawatee in Murray County, Fort Talking Rock in Pickens County and "Fort Buffington, near Canton, in Cherokee county."

Mooney, who gathered the story from people who had lived it, wrote: "Families at dinner were startled by the sudden gleam of bayonets in the doorway and rose up to be driven with blows and oaths along the weary miles of trail that led to the stockade. Men were seized in their fields or going along the road, women were taken from their wheels and children from their play." Looters followed the soldiers, and many families, looking back from a ridge, "saw their homes in flames." A Georgia volunteer later said: "I fought through the civil war and have seen men shot to pieces and slaughtered by thousands, but the Cherokee removal was the cruelest work I ever knew."

When about seventeen thousand people had been gathered into the stockades the removal began. Mooney says "hundreds died in the stockades and the waiting camps," mostly from the rations, and that "over 4,000" Cherokee died as a direct result of the removal.

Nothing in the record says what Gilliam saw or did that summer. The jury lists place him in the county; they do not say where he lived in it. But when he was called to serve on 5 November 1838, the Cherokee families of his county had been gone from their farms for some months. By 1853 he was on the tax lists of Montgomery County, Arkansas, and in January 1864 he volunteered as a Union private at the age of 45.

quotes.t: I fought through the civil war and have seen men shot to pieces and slaughtered by thousands, but the Cherokee removal was the cruelest work I ever knew.
quotes.c: A Georgia volunteer, quoted in James Mooney, Myths of the Cherokee (1900), p. 130

src: Gilliam Graves's Cherokee County jury service (Dec 1835 and 5 Nov 1838) as given on his own page; James Mooney, Myths of the Cherokee, 19th Annual Report of the Bureau of American Ethnology (1900), "The Removal, 1838-39," pp. 130-133, and the note "Removal forts, 1838" (https://archive.org/details/mythsofcherokee00moon); Wikipedia, Cherokee County, Georgia (land lottery of 1832; Etowah, now Canton, county seat 1833)
kv: 10 May 1838, Gen. Winfield Scott at New Echota
Montgomery Co., Ark., tax lists by 1853; Union volunteer 1864
stories.note: Gilliam's jury service comes from the Graves family compilation cited on his own page; Mooney does not mention him or any juror. The page numbers are those of the Annual Report edition. This is a place-and-time story: nothing seen says Gilliam took any part in the roundup.
stories.place: Cherokee County, Georgia

stories.title: "Hung up to the first limb": Doaksville, June 1861
stories.hook: In the first week of June 1861 a Northern missionary learned that a meeting at Doaksville, the town where Vincent Tims kept store, had called for hanging men who would not take the South's side.
body: John Edwards, a Presbyterian missionary from New York, had taught at Spencer Academy and since 1853 ran Wheelock Seminary for Choctaw girls. In 1861, as the Choctaw Nation was pressed toward the Confederacy, he refused to pledge himself to take up arms for the South. His account of what followed was printed by the Oklahoma Historical Society a century later, with the editor's remark that a writer at Goodland had told her of the story, "It just would not do to print!"

A few weeks earlier, riding back from Pine Ridge, Edwards had come through Doaksville and found that "The Confederate flag was flying over the town." On 1 and 2 June the Principal Chief, George Hudson, and Peter Pitchlynn stayed with the Edwardses on their way to a special council at Doaksville. Hudson carried a message recommending neutrality; Edwards later heard "that he was compelled by a vigilance committee to change it recommending the Choctaws to join the South."

Then, he writes, "On Thursday afternoon I learned that on Wednesday a public meeting had been held at Doaksville, the capital, at which Capt. Robert M. Jones, the wealthiest Choctaw, took the ground that 'every man that was not with them must be hung up to the first limb between heaven and hell.'" The next morning a neighbor, Mrs. Dukes, came to say "the committee are to be here today to hang you." He handed his keys to a friend, had his pony Jerry saddled, prayed with his wife and was on the road "probably within 15 minutes of the time the word came." His plan was that Mrs. Edwards would follow with the children, and the editor credits her with managing the family's escape.

Jones, the editor's note says, owned about 500 enslaved people, plantations on the Red River and "a large store at Doaksville." His house, Rose Hill, stood east of present Hugo; the state encyclopedia says it burned in 1912.

Vincent B. Tims had been a trader at Doaksville since the late 1830s, in the firm of Doak & Tims, and in 1864 he signed Confederate mail contracts there as "V. B. Tims, P. M." The Edwards account never names him, and nothing seen says what Tims said or did that week. It records only the town where he did business and the climate in it.

quotes.t: every man that was not with them must be hung up to the first limb between heaven and hell.
quotes.c: Capt. Robert M. Jones, as reported by John Edwards, Chronicles of Oklahoma 43 (1965), p. 72

quotes.t: The Confederate flag was flying over the town.
quotes.c: John Edwards, Chronicles of Oklahoma 43 (1965), p. 70

stories.place: Doaksville, Choctaw Nation

stories.title: The logging train that ran away, 25 June 1915
stories.hook: A log hauler jumped from a runaway train on the Pine Belt Lumber Company's railroad near Fort Towson and broke his leg; the company said he had signed away his right to sue.

subject.name: The Pine Belt logging train, 25 June 1915

body: The Pine Belt Lumber Company ran a mill, dry kilns and planers at Fort Towson and a railroad about 15 miles north into the woods, along which it logged. Clifford Riggs hauled logs by wagon and team and was paid $2 a day. His petition says the company gave its workers passes to ride the train between Fort Towson and the woods.

On 25 June 1915, Riggs says in his petition, he boarded a train near his work and "the train in going down a steep grade got out of the control of the train men operating the same and ran away down the grade." He "believed that the only chance to save his life was by jumping." He landed with a compound fracture of the right leg and ankle, was in bed 32 days, and said his injuries were permanent. He sued in the Choctaw County district court for $6,000, charging that the air brakes and steam brakes were old, worn and insufficient, and had been for a long time.

The company answered that its track was only a tramway for hauling logs and not a common carrier, that Riggs had been careless and had accepted the risk, and that before boarding he had signed a paper releasing it from any claim for injuries on the train. A jury found for Riggs.

On 6 April 1920 the Oklahoma Supreme Court affirmed. A contract, it said, "whereby the servant, in consideration of the employment, or of the wages, agrees to release and discharge his master from liability on account of injuries caused by the negligence of his master" is forbidden by the state constitution and "void as against public policy." The opinion does not state how much the jury awarded.

Two years after Riggs jumped, Grady Moffitt, 25, put "timberman" and "C. D. Neese, Ervin, Oklahoma" on his draft card in the same county. Which sawmill bought his timber is not recorded, and the county's biggest sawmill was the Pine Belt company's at Fort Towson. Nothing links Riggs to the family. The case shows what a timber hand's day could end in, and what a signed paper did not protect against.

quotes.t: the train in going down a steep grade got out of the control of the train men operating the same and ran away down the grade

stories.title: A Sunday in August 1898: the Austin murder at Hagansport
stories.hook: In August 1898 a farmer near Hagansport was shot on his way to his field by a man hired at the sawmill; the court cases ran until 1906.

subject.name: J. P. Austin, killed near Hagansport

body: On Sunday, 28 August 1898, J. P. Austin walked from his house toward his field in the bottom, "across the lake," and did not come home. His wife Ella took the children to church at Hagansport, a mile or a mile and a half away. That night he was still gone. On Monday morning she went back to Hagansport and asked a neighbor named Martin to look for him, and told him to try the trail from the lake to the field.

He was found there, killed. The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals later said the killing occurred "twelve or thirteen miles north" of Mount Vernon. Ella Austin, by then Mrs. Johnson, told the jury why she knew where to send Martin. She said that H. J. Carbough "wanted me to take the life of my husband so that he and I could marry," and that she refused. Weeks later he said he would not do it himself, "but would get some one that would." In July he told her "there was a man at the sawmill by the name of T. C. Wallace and that he would be all right to do the work," for "seventy-five or a hundred dollars." The week before the killing, she said, Carbough warned her not to let the oldest little boy go with his papa.

On the evening of the killing, she testified, Wallace came to her house on foot, carrying a long bundle wrapped in a sack, and said: "Your man is down yonder; the work is done; the man is down yonder between the fields on the trail. You know me by Carbough."

Wallace was held in jail for months before he was indicted, and was tried in Franklin County five days after the indictment, some five years after the killing. The jury gave him death. On 8 June 1904 the Court of Criminal Appeals reversed, finding that he should have had a continuance to bring in witnesses and that the prosecutor had urged the jury that if he was not at the scene, "in God's name he should have told where he was." The case was moved to Camp County and tried again; on 31 May 1905 the court reversed that verdict too, for errors in instructing the jury about the testimony of accomplices. Carbough was tried in Camp County as an accomplice and given life in the penitentiary, and on 7 March 1906 the court affirmed.

The opinions do not say what became of Wallace after the second reversal, or whether the widow was ever charged. They place the murder in the Hagansport neighborhood during the years the Smiths were farming there: Charles Oscar was nine in the summer of 1898, and by 1900 his father owned the farm. Nothing seen connects the family to anyone in the case.

stories.title: A quarrel over the log count at the Frogville sawmill
stories.hook: In July 1912 a log cutter shot the scaler at the Frogville sawmill five times over a pay settlement, thirteen years before John Moffitt was born there.
body: Frogville, on the Red River in Choctaw County, was a place of about forty families when John Winfred Moffitt was born there in October 1925. Thirteen years earlier it had a sawmill, and the sawmill had a log scale. Sloan Pool kept it; a man named Wyrick was the sawyer. The log count in the scaler's book was what a cutter's settlement was figured from, so what he wrote was money.

On 18 July 1912 Pool went out to scale logs with Jess Allen and the old logger A. F. Buxton. A. F. Buxton's son John joined them. Allen, an eyewitness, said they all sat on a log while Pool showed John the book, with every log set down. John said he did not want it to be "like the last month's pay day," and the two argued about whether Pool had "figured" him out of money. Allen said that Pool replied, "in that way I mean to dispute your word," and "John shot him." Pool was hit five times. Allen swore that John stood over the body and said, "the next log you scale will be in hell," and shot him again. Then, Allen said, John took Pool's knife from his pocket, asked "how are you going to swear about this?", cut his own arm with it and pressed the knife into the dead man's hand.

Witnesses said Buxton had been talking for weeks. On the day, a man heard him say he would have his settlement from "those damned fellows over there." At the start of July another had heard him say that "the company was beating him" and that he meant to kill Pool. Buxton swore the opposite: that Pool had cut him once on the breast and twice on the arm with "a little old pocket knife," that he had been carrying the pistol because he was told two men were waiting in the woods to kill him, and that "I shot him to keep him from killing me." His sister, Mrs. Ruth Holden, said Allen had told her in jail that he had sworn falsely against her father.

The jury in the Choctaw County district court found John Buxton guilty of murder on 21 November 1912 and set his punishment at death; his father was found not guilty. The judge sentenced him on 27 November to be hanged. On 22 September 1914 the Criminal Court of Appeals affirmed. Because a new state law on executions had taken effect while the appeal was pending and the date fixed had passed, it sent the case back to Choctaw County to set another day. The opinion says nothing about what followed.

The Moffitts were not yet in the county in 1912; at the 1910 census Grady, 18 or 19, was in Stone County, Arkansas, making barrel staves. By 1917 he was a timberman at Ervin, in this same timber country. The record shows what a day at a mill in Choctaw County could come to when the scale and the pay disagreed.

quotes.t: the next log you scale will be in hell
quotes.c: John Buxton, as testified by Jess Allen; Buxton v. State, 11 Okla. Crim. 85 (1914)

stories.place: Frogville, Choctaw County, Oklahoma

stories.title: Jesse and Hannah: a license, a grant and a widow who remarried
stories.hook: Jesse Blackshear bought a marriage license in Jones County about 1788, took up 77 acres in 1796, and vanishes from North Carolina; his widow Hannah is the one who shows up in Tennessee court in 1814.
body: Jesse's North Carolina paper trail is short. A 1954 Blackshear genealogy lists him as a chain-bearer on a Jones County survey in 1782 and again in 1789. Between 1787 and 1789 he paid ten shillings for a marriage license in Jones County, with no bride named. The 1790 census for Jones County counts him as one man over sixteen with two females in the house. In 1794 he entered a plea for land, and in 1796 he was granted 77 acres on the south side of the Trent River (Grant Book 91). After 1796 the book says he was 'not found in N.C.'

The Tennessee record picks him up. In October 1814 the Williamson County court settled the estate of 'Jesse Blackshare, Dec'd.' His widow and administrator, by then 'Hannah Mairs, wife of Isaac Mairs,' showed a balance of $227.30 'subject to a division between Penny Blackshare and James Blackshare and the above named Legatees,' who are named as Ezekiel, Elisha, Luke, David, Elijah, Jacob and Jesse. So Jesse had at least nine living children in 1814, and one of them is called Penny, the name Penelope Blackshear Grimes went by.

Hannah was a Huggins. A WikiTree profile gives her birth as 20 May 1771 in Jones County and her death as 4 June 1829 in Wayne County, Tennessee, buried in Brown Cemetery, with a second husband, Isaac Mairs or Marrs, and a child by him born about 1807. Her youngest Blackshear child is given as born in March 1804, so Jesse's death and her second marriage fall between 1804 and about 1807. Her father is very probably the Luke Huggins whose Jones County will of 1784 names a daughter Hannah.

The two families were tied twice. Jesse's father, Elisha Stout Blackshear, named 'James Huggins' as a son-in-law and his granddaughter 'Susanna Huggins' in his will, so a Huggins had already married a Blackshear daughter; Hannah, a Huggins, married a Blackshear son. Both families lived in Jones County.

stories.note: Jesse's father is stated in a printed genealogy, not in his father's will: Elisha Stout Blackshear's will names only sons Moses and Jacob, and the book says the other sons had already had their share and left. The book names no wife for Jesse; Hannah Huggins rests on WikiTree and a Texas family website. WikiTree's date of 26 July 1803 for Jesse's death sits oddly beside an estate settled in 1814, and WikiTree's 1814 death for Penelope is wrong if she was alive in 1850. Penny as the wife of John Grimes is probable, not proved; the next link down (that David H. Grimes of Wayne County was their son) is only a lead.
stories.place: Jesse was born in Jones (or Craven) County, North Carolina, about 1767, married there about 1788, and took his family to Williamson County, Tennessee, between 1800 and 1810. Hannah Huggins, born in Jones County in 1771, outlived him, remarried, and died in Wayne County, Tennessee, in 1829. Their daughter Penny is the probable wife of John Grimes.

stories.title: Luke Huggins and his 1784 will
stories.hook: A Jones County planter's will leaves a shilling each to his older children and the rest to the youngest, and one of the youngest is Hannah.
body: Luke Huggins was born about 1715, probably in North Carolina, and was a planter in Jones County, which was cut off from Craven County in 1779. He made his will on 8 March 1784 and it was proved in December of that year.

A published abstract of the Jones County wills reads: to his wife Nelly, the plantation where he lived 'as long as she is a widow or as long as she lives'; to daughters Phebe Shelfer, Sarah Standley and Nelly Littleton, and sons James, Luke and Isaac, one shilling each; to his son Jacob, the land where he lived 'with all the rest of my lands'; and the remainder of the estate to 'my youngest children, namely: Esther, Hannah, Thomas, Charles, and Temperance Huggins,' at his wife's death. Simon Spight and John Parry were executors, and Nathan Bryan, Waxel Parry and Adonijah Parry witnessed.

Hannah was about thirteen. She married Jesse Blackshear a few years later, and the Jones County papers show other ties between the two families: Jesse's father named a James Huggins as son-in-law. A James is also among Luke's sons, so the two families may have married in both directions.

quotes.t: my youngest children, namely: Esther, Hannah, Thomas, Charles, and Temperance Huggins
quotes.c: Will of Luke Huggins, Jones Co., N.C., 8 Mar 1784 (abstract in Gwynn, Abstracts of the Wills, vol. A)

Luke's wife is called Nelly in the will; WikiTree's dates for her (born 1718, died 8 March 1784) match the date of the will, so they are not her own, and none are given here.

stories.title: Elisha Stout Blackshear's will: a black horse named Pal
stories.hook: Elisha's 1808 will leaves a granddaughter a black horse called Pal and a bed, and gives two grown sons nothing but their clothes because they had already had their share.
body: Elisha Stout Blackshear was born near Little Creek in Kent County, Delaware, about 1736, the son of Alexander and Agnes Blackshear, who left Delaware for Craven County, North Carolina, in the 1740s. His wife was Susanna. A 1954 Blackshear genealogy calls her 'probably Ward': Enoch Ward of neighboring Carteret County named a daughter Susannah in his will, and Elisha's youngest son Jacob later named a son Enoch and lived beside an Enoch Ward in Georgia. No marriage bond has been found for either of them.

He was his father's executor. When Alexander's will was proved in Jones County in September 1786, 'Elisha Blackshear one of the Executors herein named qualified.' His mother's will of 1793 left him 'one Stone Jug for the service he hath done,' and her granddaughter Agnes, 'Elisha Blackshear's Daughter,' eight barrels of corn and her pockets and silver clasps.

His own will, dated 11 December 1808 and proved in November 1810, starts: 'I lend to my wife Susanna Blackshier (during her life or widowhood) my black Horse called Jack and all my household & kitchen furniture.' His sons Moses and Jacob get 'all my wearing clothes only, they having had their proportionable part of my Estate'; the daughters Rebecca, Susanna and Agnes 'have received their proportionable' share; Nancy gets an enslaved man and a young horse called Ball, Elizabeth gets the sheep, and Temperance gets the cattle, the hogs and the rest. To granddaughter Susanna Huggins he leaves 'my black horse called Pal, and one bed & furniture,' and to a granddaughter Koonce a bed. His sons-in-law James Huggins, Samuel Westbrook and Elijah Koonce share his carpenter's and plantation tools.

Jesse, our line, is not named in the will. The genealogy lists Jesse among the eleven children, says he 'moved to Tenn., and had Ezekiel,' and explains that the sons not named in the will, Alexander, James and Jesse, were presumed to have gotten their share earlier and 'struck out to find their fortunes in other parts.' Jesse's birth about 1767 fits Elisha, who would have been about thirty-one.

stories.title: Alexander and Agnes: from Delaware to the Trent
stories.hook: A Delaware clerk took Agnes aside in 1741 to ask whether she really agreed to sell the family farm; her own will of 1793, made with her mark, remembers a stone jug and some silver clasps.
body: In 1735 Robert Blackshaw deeded 100 acres at Little Creek Hundred in Kent County, Delaware, to 'My Son Alexander Blacksliare,' for 'the natural love I bear him.' The land was part of a tract called Blackshier Range, and Alexander already held a proprietary grant to survey it. Robert had been born in New Jersey and had come down the Delaware.

On 12 February 1740 (old style) Alexander and 'Agnis his wife, of Little Creek Hundred,' confirmed the sale of the 100 acres to the executors of Robert Carter of Dover Hundred, who had bought it in his lifetime for fifty pounds. The deed was acknowledged in the Court of Common Pleas on 14 May 1741, when, the clerk wrote, Agnes 'being secretly examined out of the hearing of the said husband did declare that she freely & voluntarily became a party.' Alexander signed with his mark. By 1747 Alexander was witnessing a will in Craven County, North Carolina; in 1748 he petitioned the council at New Bern for a grant.

Over forty years he built up a farm on the south side of the Trent. In 1779 he was taxed in Jones County on 517 acres and five enslaved people. He also turns up in the North Carolina Revolutionary army accounts of 1777 and 1786, in small amounts. His will, dated 3 October 1785, leaves his wife all his estate for her life, 'one Large Bible and one pair of Brass-headed Hand Irons' to his son James, a small house and one acre to his daughter Eleanor Bailey, 100 acres on the south side of the Trent to his son Abraham and then to Abraham's son Alexander, and 82 acres to Elisha until 'my Grandson Jacob Blackshear son of my son Elisha' reached twenty-one. Elisha and Nathan Bryan were executors, and it was proved in September 1786.

Agnes outlived him by seven years. Her will of 6 July 1793 gives 'Elisha Blackshear, my son, one Stone Jug for the service he hath done,' Abraham 'one barrel of Vinegar and my Garden,' and her granddaughter Agnes, 'Elisha Blackshear's Daughter,' eight barrels of corn due from a neighbor and 'my pockits and Silver Clasps.' She signed it 'Agnes B. Blackshear, her mark.' Her maiden name is not recorded.

stories.note: Both wills name Elisha as a son, which proves that link as the printed texts read; the printed texts are the book's transcriptions, not images. Agnes's maiden name is not known. The book says 'probably Stout' (Elisha Stout is the son's name), and WikiTree makes her a daughter of Benjamin Stout and Agnes Truax of Delaware. Stillwell's Stout genealogy lists only sons Charles, Benjamin and Jacob for that Benjamin, a wife Agnes of unknown surname, and no daughter Agnes. That Stout daughter is not accepted here.
stories.place: Alexander was born in Kent County, Delaware, about 1708 and farmed at Little Creek Hundred. He and his wife Agnes sold their Delaware land in 1740, were in Craven County, North Carolina, by 1747, and settled on the Trent River in what became Jones County, where he died in 1786 and she in 1793.

stories.title: Robert Blackshaw, yeoman of Little Creek
stories.hook: The Blackshear name in this family began as Blackshaw and drifted to Blackshare, Blackshier and Blackshear through the spelling of clerks writing down what they heard.
body: Robert Blackshaw is the earliest of the line the Blacksheariana can follow through records. He was born at Piscataway, New Jersey, on 24 August 1677, 'son of Ellenor and Thomas Blackshaw.' By 1708 he had bought a lot on Second Street in Lewes, Delaware (Sussex County Deed Book A-1, p. 281), and in 1712 that purchase came up at the Court of Quarter Sessions. In 1716 the Proprietaries' commissioners at Philadelphia issued warrants for 200 acres and 200 more in Kent County, and a survey of 207 acres near the head of Dover River.

He is listed as a yeoman and a farmer. In 1725 he deeded 200 acres, the grant of 1716, to 'Son Randall,' and in 1735 100 acres of 'Blackshares Range' to 'Son Alexander.' The book remarks that his own surname 'began one of its many changes with this Robert, who started out with Blackshaw and ended with Blackshare; his sons went to Blackshere, Blackshier and Blackshear.'

Robert's wife is not named in any of the records the book cites. Robert's son Randall, who married Eve, stayed in Kent County, and Eve's will of 1762 is in the Kent County probate records; Alexander left for North Carolina after selling the land his father gave him.

stories.title: Thomas and Ellenor Blackshaw at Piscataway
stories.hook: Six babies in eleven years, four of them dead by 1688: all that is left of the first Blackshaw couple in the Delaware Valley.
body: The Blacksheariana says most American Blackshears descend from 'Robert Blackshaw, first documented as son of Thomas and Ellenor of Piscataway, N.J., 1677.' Thomas appears on a 1 January 1677-78 promissory note to Thomas Bloomfield of Woodbridge, for 'Good Merchantable Tobacco,' and as a freeholder in 1683 and again in a later list. He paid quit rents on 37 acres and is listed as an early patentee. He is not in the probate records of Middlesex or Monmouth counties.

The New Jersey Archives record the births: Robert on 24 August 1677; a Thomas on 5 January 1679-80, dead two days later; Joseph on 13 April 1681, dead in October 1687; Timothy on 22 December 1682, 'd. soon'; a second Thomas on 3 September 1685, dead 24 October 1687; and a second Joseph on 15 May 1688. Only Robert and the second Joseph outlived their father.

The author guesses that Thomas was the son of John Blackshaw and Maude Barlowe of the parish of Prestbury, Cheshire, whose son Thomas was baptised on 25 September 1631 in the parish of Prestbury, who 'could very well be the first Blackshaw to establish a family in America.' The author could not locate that Thomas's marriage or death in Cheshire.

stories.title: William and Viney Clark: a bond with Henry Willis
stories.hook: In 1808 a Pulaski County marriage bond was signed by the groom and by Henry Willis; a veteran named Henry Willis said in his pension application that he had lived with William Clark during the War of 1812.
body: A WikiTree profile for William Clark, built from the Kentucky War of 1812 soldiers list, the censuses of 1840 and 1850 for Butler County, and the 1856 Kentucky death register, gives his birth as 13 October 1785 in Granville County, North Carolina, and his death as 6 January 1856 in Butler County. His wife appears in the 1850 census as 'Vina Clarke' in his household and in the 1860 census as 'Luvina Clark.'

They married in 1808 in Pulaski County, Kentucky. The county marriage book (Book 1, 1799-1850, p. 28) has the couple's names in the wrong places in the index: 'William Willis & Livina Clark.' The Kentucky marriage index files the same record under 'Viny Willis' and 'William Clark,' 1808. A discussion on WikiTree's Henry Willis page says William Clark and Henry Willis stood as bondsmen.

Their first child, Lewis, was born in Pulaski County on 16 April 1809. The family moved to what became Butler County, where Mary (1815), Newton Jasper (6 August 1817), and Emeline (1820) were born, and then to what became Edmonson County, where Harvey was born in 1826. Lewis and Emeline died in Edmonson County and Mary and Harvey in Butler.

Compiled profiles report that Newton married Polly Elms in Butler County in January 1839. Melvina’s death certificate names Newton Clark and Mary Dunn as her parents; identifying her mother with Polly Elms remains probable and the surname difference is unresolved. Melvina married a Johnson, and her daughter Samantha married John C. Satterfield, who is our line.
