stories.title: Henry Willis: bondsman, levy-exempt, dead by 1818
stories.hook: The documents agree that a Henry Willis stood bond for Lavina Willis in 1808; they do not say whether he was her father.
body: A Henry Willis and his wife Mary sold land on the waters of Clifty Creek and Fishing Creek in Pulaski County, Kentucky, before 14 October 1800. In November 1807 the Pulaski County court excused Henry from the county levy because of old age and infirmity. The next year he is the Henry Willis who stood bond with William Clark for the marriage of Lavina Willis. By 1818, a Pulaski County tax record shows Mary alone, which is the basis for his death date. In the spring court of 1820 a suit named John, George and Daniel Willis as his heirs.

The WikiTree discussion of this family traces a Henry Willis through Washington County, Virginia, where he took title to 400 acres in Rich Valley in 1781-82 and was presented by a grand jury in 1773 for living with Mary Cochran, then to Greene County, Tennessee, and then to Kentucky. It calls the identification of these as one man 'most likely' but admits he disappears from each place just as a man of the same name shows up in the next.

That discussion lists Lavina among the children only as a presumption: 'Lavina (aka Viney) Willis married William Clark in 1808. William Clark and Henry Willis stood as bondsmen. The presumption is that Viney is Henry's daughter.' Another Henry Willis, born about 1793, lived later in Edmonson County, drew a War of 1812 pension, and said he lived with William Clark in Pulaski County; the WikiTree author reads that as showing that William Clark lived in the household of Henry and Mary, which is how he would have met Viney.

quotes.t: The presumption is that Viney is Henry's daughter.
quotes.c: WikiTree Willis-11599, discussion section, 7 Nov 2022

stories.title: A family quarrel ends in a stabbing, January 1938
stories.hook: Oscar Hulsey, 27, was arrested after a two-day search in the mountains north of Millerton for stabbing his wife's brother.
body: In the last week of January 1938, Oscar Hulsey and Eddie Stevenson of Millerton, named as his brother-in-law, had a family quarrel that ended with Stevenson stabbed. The Valliant Tribune of 4 February 1938 put it in six sentences, and the McCurtain Gazette of 2 February ran the headline "Oscar Hulsey Arrested on Assault Count."

The Tribune says: "Oscar Hulsey faces a charge of assault with attempt to kill after his arrest Monday night by Deputies James Houston and Bud Butler. He was charged in connection with the stabbing Saturday night of his brother-in-law Eddie Stevenson of Millerton. Stevenson is in the Sanitarium of Paris, where his condition was reported as satisfactory Monday afternoon. The stabbing followed a family quarrel, officers said. Hulsey was arrested in a remote mountain area 30 miles north of Millerton after a two-day search." By its dates the stabbing was Saturday night, 29 January, and the arrest Monday night, 31 January.

The charge did not go away quickly. The McCurtain Gazette's published district court dockets of 17 and 28 September and 5 October 1938 list "the State of Oklahoma vs. Oscar Hulsey" as assault and battery with intent to kill for the October 1938 term, and the dockets printed on 16 and 20 September 1939 list it again, set for Saturday, 14 October 1939. No sentence, plea or dismissal was found in the pages that could be read. By April 1940 Oscar was back in Arkansas at South Fork in Montgomery County, working on a government job, and in 1941 his marriage to Katie ended in divorce.

stories.title: Killed on his bicycle, July 1947
stories.hook: Bennie George Hulsey, 13, turned in front of a pickup truck west of Hugo and died within the hour.

subject.name: Bennie George Hulsey and the pickup truck

body: The clipping reads: "Choctaw County's second highway fatality was suffered Tuesday night when Bennie George Hulsey, 13, died of injuries received when he turned in front of a pickup truck on his bicycle, the local highway patrol unit reported." Three eyewitnesses told the patrolmen that the boy turned directly into the path of a truck driven by Mack Flinn, 29, of Grant, on U.S. 70 two miles west of Hugo in front of Leon Griffin's store, about 7:30 p.m.

"The boy, son of Mrs. Katie Hulsey, Hugo Route One, was rushed to the Hugo hospital but he succumbed 45 minutes later from a compound fracture of the skull and internal injuries." The patrol said he was knocked 75 feet; Flinn's truck swerved off the road, jumped a four-foot fill and turned over once and a half. Flinn had only a few bruises and two other men in the truck were slightly hurt. The boy's death "marked the second road fatality in Choctaw County during 1947."

Services were set for 11 a.m. Thursday at the Coffey Funeral Home chapel, with burial at Mount Olivet. He was a member of the Assembly of God church and had been born in Danville, Arkansas, the paper says, and had moved with his mother and family to a place on Hugo Route One. The survivors named in the continuation are his mother, his father Oscar Hulsey of Wright City, two sisters, Mrs. Delphia Murphy of Oregon and Mary of Hugo, and four brothers, Leon, Glen, Charles and Willis, all of Hugo. Mary was his sister Mary Ellen, then eight years old.

stories.title: Two courthouses and a second wife
stories.hook: Oscar and Katie were divorced in Arkansas in 1941, he remarried five weeks later, and Katie filed again in Oklahoma in 1945.
body: Oscar and Katie Hulsey's marriage ended in two different courtrooms. The Arkansas divorce index records the divorce of "Oscar Hulsey" and "Katie Hulsey" on 26 September 1941 in Montgomery County. On 3 November 1941, five weeks later, the county marriage index shows Oscar Hulsey, 31, of Mount Ida, marrying Hester May Whittington; the state certificate gives his birth date as 27 October 1910.

Katie went back to Oklahoma and appears to have brought a second action there. In the McCurtain Gazette's court docket of 10 October 1945 the entry reads "Katie Hulsey vs. Os[car Hulsey], divorce," and from 24 November to 15 December 1945 the Gazette ran a notice by publication in the district court, case no. 12,652, with Katie Hulsey as plaintiff and Oscar Hulsey as defendant, addressed "To: Oscar Hulsey." The text of the petition itself was not readable.

By the 1950 census Katie, 40, is head of a household at Jeter in Choctaw County with her children Glen, Mary, Charley and Willis, marked "Separated" and "Keeping house." An Oscar Hulsey, "Divorced," lives alone as a farmer on the road between Wright City and Gloster in Sulphur Township, McCurtain County, the township where his parents had farmed; the index puts him at 38, born in Oklahoma, so the match is probable, not certain.
The records give no reason for either divorce.

stories.title: Lydia Payne's parents, in her son's words
stories.hook: The only direct statement of who Lydia Payne's parents were comes from her preacher son: William Payne, a six-month Revolutionary militiaman, and Catherine Arnold.
body: Rev. Elam Stevenson's wife Lydia is the mother of Abner and the grandmother of Frank Stevenson, but her own people were not named in any record the family kept. The answer comes from her son, Rev. John Baxter Stevenson, who wrote a short note about his mother. As the Casey family history and a Skinner family book print it: "My mother was born in Burke Co., N.C., Aug. 16. Her father was William Payne. Her mother was Catherine Arnold. Her ancestry were of English extraction. Her father belonged to the militia during the Revolutionary War, and was in the service six months." The Casey version adds that she joined the Methodist church in August 1802 and that "her parents were both of the Methodist Church." The Skinner book also cites a printed "Table of Descents," published at Nashville, for the same two names.

That makes the link a son's own written statement about his mother's parents, which is as direct as a family record gets, but it is a recollection and not a birth or marriage record, and no will or deed naming Lydia as William's daughter has been seen. The place fits the Stevenson story: the Skinner book says Elam married Lydia Paine in North Carolina in 1805, and Burke County lies in the same western North Carolina country as Elam's birthplace in what is now Alexander County.

A William Paine household, spelled "Wm Pain" in 1790, is on the Burke County censuses of 1790 and 1800 as WikiTree transcribes them (twelve people in 1790, thirteen in 1800), and a widow of the name is on the 1810 census. WikiTree gives William's death as 15 October 1807 and carries a gravestone memorial at Rocky Mount Cemetery, Granite Falls. It lists four children: Thomas; Abner Burgess Payne (1777-1845); Sarah, who married a Boyce; and Lydia C. Sarah's profile puts her at Bee Spring, Giles County, in the 1830 and 1840 censuses, with a grave in the Bee Spring Cemetery, so Lydia seems to have had a sister in the same church neighborhood. McFerrin's history of the Bee Spring society names a Rev. Meshach Boyce among its first members and says he is buried in the churchyard there; that he was Sarah's husband is a guess (lead).

WikiTree makes William a son of John Paine of Spotsylvania County, Virginia, whose 1764 will names a son William (see "A Spotsylvania will with six sons"). The same page says two different men named William Paine have been attached to Catherine Arnold's family and that more research is needed to rule one out, so the step back from William Paine of Burke County to John Paine is a lead.

quotes.t: Her father was William Payne. Her mother was Catherine Arnold. Her ancestry were of English extraction.

stories.title: A Spotsylvania will with a daughter 'Catey'
stories.hook: A 1774 Spotsylvania will names a daughter Catey, and a tree makes her Catherine Arnold, wife of William Payne of Burke County.
body: WikiTree's page for Catherine Arnold says she was born about 1751 in Spotsylvania County, Virginia, a daughter of William Arnold (about 1714 to after 1774) and Lydia Bell. The one record it cites is Spotsylvania Will Book E, page 119, the will of William Arnold, who died there on 17 September 1774 and "names a daughter Catey." The page marks her marriage to William Payne "Citation Needed."

The Spotsylvania origin is the only thing that makes the link plausible: WikiTree also puts William Paine's own family in Spotsylvania, and says he and his wife sold his share of his father's estate there on 20 November 1777 before the family moved to Burke County, North Carolina. A daughter named Lydia (Lydia Stevenson) may echo Catherine's mother Lydia. None of this has been checked against the will, the deed or a record that gives Catherine's age or origin, so Catherine Arnold's parents are carried here only as a lead.

stories.title: A 1955 note on the Stevenson immigrant
stories.hook: A family compiler's 1955 notes say James Stevenson of Iredell County was the son of an Irish immigrant James, not of the William some trees give him.

subject.name: James Stevenson, immigrant from Ireland, & Sally Kelly

body: A family book on the Skinner ancestry covers the Stevensons because Rev. Elam Stevenson's descendants married into that line. Its Stevenson chapter first follows a chart that starts with William Stevenson, born in County Antrim, Ireland, who came to Pennsylvania in 1748 and to Iredell County, North Carolina in 1762. Then it adds a correction from "data received May 11, 1955": "The father of James Stevenson was not William Stevenson, immigrant, but was James Stevenson, immigrant from Ireland, who died in 1820. James I married Sally Kelly of Md., who died about 1820 or 1821. James Stevenson II, who m. Jane Stevenson, died in 1828. She died 1814."

James II is the James Stevenson whose 1828 will in Iredell County names his son Elam; his wife Jane is the Jane Stevenson of the next generation. The chapter also quotes McFerrin that Elam was the son of James Stephenson of Iredell, now Alexander County, "who was a Captain in the Revolutionary War." Another passage in the same book says James Stevenson "was born in Ireland. Settled in North Carolina about 1775" and had two other sons besides Elam, which does not agree with the 1955 note (James II would then be the immigrant).

The dates do not fit well: if James II was born about 1746, an immigrant father who died in 1820 and a mother who died about 1820 or 1821 would both have been very old. The 1955 note is therefore a family compiler's statement, not a record, and the parents of James Stevenson stay a lead until a will, deed or church record names them.

quotes.t: The father of James Stevenson was not William Stevenson, immigrant, but was James Stevenson, immigrant from Ireland, who died in 1820.

stories.title: Jane Stevenson's parents: John, and a Thompson
stories.hook: The same 1955 notes say Elam Stevenson's mother Jane was a Stevenson by birth, daughter of John Stevenson, who died in 1794, and a woman named Thompson.
body: Elam Stevenson's mother is only ever called Jane Stevenson, and the compiler of the Skinner book's Stevenson chapter noted that the wives' maiden names show "Stephenson was Jane's maiden name, and not a variation" of her husband's. In the same note: "James Stevenson II, who m. Jane Stevenson, died in 1828. She died 1814. Jane was the daughter of John Stevenson (d. 1794), and a Thompson."

Nothing more is given: no first name or dates for Jane's mother, no place, no will. This is the only place found that names Jane's parents, and it is a compiler's statement from 1955 with no source printed in the excerpts that could be read, so it stays a lead. Another passage of the book puts the marriage of James and Jane about 1765 and calls James a soldier of the Revolution.

stories.title: Jesse Hulsey, the wounded soldier of Hall County
stories.hook: A Revolutionary veteran with an Indian wound and a North Carolina pension lived in Hall County, Georgia, when Salathiel Hulsey did; whether he was Salathiel's father is open.
body: The Hall County, Georgia history of the Hulsey families, as the San Diego society reprinted it, says that Jesse Hulsey, "a veteran of the American Revolution," was still living in Greenville District, South Carolina, in 1800, one of only two of the family left in the state, was in Hall County in 1820, and drew a Revolutionary land lottery lot in Troup County in 1827 (granted 12 January 1829). In the 1840 pension census he is a Revolutionary soldier, age 81, in Hall County.

WikiTree adds his North Carolina pension: on 25 November 1822 Jesse, "of Hawl Co. Ga.," named Samuel Carson his attorney to collect the pension the North Carolina legislature allowed him "in consideration of a wound which I received by the Indians in the Revolutionary War"; he appointed another agent in 1826, and a man swore in Wake County in December 1835 that he had seen him alive in September in Hall County. WikiTree calls him Jesse Hamilton Hulsey, born 1760 in Goochland County, Virginia, and lists the blacksmith Salathiel Hulsey (born about 1807, Franklin County, Georgia) among his many children by Mary Tharp.

A contemporary North Carolina resolution supplies firmer evidence for the pension. The printed Acts of the General Assembly for the 1834–35 session direct the treasurer to pay all pension arrears to Jesse Hulsey, then living in Georgia, or his agent N. Edmonson, and to continue payments for Jesse's lifetime. The resolution says his pension had been allowed by an act passed in 1824. It names no wife, children or Georgia county, so it supports the pension account without proving that Jesse was Salathiel's father. Its 1824 date also leaves a question about the 1822 power of attorney reported on WikiTree; the earlier document has not been checked here against its original.

The link to our Salathiel is a family-tree assertion. The pieces that fit are place and names: Salathiel is on the 1840 census of Hall County, and his 1850 household in Union County has a Jesse, 10, and a Jennings, 8, while the Georgia history names a Jennings Hulsey who stayed in South Carolina with Jesse in 1800. The pieces that do not fit: the same WikiTree page says a son Jesse Jr. married Mary Tharp in "1779" in Franklin County, Alabama, which cannot be right; the Georgia history treats Jesse as possibly a brother of James Hulsey Sr. of Hall County; and no will, deed or census that lists Salathiel as Jesse's son has been found.

quotes.t: in consideration of a wound which I received by the Indians in the Revolutionary War
quotes.c: Jesse Hulsey of Hall Co., Ga., 25 Nov 1822, pension power of attorney (as printed on WikiTree)

stories.title: A widower in Hopkins County
stories.hook: The 1880 census finds George W. Langley, 38, alone with two small daughters and his wife's brother and sisters in the house.
body: The 1880 census for Precinct 5 of Hopkins County, Texas, lists George W. Langley, 38, born in Georgia, as head of household. His daughters are Emma J., 12, and Eliza J., 8, both born in Texas. No wife is listed.

Living with him are Jacob Black, 29, called brother-in-law, and Sarah J. Quinton, 32, and Elizabeth Black, 23, called sisters-in-law. Two Black siblings under his roof and no wife make it likely that Mrs. Langley, a Black, had died before the count (lead).

Emma Elizabeth Langley, wife of John B. Smith, was born on 11 December 1867 in Texas, which makes her 12 in June 1880. The census gives the daughter as Emma J., so the identification rests on age, birthplace and neighbourhood (Hopkins County lies beside Franklin County, where Emma died in 1905), not on a document naming Emma Elizabeth.

stories.title: Frances Thompson and the family at Jeter
stories.hook: Frances and Simon built a household at Jeter that included three generations of the family.
body: Frances Pisachubbe was born in 1907 to Robert Pisachubbe and Lizzie Austin. Her parents came from Choctaw families whose earlier generations appear in the Dawes enrollment records: Robert and his mother Eunice on Card 1580, and Lizzie with her parents Legion and Molsey on Card 1363.

The federal enrollment process was governed by dates set in law. An act approved on 26 April 1906 authorized a limited application period for eligible children who were minors living on 4 March 1906. Frances was born the following year; her family's earlier cards provide information about her relatives, but the cutoff helps explain why she was not enrolled as one of those children.

Frances married Simon Thompson in 1925. In the 1930 census the couple shared a household at Jeter, Oklahoma, with her parents. Ten years later the 1940 census recorded Simon and Frances on a farm they owned, valued at $400, with five children in the household.

The 1950 census again placed the family at Jeter. Frances, then recorded as 42, lived with Simon, five children and her mother Lizzie Pisachubbe. Lizzie's presence connects the household directly to the earlier Austin and Pisachubbe records. Frances died in 1979 and is buried at Long Creek Cemetery.

(dwelling 421); Act of April 26, 1906, ch. 1876, section 2, 34 Stat. 137, https://govtrackus.s3.amazonaws.com/legislink/pdf/stat/34/STATUTE-34-Pg136a.pdf; National Archives, Enrollment Cards for the Five Civilized Tribes, M1186, https://www.archives.gov/files/research/microfilm/m1186.pdf; 1930, 1940, 1950 U.S. censuses as previously cited for Frances and Simon Thompson.

stories.title: Lizzie Austin and the two sisters who married two brothers
stories.hook: A seven-year-old on a Fowlerville card in 1899 became the grandmother who kept a twelve-person house at Jeter.
body: Lizzie Austin is Roll No. 3738 on Dawes Card 1363, which her father Legion filled out on 21 May 1899 for Towson County, post office Fowlerville. The clerk wrote her down as 7 years old, full-blood, the daughter of Legion and Molsey. Her 1896 census number was Towson No. 201, on the line after her mother's No. 200. The final roll, approved on 12 December 1902, carries her at 10. The age she gave the later censuses moved around as well: 42 in 1940, 58 in 1950. The roll ages point to a birth about 1892, and the 1950 age agrees.

Her small family was already losing members. The card enrolls her brother James, born 15 November 1898, with a note that he died in April 1899, and a younger sister arrived the next year: Adline, born 5 August 1900 and enrolled in June 1901. The two girls grew up to marry brothers. Adline married William Harrison Pisachubbe, and Lizzie married his younger brother Robert, the son of the widow Eunice Pisachubbe of Goodland. The children of the two marriages were double first cousins.

Lizzie's name turns up in the federal record once more before the 1920 census. In the 1916 House hearings on removal-of-restriction cases, a section for June to September 1915 lists "Lizzie Pisachubbee, nee Austin," an application to have federal restrictions lifted from her land. By 1917 Robert was 28, married with a child, and farming for himself at Speer. In 1920 Lizzie and Robert owned their farm in Jeter Township with their daughter Frances, Robert's widowed mother Eunice, and a young cousin.

The house grew crowded as the old generation died. Her mother Molsey died in 1924 and Eunice in 1927. Adline died at Speer in 1929 and her husband William Harrison in 1937, leaving their children, and the 1940 census at Jeter finds Lizzie and Robert in one household with Frances, her husband Simon Thompson and their five children, and Alice, Eli and Edward, the orphaned niece and nephews: twelve people. Frances had married Simon in 1925, and so the Austin and Pisachubbe families were joined with Joseph and Betsy Thompson's line. Lizzie was still in that household in 1950 and died in 1964. She is buried at Long Creek Cemetery near Hugo, the cemetery where Simon and Frances lie.
src: Dawes Card 1363; House Committee on Indian Affairs, Five Civilized Tribes of Indians, hearings (1916), list of removal-of-restriction cases, Choctaws.; James Austin birth affidavit, sworn 2 May 1899, Dawes Card 1363 enrollment jacket, National Archives; Dawes Card 1363. 1920, 1940 and 1950 U.S. censuses (Jeter, Choctaw Co., Okla.); Dawes Card 1363 (1896 census Nos. 199-201; final roll approved 12 Dec 1902); House hearing 1916 removal-of-restrictions list (June-Sept 1915).

stories.title: The old place north of Doaksville
stories.hook: Vinson Tims farmed north of Doaksville, where his daughter Betsy married Joseph Thompson in 1889 and where he is said to be buried.
body: Vinson W. Tims was born in 1838, the elder son of the Doaksville trader Vincent B. Tims. He and Emeline farmed in the High Hill neighborhood of Towson County, 'about four miles north and a little west of Doaksville,' on land later called the Charley Blankenship place. Their children included James, Mitchell, Betsy (Mrs. Joseph Thompson), John, Rev. Robert Tims, Willie, Rosie (Mrs. James Wilson) and Calvin.
Betsy married Joseph Thompson at that house in 1889. Joel remembered his grandparents as 'buried there at the old place,' which fits the marker at High Hill, a cenotaph whose dates cannot be read.

A memorial for him at High Hill Cemetery gives 1838 to 25 October 1891. The 1896 Choctaw census, pictured here, appears to list Vinson with Emeline and their family in Towson County, and on the 1899 card Betsy's father is named 'Vincent Tims,' dead. So his death date is unsettled: 1891 on the memorial, after 1896 if the census line is his.

A memoir of his son Robert, printed in 1944 in the Methodist Indian Mission's minutes, says Robert was "the son of Vincent and Emiline Tims." That is the same first name the 1899 Dawes card gives for Betsy's father, so the family's own church record used "Vincent" for him where the High Hill marker says "Vinson."

Vinson never enrolled, because he was gone by 1899, but his name is on the cards of his children. Written by Dawes clerks in 1899, it appears as "Vinson W. Tims" on James B.'s card, "Vincent Tims" on the cards of Betsy, Robert and Willie, and "Benson Tims" on Mitchell's. In every case the column marks him dead and gives Towson County, where the family lived.

stories.title: Eunice Pisachubbe’s family and allotment
stories.hook: An enrollment card and a later court petition trace a Choctaw mother’s family and land across nearly three decades.
body: After Eunice died on 19 May 1927, her sons Robert and William H. Pisachubbe, "the lawful issue of the marriage between Joseph Pisachubbe and Eunice Pisachubbe," petitioned the Choctaw County court to approve the sale of her allotment of about 159 acres for $1,200. As full-blood Choctaw land, it could not be sold without a judge's approval. The petition also records that Joseph had died long before her and that she never remarried.

Eunice's Dawes card, 1580, was made out for Kiamitia County, post office Goodland, on 10 May 1899. It lists "Pisachubbe, Eunice," age 49, full-blood, Roll No. 4465, with her parents named as "Jackson Gardner" and "Viney Gardner," both dead, of Blue County. Her sons William H., 16 (on the 1896 roll as "William Harrison"), and Robert, 11, are on lines 2 and 3, fathered by "Joseph Pisachubbe," dead. Line 4 is not a son: Edward Pisachubbe, 17, is written as her ward, with his own dead parents named as Simpson and Sallie Pisachubbe of Jackson County, and the card notes that he was the husband of Frances Byington, Card 956.

The tribal-enrollment columns of Card 1580 add the 1896 census numbers: Eunice is Kiamitia County No. 10432, her son Robert No. 10433 and the ward Edward Pisachubbe No. 10434, the three of them on consecutive lines of one household. William is not with them. He appears on the same card as No. 5759, a far earlier number, with a note "No. 2 on 1896 roll as William Harrison," which fits the 1911 finding that he was also listed separately as a student at Armstrong Academy and enrolled twice. All four were approved by the Secretary of the Interior on 12 December 1902.

A note on the card sends the reader on for William's child: "For child of No. 2 see N.B. (Apr. 26, '06) Card No. 1203," the 1906 newborn card for his son Colbert. On the back of the 1911 duplicate-enrollment file, the Commissioner's letter of 1 August 1911 lists the testimony of four witnesses taken to settle the question: William H. Pisachubbe, Eunice Pisachubbe, Harrison Nohio and Thomas Hunter.

The court petition describes Eunice’s land in Section 29 of Township 5 South, Range 17 East, and subtracts two strips for the St. Louis and San Francisco Railway’s right of way: 10.80 acres from one tract and .01 acre from another. It gives the remaining allotment as 159.19 acres. Robert and William asked the court to approve a $1,200 deed to L. C. Hudgens; the petition itself records the request and does not establish whether the court approved it.
src: Choctaw County Court, Estate of Eunice Pisachubbe, petition for approval of full-blood deed (1927); Dawes Card 1580; Dawes Card 1580 (1896 census numbers and marginal notes); Choctaw Commissioner's letter, 1 Aug. 1911 (jacket 7-1580); Choctaw County Court, Estate of Eunice Pisachubbe, Petition for Approval of Full Blood Deed, 1927; Choctaw by Blood enrollment card 1580, National Archives.

stories.title: Joseph Pisachubbe, the father who is on a card only as 'dead'
stories.hook: The Dawes clerk recorded him as the deceased father of two sons; probate records preserve more of his family.
body: On Dawes Card 1580, made out on 10 May 1899 at the Goodland post office in Kiamitia County, Joseph Pisachubbe holds a single word. The card is his widow Eunice's. Her two sons stand on lines 2 and 3, William H., 16, and Robert, 11, and in the father column of each the clerk entered "Joseph Pisachubbe," the year column reading "Dead" and the county Kiamitia. He is recorded as deceased when the card was made; no enrollment card of his own has been identified. His sons were born about 1883 and 1888, so he was alive into the late 1880s. Eunice, Robert and their ward Edward Pisachubbe are on consecutive lines of the 1896 census, Nos. 10432 to 10434, and he is not listed with them; that alone does not establish his date of death.

Eunice's widowhood is the rest of his record. When she died on 19 May 1927, her sons Robert and William H. petitioned the Choctaw County court as "the lawful issue of the marriage between Joseph Pisachubbe and Eunice Pisachubbe," and the petition adds that he died long before her and that she never remarried. The 159-acre allotment she asked to sell lay in Section 29, Township 5 South, Range 17 East, the same section where Robert's own allotment lies.

The only account of where the family came from is a family history printed in the Hugo Daily News on 11 May 1937 at William Harrison's death, given by his relative Judge T. W. Hunter: the Pisachubbes came from Mississippi in 1832 with the first group of Choctaw exiles and settled at Fort Coffee, near present-day Spiro. The date has to be read with care. Fort Coffee was established on the Arkansas River only in June 1834, so the family's "in 1832" and "at Fort Coffee" describe the neighborhood by the later landmark; by 1899 they were in Kiamitia County, where a Presbyterian mission had worked at Goodland since 1848. The family history does not say whether Joseph himself was born in Mississippi or among the first children born in the new Nation.

His own parents are unknown. Family trees give them as a man called Pisachubbe or Wilson and Nancy Te-hol-ba-ta-bi, but the Nancy on Dawes Card 1278 was listed as 69 in 1899, born about 1830. Her age alone does not establish or rule out a mother-and-son relationship; no examined record links her to Joseph (lead only). A "Case Pisachubbi" has his own jacket at Idabel, and a Sarah Pisachubbi is Roll 3471, but nothing connects either to Joseph. What his descendants can be certain of is the name, which they carry through Robert and Lizzie to Frances Thompson, and which the clerks spelled Pisachubbe, Pisachubbee and Pisachubbi from one document to the next.

stories.title: John and Betsy Thompson, Joseph's parents
stories.hook: Two names on the first line of a Dawes card, and a grandson's memory of a burial, are all that survive of the parents of Judge Joseph Thompson.
body: Joseph P. Thompson's card, No. 1283, was filled out on 1 May 1899 in Cedar County, post office Doaksville, and its first line, Joseph himself, names his parents: "John Thompson," dead, of Cedar County, and "Betsy Thompson," dead, of Cedar County. Joseph's wife shared his mother's first name, and both women were Betsy. Joseph was born in December 1861, two miles west of High Hill church, the year the Choctaw Nation sided with the Confederacy, and he gave the 1910 census taker Mississippi as the birthplace of both his parents.

His son Joel, interviewed in Hugo in 1937, supplied what the card does not. Joseph was the second of nine children. John died when Joseph was nine, about 1870, and was buried near the family home toward Spencer Academy. Spencer, which had closed in 1861, reopened in 1871, and Joseph, who had lost his father the year before, was of school age during its reopened years; the 1891 sketch of him says he was educated at Spencer, and from there he went east to Roanoke College in Virginia.

Betsy's side was a harder subject. Joel said his father's mother's people "had some sort of a Choctaw name" and never took a white man's name, which fits the pattern the Dawes cards show elsewhere on this line: surnames such as Thompson, Austin and Gardner came into use among the Choctaw after the 1830s, often borrowed from the given name of a respected white man, while others, like Pisachubbe and Ata-sa-ha-bi, kept their Choctaw names to the end.

The neighborhood that marked their lives was High Hill, where the Methodist church stood two miles east of their son's birthplace; Joseph later built his white house 300 yards from it, and Emeline Tims, his mother-in-law, is buried in its cemetery. Henry W. Thompson, who was enrolled on the next card the same day, is not their son: his parents are written as Simon and Lucy. The names of Joseph's eight brothers and sisters have not been found in the records cited here.
src: Dawes Card 1283; WPA interview #7392 (Joel J. Thompson, 1937); Dawes Card 1283. Dawes Card 1283; 1910 U.S. Census, Wilson Twp, Choctaw Co.; H. F. O'Beirne, Leaders and Leading Men of the Indian Territory (1891), p. 162; Spencer Academy NRHP nomination (NRIS 75001562).

stories.place: Full-blood Choctaw of Cedar County, named as Joseph's parents on his 1899 Dawes card, both dead. Joel said John died when Joseph was nine and was buried near the family home toward Spencer Academy, and that his grandmother's people "had some sort of a Choctaw name" and had not taken an English one.

stories.title: Legion Austin and a father’s affidavit
stories.hook: A birth form altered by hand records a Choctaw father, a neighbor and a child whose enrollment records do not agree.
body: Dawes Card 1363, line 1, lists 'Austin, Legion,' 33, male, full blood, on the 1896 census of Towson County as No. 199, living near Fowlerville. The card names his father as Ata-sa-ha-bi and his mother as Lotima, both dead and both of Towson County. His wife Molsey is on line 2, with her parents Brazil and Siney of Red River, also dead.
Fowlerville's post office was established on 7 July 1894 and renamed Valliant on 23 June 1902.

The application was filed on 21 May 1899 for Towson County, post office Fowlerville. The card lists five people: Legion, Molsey, their daughter Lizzie, a son James, whose date of death is recorded differently in the documents, and a baby daughter Adline, born on 5 August 1900. Legion himself wrote to the Commission from Garvin in October 1900 asking for a blank application for an infant child; the Commission sent it on 9 October. The baby was enrolled on 4 June 1901, as a Commission letter of 5 June 1901 to William Swink at Fowlerville records: "Adline Austin, the infant daughter of Leageon and Muley Austin, born August 5, 1900," the clerk's spellings of Legion and Molsey.

The enrollment card records that James died in April 1899 and that proof of death was filed; his enrollment was cancelled in 1904. A birth affidavit signed by Legion and neighbor Leonidas Willis, dated 2 May 1899, retains the printed words that James was then living. The two documents therefore disagree, and the date on the form or the recorded death requires further checking.

The card's tribal-enrollment columns tie him to the 1896 Choctaw census: Towson County, No. 199, with Molsey at No. 200 and Lizzie at No. 201, and the clerk's note "No. 1 on 1896 roll as Legend Austin." The Commission approved lines 1, 2, 3 and 5 on 12 December 1902. On the final roll he is Choctaw by Blood No. 3736 and the age beside his name is 36, three years more than the 33 written on the 1899 card. The ages on one card do not agree with each other, or with his own testimony in November 1902 that he was "about fifty".

He signed by mark. On the affidavit for his infant son James, sworn at Fowlerville in early May 1899, the clerk crossed out the form's printed "Affidavit of Mother" and wrote "Father" above it, and Legion, "33 years of age and a citizen by blood," swore as the husband of Molsey that the boy was born 15 November 1898. The man who vouched for the birth was a neighbor, Leonidas Willis, who also signed with a mark and is written in as "a Neighbor," not a physician. Nobody named a doctor or midwife for that birth.

stories.title: Molsey Austin and Adline’s birth affidavit
stories.hook: In 1901 Molsey and a midwife each made their mark on a record of her daughter’s birth.
body: On 19 April 1901, Molsey Austin signed an affidavit concerning the birth of her daughter Adline. The document records that Adline was born on 5 August 1900, and names her father as Legion Austin. It gives the family’s post office as Fowlerville, Indian Territory, and identifies both parents as citizens of the Choctaw Nation.

Molsey’s statement appears above a second affidavit made by Sinie Hall, the midwife who attended the birth. Both women signed by mark. J. R. Moore and Sallie Johnson witnessed the marks, and William Swink signed as notary. The page preserves a mother’s account and the name of the woman who helped at the birth.

The family’s enrollment card names Molsey’s parents as Brazil and Siney of Red River County. It also lists Molsey and Legion’s daughter Lizzie, their son James, who died in April 1899, and Adline. The name Siney appears both for Molsey’s mother and in a similar form for the midwife, but the surviving page does not establish whether the two women were related.

The federal enrollment records recorded the family under several spellings, including “Mulcy” for Molsey and “Leageon” for Legion. A later land-restriction list uses “Molsey Pisachubbi, Austin,” suggesting she later carried the name Pisachubbi.
src: House Committee on Indian Affairs, Five Civilized Tribes of Indians, hearings (1916), "Removal of restriction cases received in the Indian Office since Jan. 1, 1915," Choctaws, p. 93; Dawes Card 1363 (front and back) and jacket 7-1363, NARA Dawes Enrollment Jackets (Choctaw by Blood); Dawes Card 1363 and enrollment jacket 7-1363, Choctaw by Blood; Adline Austin birth affidavit sworn 19 April 1901, National Archives; House Committee on Indian Affairs, Five Civilized Tribes of Indians, hearings (1916), removal-of-restrictions list, p. 93.

stories.title: John Steadman on Card 778
stories.hook: The one name on a Choctaw card whose county column reads 'Non Citz': the father of the Doaksville midwife.
body: On Card 778, in the father column of line 1, the clerk wrote "John Steadman," with "Dead" and "Non Citz." in the adjoining columns. Emeline was enrolled as a Choctaw citizen by blood, and the card records her mother as O-we-na. The noncitizen label does not by itself establish John's race or birthplace. The card gives Emeline's recorded blood fraction as one-quarter, but does not record a fraction for either parent; it cannot establish O-we-na's ancestry on its own.

Emeline was born on 26 January 1842, while Fort Towson was still an army post and Doaksville a trading town. Her father's surname is Steadman on the Dawes card; her own grandson Joel Thompson could not recall her maiden name when he was interviewed in 1937, so the name comes from the card and not from family memory. Her 1896 census entry is Towson County No. 12116, written there as Emeline Tims, and the clerk gave her age as 57 against a final-roll age of 60.

He may have been Irish (lead). The card gives no birthplace, residence or death year, only that he was dead by 1899. What the card does show is how far his line travelled from him. His daughter married Vinson W. Tims, a son of the Doaksville trader Vincent B. Tims, and bore eight children, among them Betsy, who married Judge Joseph P. Thompson in 1889. Emeline herself lived to see her grandson Simon born on 4 May 1899, attended his birth as midwife and swore the affidavit that put him on the roll.
src: Dawes Card 778 (NARA). Joel J. Thompson, Indian-Pioneer Papers #7392 (Hugo, 1937); Dawes Card 778 and Card 1283 file (affidavit of 17 Oct 1899).

stories.title: O-we-na, the mother who is a name and a county
stories.hook: Emeline Tims’s mother is named on an 1899 enrollment card, with Towson County beside her name.
body: O-we-na is the only parent on Dawes Card 778 who has a Choctaw county beside her name. The clerk wrote her in the mother column of line 1, the year marked "Dead," the county Towson, the same county in which her daughter Emeline Tims was counted in 1896 (No. 12116) and lived near Doaksville in 1899. Emeline's father, John Steadman, is the one parent on the card marked "Non Citz". The card identifies O-we-na as Emeline’s mother but does not provide a separate enrollment entry for her.

The hyphens are the clerk's. Dawes clerks wrote Choctaw names by ear and broke them into syllables, and O-we-na may have been spelled differently by the person who said it. Its meaning is not recorded. The card gives no year of birth or death for her. Emeline's birth on 26 January 1842 is the one date that frames her.

The commission recorded Emeline as one-quarter Choctaw and listed John Steadman as a noncitizen. It did not record O-we-na’s ancestry or a fraction for her, so the card cannot by itself establish those details. Through Emeline, O-we-na is an ancestor of the Tims and Thompson families of High Hill.
src: Dawes Card 778 (National Archives).

stories.title: Jackson and Viney Gardner of Blue County
stories.hook: Eunice Pisachubbe's parents, written 'dead' on an 1899 card, lived in the county that held Armstrong Academy.
body: Their daughter Eunice's Dawes card names them in the parents' columns of line 1: "Jackson Gardner," dead, of Blue County, and "Viney Gardner," dead, of Blue County. The card was made out on 10 May 1899 at Goodland in Kiamitia County, when Eunice was 49, which puts her birth about 1850. Her own number, 10432 on the 1896 census in Kiamitia, comes from her husband's county, not from her parents'.

Blue County in the Choctaw Nation lay in the Pushmataha District, and Armstrong Academy, the Choctaw boys' school where Eunice's son William Harrison's name turned up on a student list in August 1899, stood in it. By the 1894 printed laws Blue sent one senator, like Kiamichi, Atoka and Jack's Fork. In 1886 the Council cut a new Jackson County from Kiamitia, Blue and Atoka. Samuel G. Gardner of Blue County was a probate judge, but nothing connects Jackson and Viney to him (lead).

The family tree suggests that Jackson was born in Mississippi around 1820, but no examined record establishes his birthplace or birth year (lead). A Carney maiden name and other given names for Viney also appear in trees and need independent evidence. Their daughter Eunice married Joseph Pisachubbe and lived at Goodland, where she raised two sons and a ward. After her death on 19 May 1927, her sons petitioned to sell her 159-acre allotment in Section 29, Township 5 South, Range 17 East.

The Dawes card points to an older set of Choctaw Nation records. The Nation conducted its own censuses decades before the federal commission compiled its rolls; a surviving 1860 Towson County census, for example, records households, ages, occupations and places of birth. These records may help trace earlier generations, but a name match alone does not establish that a person is this Jackson or Viney. The Choctaw Nation Genealogy Department recommends following evidence through census records, application packets and other records to verify each link.
src: Dawes Card 1580; Constitution and Laws of the Choctaw Nation (1894), archive.org constitutionand00watkgoog; Choctaw County Court, Estate of Eunice Pisachubbe (1927); Choctaw Nation, Biskinik, February 2020, p. 12, https://www.choctawnation.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/feb2020-biskinik.pdf; Choctaw Nation Genealogy Department, https://www.choctawnation.com/services/genealogy/.

stories.title: Brazil and Siney of Red River County
stories.hook: Dawes Card 1363 records the names of Molsey Austin's parents, Brazil and Siney, in the Choctaw Nation's Red River County.
body: Dawes Card 1363 names them in the parents' columns on line 2, the line of their daughter Molsey Austin: "Brazil," dead, of Red River, and "Siney," dead, of Red River, with the clerk setting the mother's name in quotation marks. The quotation marks may mean the clerk was unsure of the spelling or that it was a nickname. Brazil is written with no surname.

Red River County was one of the Choctaw Nation's counties along the Red River on the Texas border. Molsey was counted in Towson County in 1896 (No. 200), after her husband Legion Austin, so she had moved from Red River County to Towson. Molsey was about 25 in April 1901, which puts her birth about 1876.

A midwife named Sinie Hall attended the birth of Molsey's daughter Adline on 5 August 1900, and signed the affidavit with her mark at Fowlerville. The two spellings may be the same name; the affidavit does not state any kinship. What Brazil and Siney left is Molsey, who signed with her mark as "Mulcy Austin" and was later listed in the 1916 hearings as "Molsey Pisachubbi, Austin," and the children on Card 1363: Lizzie, James and Adline.
src: Dawes Card 1363. Dawes Card 1363 and jacket 7-1363; Adline Austin birth affidavit, 19 Apr 1901.

stories.title: Ata-sa-ha-bi and Lotima of Towson County
stories.hook: Legion Austin's parents survive only as two Choctaw names copied from the 1896 census.
body: Legion Austin's parents are on Dawes Card 1363 in the parents' columns of line 1: "Ata-sa-ha-bi," dead, of Towson County, and "Lotima," dead, of Towson County. The card writes "Ded" beside both, gives no year of death, and gives neither a roll number. Because Legion was already on the 1896 Choctaw census as "Legend Austin" (Towson No. 199), the clerk had the parents' names from that roll and not from fresh testimony in 1899.

The first name ends in abi, which the Choctaw linguist Ovid Vickers calls a war-name element; "a great proportion of those who had earned second names as a result of participation in a war were given names carrying the termination abi signifying killer." The Choctaw Nation's language staff cautions against reading the ending simply as "killer," and the meaning of Ata-sa-ha-bi is not recorded.

Legion himself bore an English surname, Austin, and signed by mark. The 1899 card gave his age as 33, but in November 1902 he testified he was "about fifty," so his birth falls somewhere between about 1852 and 1866. He had a grown daughter, Viny, born about 1879 to an earlier wife named Betsy, and he raised his nephew Nicholas Greenwood, so the household was wider than the card shows. His daughters Lizzie and Adline married the Pisachubbe brothers Robert and William Harrison, and the line runs through Frances Pisachubbe Thompson.
src: Dawes Card 1363 (NARA); Dawes Card 1363. Dawes Card 1363 and jacket 7-1363; Ovid Vickers, 'Mississippi Choctaw Names and Naming' (Names).

stories.title: The fifth child, who was eight the summer her brother died
stories.hook: Born at Broken Bow in 1938, Mary Ellen Hulsey grew up between two courthouses and married into the Thompson family of Choctaw County.
body: Mary Ellen Hulsey was born on 22 August 1938 at Broken Bow, Oklahoma, the fifth child of Oscar and Katie Hulsey. Broken Bow had grown up around the Dierks lumber company and was incorporated in 1911, a mill town in the pine hills of McCurtain County; her father's work in the Ouachita timber country is told in "A WPA laborer in the Ouachitas." In April 1940 the census found her at 2, with her parents and four older brothers and sisters, at South Fork in Montgomery County, Arkansas.

Her parents' marriage came apart in her childhood. An Arkansas divorce was entered in Montgomery County on 26 September 1941, when she was 3, and Katie filed again in McCurtain County, Oklahoma, in 1945 (see "Two courthouses and a second wife"). In July 1947 her brother Bennie George, 13, was killed on his bicycle west of Hugo; she was 8. By April 1950 she was 12 and living at Jeter in Choctaw County with her mother, enumerated as head of household and "Separated," and three brothers, Glen, Charley and Willis.

She married William 'Junior' Thompson Jr. (1934-2007), which joined the Hulsey line from Arkansas and Georgia to the Thompson family of Choctaw County. She died at Hugo on 4 November 2002, aged 64, and is buried at Woodlawn Cemetery in Choctaw County beside her husband. Her mother Katie outlived her by more than six years, and when Katie died in 2009, Mary was among the children she had already buried.

stories.title: Katie, who lived to ninety-eight
stories.hook: Born at Danville, Arkansas, in 1910 and married at 17, Katie Stevenson Hulsey raised her children alone at Jeter and Hugo and buried four of the people she raised.
body: The census taker at Danville, Arkansas, wrote down seven children in Frank Stevenson's rented house, and the last was "Katie, a baby." She was Katie Cornelia Stevenson, born 15 October 1910, the youngest of Gilbert Franklin 'Frank' and Parsis Jane (O'Neal) Stevenson. (The census day was in April and her recorded birthday is in October, so one of the two is off by months; the 1920 census, which gives her as 'Kate, 9,' agrees with a birth in 1910.) Danville was a Yell County seat laid out in 1841 and named for a steamboat on the Petit Jean River; her father was a Methodist clergyman there and had children born in Indiana, Texas and Oklahoma before her.

By 1920 the family was farming a rented place on the South Millerton Road in Kirk Township, McCurtain County, Oklahoma, near Valliant, a railroad town founded in 1902 in the Choctaw Nation. On 27 October 1927, twelve days after her seventeenth birthday, Katie married Oscar Hulsey, the son of the Rev. George Washington Hulsey and Sarah Rebecca Graves. Two preachers' families, one from Tennessee and Indiana, the other from Georgia and Arkansas, were joined, and their children grew up in the Ouachita hills at places like South Fork, Montgomery County, where the 1940 census found them.

The 1930s were hard on the marriage. Oscar was charged after a stabbing in January 1938 that involved Katie's brother Eddie Stevenson ("A family quarrel ends in a stabbing"). An Arkansas divorce was entered on 26 September 1941, and Katie filed in McCurtain County in 1945 (suit no. 12,652). In July 1947 her 13-year-old son Bennie George died after turning his bicycle in front of a pickup truck west of Hugo, and she moved to Hugo that year. In April 1950 she was enumerated at Jeter, Choctaw County, as "Kattie," 40, "Separated," head of household, with Glen, 14, Mary, 12, Charley, 9, and Willis, 6.

She died at Hugo on 30 January 2009, aged 98, with services on 2 February and burial at Mount Olivet Cemetery, where her parents lie in Block 2. Her obituary counted 16 grandchildren, 32 great-grandchildren and 26 great-great-grandchildren, and named daughters Delphia and Mary and sons Willis, Bennie and Glen as having died before her. Her daughter Mary Ellen's marriage into the Thompson family connects this line to the Choctaw County side of the tree.

stories.title: From Arkansas to the Oregon coast
stories.hook: Sarah Rebecca Graves arrived on 5 May 1884, married a Hulsey at 17, bore ten children, and ended her life on the Oregon coast.
body: Sarah Rebecca Graves was born on 5 May 1884. A family genealogy identifies Margaret Crumpton as her mother and says Margaret died the same day, but neither claim has been confirmed by a primary record. A 1977 family-history query names Jesse Graves as Sarah's father and lists Margaret as one of his wives, without stating which wife was her mother. An 1884 Garland County marriage record names a Jesse Graves and Margaret Crumpton; the groom's recorded age differs from other accounts of Jesse, so the identification needs more research.

On 22 December 1901, at 17, she married George Washington Hulsey in Arkansas. They farmed in Sulphur Township and between 1904 and 1925 had ten children, from Roy, the eldest, to George Paul, the youngest, with Oscar, the father of Katie's children, among them ("The oldest of the ten Hulsey children"; "George Paul, the last child"). By 1920 the family was in McCurtain County, Oklahoma. In September 1918 George Washington was a laborer at Camp Pike near Little Rock while she was at Story, Montgomery County; he died in 1935 and she was a widow at 51.

An index to an Arkansas Gazette obituary for Abe N. Graves, published on 4 February 1943, lists Mrs. Rebecca Hulsey as his sister. It is consistent with the family's account of her Graves relatives, but does not name her parents. The Graves family genealogy says Jesse was the son of Gilliam Graves, who came from North Carolina by way of Georgia and Alabama to Cedar Glades in Arkansas and volunteered for the Union army in January 1864.

She died on 23 December 1972 at Bandon, on the Oregon coast, at 88, and is buried at Hawthorne Memorial Gardens, Grants Pass. Her grandson Glen, Oscar and Katie's son, died at Veneta, Oregon, in 2001, so more than one branch of the Hulsey family ended up in Oregon.

stories.title: The preacher's son who followed the road west
stories.hook: Born in 1861 at Pulaski, Tennessee, Frank Stevenson was one of fifteen children of a Methodist preacher and went on to preach and farm in Indiana, Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas.
body: In April 1910 the census taker at Danville, Arkansas, wrote "Clergyman" after Frank Stevenson's name. He was 51, renting, married for 25 years, and his seven children had been born in Indiana, Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas. He had begun life in a Tennessee circuit preacher's household: Gilbert Franklin Stevenson was born on 17 November 1861 near Pulaski, Giles County, one of fifteen children of Rev. Abner Arrington Stevenson and Martha Still Watson, and the twin of George Washington Stevenson.

He was five months old when Federal troops first reached Pulaski in April 1862. Goodspeed's county history says Giles County was "continually overrun with both Federal and Confederate soldiers" and that in 1863 the Federals relieved the county of "horses, cattle and grain." His first cousins Coleman and Wilbur Stevenson served in the Confederate 32nd Tennessee. In 1870 he and George, both 8, were in their father's household with younger children; in 1880 he was 18 and a farmer. In January 1881 The Pulaski Citizen reported that his father had "abandoned the idea of going to Texas," and that May that "Judge Geo. Stevenson, son of Rev. A. Stevenson, returned from Texas last week." Texas was in the family's talk before Frank himself lived there.

He married Parsis Jane O'Neal of Gibson County, Indiana, whose father Daniel had served in the 42nd Indiana. Their older children were probably born in Indiana; later ones were born in Texas (Willie, Frank and Elisha) and Oklahoma (Eddie), and the youngest, Katie, at Danville in 1910. By January 1919 his mother-in-law's obituary placed his wife as "Mrs. Frank Stevenson of Valiant, Oklahoma," and in 1920 he farmed a rented place on the South Millerton Road in Kirk Township, McCurtain County. The road he took is traced in "Frank Stevenson's road: Pulaski to Indiana to Danville to Valliant."

He died at Hugo on 9 May 1950, aged 88, and lies in Block 2 of Mount Olivet Cemetery next to Parsis. The stone, as canvassed in 2000, reads 'Stevenson, Frank N., 1860-1950.' The year of birth is a year off the family record, and the census ages of 1870, 1880 and 1910 range from 1859 to 1862. His youngest daughter Katie married Oscar Hulsey, and she outlived him by almost sixty years.

stories.title: The farming preacher of Bee Spring
stories.hook: For 54 years Rev. Abner Stevenson rode the Giles County circuits, and in 1880 he gave the census taker his trade as "Farming Preacher."
body: When the census taker came to District 10 of Giles County, Tennessee, in 1880, Abner Arrington Stevenson gave his occupation as "Farming Preacher." He was 64. He had been born on 16 March 1816, the fourth of eleven children of the Rev. Elam Stevenson and Lydia Payne, in a family that produced five Methodist-preaching brothers; Elam had organized the Bee Spring church in 1815 and moved to Tennessee in 1813. A grandnephew's letter of 1932 gave the family totals as years in the pulpit, and set down "Uncle Abner 54 years." The 1956 Methodist history of middle Tennessee calls him "a Godly man" who "lived to be very old."

On 8 December 1838 he married Martha Still Watson, born 19 February 1823, and between 1840 and 1866 they had fifteen children. The twins Gilbert Franklin and George Washington were the twelfth and thirteenth; one son, James Willis, became a minister and lived to 1943 ("Fifteen children at Bee Spring"). A son-in-law, John Newton Andrew, married three Stevenson women in turn. The household was a farm first and a pulpit second: The Pulaski Citizen of 21 November 1878 gave him "Blooming Grove, 4th Sunday, 11 a. m." on the Mt. Pisgah circuit, and on 29 May 1884 a column noted two sermons at Rocky Point, "one by Abner Stevenson."

The war came to his farm. His twins were infants when Federal troops reached Pulaski in April 1862, and Goodspeed says the county was "continually overrun with both Federal and Confederate soldiers." His nephews Coleman L. and Wilbur M., sons of his brother William P., served in the Confederate 32nd Tennessee. His own sympathies are not recorded. In January 1881 the Citizen reported that he had "abandoned the idea of going to Texas and will remain where he is now living," and that May his son "Judge Geo. Stevenson" had "returned from Texas last week." Another son, Frank, lived in Texas himself in the 1890s.

Martha died on 12 July 1887, and her stone reads "Wife of Rev. A. A. Stevenson." Abner died on 30 July 1896 and was buried at Bee Spring, the church his father founded. The church was destroyed by a tornado on 29 April 1909 and the congregation rebuilt at Bryson; the 1956 history says "All that remains of this today is the cemetery." His son Frank carried the preaching and the road west to Arkansas and Oklahoma, where Frank's youngest daughter Katie married a Hulsey.

stories.title: A blacksmith in the old Cherokee gold country
stories.hook: The 1850 census records a Georgia blacksmith and a household that may connect to the Hulseys later recorded in Arkansas.
body: The original 1850 census of Union County, Georgia, records Salathiel (indexed as Salathel Halsey), 43, a Georgia-born blacksmith with $50 in real estate. In dwelling and family 998 are Elizabeth, 35; Maryan, 19; Robert, 17; Elizabeth, 12; Jesse, 10; Jennings, 8; a girl transcribed as Lillean, 6; Benjamin, 3; and Nancy, 1. Arminda Burnett and J. C. Bell are listed in the same household. The page was enumerated on 11 November. The census did not record family relationships, so the apparent spouse and child relationships are inferred. In 1840 Salathiel was counted in Hall County.

Union County, in the northern mountains, was formed in 1832 from the country the Cherokee had held until their removal in 1836-39, once a gold-rush district; settlers there were hardscrabble farmers, mostly from Virginia and North Carolina, and few kept slaves. A blacksmith in such a place shod horses and mended plows. The census gives Salathiel's birth about 1807 and Elizabeth's about 1815, but it does not establish how Elizabeth and Maryan were related. He is gone by the early 1850s.

The original 1860 Hempstead County, Arkansas census records a Georgia-born Robert Hulsey, 27, with Sarah A., 20, and an infant male. His age and birthplace fit a possible continuation of Robert in the Georgia household, but neither census gives him a middle initial. The infant’s name, indexed as Selatha G., is uncertain in the handwriting; the published reading Salathel G. cannot securely link him to Salathiel. Family accounts also place Benjamin in Story, Arkansas, with a son named Martin Salatheil. The original 1850 age of three removes the apparent conflict with Benjamin’s reported 1847 birth, but neither his identity with the Arkansas man nor his relationship to George Washington Hulsey is established.

Salathiel's father may be Jesse Hulsey, the wounded Revolutionary pensioner of Hall County; online trees say so, but they also name Jesse Hamilton Hulsey and Mary Tharp, and no record supports either (lead).

stories.title: Eleven in the census, a bride at sixteen
stories.hook: Parsis O'Neal was 11 and "works at home" in Gibson County in 1880; by 1884 an Arkansas index has her a bride, and she died at Hugo in 1956.
body: In the Columbia Township, Gibson County, Indiana, census of 1880, Parsis J. O'Neal, 11, is listed as "Works At Home" in her father's house. She was the fourth of the ten children of Daniel Waters O'Neal, a veteran of Company F, 42nd Indiana, and Vashti Pearson. Her grandmother Parses (Shaw) Watt, widow of Archibald O'Neal, was on the old home farm near Oakland City, and her brothers in the household were William (16), John (13), George J. (4, born in Missouri) and Daniel G. (2). She was born on 26 March 1868, three years after her father came home from the war.

At 16 she may already have left. A marriage index for Arkansas records "Parsis J O Neal and Otho Louderback" married on 25 December 1884 in Pulaski County, Otho 40 and Parsis 16, and the Find a Grave memorial for her grave at Hugo carries the name Louderback (lead). Her sister Mary was in Arkansas by February 1884. The 1910 census says she and Frank Stevenson had been married 25 years, which puts the Stevenson household in 1885, and the oldest children, Delphia and George, were born in Indiana ("A sixteen-year-old bride in Pulaski County").

The Stevensons then followed the work. Willie, Frank and Elisha were born in Texas between about 1894 and 1904, Eddie in Oklahoma about 1907, and Katie at Danville, Arkansas, on 15 October 1910, when Parsis was 42. By January 1919 her mother's obituary called her "Mrs. Frank Stevenson of Valiant, Oklahoma," and in 1920 the family farmed a rented place in Kirk Township, McCurtain County. Her son George Sherman died at Kilgore, Texas, in 1978, and the death certificate names her as his mother.

She died at Hugo on 26 January 1956, aged 87, and lies in Block 2 of Mount Olivet Cemetery beside Frank. The stone, as canvassed in 2000, reads 1887-1956; every record made in her lifetime, from the 1880 census to her children's births, puts her birth in 1868, so the 1887 is a carving or reading error. Her brothers stayed in Gibson County and her sister Mary lived to 100 at Tuttle, Oklahoma ("A hundred years from Indiana to Oklahoma").

stories.title: Vashti O'Neal's six hours of apoplexy
stories.hook: Married at 15 in 1860, Vashti Pearson O'Neal raised ten children in Gibson County, Indiana, sent a husband to the Union army, and died there in 1919.
body: Vashti Elizabeth Pearson was born on 18 May 1844 and married Daniel Waters O'Neal on 5 January 1860, when she was 15 and he 21. Daniel's father Archibald had come to Gibson County, Indiana, from Tennessee in 1839 and died in 1841, leaving his widow Parses on the farm. In October 1861, with Vashti 17 and their first child, Mary Elizabeth, a year old, Daniel enlisted in Company F of the 42nd Indiana, the company raised at Oakland City, and the war carried much of the regiment from Perryville to Atlanta ("Union soldier, 42nd Indiana"). A family biography has him discharged for disability at Nashville in March 1862.

Between 1860 and 1887 she bore ten children: Mary Elizabeth (1860, who lived to 100), William Allen (1863), John Sherman (1866, born the year after the war), Parsis Jane (1868), J. A. (1871, an infant death), George Johnson (1875), Daniel Clinton (1878), David Commodore (1881), Nora (1884, an infant death) and Charity Louisa (1887). The 1880 census shows the family in Columbia Township, with George, the child born in 1875, listed as born in Missouri. Her five surviving sons lived into their fifties or later, and three of them died at Somerville.

She died at Somerville on 16 January 1919, of "apoplexy, 6 hrs." She professed faith early in life and was a faithful member of Somerville's United Brethren Church. It named her husband, her five sons William, John, George, Clinton and Commodore, two daughters, "Mrs. Frank Stevenson of Valiant, Oklahoma," and Mrs. Fred Skomp of Somerville, and a brother, James Pearson of Elberfeld. Her eldest daughter Mary Elizabeth was in Oklahoma in 1919 but is not named in the notice, and Parsis's marriage to Frank Stevenson tied the O'Neals to the Stevenson family of Arkansas and McCurtain County.

The 1884 county history shows a Pearson family in Columbia Township long before she was born: in 1827 "Solomon Brown and William Pearson had charge of the poor." No record ties that William to her father John. Her restored family stone stands with Daniel's at Somerville, and her own marker reads "Vashti, 1844-1919."

stories.title: Martha Still Watson, fifteen children and a preacher's stone
stories.hook: Married at 15 in 1838, Martha Watson Stevenson bore fifteen children in Giles County and is remembered on her stone only as a preacher's wife.
body: The Stevenson family history says that on 8 December 1838 Abner Stevenson "married Martha S. Watson," born 19 February 1823 in Tennessee, "the daughter of Mary Watson." She was 15. Between 1840 and 1866 she had fifteen children, the last of them about the time she turned 43, among them the twins Gilbert Franklin and George Washington in November 1861, five months before Federal troops reached Pulaski.

For a Methodist circuit preacher's wife that meant a farm and a houseful of children during the years her husband was riding to Blooming Grove, Rocky Point and the Mt. Pisgah circuit (see "Fifteen children at Bee Spring"). She died on 12 July 1887, and the Nashville Christian Advocate abstracts of 20 August 1887 carry the notice of her death. Her stone at Bee Spring is reported to read "Wife of Rev. A. A. Stevenson."

Her mother is given only as Mary Watson. WikiTree names William Watson and Mary Brown as her parents; no record is cited and the middle name Still is unexplained, so her ancestry stops at Mary (lead). Her son Frank carried the line to Arkansas, where Frank's youngest daughter Katie married Oscar Hulsey.

K. T. Smith); Casey family history of the Stevensons.

stories.note: Her parents are not proven. The Casey family history names her mother as Mary Watson; WikiTree's William Watson and Mary Brown rest on no cited record. The Isham Brown of Giles County lead noted elsewhere remains unchecked. The published abstract of her notice in the Nashville Christian Advocate of 20 August 1887 gives her death as 12 July 1886 and her marriage as 6 December 1837. Family compilations and the existing grave-memorial dates instead give death in 1887 and marriage on 8 December 1838. The original newspaper notice and marriage entry have not been examined, so these conflicts remain unresolved; the tree’s existing dates are retained pending verification. Her parents remain unproved.

stories.title: The Pearsons behind Vashti
stories.hook: John and Elizabeth Pearson are known only through their daughter's 1919 obituary, a grave memorial, and a son in Elberfeld.
body: John and Elizabeth Pearson were the parents of Vashti Elizabeth, born 18 May 1844, who married Daniel Waters O'Neal in Gibson County, Indiana, on 5 January 1860. Both were dead by January 1919, when Vashti's obituary appeared. The only brother it names is James Pearson of Elberfeld, Indiana, a Warrick County town a few miles from Gibson County. Elizabeth's maiden name, Carman, comes from the memorial for her grave.

The 1884 History of Gibson County shows that a Pearson family had been in Columbia Township since at least 1827, when "Solomon Brown and William Pearson had charge of the poor." No document names that William as John's father or brother. Their daughter's story, with ten children and a husband in Company F of the 42nd Indiana, is told under Vashti's name.
src: Obituary of Vashti O'Neal (1919), family transcription on Find a Grave. History of Gibson County, Indiana (1884), Columbia Township, p. 213.
stories.place: Named as Vashti's parents in her 1919 obituary, both dead by then. Her only surviving brother was James Pearson of Elberfeld, Indiana. The maiden name Carman comes from her grave memorial.

stories.title: A Tennessean who lived two years on the Gibson County farm
stories.hook: Archibald O'Neal came to Gibson County, Indiana, in 1839 and was dead by April 1841, leaving a widow, a baby son, and a farm that stayed in the family for decades.
body: The 1884 History of Gibson County, Indiana, puts it in one plain paragraph: "Archibald O'Neal was an early settler. He came here in 1839. He was a Tennesseean by birth. He died April 25, 1841." He farmed in Columbia Township with his wife Parses, whom the book calls "a native of Lawrenceburg, Ohio." Their son Daniel Waters had been born in Tennessee in October 1838, the year before the move.

The book prints his death date twice, and the two differ. The township narrative (p. 212) gives 25 April 1841; the directory on p. 239, listing him under his widow, reads "Died Ap'l 22,'41," "First Husband of Mrs. P. W." The year is certain, the day is not. His widow Parses then married Hugh Watt, an Irishman from County Down, who died in September 1871. In 1884 she was still on the old home farm, and she died in 1901 ("Parses Watt and the old home farm").

Online trees give Archibald a birth in Virginia in 1796 and parents named Charles and Martha, which rests on an uncited memorial; the county history says Tennessee. His son Daniel enlisted in Company F, 42nd Indiana Infantry, in October 1861, married Vashti Pearson, and had ten children, among them Parsis Jane, who married Frank Stevenson.

stories.title: Parses Watt and the old home farm
stories.hook: In an Indiana township directory, a widow and farmer appears alongside the names of both her husbands.
body: In 1884, a Gibson County directory listed “Mrs. Parsis Watt” as a farmer in Section 32 near Oakland City, Indiana. The entry gave her birthplace as Lawrenceburg, Ohio, and the year she came to the county as 1839. The directory set two more names immediately below hers: Archibald O’Neal, her first husband, and Hugh Watt, her second.

Archibald O’Neal came to Gibson County in 1839 and farmed there. He died in April 1841, leaving Parses a widow. She later married Hugh Watt, an Irishman from County Down. The county history says that, decades after Archibald’s death, she was still living on the old home farm.

The directory records Hugh’s death in September 1871. By the time the book appeared thirteen years later, Parses was listed under her own name and occupation. Its pairing of a widow’s farming entry with the names of two deceased husbands preserves a compact account of a household that had changed over more than forty years.

The same book gives conflicting dates for Archibald’s death: its biographical sketch says April 25, 1841, while the directory says April 22. Both agree on the year. Parses died in 1901, according to the family record.

stories.title: The Iredell Presbyterians who raised a Methodist preacher
stories.hook: James and Jane Stevenson lived out their lives in Rowan and Iredell counties, North Carolina, and their son Elam took the family into Methodism and Tennessee.
body: James Stevenson was born in 1746 and died in 1828. His will of June 1828, made in Iredell County, North Carolina, names his son Elam among his heirs, and the State Records of North Carolina list him in the Rowan County militia in 1781. He and Jane Stevenson, Presbyterians, were married in 1781, though a compiler's note puts the marriage about 1765 and calls James a soldier of the Revolution. Jane died in 1814, fourteen years before her husband.

Their son Elam was born on 24 September 1787 in what is now Alexander County, North Carolina. He was the first of the family to join the Methodists, married Lydia Payne in Burke County, was licensed to preach in 1813 and that year moved his family to Giles County, Tennessee, by pack horse. In 1869 he wrote his own account of those years ("In his own words, 1869"), and the Christian Advocate printed his obituary in April 1875. Five of his sons became preachers; Abner, whose farm and pulpit were near Pulaski, is the next generation of this line.

A 1955 note in a family book gives James's father as another James, an Irish immigrant who died in 1820, and his mother as Sally Kelly of Maryland; it gives Jane's parents as John Stevenson (d. 1794) and a Thompson. These are compilers' statements only (lead). The dates are strained: a father who died in 1820 and a mother in 1820 or 1821 would both have been very old. See the entries for each.
src: Will of James Stevenson, Iredell Co., NC (1828); State Records of North Carolina, vol. 17; Christian Advocate obituary of Elam Stevenson (1875).
stories.place: Presbyterians of Rowan, later Iredell County, North Carolina, married in 1781. James's will of June 1828 names his son Elam among his heirs. He served in the Rowan County militia in 1781.

stories.title: Noble Shaw's 268 acres at Oak Ridge
stories.hook: A Quaker farmer of Guilford County, North Carolina, Noble Shaw died on Christmas Day 1855, and his widow sold his land in the spring of 1857.
body: On Thursday, 26 March 1857, The Times of Greensboro carried a notice headed "Land Sale." Having qualified as administrators on the estate of Noble Shaw, with a will annexed, J. H. Leak and Sicily Shaw would sell on 16 April "a tract of land, consisting of 268 acres, well timbered and well watered, convenient to the Oak Ridge Institute, and on the direct road from Danville, Va., to Salisbury," on credit. It is signed at Oak Ridge, 24 March 1857.

Noble was born on 22 April 1787 and was a member of Dover Monthly Meeting, whose register lists his wife Sicily and children Aaron (16 December 1809), Parris (7 July 1817, died 30 May 1818) and Mary (17 November 1820). He died on 25 December 1855. The Dover register fits a time when Friends were leaving for Ohio and Indiana: Weeks counts seventy-one certificates from Dover between 1816 and 1860, nearly all of them to Indiana. The Shaws stayed.

Parses Watt of Gibson County, Indiana, who was born about 1811 and died in 1901, is thought to be the Shaws' daughter, but the Dover register shows only a Parris who lived a year; she would have to be an earlier child missing from the page (lead). If she is theirs, her son Daniel O'Neal's Union service and her great-granddaughter Katie Stevenson's marriage to a Hulsey tie the Guilford County Quakers to the Ouachita hills of Arkansas and Oklahoma.
src: Hinshaw, Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy, vol. 1 (Shaw family entry); U.S., Quaker Meeting Records, 1681-1935 (Dover MM birth and death of Noble Shaw); U.S., Quaker Meeting Records, 1681-1935 (Dover MM register, Noble Shaw family) The Times (Greensboro, N.C.), 26 March 1857, p. 3, and 2 April 1857, p. 4; Weeks, Southern Quakers and Slavery (1896).

stories.title: The widow who signed the land sale
stories.hook: Sicily Nordyke Shaw, born in 1790 to Quaker parents in North Carolina, outlived her husband Noble by five years and signed the notice that sold his farm.
body: Hinshaw's Quaker records list "Sicily b. 8-2-1790" first among the children of Aden and Martha Nordyke, which gives 2 August 1790 for her birth. Her father Aden had been born in Burlington County, New Jersey, in 1762, shot in the arm in a Georgia attack, and married Martha Johnson in 1787 at Deep River Meeting in Guilford County. Sicily married Noble Shaw of Dover Monthly Meeting and lived out her years in Guilford County while her father went to Indiana.

In the spring of 1857, aged 66, she and J. H. Leak signed, as administrators, the notice in the Greensboro Times offering Noble Shaw's 268-acre farm at Oak Ridge at public sale on 16 April ("Noble Shaw's land, advertised at Oak Ridge in 1857"). The court trusted her, with Leak, to carry out her husband's will. She died on 16 May 1861, four years later.
src: Hinshaw, Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy, vol. 1 (Nordyke family entry); U.S., Quaker Meeting Records, 1681-1935 (Union MM birth of Sicily Nordyke) Weeks, Southern Quakers and Slavery (1896); The Times (Greensboro, N.C.), 26 March 1857.

stories.title: The Quaker bride at Deep River, 1787
stories.hook: Martha Johnson was born at Deep River in the Quaker country of Guilford County and married Aden Nordyke there in December 1787.
body: On 12 December 1787 a Quaker marriage entry in Hinshaw's index reads: "Martha, dt Robert & Cecilia, Surry Co., m Adin Nordyke." She was Martha Johnson, born in 1766 and living with her family in the Quaker settlements of the North Carolina piedmont. Another genealogy gives her parents as Robert Johnson and Virginia C. Elmore, daughter of Thomas Elmore and Cecilia Ellyson; Cedar Creek Meeting in Virginia recorded the couple as moving to North Carolina on a certificate dated 29 March 1766. Hinshaw's index gives her mother as Cecilia, while the Cedar Creek minutes name Robert's wife as Virginia, and the minutes do not name Martha at all (lead).

Her husband Aden was born in 1762 in Burlington County, New Jersey, the oldest son of Abraham Nordyke and Mary Rogers. Their daughter Sicily, born 2 August 1790, married Noble Shaw. Martha died in 1844, two years after Aden, who is said to have died in Indiana in 1842.
src: Hinshaw, Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy, vol. 1, Nordyke family entry and 12 December 1787 marriage; U.S., Quaker Meeting Records, 1681–1935, Deep River Monthly Meeting, 12 Dec 1787 (as cited in Aden Nordyke’s profile). The proposed Cedar Creek parentage remains a lead.
stories.place: Born at Deep River, North Carolina.

stories.title: Six homes in forty-four years
stories.hook: Abraham Nordyke and Mary Rogers married in a New Jersey Quaker meeting in 1761 and kept moving, through Virginia, Georgia, North Carolina and Tennessee, until they reached Ohio in 1805.
body: Abraham Nordyke and Mary Rogers were married on 1 June 1761 in Burlington County, New Jersey, and were members of Chesterfield Monthly Meeting. Mary was the granddaughter named in her grandfather Thomas Staples's will of 1758, where he left bequests to "Mehetable and Mary Rogers", the daughters of his daughter Ann and her husband Thomas Rogers. Abraham was probably the son of Henry Nordyke and Rebecca Perkins, who married at Willingboro in 1731.

The Terrell-Nordyke Genealogy of 1960 gives their moves in order. In 1771 they transferred to Hopewell Monthly Meeting near Winchester, Virginia. They then lived for eight years in Georgia, where their son Aden was shot in the arm in an Indian attack (Ohio county history), and where their son Micajah, born in 1771, hid through a night in the woods when an invasion was feared. In 1788 they joined Deep River Meeting in North Carolina, where their son Aden had married Martha Johnson the December before. In 1798 they moved to Lost Creek Meeting near Knoxville, a settlement whose Friends had been refused leave to meet in 1787 because the land title was still disputed with the Indians, and in 1805 to a farm near New Vienna in Clinton County, Ohio, where they helped start East Fork Meeting.

Their children included Aden, Israel, Benajah, Beulah, Micajah, Daniel, Phebe and Hiram, and the Quaker habit of recording the hour of birth survives: "Aden was born at 7:00 P.M.; Israel at 3:00 P.M.; Benajah at 9:00 P.M." Mary died in 1814 and Abraham's burial at East Fork was recorded in 1825, at 89. Aden's daughter Sicily, born in 1790, married Noble Shaw in Guilford County, North Carolina; if Parses Shaw of Gibson County, Indiana, was their daughter, the line runs on to the O'Neals, the Stevensons and the Hulseys of Arkansas.
src: C. Clayton Terrell, Terrell-Nordyke Genealogy (1960), pp. 13-15 Weeks, Southern Quakers and Slavery (1896), pp. 251-54 (Lost Creek, 1787); site story 'Six homes in forty-four years'.
