stories.title: The man who owed Jacob Perkins money
stories.hook: Henry Nordyke married Rebecca Perkins at Willingboro, New Jersey, on 6 January 1731, and the Perkins estates were settled around him that same year.
body: Henry Nordyke and Rebecca Perkins were married at Willingboro (Wellingborough), Burlington County, New Jersey, on 6 January 1731. The name looks Dutch, and a compiled family page gives Henry's birth as 2 January 1710 in the Netherlands, but the marriage records say only "Henry" and no ship or church record has been found; a Dutch origin is a lead.

Henry's name appears again in the estates of his wife's family. Her father, Jacob Perkins Jr., made his will on 26 October 1731, naming his wife Sarah and ten children, among them Rebeckah, and listing bonds due him "from James Smith, Esq., John Shinn and Henry Nordike." He left ten pounds to St. Mary's Church, Burlington. The will was proved on 7 December. Rebecca's brother David then died too; his will of January 1731/2 names "Sister, Rebecca, wife of Henry Nordike" and was witnessed by Henry himself, and it was proved on 4 March 1731/2 ("A cane and a sword").

Their son Abraham, who died at 89 in 1825, was born about 1736; he was a member of Chesterfield Meeting when he married Mary Rogers in 1761. From there the line goes to Guilford County, North Carolina, to Ohio and Indiana ("Six homes in forty-four years").
src: Wills of Jacob Perkins Jr. (1731) and David Perkins (1731/2), Calendar of New Jersey Wills, Lib. 3 p. 102 and Lib. 8 p. 184.

stories.title: Mary Tinsley Shackleford
stories.hook: Born in Etowah County, Alabama, in 1895, Mary raised her family with Grady and is buried at Shoat Springs Cemetery.
body: Mary was born on 4 June 1895 in Alabama and is the "May, 5" in her parents' 1900 household at Gilbert, Etowah County. Her parents were John Morgan and Lizzie (Newton) Shackleford. She married Grady Moffitt about 1914 and bore at least eleven children, two of whom died as toddlers.
In 1930 she and Grady and their six boys were living with her parents in Martin County, Texas. She died in Paris, Texas, on 26 August 1962 and is buried beside Grady at Shoat Springs Cemetery, Hugo.

stories.title: Twenty-two years a widow at Herpel: Hannah Grimes Moffitt
stories.hook: Her birthplace is a Mississippi River landing or Illinois, depending on the tree, but her stone is in the Rocky Bayou hills and reads "Wife of Henry H Moffitt."
body: The 1910 census finds Hannah Moffitt, a widow of 53, renting a house in Franklin Township, Stone County, Arkansas. Two sons live with her: Thomas, who works as a railroad section hand, and Grady, who makes barrel staves. The census asks every mother how many children she has borne and how many are living, and Hannah's answer is seven and six. The household was already nine years into her widowhood: her husband Henry H. Moffitt had died at Mountain View in 1901, and she lived on without him until 1923.

Henry and Hannah were the same age. Henry was born in 1855, when his father Nathan Moffitt, the wheelwright, and Rebecca Williams were farming in Lawrence County; Hannah was born in July 1855, the daughter of David H. Grimes of Wayne County, Tennessee. Their children were Josephine, Jesse Gee (1879-1957), Gimsa, Bertha, Thomas Berry (1889-1953) and Grady (1891-1972). The 1910 age of 53 would put Hannah's birth nearer 1857 than 1855, and where she was born is itself in dispute: a family tree gives Arkansas City, Desha County, a second WikiTree profile gives Illinois, and the 1855 date has no original record behind it; WikiTree lists only Tom and Grady as her children. The Desha County name cannot be right as written. In 1855 the Mississippi River landing that became Arkansas City lay in Chicot County and had seen little growth; the town was not incorporated until 1873 and was not in Desha County until the boundary moved in 1879.

What the records do show is where she ended up. By 1910 she was among the Moffitts of Stone County, a county only 37 years old, whose seat Mountain View had barely 100 people in 1880. Her brother-in-law Patrick Moffitt also lived in Stone County, and his wife Alice Ann died in May 1901, a few months before Henry. After Henry's death Hannah kept a household of grown sons going on rented ground, and the two sons at home worked for wages, Tom on the railroad and Grady making barrel staves.

She spent her last years at Herpel, a Rocky Bayou community about six miles east of Mountain View, with a grist mill, a cotton gin, a stave mill and a sawmill. Its post office ran from 1907 to 1957. The Herpel Missionary Baptist Church laid its cornerstone on 5 March 1923, and Hannah died on 4 April 1923, about a month later. She is buried in Herpel Cemetery. Her stone reads "Wife of Henry H Moffitt," the only memorial the couple have, since Henry's own grave has not been located.

Hannah’s marriage connected the Grimes and Moffitt families. Through her husband she was the daughter-in-law of Nathan and Rebecca, whose road led from Randolph County, North Carolina, to Arkansas and Missouri; through her father David she belonged to the Grimes family of Hardin Creek in Wayne County. Her youngest son Grady carried both lines to Hugo, Oklahoma, where he raised his family.

stories.title: Rebecca's bond: a £500 promise in Randolph County, 1835
stories.hook: On 13 October 1835 two Moffitt brothers put up £500 to the Governor of North Carolina so that Nathan could marry Rebecca Williams.
body: The paper that proves the marriage is a printed form from the North Carolina Governor's office, filled in by hand. "KNOW all men by these presents, that we Nathan Moffitt & David Moffitt are held and firmly bound unto David L. Swain Esquire, Governor, &c.... in the full sum of five hundred pounds current money," and it is dated the 13th of October 1835. The condition reads that Nathan "hath made application for license for marriage to be celebrated between him and Rebecca Williams of the County aforesaid." The bond would be void if no lawful impediment appeared. Both men signed with seals. David Moffitt was almost certainly Nathan's older brother, born in 1802, one of Robert and Martha's nine children.

The form names her "Rebecca," and so does every later record. She is Rebecca Moffet in Nathan's household in Strawberry Township, Lawrence County, Arkansas, in 1850 and Rebecca Moffit in his household again in 1870. The county marriage index (FHL film 2,447,732) lists the marriage as Rebecca Williams to Nathan Moffitt, 13 October 1835. The profile title carries "Mary Rebecca," but every record calls her Rebecca. Her birth is given as 1814 in the dates above and as about 1816 in other tables, in Randolph County. No document names her parents. Ancestry suggests James S. Williams and Polly Garner, but the Williams families of Randolph County were numerous and none can be tied to her.

Her husband's family surrounded her. Nathan's mother Martha Chamness, who was born in 1778 and lived until 1865, was in the same county when Rebecca married, and Rebecca's sister-in-law Thalitha Williams (born 1804 at Deep River) had married Nathan's brother William C. on 7 August 1827. Whether the two Williams women were sisters is not shown. A son, Calvin Vestal, was born in Randolph County on 4 December 1841. By 1850 the couple were in Arkansas, where Patrick Green was born in May 1853, and in 1860 Nathan was a wheelwright with 1,200 dollars in land. Nathan's sister Sarah went to Iowa with her husband, Rev. Beeson Barker, and his brother Robert followed him to Strawberry Township by 1860.

Her last move was to Missouri. In 1870 she and Nathan were farming in Dent County, Missouri, with no land of their own, and she was still living in June of that year. She died in Oregon County, Missouri, in 1871 by the family tree, a year after the census date this profile carries, and Nathan married the widow Nancy (Rowe) Cole that same year. Her sons were Calvin Vestal (1841-1913) and Patrick Green (1853-1905), among others, and one of the others, Henry, married Hannah Grimes and raised the Moffitts of Stone County.

stories.title: David Grimes of Wayne County, and the daughter born on the river
stories.hook: Born in 1829 into a Tennessee farm family on the Highland Rim, David H. Grimes is known to us mainly through the daughter who married a Moffitt.
body: David H. Grimes was born in 1829 in Wayne County, Tennessee, a young county on the western edge of the Highland Rim. The legislature created Wayne County in 1817 and had to pass the act again in 1819 because the clerk never signed it; its first county court met at the home of Benjamin Hardin on Factor's Fork, where the old Natchez Trace crosses Shoal Creek. It was wooded country of ridges and hollows with iron deposits, and Clifton, on the Tennessee River, became its main commercial town and shipped cotton, livestock, lumber and cross ties downriver. David's world was the Hardin Creek farm of John Grimes and Penelope Blackshear, his probable parents, whose children were James B., Elisha S., John Anderson and William Jasper.

His father John died on 14 June 1844 and was buried on the Haggard farm, when David was about fifteen. His brothers stayed. John Anderson was farming on the home place in 1860 and 1900, and in 1872 William Jasper left a will naming "John A. Grimes, my brother, as executor." David is not named in that will. His birth in 1829 fits the unnamed son the Grimes family site lists between William Jasper (1826) and the end of the children, and a family tree names John Grimes as his father, but the link is unproved.

The rest of his life is in his daughter's records. A family tree has Hannah born in July 1855 at Arkansas City, Desha County, and David dying there in 1876. The place name is a later label: in 1855 the Mississippi landing now called Arkansas City was in Chicot County, and Desha County took in the area only in 1879. Hannah's 1910 age of 53 would put her birth nearer 1857, and a second profile gives Illinois. Whatever the town, the tree puts David in the lower Mississippi country of Arkansas by the mid-1850s, a long way from Hardin Creek, and has him dying in 1876. His daughter's stone in Herpel Cemetery reads "Wife of Henry H Moffitt."
src: Tennessee Encyclopedia, 'Wayne County' (tennesseeencyclopedia.net/entries/wayne-county/); Encyclopedia of Arkansas, 'Arkansas City Commercial District'; Genealogy.com Grimes forum postings of P. Bryant (2002-2003)

stories.title: The recorder of Cane Creek, and eleven children in twenty years
stories.hook: Joseph Chamness wrote the Cane Creek marriage certificates from 1764, lost his wife the year the youngest was born, and lived to see every child married.
body: Joseph Chamness was in his twenty-third year when he married Margaret Norton at Cane Creek Meeting on 17 March 1763. The certificate names him as the son of Anthony and Sarah Chamness of Orange County and her as the daughter of Edward and Elizabeth Norton of Rowan County; all four parents signed as witnesses. The next year, in 1764, the meeting made him its Recorder of Marriage Certificates, and the certificate book in his handwriting was kept in the vault at Guilford College when Zimri Hanson wrote the family's history in 1922. He was born in Baltimore County, Maryland, in 1740, and had come south with his father at the age of nine.

Eleven children were born to Joseph and Margaret between 1764 and 1784, the first three in Orange County and the rest in what became Randolph. Hanson lists Sarah (1764), William (1766), Elizabeth (1768), Mary (1770), Joseph (1771), Anthony (1773), Margaret (1776), Martha (1778), Lydia (1780), Edward (1782) and Mourning (1784). Joseph later took a certificate of removal from Cane Creek to Providence meeting in Randolph County, where he owned a farm. Martha, the eighth child, married Robert Moffitt at Providence in 1797, joining the Chamness and Moffitt families.

On the 12th of Fourth month 1784 Margaret died, with the youngest of her eleven, Mourning, a newborn. Hanson's account is that the eldest daughter, Sarah, then in her twentieth year, took charge of the infant and was the guiding star of the household until a stepmother appeared; some three years after her mother's death she married Obadiah Elliott in Randolph County and took the little sister into her own home. Joseph's second wife was Hannah Beeson, daughter of William and Mary Beeson, and they were married at Deep River meeting on 6 March 1786. Their daughter Susanna, born in 1788, was the twelfth child. Hanson counts twelve Beesons among the relatives of the bride when Joseph's son William married Isabel Beeson in Providence meeting, and records that William's stepmother signed that certificate too.

Joseph died on 17 May 1818 in Randolph County and is buried at Providence Cemetery. By Hanson's count he lived to see all his children married and settled, the youngest, Susanna, then about thirty. His own wedding certificate, printed in Hanson's book (pp. 17-18), is the document that ties the Chamness line to the Nortons, and his daughter's marriage to Robert Moffitt in 1797 tied both to the Moffitts.

stories.title: Pearl's family across the Red River
stories.hook: A Kentucky-born girl became a Texas farm neighbor, married Oscar Smith, and raised four children in southeastern Oklahoma.
body: Artie Pearl Satterfield was born in Butler County, Kentucky, in 1898, into the household of John C. and Samantha Johnson Satterfield. By 1910 the family had moved to Hagansport in Franklin County, Texas. Eleven-year-old Pearl and nineteen-year-old Oscar Smith appeared a few households apart on the same census route. They married in 1914. Their first daughter, Nellie Mae, was born at Talco, Texas, on 3 April 1917.

The Smiths crossed the Red River to Choctaw County, Oklahoma. In 1920, Pearl, Oscar and little Nellie were living on a rented farm in Oakes Township. By 1930 they were at Jeter with four children: Nellie, Robert Lee, Virgil and Faye. Faye had been born at Forney on 23 March 1929. The 1940 census still placed the household on rented farmland along Hugo Route 1. Pearl's family had gone from Kentucky to Texas to Oklahoma in one generation; the children's records preserve the different stops.

Pearl outlived Oscar and her eldest daughter. Nellie Mae Choat died in Paris, Texas, on 7 July 1973, aged 56, after breast cancer; her death certificate names her parents as Charley O. Smith and Pearl Satterfield. She was brought home to Hugo for burial at Mount Olivet Cemetery. Pearl lived until 1983 and was buried beside Oscar at Grant Cemetery. Her youngest daughter Faye lived until 2014, carrying the Smith and Satterfield connection into the Moffitt family.

stories.title: John B. Smith, who owned his Hagansport farm free and clear
stories.hook: A farmer on the Sulphur River divide who buried his wife at thirty-seven and lay beside her under a wooden stob.
body: The June 1900 census for Justice Precinct 2 of Franklin County, Texas, finds John B. Smith, 44, farming land he owned free of mortgage. With him were his wife Emma, their son Oscar, 10, daughters Vera, Luina, Lona and Allie, and a baby, Jimmie. The family lived around Hagansport, a community that grew up at a Sulphur River crossing called Hagan's Port and that by 1884 had about 150 people, four churches, a one-room school, a mill and a gin. Oscar, later Charles Oscar Smith, had been born there on 29 May 1889.

Emma Elizabeth Langley was born on 11 December 1867 in Texas. The only census household that fits her is that of George W. Langley, a Georgia-born widower of Precinct 5 in neighboring Hopkins County in 1880, who had two daughters, Emma J., 12, and Eliza J., 8 (probable). She died on 15 March 1905, aged 37, and her stone in Hagansport Cemetery reads "Emma / Wife of / J.B. SMITH / Gone but not forgotten." Six children were in the house in 1900, the youngest a baby.

John did not stay a widower. By April 1910 he had remarried, and Oscar, 19, was working on the home farm. On the same census route, a few doors away, the census taker recorded John C. Satterfield, lately of Kentucky, with his wife Samantha and their daughter Pearl, 11. Oscar and Artie Pearl Satterfield married in 1914. Owning rather than renting set John apart in the county: in 1900 only 44.1 percent of Franklin County farms were run by their owners, and the usual tenant gave up half the crop.

John B. Smith died in 1918 and was buried at Hagansport beside Emma; his grave is marked with a wooden stob. His own parents are not established: Ancestry trees suggest Noah Smith and Mary P. (Keith), but no census, marriage or death record naming them is in hand (lead) and his Texas death certificate is not indexed. His son Charles carried the farm tradition across the Red River to Choctaw County, Oklahoma, where he is buried at Grant.
src: 1900 and 1910 U.S. Census, Franklin Co., Tex.; Find a Grave (Hagansport Cemetery); obituary of Lona May Ottinger (1975). Handbook of Texas, 'Hagansport'; Soil Survey of Franklin County, Texas (1908), pp. 931-947; 1880 U.S. census, Precinct 5, Hopkins Co., Tex.
kv: George W. Langley, b. c.1842 Georgia: 1880 census, Hopkins Co., Tex., daughter Emma J., 12

Ancestry suggests Noah Smith and Mary P. (Keith); no census, marriage or death record naming them has been seen. His Texas death certificate of 13 Apr 1918 (Franklin Co.) did not turn up in the Texas Death Certificates index; the Find a Grave memorial for John B. Smith names only his wife and daughters.

stories.title: Thomas Staples and Hananiah Gaunt's daughter
stories.hook: Thomas Staples's will of 1758 names a daughter Ann and two granddaughters, and through one of them the line passes to the Nordykes.
body: Thomas Staples of Burlington, New Jersey, wrote his will on 25 October 1758, naming his daughter "Ann, wife of Thomas Rogers" and his granddaughters "Mehetable and Mary Rogers." His wife Mehitable was the daughter of Hananiah Gaunt of Springfield Township, whose 1720 will names "Mahitable Staples" and "son-in-law Thomas Staples." Ann married Thomas Rogers at Upper Springfield Meeting on 30 October 1736.

A Burlington County administration of 6 December 1748 may belong to the next generation: "Staples, Thomas, Jun'r, of Burlington Co., innholder" died without a will, and administration went to Thomas Rogers, the husband of Ann Staples, with John Deacon and John Antram of the City of Burlington as bondsmen. The inventory was only 30 pounds 7 shillings. If this Thomas Jr. was Ann's brother, it fits Thomas Rogers acting for the estate (probable).
Granddaughter Mary Rogers married Abraham Nordyke on 1 June 1761 ("Three wills from Quaker New Jersey").

stories.title: John Rodgers and a third of the residue
stories.hook: John Rodgers of Burlington left his son Thomas one-third of the residue in a will proved in March 1767.
body: John Rodgers of Burlington, New Jersey, made his will on 23 January 1764. The published New Jersey will calendar abstracts his gift to his son Thomas as one-third of the residue. An inventory was made on 7 March 1767 and the will was proved on 26 March. The other thirds went to his daughter-in-law Elizabeth, then wife of William Lyndon, with her three daughters, and to the children of his daughter Martha, wife of Robert Hosier.

The son Thomas is identified in this family as Thomas Rogers, who married Ann Staples at Upper Springfield Meeting on 30 October 1736; their daughter Mary married Abraham Nordyke in 1761. The will abstract names Thomas but does not name his wife, and it gives no name for John’s own wife or parents.

The proposed connection to Martha Middleton and to the John Rogers born in 1687 to John and Mary Groom remains a lead. A separate calendar entry records John Rogers of Windsor, Middlesex County, whose will was dated 6 January 1769 and proved 10 April 1776. It names sons Isaac, Abraham, Joseph, John, Robert, Amos and Mathew, and daughters Mary and Martha; no Thomas is named in that abstract. Those dates and beneficiaries distinguish the Windsor estate from the Burlington estate proved in 1767. They do not establish which family belongs to the 1687 birth record.

Independently examined printed abstract: https://archive.org/details/calendarofnewjer04newj/page/360/mode/2up . Calendar of New Jersey Wills, vol. V, 1771–1780, p. 431, John Rogers of Windsor, will dated 6 Jan 1769, proved 10 Apr 1776; citing Lib. 17, p. 354. Independently examined printed abstract: https://archive.org/details/calendarofnewjer05newj/page/431/mode/1up . Proposed earlier family: WikiTree Rogers-3993 and Rogers-3994; Martha Middleton’s 1712 will. The original manuscript wills have not been examined here.

stories.title: Hananiah Gaunt: from a Quaker wedding at Sandwich to 500 acres at Hananicon
stories.hook: Hananiah Gaunt married a Quaker neighbor's daughter at Sandwich in May 1678, traded his Cape Cod land for New Jersey land the next day, and died on his own acres in Springfield Township.
body: On 3 May 1678 Hananiah Gaunt posted his intention to marry Dorothy Butler at the Sandwich Friends Meeting on Cape Cod. The next day he and his brother Israel exchanged their Sandwich land for land in New Jersey. On 10 May they were married. His father Peter Gaunt, who had been fined in cattle by the Plymouth Colony court for Quaker meetings, is recorded as dying on 10 May 1678, the same day; one of the two dates is probably wrong ("No publicke vizable worship now in the world"). Dorothy's brother Daniel had been whipped for helping a Quaker in 1660 ("Daniel Butler's whipping").

The couple lived at Dartmouth, Massachusetts, until about 1685. On 11 May 1685 George Hutcheson of Burlington conveyed "to Hananiah Gaunt of Rhode Island, yeoman, for 500 acres in the First Tenth," and the proprietors' survey of July 1685 enters "500 a. near Honeonickon" (later Oneanickon, then Springfield Township). On 18 May 1687 "Hananiah Gaunt of near Oneanickon, yeoman," sold 100 acres to William Bustill, a carpenter of Shrewsbury, and in 1690 Hutcheson deeded him one twenty-fourth of a share of West Jersey, a proprietary right to land.

The county history, quoting Revel's Book of Surveys, shows him as a settled neighbor. Land "surveyed for William Biddle, at Oneanickon, 8th month, 1686, two hundred and seventy acres of land, and in 4th month, 1689, one tract of two hundred and thirty acres, and two other tracts, containing together three hundred and twenty-three acres" adjoined "lands of Hannaniah Gauntt, John Days, Peter Harvey, Charles Read, Samuel Barker, Daniel Leeds, Michael Buffin, John Browne, and John Shinn."

Dorothy died there on 26 April 1714. Hananiah made his will on 17 July 1720, naming his children Daniel, Zebulon, Mahitable Staples and Mary Webb, and his son-in-law Thomas Staples; it was proved on 17 November 1721. His daughter Mehitable's daughter Ann married Thomas Rogers in 1736, and Ann's daughter Mary married Abraham Nordyke in 1761, so the farm at Hananicon is where this line's New Jersey roots begin.

stories.title: The charge against the women's minutes
stories.hook: In December 1766, Cane Creek Friends expelled Charles Davies after a dispute over the truth of the women's meeting record.
body: At Cane Creek Monthly Meeting on 6 December 1766, Charles Davies's name entered the minute book as a disciplinary matter. His complaint concerned the women's minutes: he had charged them with being mixed with an untruth. The record does not preserve the passage he disputed or explain his side of the argument. It records what the meeting decided to do about it.

Friends had already made repeated efforts to change his mind. Their minute says the labor had been to no purpose, and the meeting therefore disowned him. On the same page, ordinary business continued around the dispute: certificates of membership, a marriage report and appointments to attend the quarterly meeting. The break with Charles was entered in the same practical hand as those routine decisions.

Charles and Hannah Matson Davies had raised the family from which Mary Davies married William Moffitt in 1763. Charles owned 187 acres purchased in 1758 and was recorded as a minister in 1761. The 1766 decision shows a rupture within that Quaker community; it does not establish that he left North Carolina or ceased to believe. He lived until 1801. His daughter Mary's own will, written more than fifty years after the dispute, still used the numbered-month date familiar in Quaker records.
src: Radnor MM marriage certificate (1732/3); Davis, Davis: A Quaker Family (1985); Hinshaw vol. 1; U.S., Quaker Meeting Records, 1681-1935 (Cane Creek MM minutes, 6 Dec 1766); Cane Creek Monthly Meeting minutes, 6 December 1766, manuscript page 36, U.S. Quaker Meeting Records, 1681–1935.

stories.title: Married as an orphan at West Nottingham: Elizabeth Brown and Edward Norton
stories.hook: Elizabeth Brown was about eight when her father died. At twenty she married a Quaker born in Ireland, and their road ended at Cane Creek.
body: The Nottingham Monthly Meeting certificate of 16 October 1739 gives both sides in a few lines. The bridegroom was Edward Norton of West Nottingham, Chester County, son of the late Edward Norton of the Parish of Armagh in the Kingdom of Ireland. The bride was Elizabeth Brown, "dt William & Elizabeth (Cowgill), both dec." She had been born about 1718. Her mother died before her father married again in March 1721/2, and her father, William Brown Jr., died about 1727; her stepmother, Margaret Davis, then married William Kirk. Her grandfather, the emigrant William Brown, was an elder of the meeting.

Edward's own connections were tangled with hers from the start. His sister Mary Norton had married Elizabeth's uncle Richard Brown in November 1733, and both couples took certificates to Hopewell Monthly Meeting in Virginia, Edward and Elizabeth on 19 January 1739/40. Richard died before 1747, and when Fairfax meeting looked into the settlement of his will to protect his children, Mary married William Kirk, the widower of the same Margaret Davis who had been Elizabeth's stepmother.

From Hopewell the Nortons went on to Fairfax and then south. They reached Cane Creek in 1762, and the next March their daughter Margaret, born about 1740, married Joseph Chamness. The certificate calls the bride's parents "Edward Norton and Elizabeth, his wife, of Rowan County," and both signed as witnesses. Edward died in 1776 and is buried at Providence, Randolph County. Their granddaughter Martha married Robert Moffitt in 1797, which is how an orphan from West Nottingham and a family from Armagh come into the Moffitt story.

stories.title: John Matson of Merion, and the daughter who married at a justice's house
stories.hook: John Matson gave his consent in February 1733 for his daughter Hannah to marry Charles Davis; their daughter Mary married William Moffitt at Cane Creek.
body: The document that puts John Matson on record is his daughter's marriage certificate. In the twelfth month of 1732, by the Friends' count, Charles Davis of Blockley and Hannah Matson, "daughter of John Matson of Merion in the same county and province aforesaid with consent of her father," published their intentions under a Pennsylvania law against clandestine marriages and met at the house of Charles Read, Esq., a justice of the peace for Philadelphia. The witnesses were John Matson Jr. and Daniel Matson, probably Hannah's brothers, along with Evan and Jane George, Richard and Thomas George, Ellin Jones and Mary Andrew. Hannah was born about 1715.

John was a Quaker farmer of Merion, in the Welsh settlement west of Philadelphia. By the usual reckoning he was born about 1686 at Upper Merion and married a woman named Margaret before 1709. Their children were Daniel, Hannah, Morris, Catherine, John, Peter and Joseph. Matson is a Swedish name, and Swedes had farmed along the Schuylkill and the Delaware before Penn's grant, but the Swedish Colonial Society's study and the Mattson genealogy of 1983 do not make him a son of the Swede Johann Mattson; his parentage is undocumented. In 1742 he and his wife took a certificate from Chester Monthly Meeting to Goshen.

John Matson was buried on 3 May 1748, and his will was proved in Chester County on 16 July 1748. By then his daughter Hannah and Charles Davis had left Pennsylvania for Virginia and then Cane Creek, North Carolina, where Charles was disowned by the meeting in 1766 and died in 1801; Hannah lived until 25 October 1812. Their daughter Mary married William Moffitt there on 2 April 1763, sixteen days after the Chamness-Norton wedding, and her son Robert married Martha Chamness in 1797. John Matson of Merion is Robert Moffitt's great-grandfather on his mother's side.

stories.title: Joseph Cole's will, and the two-year-old who became Sarah Chamness
stories.hook: Joseph Cole made his will on 22 January 1720/1, leaving a widow and a daughter, Sarah, not yet three, who later married Anthony Chamness.
body: Joseph Cole of Baltimore County, Maryland, was the son of John Cole and Johanna Garrett. Barnes's Baltimore County Families lists him as "Cole, Joseph (6), s. of John (5) and Johanna." In November 1712 his father conveyed him part of a tract called "Daniel's Whimsey." His mother's father was Dennis Garrett, the early settler killed in 1691.

He made his will on 22 January 1720/1, and it names his wife Susanna and his daughter Sarah. Sarah was born on the 1st day of the 5th month 1718 in the Friends' register, so when her father wrote the will she was not yet three. The Cane Creek register later wrote her down as the "daughter of Joseph and Susanna Cole, of Baltimore Co., Md., now married to Anthony Chainness."

On 24 November 1735 Sarah married Anthony Chamness at St. Paul's Parish, Baltimore County. Anthony, a London-born servant who had finished his indenture, was about twenty-two, and she was seventeen. They went to Monocacy, then to Carver's Creek in 1749 and Cane Creek in 1751, and Sarah bore thirteen children. Zimri Hanson's 1922 history describes their farm, a mile west of the Cane Creek meetinghouse: a hewn-oak log house with a porch the length of the front, a grist mill on a small creek and large meadows on either side. Sarah died about 1773 and is buried in the Friends' graveyard at Cane Creek. Her son Joseph Chamness married Margaret Norton, and their daughter Martha was Robert Moffitt's wife.
src: Will of Joseph Cole; Barnes, Baltimore County Families. Zimri Hanson, History and Genealogy of the American Descendants of John and Ann Chamness (1922), on Sarah Cole and the Chamness farm

stories.title: John Cole of Cole's Adventure: a witness at his father-in-law's trial
stories.hook: John Cole was about twenty-two when he was named as a witness in the Garrett case, and about sixty-seven when he gave evidence on the bounds of his own land in 1738.
body: John Cole's name is in the Provincial Court record of the death of his wife's father. The court's 1692 indictment of John Oldton for the sword blow that killed Dennis Garrett listed its witnesses: Philip Roper, Nicholas Hale, "John Cole (son-in-law of the deceased)," Thomas Stone, Abraham Vaughan and Barbara Garrett, the widow. John had married Dennis's daughter Johanna. Oldton was condemned to hang and was pardoned; he later served as captain of the county's rangers. John Cole was then about twenty-two.

The records that follow are surveys. William B. Marye's 1921 study of the old garrison roads of Baltimore County lists "Cole's Choice," surveyed for him on 28 July 1694 and never patented; "Cole's Addition," 67 acres surveyed on 29 May 1698 "on the north side of Patapsco River in the woods"; and "Cole's Adventure," surveyed in 1706 on a run called Gwin's Run. In March 1737/8, when a land commission sat on Cole's Adventure, "John Cole, Senior, aged about 67 years," testified that the beginning tree stood about a hundred yards east of Gwinn's Run.

In August 1750 another commission took depositions about Cole's Addition from men who had known him. John Ensor, Sr., aged 55, called him his father-in-law and said that about eighteen years earlier, around 1732, Cole had come with him to the spot and shown him where the boundary oak stood. By then Cole had died, in 1746, at about seventy-six. His land lay in and around the site of Baltimore, which was laid out as a town in 1729.

The family is easy to follow. His son Joseph made a will in 1720/1 and left a daughter, Sarah, who married Anthony Chamness in 1735; a son named Dennis Garrett Cole received land from his grandmother Barbara Garrett Broad in 1712. Sarah's son Joseph Chamness was the father of Martha, who married Robert Moffitt in 1797.

stories.title: Ann Mercer’s six children and her Quaker ministry
stories.hook: Ann Mercer bore six children with William Brown and was remembered among the Friends who spoke in meeting.
body: An original Ringwood Quaker entry records Ann Mercer, daughter of Thomas and Ann Mercer of Ringwood, born on the twenty-fourth day of the twelfth month 1666: 24 February 1666/7, or 1667 in modern year numbering. Her identification with Ann Mercer, William Brown’s second wife in Pennsylvania, remains probable. Later accounts place Thomas at Andover before he and his daughter crossed to Pennsylvania about 1682–83 and settled in Aston Township, Chester County. William’s original Wellingborough Quaker birth entry records him on the twenty-ninth day of the first month 1658 (29 March, Old Style), the son of Richard Browne; it does not name his mother. William had married Dorothy in England, and their son Joseph was born there on 12 June 1682. Dorothy died at sea on the voyage to the Delaware. William went first to his brother James, a weaver at Marcus Hook, and in 1684, when Ann was seventeen, he married her.

Gilbert Cope's 1864 list of the family, built from the Nottingham Monthly Meeting registers, gives the children Ann bore him: Mercer, born the 27th of the 12th month 1685; Ann, 1st of the 10th month 1687; William, 21st of the 7th month 1689; John, 3rd of the 5th month 1691; Richard, 31st of the 1st month 1693; and Thomas, 17th of the 11th month 1694. Mercer, named for her family and often written "Messer," was the first. Ann Mercer died in 1696; a 1709 Quaker list of Friends who died in Pennsylvania names her as "Ann Browne daughtr of said Thoms Mercer." Her father Thomas had died on 22 November 1694, eight weeks before her youngest, Thomas Brown, was born in January 1695.

Ann also had a public religious role. A catalogue read at the Yearly Meeting in 1709 remembered Anne Browne among the deceased Public Friends—the people who spoke in meeting. It names her as Thomas Mercer’s daughter, says she crossed with her father and received a Testimony for Truth after arriving, and records her burial in 1696. Her place in that list preserves a part of her life beyond the names and dates of her children.

William married Catharine Williams of Philadelphia in 1699, and in 1702 he moved to the Nottingham Lots on the Pennsylvania-Maryland line, where Lots 23 and 33 were assigned to him. A 1902 history of the Brick Meeting House says that he "was the first Friend to settle on the Nottingham lots" and that the first meeting was held at his house in 1704. His fourth wife, whom he married in 1711, was Mary Matthews. The family memorandum entered at East Nottingham Monthly Meeting in 1786 calls him an elder and a substantial Friend, and puts his death in 1746 in his ninety-first year; the Wellingborough register, which gives his birth in 1658, would make him about eighty-eight.

Ann Mercer’s descendants connect several branches of the family. Her son William married Elizabeth Cowgill in 1715; her son Thomas married Elizabeth's sister Ellin in 1718/9; her son Richard married three times and ended with Mary Norton of Armagh in 1733; and William's daughter Elizabeth Brown married Mary's brother Edward Norton in 1739. Their daughter Margaret Norton married Joseph Chamness, and Margaret's daughter Martha married Robert Moffitt. Ann Mercer is Martha Chamness's great-great-grandmother, and so the ancestor of every child Martha bore Robert Moffitt.

stories.title: Chamniss of Wapping: the London parents of a boy bound for Maryland
stories.hook: John Chamness married Ann Weary at St John's, Wapping, in January 1704; twenty years later their son Anthony was bound as a servant for seven years in Maryland.
body: John Chamness and Ann Weary were married on 4 January 1704 at St John's Church, Wapping, the riverside parish beside the Thames, east of the Tower. The register spells the name "Chamniss," and Ann's surname Weary or Wearey. Online trees that call her Ann Jones have nothing behind them. Their children came steadily: at least eight between 1705 and 1717, baptized in the same parish. Anthony, the one who matters here, was baptized in February 1713 when he was eighteen days old. Cane Creek Meeting later wrote him down as "Anthony Chamness, s. John & Ann, b. about 2 mo. 1713, Est. Smithfield, London," so the family lived at East Smithfield, close to Wapping.

Anthony was bound as a servant on 9 February 1724/5. The indenture, which describes him as of Whitechapel, bound him for seven years to John Cooke, a London victualler, for service in "Maryland (his Majesty's Plantation in America)." It gives his age as fifteen; counted from his baptism he was about eleven. Either way he was out of his time by 1732 and was in Baltimore County, where on 24 November 1735 he married Sarah Cole, the great-granddaughter of the murdered Dennis Garrett.

The title of Zimri Hanson's 1922 family history, History and Genealogy of the American Descendants of John and Ann Chamness of London, England, names John and Ann as the founders of the American line. John and Ann themselves leave only the parish registers: no will, no trade and no death date. Their son, the boy sent to Maryland at the age of eleven or fifteen, became overseer of the Cane Creek meeting and in 1751 took up 490 acres there.

stories.title: Henry Satterfield, who died in 1861 with twelve children
stories.hook: A Tennessee-born farmer in Allen County, Kentucky, and the Garrison daughter who outlived him by thirty-five years.
body: The 1885 Butler County sketch of his son James names Henry Satterfield in one sentence: "a native of Maury County, Tenn.; died in 1861, at the age of fifty years." His death register entry, 24 December 1861, names his parents as Ephraim and "Rutha" Satterfield. He was born about 1811, two years after Ephraim Satterfield married Ruth Knowles in Warren County, and Maury County is where the sketch places the young couple. His son James was born in Allen County on 14 April 1838.

Henry married Mary Garrison, born 17 October 1811, the daughter of John M. Garrison of Allen County and of Martha "Patsey" Cannon (lead). The 1885 sketch names their twelve children: Louisa J. (Roy), David E., Samuel A., James H., Ruth M. (Massey), John E., Euphema P. (Liles), Hettie C. (Jones), Martha C. (deceased), Sarah E. (Hues), Joseph W. H. and Abraham W. Of the twelve, James H., born in 1838, married Melissa Gibson in 1859 and is the line to the Smiths. In 1861, the year his father died, James enlisted in the Ninth Kentucky, and an S. A. Satterfield, perhaps their son Samuel A., was sued with A. W. Garrison in 1871 in Warren Circuit Court over lot 74 in Bowling Green (Garrison v. Clark, 151 Ky. 565); the opinion gives only initials (lead).

Mary's parents' marriage ended in the legislature. In 1847 the Kentucky General Assembly dissolved the marriage of her father John M. Garrison and Patsey; Mary was then 36. She outlived Henry by thirty-five years and died on 2 March 1896.

quotes.t: His father, Henry Satterfield, a native of Maury County, Tenn.; died in 1861, at the age of fifty years.

stories.title: James and Cynthia Gibson of Allen County, Melissa's parents
stories.hook: Two names from a county history, and the daughter who married a Satterfield in 1859.
body: James and Cynthia (Woodcock) Gibson are named once, in the 1885 sketch of their son-in-law James H. Satterfield of Butler County: Melissa A., his first wife, was the "daughter of James and Cynthia (Woodcock) Gibson, of Allen County." The Allen County marriage register confirms Melissa's wedding to James Satterfield on 17 September 1859.

Allen County, created in 1815 from Warren and Barren, was where both families lived. Melissa and James had children together; the 1885 sketch names Henry W., John C., Sidney R., James D., Martha A. and Mary C., among them John C., born in February 1864. In 1867 the Satterfields left for Dakota County, Minnesota, and returned in 1875 to Warren County and then, in 1876, Butler County. Melissa died on 2 May 1877, the year after the move. A fire at the Allen County courthouse in 1902 destroyed some county records.

Melissa's son John C. Satterfield farmed at Horse Mill in Butler County and moved to Hagansport, Texas, about 1907. His daughter Artie Pearl Satterfield married Charles Oscar Smith in 1914, and their daughter Faye (Smith) Moffitt is the link to this family.

stories.place: Allen County, Kentucky. Parents of Melissa A. (Gibson) Satterfield.

stories.title: Ephraim Satterfield, a Virginian by his grandson's account
stories.hook: One of thirteen children named in a Warren County will, he married a Knowles in 1809 and is gone by 1850.
body: The Butler County sketch of 1885 introduces Ephraim in a subordinate clause, as the father of Henry Satterfield and "a native of Virginia, who died about 1850." Warren County, Kentucky, supplies the documents. John Satterfield's will, recorded in Will Book D at page 262 and proved on 10 November 1847, names Ephraim among thirteen children: Uriah, Ephraim, Rebecca, Mary, Jeremiah, Phoebe, Nancy, Moses, Sarah, Jesse, Leah, Reuben and John. On 12 November 1809 Ephraim married Ruth Knowles in Warren County, and Ruth's father Joshua Knowles named "Ruth Saterfield" among his daughters in a will of 1824.

Their son Henry was born about 1811, in Maury County, Tennessee, by the 1885 account. Henry's own Kentucky death register entry of 24 December 1861 names his parents as Ephraim and "Rutha" Satterfield, and that is the document that ties Henry to this Ephraim and Ruth (probable). The sources disagree about Ephraim himself. WikiTree has him born in South Carolina in 1787 and dead in 1848, with Henry born in Warren County, while the 1885 sketch gives Virginia and Tennessee. A birth in South Carolina fits the will of his father John, who had lived in South Carolina before Kentucky.

By 1850 Ruth was a widow in Allen County, living with her daughter Elizabeth. Ephraim's death falls between his father's will of 1847 and that census, and the 1885 sketch dates it about 1850. His grandson James H. Satterfield, who supplied the sketch, was twelve in 1850.

stories.title: Melvina Clark: a birth date and age that disagree
stories.hook: Her 1929 death certificate names both parents, but its birth date and recorded age disagree.
body: Melvina’s original Kentucky death certificate uses the married spelling Johnston. It records her death at Big Reedy in Edmonson County on 17 January 1929, describes her as a widow, and names her father as Newton Clark, born in Kentucky, and her mother as Mary Dunn. Polly Nash of Big Reedy supplied the information. The space for her husband’s name is blank; this record does not identify him.

The certificate’s birth date is read and indexed as 10 November 1851, although the final year digits are not perfectly clear. It also records an age of 78 years, 2 months, 6 days. That age is inconsistent with the written birth and death dates. Both fields are preserved here without choosing a corrected birth year.

The original 1850 census for Newton Clark’s Butler County household lists Newton, 32; Polly, 32; Martha, 10; Granville, 9; Stanford, 8; Hester, 6; William, 5; a girl aged 3 indexed as Vina; and Mary, 11 months. The handwriting of the age-three girl’s name does not unambiguously identify her as Melvina. The former claim that this census establishes Melvina’s birth about 1847 is therefore withdrawn. The census has no relationship column, and the identification of Vina with Melvina remains open.

Compiled family profiles identify Newton’s wife as Polly Elms and link the family to William and Lavina (Willis) Clark. Melvina’s death certificate instead gives her mother’s maiden name as Dunn. No examined marriage record reconciles Dunn and Elms or proves that the same woman bore both names. The identification of the mother named in 1929 with Polly in Newton’s 1850 household remains probable, rather than an established maiden-name sequence.

Her married name was Johnson; her husband's first name is not recorded on the memorials. Samantha D. was born on 28 March 1872 and Charlie in 1885. Samantha married John C. Satterfield in 1892, moved with him to Hagansport, Texas, about 1907, and crossed the Red River to Choctaw County, Oklahoma, after marrying Bird Alexander Stephens in 1917. She died on 1 October 1928 and is buried at Soper Cemetery.

The death certificate records burial at Mount Pleasant on 18 January 1929. The family memorial identifies this as Mount Pleasant Cemetery at Big Reedy. Samantha had died on 1 October 1928; the records examined do not establish that Melvina attended her Oklahoma burial. Charlie remained in Butler County and died in 1959.

stories.title: The Norton from Armagh who left a son and a daughter in Pennsylvania
stories.hook: Edward Norton of Armagh is known only from what his children's marriage certificates say of him, but it is enough to place his family in Ireland.
body: The Nottingham Monthly Meeting certificate of 16 October 1739 describes the bridegroom as "Edward Norton of West Nottingham, Chester County, son of Edward Norton of 'ye City and Parish of Armagh,' Ireland, deceased." That is all it says. His wife's name is not given, nor is his trade or the year of his death. He was dead by October 1739. Albert Cook Myers, who collected the certificates of Irish Friends settling in Pennsylvania between 1682 and 1750, prints the two Norton marriages together on p. 376 of his 1902 book, one under the other.

The other marriage is his daughter's. On 24 November 1733, "Mary Norton, daughter of Edward Norton, 'of ye County of Armagh,' Ireland," married Richard Brown, son of William Brown of West Nottingham. Cope's genealogy of the Browns gives the same marriage as the 24th of the 5th month and calls her "dau. of Edward Norton of Co. Armagh, Irel'd." She was Richard's third wife. Together the two certificates put two adult children of the same Armagh Quaker in Chester County, near the Maryland line, within six years, part of the Irish Friends' emigration that Myers traced.

Both Norton marriages were into the Brown family, and both couples went on to Virginia. Edward Norton the younger and Elizabeth Brown are the Moffitt ancestors; their daughter Margaret married Joseph Chamness at Cane Creek in 1763, and Margaret's daughter Martha married Robert Moffitt. Mary and Richard Brown had three sons, Richard, Joseph and Mercer; Richard died before 1747, and in April 1747 Mary married William Kirk. The elder Edward, who stayed in Armagh as far as the certificates show, is the earliest Norton on this line.

stories.title: Two Cowgill sisters, two Brown brothers, and a daughter left behind
stories.hook: William Brown Jr. married a Cowgill in 1715, buried her within six years and a second wife by 1730, and left a daughter who married at West Nottingham as an orphan.
body: William Brown Jr. was born on the 21st day of the 7th month 1689, the third child of the Nottingham pioneer William Brown and Ann Mercer. In 1715 he married Elizabeth Cowgill, born on the 24th of the 6th month 1694 at Middletown, Bucks County, to John Cowgill and Bridget Croasdale. Her father had come from Yorkshire in 1682; accounts differ on which ship carried the Settle families. He was a tanner who moved about 1713 or 1714 to the Delaware shore, where on 10 May 1718 he asked for another hundred acres, "having erected a tan-yard on a branch of Black Bird's Creek." The marriage was recorded in Duck Creek Monthly Meeting as that of Elizabeth Cowgill, "daughter of John Cowgill, of Duck Creek in New Castle," and William Brown, "son of William Brown, of Nottingham."

Cope's list gives the couple two children. John was born on the 27th of the 2nd month 1717 and died on the 12th of the 7th month 1723, aged six. Elizabeth was born in the twelfth month of 1718, which in modern dating is early 1719. Her mother died within about three years of that birth, before March 1721/2, when William married Margaret Davis. That marriage produced William (1722) and Jacob (1724), and William Jr. himself died about 1727. His widow married William Kirk on the 6th of the 3rd month 1730. Her stepdaughter Elizabeth was eight or nine when her father died. In 1739 the Nottingham book called her "dt William & Elizabeth (Cowgill), both dec."

The Cowgill sisters had already made two marriages with the Browns. Elizabeth's sister Ellin, born on the 14th of the 10th month 1700, married William's brother Thomas Brown in 1718/9; Thomas died on 19 February 1746/7, and Ellin lived to 5 January 1772, aged 71. Two immigrant families, one from Yorkshire and one from Northamptonshire and Hampshire, had become a single network of cousins at Nottingham.

The child they left carried the line. Elizabeth Brown married Edward Norton at West Nottingham on 16 October 1739, her uncle Richard Brown having married Edward's sister Mary six years before, and their daughter Margaret married Joseph Chamness at Cane Creek in 1763. Through Elizabeth Brown, the Cowgill and Brown families became part of the Norton and Chamness lines.

stories.title: John Satterfield's will, with thirteen children in a single line
stories.hook: Born in Orange County, North Carolina, and dead in Warren County, Kentucky, at about eighty-one.
body: John Satterfield was born about 1766 in Orange County, North Carolina, a county formed in 1752 and since divided so that his birthplace lies in Person County. He lived in South Carolina and later settled in Warren County, Kentucky, where he made a will recorded in Will Book D at page 262 and proved on 10 November 1847. It lists thirteen children: Uriah, Ephraim, Rebecca, Mary, Jeremiah, Phoebe, Nancy, Moses, Sarah, Jesse, Leah, Reuben and John.

His wife Mary, born about 1768, is named in the will. Her maiden name is not settled: Find a Grave gives Jones, and a 1786 marriage record from Surry County, North Carolina, gives Haga. John's own father is disputed and is not shown here. Ephraim's place in the list is the link to this family. Ephraim's son Henry died on 24 December 1861, and the Kentucky register names Henry's father as Ephraim, which matches the Ephraim of the will (probable).
The sources differ on where Ephraim was born: WikiTree has South Carolina in 1787, where John had lived, while the 1885 sketch by his grandson calls him a Virginian.

stories.title: Ruth Knowles Satterfield, who died in Missouri at eighty-one
stories.hook: Born in Virginia, married in Warren County in 1809, widowed by 1850, and buried a long way from either.
body: Ruth Knowles was born about 1783 in Virginia, the daughter of Joshua Knowles, whose 1824 will names "Ruth Saterfield" among his five daughters. On 12 November 1809 she married Ephraim Satterfield in Warren County, Kentucky. Her son Henry was born about 1811 and his death register entry of 24 December 1861 names his parents as Ephraim and "Rutha" Satterfield.

By 1850 she was a widow in Allen County, living with her daughter Elizabeth. In 1860 the census found "Rutha Satterfield," about 77, in the household of Elizabeth and her husband Jesse Agee in Gasconade County, Missouri. She died there in 1864, having outlived her husband by about fourteen years and her son Henry by three.
Her reason for going to Missouri is not stated in any source. The identification of Ruth with our Ephraim's wife rests on Henry's death register and her father's will (probable).

stories.title: Joshua Knowles's will: a wife named Jemima and five daughters
stories.hook: A Warren County man past eighty who wrote his will in 1824 and lived another eight years.
body: Joshua Knowles was born about 1747, and the 1830 census counted him in Warren County, Kentucky, between 80 and 90. He wrote his will on 11 November 1824, and it was proved in October 1832. It names his wife Jemima, his son Matthew as executor, his son John of Franklin County, Virginia, and five daughters: Sarah Hays, Polly Stephens, Leaner Jones, Ruth Saterfield and Elizabeth Bailey. Ruth was born in Virginia.

Ruth is the daughter that matters here. She had married Ephraim Satterfield in Warren County on 12 November 1809, and her father's will, written fifteen years later, calls her "Ruth Saterfield" in the clerk's spelling. The will does not say whether Jemima was Ruth's mother or a later wife.
His burial place is Knowles Cemetery at Motley in Warren County (Find a Grave). The will is cited from WikiTree and has not been read in the original (probable).

stories.title: Thomas Mercer of Andover, who crossed with his daughter Ann
stories.hook: A Hampshire Quaker widower brought his teenage daughter to Pennsylvania in 1682-83; she married at seventeen, and he died there in 1694.
body: Thomas Mercer and his wife Ann lived at Ringwood in Hampshire when their daughter Ann was born. The original Quaker register names both parents and dates the birth to the twenty-fourth day of the twelfth month 1666. In the Friends’ calendar then in use, this means 24 February 1666/7, or 1667 in modern year numbering. The entry gives the mother’s first name but no maiden surname. Later family accounts place Thomas at Andover before crossing to Pennsylvania with his daughter about 1682–83; identification with the Ringwood family remains probable.

He took up land in Aston Township, Chester County, and his daughter was married there in 1684 to William Brown, born in Northamptonshire, who had landed a year or two earlier. Ann was seventeen. Her first child, born in February 1685/6, was named Mercer for her family. Thomas Mercer lived long enough to see five grandchildren born, and died on 22 November 1694. A 1709 Quaker list of public Friends who died in Pennsylvania names him and "Ann Browne daughtr of said Thoms Mercer," who died in 1696.

Thomas Mercer's own parents are unknown. Through Ann his line runs to her son William Brown Jr., his daughter Elizabeth Brown, her daughter Margaret Norton and her daughter Martha Chamness, who married Robert Moffitt.

The two Anns belong to different generations: Ann, wife of Thomas, was the mother; Ann Mercer, who married William Brown, was the daughter. The elder Ann’s maiden surname and life dates remain unknown. Keeping those identities separate preserves the maternal link without supplying a name the birth entry does not give.

The 1709 catalogue gives the immigrant father and daughter their own entries: Thomas Mercer of Andover, who arrived about 1682 or 1683 and died in 1694, and Anne Browne, his daughter, who came with him and was buried in 1696. It also remembers Anne’s public testimony after her arrival. The list names Andover’s county as Wiltshire, a discrepancy retained in the source citation; it supplies no further parents for Thomas or maiden surname for his wife.

Ann died before the voyage; Thomas crossed about 1682–83 with their daughter Ann and settled in Aston Township, Chester County, Pennsylvania, where he died on 22 November 1694. A 1709 Quaker list of public Friends who died in Pennsylvania names him and 'Ann Browne daughtr of said Thoms Mercer', who died in 1696.

stories.title: Mary Dockery and the Newton household
stories.hook: An 1867 marriage and an 1880 census offer a possible name for Lizzie Newton’s mother.
body: A St. Clair County, Alabama, marriage register records a license issued on 11 February 1867 for Bailus Newton and Mary Ann Dockery. The marriage return in a second entry places the ceremony at a Gibson residence; the day in the return is not clear enough to resolve the differing index dates.

In 1880 Balus Newton and his wife Mary lived in Etowah County with children including Elizabeth, seven. The original census image gives the surname Newton, though the index reads Keaton. Balus’s name, the county and Elizabeth’s age fit the father and daughter named as Balas and Lizzie in Lizzie’s 1889 marriage consent.

Mary’s work was entered as keeping house in a household of nine. The eldest boy, twelve, was already listed as a farm hand; the youngest child was an infant of eight months. Elizabeth stood between older children Ann and Lindsey and younger children Hezekiah, Amanda and the baby.

The 1880 census identifies Mary as Balus’s wife; it does not expressly identify her as Elizabeth’s mother. The earlier marriage to Mary Ann Dockery and the household make her a probable mother, but a record directly naming Lizzie’s mother is still needed. A death index for Oda Verbena Newton names parents Balous Newton and Mary Marzee Dockery; a similarly named young daughter appears in the 1880 home.

stories.title: A family name on the Armstrong school list
stories.hook: A school list preserves William Harrison Pisachubbe's name and points to a Choctaw education system built and funded by the Nation.
body: On 22 August 1899, a list of Armstrong Academy students was submitted to the Dawes Commission. It included Harrison Pisachubbe. Twelve years later, a federal official identified him as William H. Pisachubbe, son of Eunice and brother of Robert, the family's direct ancestor. The school list gave him a second enrollment number under his middle name; the 1911 letter and later roll notation document the correction. The letter does not describe his lessons or tell us how long he attended.

Armstrong Academy had opened in 1845 as part of the Choctaw Nation's school system. The Choctaw Council funded schools, often contracting with religious mission boards to operate them. The Civil War interrupted instruction, and the academy building later served as a Choctaw government meeting place before the Nation's capital moved to Tuskahoma.

In 1883 the Choctaw General Council passed an act establishing a school for orphan boys at Armstrong and appropriated money for its reopening. A separate act set a planned enrollment of fifty boys there and fifty girls at the Choctaw orphan school. The acts show the Nation making educational policy; a place on a later student list does not by itself explain a child's family circumstances or whether a parent was living.

The Oklahoma Historical Society dates the reopened orphan boys' academy to 1884. In 1898 the federal Curtis Act placed Choctaw Nation schools under United States government control. William's 1899 listing therefore belongs to a period when control over an institution begun by the Choctaw Nation was being transferred to the federal government. His own experience at the school remains to be researched.

stories.title: Clinton Sandridge: an Arkansas farmer in Broken Bow
stories.hook: A December 1961 newspaper notice follows Clinton’s move to McCurtain County and connects the family across Oklahoma, Texas and California.
body: Clinton Lamar Sandridge moved from Arkansas to McCurtain County in 1919. He farmed, belonged to the Assembly of God church and made his home in Broken Bow. His death notice appeared in the McCurtain Gazette on 20 December 1961, reporting that he had died at home early that morning.

The notice names Lemuel Sandridge of Broken Bow as a son, alongside another son, Jack, in Lake Jackson, Texas. Two daughters were in California and Houston. Clinton’s surviving brothers, Lon in Little Rock and L. P. in California, suggest routes for following the earlier Arkansas family, but the notice does not name Clinton’s parents.

His birth remains unsettled. The newspaper gives 25 September 1892, whereas the 1930 census records an age of 43, implying a birth around 1886–1887. The notice also leaves his widow unnamed. Maggie appears with Clinton and Lemuel in the census; her maiden name is still unverified.

stories.note: The newspaper directly names Lemuel as Clinton’s son. The family identification remains probable because of conflicting ages across records. Neither Clinton’s parents nor Maggie’s maiden name has been established. The newspaper’s Arkansas birthplace is printed as Burn; it has not been assigned to a modern locality.

stories.title: Barbara Phillips Livesay and the Pearland family
stories.hook: A local historical society remembered Barbara and Lester’s daughter, preserving a link between the Pearland and Carthage generations.
body: Barbara Phillips and Lester Woodrow Livesay Jr. belonged to a family with ties to Houston, Pearland and Carthage. A Texas birth index names Barbara Phillips and Lester as Wayne Woodrow Livesay’s parents. Lester’s later obituary identifies Barbara by her maiden name and records that she died before him.

In July 2014, the Pearland Historical Society remembered their daughter Carylon Livesay Bardwell. Its newsletter reports her death in Carthage on 18 June and names her parents as Lester and Barbara Livesay. It also identifies Wayne Livesay as her brother and Jimmy Bardwell as her husband, both of whom had already died.
The notice adds a daughter to the family preserved in the birth index and Lester’s obituary. It does not identify Barbara’s own parents, and they remain unknown in this tree.

stories.title: Julia’s changing names: the family behind Audrey
stories.hook: A marriage in Idabel and a daughter in Broken Bow help connect Julia Myers, Nelson, Stevens and Ratcliff.
body: Julia’s family appears under several surnames in the records of McCurtain County and neighboring Arkansas. A county marriage record names Julia Myers, forty, and William A. Nelson, forty-six, marrying at Idabel on 1 July 1916. The original page has been examined. Their names, place and ages make this a probable match for the parents in Audrey Nelson’s later household; the marriage does not establish that Myers was Julia’s birth surname.

In 1920, William and Julia Nelson were living in McCurtain County with two-year-old Audrey. William was recorded as forty-nine, born in Arkansas, and Julia as forty-seven, born in Texas. The household also included Homer, Willie and Edith Nelson, and Hattie Myres, indexed as William’s stepdaughter. Those entries suggest a family formed through more than one parental relationship. They do not identify Hattie’s father or prove who Julia’s own parents were.

Ten years later, the Broken Bow census places twelve-year-old Audry Nelson with a divorced, Texas-born parent indexed as Julian A. Stevens, fifty-four. The daughter’s name, age and birthplace make this a strong probable continuation of Audrey and Julia’s family. An original notice in The Broken Bow News on 10 October 1929 names her mother as Mrs. Stevens and her sister as Miss Audrey Nelson, providing another connection between the names.

An original Arkansas marriage record names Julia Ann Stevens, seventy-six, marrying Charles M. Ratcliff on 19 August 1950. An original notice in the McCurtain Gazette on 29 September 1956 names Mrs. Lemuel Sandridge and Homer E. Nelson among Mrs. C. M. Ratcliff’s children. Together these records strongly support Julia’s later identity. The notice reports a Bowie County, Texas, birth on 17 November 1873 and death on 26 September 1956, but its stated age of seventy-two conflicts with that birth date. The notice places her move to Broken Bow in 1921, after the 1920 census recorded the family elsewhere in McCurtain County.

Julia’s exact birth date and the circumstances of each surname change still need checking. The 1916, 1920 and 1930 ages imply different birth years. Robbins is the maiden name supplied by Audrey’s reproduced obituary, rather than a name established by these marriage records. Her parents remain unassigned while the conflicting records are investigated.

stories.title: Hattie Myers Kilgore: Audrey’s older sister
stories.hook: A young woman’s 1929 death notice helps connect Audrey Nelson with her mother’s Stevens surname.
body: Hattie Myres was eleven in the 1920 Nelson household in Frisco Township, McCurtain County. The original census calls her William Nelson’s stepdaughter. Two-year-old Audrey Nelson was in the same household with William’s wife Julia. Hattie’s different surname preserves a clue to the family before Julia’s Nelson marriage.

Nine years later, a notice in The Broken Bow News on 10 October 1929 identifies Mrs. Gordon Kilgore as the former Hattie Myers. It names her mother as Mrs. Stevens of Broken Bow and Miss Audrey Nelson among her sisters. This recurring mother-and-sister combination strongly supports identifying her with the girl in the Nelson household. The notice does not say whether the sisters shared both parents, and Hattie’s father remains unknown.

The original Texas death certificate records Mrs. Gordon Kilgor’s death at the Sanitarium of Paris on 8 October 1929, at age twenty. Her usual residence was Idabel, Oklahoma, and the certificate records burial there. It gives 1909 as her birth year, with month and day unobtainable, and supplies no parental names. The memorial’s birth date, 23 September 1906, conflicts with both that certificate and her census age. The earlier date has therefore not been adopted as settled fact.

stories.title: A Camden visit brought three generations together
stories.hook: In 1940, Nona Alford’s visit to Broken Bow ended with Audrey, young Larry and their mother Julia joining her in Arkansas.
body: Nona Alford and her married daughter traveled from Camden, Arkansas, to visit friends and relatives in Broken Bow. When they went home, the visiting party grew: Nona’s sister Mrs. L. L. Sandridge, her son Larry, and their mother Julia Stevens accompanied them for several days. The Broken Bow News recorded the trip on 7 March 1940. Audrey Sandridge and young Larry belonged to this same family, connecting the brief newspaper item with the direct maternal line.

Nona already had a family of her own. An original Bowie County, Texas, register records Wesley E. Alford and Nona Myers marrying on 20 June 1919. The 1930 Broken Bow census lists their daughters Mable and Gerldene, names later recorded as Mabel and Geraldine. Both daughters’ Social Security entries name Nona A. Myers and Wesley E. Alford as their parents, preserving the Myers surname behind Nona’s married name.

The newspaper calls Nona’s daughter Mrs. Edwin Chidester. A 1940 Camden census names Mabel as Edwin Chidester’s wife, and her Social Security record uses the name Mabel Alford Chidester, making this a strong identification. Mabel later appears under Crowl; an obituary index for Geraldine Forkner names Mabel Crowl as her sister. These separate records help keep the two daughters connected as their surnames changed.

Julia was the older generation traveling with her daughters and grandchildren between Broken Bow and Camden. The visit preserves her Stevens surname alongside Audrey’s Sandridge and Nona’s Alford names. It also gives Nona a clear place beside Audrey in the maternal family.

stories.title: Sadah’s Indiana beginnings
stories.hook: A Texas death certificate supplies dates and a father’s initials, while an earlier census offers a household to investigate.
body: The 1920 census places Sadah and Lester W. Livesay in Harris County with their children. Their son Lester’s 2001 obituary names his mother as Sadah McCormick. A Harris County marriage index records Lester W. Livesay and Sadah H. Mc.Cormick in 1911, volume 4, page 402, certificate 22072; this is an index entry, not an examined marriage license.

An original Texas certificate records Sadah Livesay Vaughan’s death in Houston on 29 April 1978, aged 84. It gives her birth as 13 August 1893 in Anderson, Indiana, and names the informant as Alice Livesay Kauitzsch. The combination of the unusual given name, Livesay surname and informant supports the probable identification with Lester’s wife. Alice’s Social Security NUMIDENT index names her parents as Lester W. Livesay and Sarah H. McCormack and includes the Kauitzsch surname; Sarah and Sadah remain recorded variants rather than a silently corrected name.

The certificate names Sadah’s father as J. T. McCormack and gives her mother’s maiden name as Unknown. It does not expand his initials. The dates now shown in the tree come from this certificate, whose birth information was reported many decades after the event.

An earlier original census offers a possible family connection. On 18 April 1910, in Brazoria County’s Justice Precinct 5, Jay T. McCormick, 41, and his wife Frances, 40, were listed with a daughter Sadie, 17, born in Indiana. The father’s initials, daughter’s age and birthplace fit the later certificate, but no examined record yet establishes that Sadie and Sadah are the same person. Jay T. and Frances remain unattached research leads. The census supplies no maiden surname for Frances.
